Moreover, these models are generally black boxes, and their ability to generate low-energy structures containing hundreds or thousands of atoms remains uncertain, particularly when trained primarily on small crystals. Generated structures must still be checked through energy calculations and relaxation, and their quality for systems far outside the training data remains uncertain. This leaves a need for methods that search directly for favorable atomic arrangements in large systems.

Several established methods search directly for low-energy structures. Random structure searching generates and locally relaxes many independent trial structures [31], while basin hopping and minima hopping alternate local relaxation with moves that explore other minima [38, 12]. Particle-swarm optimization guides a population of candidates using information from previously found low-energy structures [39]. Genetic algorithms provide a powerful approach to this search by maintaining and evolving a population of candidate structures [6, 29, 11, 5]. Candidates are ranked by their energy or another specified objective, and better candidates have a higher chance of being selected as parents. Crossover creates a child by combining parts of two parents, while mutation introduces changes such as moving, adding, or removing atoms. Each new candidate is locally relaxed before it is evaluated for selection. Repeating these steps over successive generations allows the search to explore many local minima. This approach has been successful in predicting crystal structures, particularly for small and moderately sized unit cells, and developments such as USPEX have substantially extended its capabilities [29, 11, 24]. Frameworks such as FANTASTX also combine discrete-atom genetic operations and local relaxation with experimental constraints to guide atomic-structure searches [22].

For large systems, conventional genetic algorithms can struggle to find low-energy structures from random starting configurations. Local relaxation often leaves these candidates trapped in disordered arrangements, and combining two disordered parents can simply produce another poor structure [25]. Further improvement requires larger rearrangements that crossover and mutation may take many generations to produce. Introducing order into the initial population and preserving favorable local arrangements can improve convergence, as demonstrated by USPEX [25, 24]. However, obtaining a useful starting structure can itself be difficult. For example, Yu et al. reconstructed a gold nanoparticle containing thousands of atoms, but their search began with crystalline candidates whose orientation was already known experimentally and still proceeded over thousands of generations [43]. Such initialization supplies substantial structural information that may be unavailable for an unknown defect or disordered material. This motivates methods that can more readily escape poor local minima without relying on an ordered starting structure.

Effective Atom Theory (EAT) offers a way to address this difficulty [36]. It represents each site as a mixture of elements and a null species corresponding to an absent atom, allowing the mixture weights and atomic position to vary continuously during relaxation. A site can gradually change from one element to another, disappear as its weight shifts to null, or reappear as its weight shifts back to a real element. For example, an atom can gradually disappear to allow neighboring atoms to rearrange, avoiding an unfavorable configuration that positional relaxation alone would encounter. Such changes can open paths to lower-energy structures even when the starting configuration is a local minimum with respect to atomic positions. The system is then driven toward a final structure in which each site is either assigned a single real element or removed, leaving only conventional atoms with definite chemical identities.

As originally formulated, EAT is a local optimization method. It follows gradients from a given starting configuration and can still become trapped in a local minimum, especially in a large system. We therefore introduce Hereditary Effective Atom Theory (HEAT), a genetic algorithm that uses the effective-atom representation of EAT to enable efficient global search. Central to the method is a novel crossover operation that directly superimposes and subsequently relaxes two parent structures, allowing atoms from either parent to move, change identity, or disappear. The child can thereby retain favorable parts of both parents while removing redundant or unfavorable atoms. Importantly, the method does not require an ordered initial structure, making it more flexible than conventional genetic algorithms.

papers.title: Local and Sparse Kernel Operator Learning for Incompressible Flows: An Operator Lagrange Formulation
papers.abstract: We present a local and sparse kernel method for learning the solution operators of incompressible flows. It builds on our earlier property-preserving kernel method, whose global output reconstruction and dense operator regression scale poorly. Our method replaces the global output reconstruction by local divergence-free interpolants with divergence-free polynomials of any degree, solved in parallel on the GPU. These interpolants are divergence free, periodic on periodic domains, and, with a multiscale kernel, approach Kolmogorov statistics under refinement. A compactly supported kernel, positive semidefinite in any input dimension, makes the operator regression sparse. Its support radius, and hence the sparsity, is fitted to data, and optional affine polynomials in the input capture global trends. Operator Lagrange weights join the two. They cost one sparse solve per new input and act on the training fields before the output reconstruction, so their local coefficients are never formed. We show that, unlike direct evaluation, Lagrange evaluation does not amplify solve errors by the cancellation among spatial coefficients. On ten fluid benchmarks, validation selects sparse matrices nearly everywhere, with densities that mostly decrease as the training set grows, and affine augmentation lowers the error by more than an order of magnitude for forced isotropic turbulence. These sparse models are at least as accurate as our earlier dense method and more accurate than neural operators. Lagrange evaluation is as accurate as direct evaluation with local output reconstructions, and up to nearly three orders of magnitude more accurate with global ones. We also present GPU timings and storage.

papers.intro:
Uncertainty quantification, design, and inverse problems for incompressible flows require the velocity field for many initial conditions, boundary conditions, or forcing functions, and the repeated solution of the Navier–Stokes equations then dominates the cost [60, 43, 59, 61]. One remedy is to learn the solution operator, the map from the problem data to the velocity, from a collection of simulations [7]. Reduced-order models have long served this purpose [42, 5], and neural operators such as DeepONets, Fourier and graph neural operators, transformer-based models, and kernel neural operators now learn such maps from large data sets [37, 33, 34, 32, 70, 36]. We seek an operator learner for incompressible flows that satisfies four criteria. First, every prediction should be divergence free, and periodic on periodic domains, however accurately the operator itself is learned. Second, the cost of the output representation should grow linearly with the number of output points, so that fine three-dimensional outputs remain affordable. Third, the regression should handle ten thousand or more training functions without factoring a dense matrix. Fourth, every stage should run in parallel on a graphics processing unit (GPU).

Third, the regression should handle ten thousand or more training functions without factoring a dense matrix. Fourth, every stage should run in parallel on a graphics processing unit (GPU).

Kernel methods offer an attractive alternative to neural operators [2, 38, 29]. Batlle et al. [2] learn an operator from point samples in two steps. An operator regression, a kernel regression on the space of sampled inputs, maps the samples of the input function to the samples of the output function. An output reconstruction, a kernel interpolant of these samples in space (or spacetime), then recovers the output function. Since both steps are kernel interpolation or regression problems, the learned operator has a closed form, few parameters, and an error analysis. For flows, the output representation is the natural place to impose physics [45, 30]. In our previous work [53], we therefore regressed the coefficients of a divergence-free kernel interpolant of the output instead of its point samples, so that every prediction is exactly divergence free regardless of the accuracy of the operator regression. We called this the property-preserving kernel method (PPKM). PPKM satisfies the first criterion, but both of its kernel problems are global. Its operator regression factors one dense kernel matrix on all NN training inputs, at a cost of O⁡(N3)O(N^{3}) operations and O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) storage, and its output reconstruction solves one dense system on all output points. Both limits bind for three-dimensional turbulence, where a training set has ten thousand or more functions and an output has thousands of points. Meeting the other criteria poses three tasks. The output reconstruction must become local without losing the properties of the global one, the operator regression must become sparse, and the two must be joined without forming the local coefficients of every training field.

The first task draws on radial basis function-generated finite differences (RBF-FD). RBF-FD methods replace a global radial basis function (RBF) interpolant, whose dense system couples all nodes, by small interpolants on the stencil of each node, so that every linear system has a fixed size and is independent of the others [62, 55, 69, 21, 20]. Over the last two decades, RBF-FD methods have been stabilized for convection-dominated problems [22, 48], applied to the Navier–Stokes equations [55, 18], extended to overlapped stencils, surfaces, and moving domains [52, 50, 51], and formulated in the least-squares sense [63]. They also have error bounds [10], node generators for irregular domains [49], and GPU implementations [6]. In particular, polyharmonic splines (PHS) augmented with polynomials converge at the order of the polynomial degree and have no shape parameter [19, 3]. For flows, the local interpolants must also be divergence free. Divergence-free kernels, obtained by applying −Δ​I+∇∇𝖳-\Delta I+\nabla\nabla^{\mathsf{T}} to a scalar kernel [40, 11, 39, 25, 66], have this property by construction and have been used both globally and in partition-of-unity form [24, 12], and Yelnyk [71] combined divergence-free PHS with polynomials in local Hermite interpolation for Stokes problems. However, the high order of PHS-based RBF-FD comes from the polynomials, so a local divergence-free interpolant of high order needs divergence-free polynomials of any degree, in two and three dimensions, that can be evaluated anywhere on the stencil.

Since the local systems are independent and of fixed size, we assemble, factor, and evaluate them in batches on the GPU, and our output reconstruction is embarrassingly parallel.

papers.title: Investigating a TeV-Halo Candidate around PSR J1928+1746 with HAWC
papers.abstract: We present an updated High-Altitude Water Cherenkov (HAWC) analysis of the crowded Galactic-plane area near PSR J1928+1746, which was previously linked to the extended source 3HWC J1928+178. With 2904 days of HAWC data, improved event reconstruction, and a multicomponent likelihood model that includes six TeV source components and Galactic diffuse emission, we describe the region using six components and find a distinct, moderately extended source close to PSR J1928+1746. This source, HAWC J1928+1750, is detected from about 2 TeV to above 100 TeV and is well-described by a log-parabola spectrum with normalization $K = 5.0 \times 10^{-15}$ TeV$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ at 12 TeV, index $α= 2.09$, curvature $β= 0.35$, and Gaussian extension $σ= 0.19^\circ$. Interpreting the emission using diffusion-halo templates under the assumption $B = 8 μ\mathrm{G}$ yields the diffusion coefficient D(100 TeV) = $2.1 \times 10^{27}$ cm$^2$ s$^{-1}$, which is about 500 times smaller than typical interstellar diffusion values at similar energies. This suggests that particle transport around PSR J1928+1746 is strongly suppressed under the TeV-halo interpretation. The TeV spectrum is consistent with leptonic inverse-Compton emission originating from pulsar-injected electrons and positrons, which requires less than approximately 1% of the pulsar's characteristic spin-down energy. However, a hadronic contribution from the surrounding environment cannot be excluded.

These systems are especially interesting because TeV halos are characterized by particle diffusion that is strongly suppressed relative to the average ISM [4]. This affects how we understand the particle injection of the pulsar and whether pulsars could explain much of the observed cosmic-ray positron excess [14]. Recent HAWC results also suggest that TeV halos might be common around middle-aged pulsars [15]. However, it is still unclear how much their properties depend on the local environment or the source’s history.

PSR J1928+1746 is a middle-aged, energetic pulsar with a characteristic age τc≃82​kyr\tau_{c}\simeq 82~{\rm kyr} and a spin-down power E˙=1.6×1036\dot{E}=1.6\times 10^{36} erg s-1 [25]. An earlier HAWC analysis modeled the emission around this pulsar with the extended component 3HWC J1928+178 and a broader component, HAWC J1928-EXT [13]. The region also includes 3HWC J1930+188, which is linked to the PSR J1930+1852 and SNR G54.1+0.3 complex, as well as the nearby source HAWC J1932+192. The origin of the emission near PSR J1928+1746 remained uncertain because no clear X-ray counterpart has been found for the pulsar-centered TeV emission, and molecular material near the source could allow for hadronic interactions [13]. In this paper, we refer to this Galactic-plane field, which includes PSR J1928+1746, the G54.1+0.3 complex and the nearby TeV emission, as the J1928 region. Several ATNF pulsars are located near the fitted TeV components in this field, which introduces potential source confusion and highlights the importance of considering possible pulsar associations in regional modeling. A recent dedicated Fermi-LAT analysis of this region identified an extended GeV component called J1929+1732E, using a source-search analysis that goes beyond the standard 4FGL-DR4 catalog model [33]. This component overlaps with the official 4FGL catalog source, 4FGL J1929.0+1729 [22], and lies in the same GeV to TeV complex as the previously reported HAWC emission near 3HWC J1928+178 [13] and the LHAASO sources, 1LHAASO J1928+1746u [24]. This region has overlapping TeV sources, possible pulsar associations, molecular material, and structured emission from the Galactic plane. Because HAWC has an energy-dependent angular resolution, with 68%68\% containment angles of order 0.3° at a few TeV and less than 0.2° at energies above tens of TeV, emission from nearby sources can overlap in the likelihood fit [12]. To understand the TeV excess centered on PSR J1928+1746, we need a model that accounts for nearby sources and diffuse emission in a consistent way. This helps ensure that flux from the surrounding area is not incorrectly assigned to PSR J1928+1746. In this study, we take another look at the region using updated event reconstruction, improved gamma–hadron separation, better energy estimation, and a clear template for Galactic diffuse emission.

Using the analysis procedure in Section III, we first construct a global model of the region that includes nearby TeV sources and Galactic diffuse emission. The resulting regional decomposition and comparison with previous TeV measurements are presented in Section IV. We then focus on the extended emission near PSR J1928+1746 in Section V. papers.title: AI-Based End-to-End Automotive Design and Software Development for SDVs
papers.abstract: This paper explores the potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to enable end-to-end automotive design and software development for Software-Defined Vehicles (SDVs). Based on our contributions within the Central Car Server (CeCaS) and follow-up EU-funded projects, we present an AI-driven toolchain integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) to automate the transformation of natural-language requirements into system architectures, executable software, and validation artifacts. The approach emphasizes traceability, consistency, and compliance with safety-critical automotive development requirements. Validation is performed on a centralized vehicle computing platform supporting adaptive cruise control and emergency braking, tested in Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) and Software-in-the-Loop (SiL) environments. We discuss current capabilities, practical limitations, and future directions toward increasingly automated, reliable, and quality-assured automotive software development with minimal human intervention.

papers.title: A Decade of Learning-Based Control: From Theoretic Foundations to Practical Deployment
papers.abstract: Motivated by ten years of Learning-Based Control Invited Sessions at the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC), this tutorial paper reviews key advances at the intersection of machine learning and control. We focus on methods that combine the flexibility of machine learning techniques with the structure and theoretical foundations of control to design autonomous systems that are capable, reliable, and safe. We first introduce core notions for establishing stability and safety guarantees, then review approaches that learn dynamics models to improve control under uncertainty, and finally discuss data-driven methods that directly synthesize or learn policies, including reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and Bayesian optimization. We further discuss representative applications and open challenges. The goal is to provide an accessible entry point to the field and to support continued progress toward reliable learning-based control in real-world systems. To support learning and practical exploration, we share implementations and illustrative examples along with our discussion, together with additional resources on our website: https://learning-based-control.github.io/tutorial/.

papers.intro:
Over the past decade, the integration of machine learning and control theory has evolved from a growing research interest into a practical approach for many real-world systems. Machine learning provides powerful tools for extracting patterns from data, while control theory offers the mathematical foundation needed to use such data-driven methods in closed-loop systems. Principled combinations of these perspectives can extend autonomous systems to more challenging operating domains, broader system classes, and more complex tasks, while preserving the closed-loop properties required for reliable deployment.

Principled combinations of these perspectives can extend autonomous systems to more challenging operating domains, broader system classes, and more complex tasks, while preserving the closed-loop properties required for reliable deployment.

Why machine learning? With the widespread availability of data and accelerated computing, machine learning methods have achieved remarkable success across many domains, especially in computer vision and natural language processing. From early milestones in image recognition [1, 2] to recent large-scale language models [3, 4, 5], these methods have demonstrated a strong capability to capture complex input-output relationships directly from unstructured data. A similar shift is taking place in control through deep RL (RL). Enabled by high-quality synthetic data and massively parallelized compute power [6, 7, 8], deep RL has expanded our ability to address challenging control problems involving high-dimensional, non-smooth, and complex dynamical systems [9, 10]. More broadly, leveraging data, whether synthetic or real, offers new opportunities to expand what autonomous systems can achieve.

Enabled by high-quality synthetic data and massively parallelized compute power [6, 7, 8], deep RL has expanded our ability to address challenging control problems involving high-dimensional, non-smooth, and complex dynamical systems [9, 10]. More broadly, leveraging data, whether synthetic or real, offers new opportunities to expand what autonomous systems can achieve.

Why control? The flexibility that makes machine learning powerful also introduces challenges when learning-based methods are deployed in physical systems. Purely data-driven models can be highly expressive, but often struggle to satisfy strict safety and reliability requirements, and may require large amounts of data that are costly or infeasible to collect on real systems. Control provides structural priors and theoretical tools for bridging this gap. By embedding control principles into the learning design, one can guide the learning process toward methods that are more sample efficient, high-performing, and safe for practical applications [11, 12, 13, 14]. The use of data to model the unknown has long been central to control, for instance, in system identification and adaptive control. However, the scale, expressiveness, and opacity of modern learning methods create new challenges in sample efficiency, verification, and reliable deployment. Addressing these challenges requires a tight and principled coupling of machine learning and control-theoretic approaches.

Where do these fields converge? To foster principled approaches that integrate machine learning and control theory beyond the standard tools of either discipline alone, the Invited Session Series on Learning-Based Control has been held at the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC) since 201611 1 The website of the CDC Learning-Based Control Invited Sessions is available at https://ics.mavt.ethz.ch/Events/learning-control-session.html.. Over the past decade, this series has hosted 30 dedicated sessions featuring 182 accepted papers, drawing contributions from over 100 distinct institutions. As reflected in Figure 2, the series captures the increasing incorporation of expressive learning paradigms into control, while maintaining a strong emphasis on principled methods with desired closed-loop properties. Recurring themes include (deep) neural networks, (deep) RL, and GP, combined with control tools such as MPC (MPC), HJ (HJ) reachability, CLF, and CBF to address performance, stability, and safety. The steady growth in citations over the past decade (Figure 3) further reflects the sustained interest in these topics and the expanding body of work contributed by the community.

In this tutorial paper, we highlight key developments and emerging trends in learning-based control over the past decade, spanning control-theoretic foundations, dynamics learning, direct data-driven control, and learning-oriented policy optimization (see Figure 1). Our intention is to draw connections among these different families of methods by highlighting how they address uncertainty, which theoretical tools are compatible with them, and what types of guarantees can be established (see Table I). Rather than providing an exhaustive survey, we focus on representative methodological directions motivated by the CDC Learning-Based Control Invited Sessions. With the discussions and examples along the way, we hope this tutorial paper serves to contextualize the progress of the past decade and illustrate how learning and control can be combined to enable more capable, reliable, and safe autonomous systems.

We then review control-theoretic foundations for certifying desired system properties and guarantees (Section III), followed by learning-based control approaches that learn dynamics and improve performance under uncertainty (Section IV). We next discuss direct data-driven control and learning-oriented methodologies, including RL, IL (IL), and BO (BO), that synthesize or optimize policies from data while preserving desired closed-loop properties (Section V and Section VI). We conclude by highlighting representative applications at the intersection of learning and control (Section VII), followed by takeaways and future research directions (Section VIII).

papers.title: B-fields In STar-forming Region Observations (BISTRO): Technical Foundations for Quantitative 450/850 $μ$m JCMT SCUBA-2/POL-2 Polarimetry
papers.abstract: We present five technical validations of SCUBA-2/POL-2 polarimetry on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope at 450 and 850 $μ$m, using 174 archival fields in 69 molecular cloud regions and subsets appropriate to each test. Extended-source calibration avoids a deterministic shift of $Δβ=-1.05$ in the dust emissivity index $β$ that would result from calibrating extended emission using peak brightness. We modeled Stokes $I$ noise with additive and signal-dependent components. The measured median ratio of surface-brightness noise at 450/850 $μ$m is 25. Independent tests of Stokes $Q,U$ noise support approximately equal additive variances and weak error correlations, providing a basis for propagating polarization uncertainties. Corrections determined for individual fields reduce additive zero-level offsets of order $1$ mJy arcsec$^{-2}$ in the 450 $μ$m Stokes $Q$ and $U$ intensities. The three-step regression leaves a median combined residual amplitude of $0.07$ mJy arcsec$^{-2}$. Independent comparisons with SOFIA/HAWC+ at 154 and 214 $μ$m support the correction in strongly affected fields. We matched the 450 $μ$m maps to the modeled 850 $μ$m beam and the common $12.6''$-$300''$ range of angular scales. We compared three reductions of the same 450 $μ$m observations across 30 sources. Taking the median angular residual relative to the final product for each source, we find that beam matching reduces the median over sources from $6.3^\circ$ to $4.7^\circ$. After matching, 29 of the 30 sources have median residuals below $10^\circ$. We also quantified how residual $Q/U$ offsets propagate in ratios of polarization fractions, differences in spectral indices, and polarization angles. These validations provide procedures and quantitative references for interpreting POL-2 measurements and combining them with polarimetry at other wavelengths.

Observations with the Planck satellite, the High-resolution Airborne Wideband Camera Plus (HAWC+) on the Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy (SOFIA), and interferometers such as the Submillimeter Array (SMA) and Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) have extended the range of wavelengths and spatial scales available for studying magnetic fields (Pattle et al., 2023, see the review by). These facilities trace the field over successive ranges of spatial scale: Planck on the scales of entire molecular clouds, single-dish telescopes such as the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT) down to ∼\sim0.1 pc dense cores, and interferometers such as ALMA from several ×1000\times 1000 au down to a few ×10\times 10 au (Hull and Zhang, 2019).

The JCMT has a long record of submillimeter imaging polarimetry. Its first-generation camera, the Submillimetre Common-User Bolometer Array (SCUBA; Holland et al. 1999), was used with the SCUPOL polarimeter (Greaves et al., 2003). The SCUPOL archive established an extensive record of 850 \micron imaging polarimetry (Matthews et al., 2009). SCUBA was replaced by the Submillimetre Common-User Bolometer Array 2 (SCUBA-2; Holland et al. 2013), which images at 450 and 850 \micron simultaneously. Its flux calibration, through flux conversion factors (FCFs), and its beam shapes have been established from observations of calibration sources (Dempsey et al., 2013; Mairs et al., 2021). Variations in atmospheric emission also introduce sky noise, while changing opacity modulates the astronomical signal (Archibald et al., 2002). papers.title: B-fields In STar-forming Region Observations (BISTRO): Dual-Wavelength Constraints on Size-Dependent Grain Alignment in Star-Forming Regions
papers.abstract: We compared 450 and 850 $μ$m POL-2 observations from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope at $12.6''$ resolution. The median absolute difference in polarization angle between bands is $6.7^\circ$ across 21 regions. For total intensity $I\proptoν^α$ and polarized intensity $PI\proptoν^γ$, 24-27 of 35 regions have $γ<α$, allowing for $3σ$ limits on weak polarized intensities. The median $γ-α$ is $-0.51$, ranging from $-0.57$ to $-0.45$ under these limits. The ratio of polarization fractions is $P_{450}/P_{850}=0.69\pm0.02_{\rm sys}\pm0.03_{\rm stat}$, with no detected dependence on the angle difference. We suggest that the dependence of alignment on grain size offers the simplest explanation of these findings. For optically thin components sharing a polarization angle and opacity law, temperature mixing reproduces the median $-0.51$ only if the warm dust is polarized less efficiently than the cold dust. If the cold dust is at 10 K or warmer and the warm dust at 40 K or cooler, the median requires a ratio of warm to cold effective polarization efficiencies $r\lesssim0.18$. We tested mixtures with opacity index $β=2$ in four fields against Herschel dust temperatures and Green Bank Ammonia Survey kinetic temperatures. We assumed equal gas and dust temperatures, ammonia tracing cold gas, and model ranges of 3-20 K for cold dust and 25-40 K for warm dust carrying at most half the mass. Mixtures matching both temperatures cannot reproduce $γ-α$ within $1σ$ in three fields, including OMC 2 tentatively, even for $r=0$. Allowing warm dust at 10-100 K and up to 95% of the mass permits solutions only for $r\leq0.041$. To explain these three fields by temperature mixing, we need wider model ranges and a very strong contrast in polarization efficiency. The origin of this contrast remains undetermined.

papers.intro:
Magnetic fields (B→\vec{B}-fields) pervade the interstellar medium (ISM) and play a central role in the dynamics of molecular cloud formation, filament evolution, and star formation (Hennebelle and Inutsuka, 2019; Pattle et al., 2023). In star-forming regions, submillimeter polarimetry of thermal dust emission is the primary means of mapping B→\vec{B}-field morphology in the plane of the sky, complementing Zeeman measurements of the component along the line of sight (Crutcher, 2012). Recent observations of nearby molecular clouds have established that field strengths in the plane of the sky lie between ∼\sim1 μ\muG in diffuse envelopes and ∼\sim10 mG in the densest star-forming cores; in the OMC 1 integral-shaped filament, Davis–Chandrasekhar–Fermi analysis yields ∼\sim6 mG (Pattle et al., 2017; Pattle et al., 2023). The Planck all-sky survey and column density maps from Herschel provide the environmental context on larger scales for interpreting these results (Planck Collaboration et al., 2015; André et al., 2010). Single-dish submillimeter polarimeters such as JCMT/POL-2 bridge these cloud scales and the scales resolved by interferometers such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), from several ×1000\times 1000 au down to a few ×10\times 10 au (Hull and Zhang, 2019). For the present sample, the 12​\farcs​612\farcs 6 POL-2 beam corresponds to ∼\sim0.008–0.5 pc at the adopted reference distances (section 2; subsection 4.2).

Submillimeter emission polarimetry probes magnetic fields in cold (T≲100T\lesssim 100 K) gas through the alignment of non-spherical dust grains with their major axes perpendicular to the local B→\vec{B}-field direction (Davis and Greenstein, 1951). Thermal emission from these aligned grains is polarized, allowing us to infer the orientation of the B→\vec{B}-field in the plane of the sky. These dust grains are a mixture of silicates and carbonaceous species comprising ∼\sim1% of the ISM by mass (Draine, 2003). These grains emit optically thin radiation whose intensity traces the column density (Hildebrand, 1983).

The high dynamic range of this system enables polarization measurements across hydrogen column densities of NH∼1020N_{\rm H}\sim 10^{20}–102410^{24} cm-2, and its ∼\sim3\arcmin field of view allows efficient mapping of extended structures. The ongoing B-fields In STar-forming Region Observations (BISTRO) Large Program (Ward-Thompson et al., 2017) has systematically mapped magnetic field morphology in various star-forming regions. Observations at 450 μ\mum remain challenging because of atmospheric variability. The companion technical paper (Paper T) presents methods to establish and validate reliable 450 μ\mum polarimetry and to quantify its systematic floors.

Optical and near-infrared extinction polarimetry differ conceptually from submillimeter emission polarimetry. In extinction polarimetry, the polarization fraction pVp_{V} and extinction AVA_{V} both scale with the column density of dust along the line of sight. Their ratio pV/AVp_{V}/A_{V} therefore cancels the dust column and isolates the intrinsic polarizing efficiency of the grain population, a quantity traditionally termed “polarization efficiency” (Serkowski et al., 1975; Whittet et al., 2008). In emission polarimetry, in contrast, the polarized intensity P​IνPI_{\nu} and the total intensity IνI_{\nu} are both weighted by temperature through the Planck function Bν​(T)B_{\nu}(T). Grains of different sizes reach distinct equilibrium temperatures, and their relative contributions vary with wavelength. The ratio Pν=P​Iν/IνP_{\nu}=PI_{\nu}/I_{\nu} therefore depends on the alignment efficiency, optical properties of the grains, and temperature structure along the line of sight. Consequently, submillimeter emission polarimetry does not have a simple analog of pV/AVp_{V}/A_{V} that isolates alignment efficiency from other factors.

The most widely accepted theory for the alignment of dust grains is the Radiative Alignment Torque (RAT) mechanism (Lazarian, 2007; Lazarian and Hoang, 2007a), in which irregularly shaped dust grains are spun up by anisotropic radiation fields (Andersson et al., 2015). Alignment efficiency should decrease as extinction increases because the RAT mechanism aligns grains through incident radiation (Lazarian, 2007; Andersson et al., 2015). This trend appears as the polarization hole: the polarization fraction PP decreases with increasing column density NN. The phenomenon was characterized in dark clouds by Goodman et al. (1995) and has been confirmed in near-infrared extinction polarimetry, as a decline in polarization efficiency with extinction (Whittet et al., 2008), and in emission polarimetry at submillimeter wavelengths (Alves et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2018; Soam et al., 2018; Coudé et al., 2019).

Both techniques integrate along the line of sight, and variations in B→\vec{B}-field orientation along that path can reduce the net polarization in either technique. Extinction polarimetry samples a pencil beam toward each background star, whereas emission polarimetry additionally averages over the finite beam of the telescope. Unresolved variations across this beam in the plane-of-sky B→\vec{B}-field orientation can further reduce the observed polarization (Whittet et al., 2008).

papers.title: Asynchronous, Generation-Free ABC: Streaming AMIS Reweighting for Heterogeneous Simulator Workloads on HPC
papers.abstract: Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) enables Bayesian inference for models with intractable likelihoods by estimating parameter posterior distributions from simulated data. Sequential ABC methods improve sampling efficiency by iteratively adapting the proposal distribution toward regions of high posterior probability. However, these methods typically operate in generations, where each generation must wait for its slowest simulation before the next can begin. On a parallel machine, this synchronization barrier leaves workers idle and reduces throughput, particularly when simulation runtimes vary substantially. We introduce a generation-free ABC sampler that updates its proposal when simulation results arrive and sends a new candidate to each available worker. The proposal is based on the best particles evaluated so far. To estimate the posterior, we reuse the full history and reweight particles against a reconstructed mixture of sampling proposals. We show how errors in approximating the mixture of sampling proposals affect the estimated posterior and establish consistency for the smooth-ABC posterior when the approximation becomes asymptotically exact. In our experiments, the method achieves well-calibrated posterior estimates where a pyABC baseline with the same kernel and bandwidth schedule under-covers. From the asynchronous run's timing alone, we predict how much a synchronization barrier would slow the sampler. These predictions agree with measured synchronization penalties ranging from 1.2x to 400x. On a Cellular Potts tissue simulator, the asynchronous sampler completes 2.1-2.4x as many evaluations as pyABC in the same hour, and the discrepancy threshold for its best 100 evaluations is 4.1x smaller. With the starting bandwidth set from prior-predictive discrepancies, it also produces a more concentrated two-parameter posterior with a larger effective sample size than pyABC.

Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) enables Bayesian inference when the likelihood is intractable but data can be generated using a simulator (Cranmer et al., 2020; Beaumont, 2019). Sequential ABC methods, such as ABC sequential Monte Carlo (ABC-SMC) and ABC population Monte Carlo (ABC-PMC) (Sisson et al., 2007; Toni et al., 2009; Beaumont et al., 2009; Del Moral et al., 2012), iteratively update a population of weighted parameter samples, to favor parameters whose simulated data better match the observations. Although simulations of individual candidates can run in parallel, the generation-based implementations considered here update their proposal and ABC bandwidth only after the entire population has been evaluated. Workers that finish early must therefore wait for the slowest simulation, which can substantially reduce throughput when runtimes vary. This is particularly relevant to cell-based tissue models, where different parameter values can produce very different numbers of cells and, consequently, simulation runtimes.

papers.title: Algorithm duality from resolvent Moreau identities
papers.abstract: Duality is classically defined as a relationship between objective functions, one that breaks down beyond convexity. We show that a more fundamental duality persists between the resolvent operators used to solve associated problems. We establish a framework from which we obtain complete characterizations of the duality-like correspondences between proximal fixed-point iterations and their alternating minimization scheme counterparts. Namely, we show the known primal-dual relationships between forward--backward splitting and Tseng's alternating minimization algorithm, and between the Douglas-Rachford method and alternating direction method of multipliers, to hold generically and irrespective of problem assumptions. The approach considered herein avoids the machinery of convex analysis entirely, providing a definitive formulation of algorithmic dualities in maximal generality while greatly simplifying their proofs. In particular, assumptions such as monotonicity, weak monotonicity, Lipschitz continuity, and injectivity of linear operators are all shown to be unnecessary. In addition, we utilize our framework to reveal and analyze a novel primal-dual relationship between backward-backward splitting and a special instance of the alternating minimization algorithm. This illustrates how our duality framework provides a principled basis for primal-dual algorithm design and analysis in nonmonotone settings. Finally, our experiments show that our backward--backward splitting--based approach reliably outperforms the FISTA and SR3 algorithms for the LASSO problem.

We show in Theorem 3.1 that even with no problem assumptions, every generalized resolvent operator possesses a unique resolvent to which it is linked in a meaningful and explicitly describable way. papers.title: VMSpec: A Decompiler-based Approach against Virtual Machine Obfuscation
papers.abstract: Malicious actors frequently obfuscate their code to hinder investigative reverse engineering efforts. Among the most formidable techniques is virtual machine (VM) obfuscation: programs are translated into bytecode for a custom VM, often with a randomized virtual instruction set and distributed alongside a corresponding interpreter. Manual analysis and deobfuscation scale poorly due to the complexity of VM obfuscation and the diversification techniques that render each VM and interpreter unique. Existing methods primarily focus on simplifying execution traces and identifying virtual execution boundaries. However, comparatively little attention has been given to recovering higher-level program semantics from VM-obfuscated code. To address this gap, we propose VMSpec, a novel decompiler-based approach that automates the construction of VM processor specifications, enabling existing, well-known decompilers to analyze the VM-obfuscated code. We evaluate our prototype of VMSpec on 147 programs from an established obfuscation benchmark, comprising hash functions, standard algorithms, and randomized functions, obfuscated with different configurations of the Tigress and Code Virtualizer obfuscators. To demonstrate real-world applicability, we additionally include six domain generation algorithms stemming from real-world malware. VMSpec completely strips VM-obfuscation from nearly all obfuscated samples, producing output comparable to Ghidra's decompilation of the original code. Furthermore, it is the first method capable of reconstructing the complete program behavior of VM-obfuscated programs with infinite, input-dependent paths and recursive calls.

papers.intro:
Program authors obfuscate their software to thwart reverse engineering and other forms of program analysis. While obfuscation can serve legitimate purposes – such as protecting intellectual property or reducing fraud – it is especially attractive for malware authors seeking to evade detection and analysis. Among the various obfuscation techniques, virtualization-based obfuscation is widely considered one of the strongest techniques available [20]. Here, the original program is translated into bytecode for a custom virtual machine (VM), which is then embedded, together with a bytecode interpreter, into the obfuscated program. The meaning of individual bytecode instructions is therefore encoded solely in the interpreter, thereby forcing human analysts to first reverse-engineer the interpreter before they can reason about the behavior of the embedded bytecode. Moreover, to hinder knowledge reuse, commercial obfuscators [10, 33, 32, 50] generate distinct virtual machine architectures, instruction sets, and interpreters by employing various diversification techniques [53].

Many techniques have been proposed to deobfuscate virtualization-based obfuscated programs [20] and obfuscated software in general [39]. Current state-of-the-art methods against virtualization-based obfuscation primarily rely on instruction traces collected during execution of the obfuscated program. These methods analyze and simplify runtime traces either directly [51, 11, 37, 47, 52] or first identify VM handlers, which then serve as an anchor point for trace simplification [18, 6, 35, 9, 23]. However, dynamic tracing approaches are inherently limited to the code path taken during a given run, thereby limiting the analysis of program behavior to the specific inputs provided. While prior work [37, 47, 52] proposes overcoming this problem using path exploration algorithms, they cannot guarantee exhaustive path coverage and remain constrained by the path explosion problem, which renders them infeasible for more complex programs. Furthermore, studies [31, 30] show that attackers can craft strong and robust primitives to explode the number of paths. Consequently, dynamic tracing approaches are unable to recover the complete behavior of virtualization-based obfuscated programs.

papers.title: End-to-End Reinforcement Learning for Quadrupedal Jumping in Lunar Gravity
papers.abstract: Legged robots can extend planetary exploration to rugged and discontinuous terrain that is inaccessible to conventional rovers. In lunar gravity, jumping further expands this mobility by enabling robots to cross obstacles and gaps that cannot be traversed by walking alone. We present a multistage reinforcement-learning approach that produces a single end-to-end control policy for commanded point-to-point jumping under lunar gravity. The resulting policy has a simple architecture and relies exclusively on mission-compatible onboard sensing, making its deployment on a real lunar mission plausible. In simulation, the learned policy performs accurate point-to-point jumps with landing errors smaller than the robot's body size. We analyze the torque and power demands of lunar jumping and characterize performance degradation under extreme outlier events, including control-update freezes of up to \SI{1}{s} during flight. Hardware transfer demonstrates that the policy can successfully execute a vertical jump under lunar-gravity offloading. Furthermore, the measured torque and power profiles are consistent with the simulation results and remain within the robot's hardware limits.

papers.intro:
Robotic exploration of the solar system is essential for advancing scientific understanding of planetary bodies and preparing future human missions. While orbiters and stationary landers provide valuable measurements, scientifically relevant targets require mobile surface systems to acquire local observations and interact with the terrain. As interest grows in sustained surface operations [1], infrastructure construction [2, 3], and scientific access to challenging terrain, missions increasingly target sites such as permanently shadowed regions, crater walls, and lunar lava tubes – areas that remain difficult to reach with conventional mobility systems [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Planetary rovers have so far relied predominantly on wheeled locomotion, which provides substantial flight heritage and reliability on comparatively benign terrain, but remains limited on steep, loose, rugged, or discontinuous surfaces [11]. In contrast, recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have substantially improved the ability of legged robots to traverse rough and unstructured terrain, motivating their investigation for planetary exploration. Beyond robust walking, the morphology of legged robots also enables dynamic locomotion modes such as jumping [12]. For a lunar robot, jumping is not intended to replace walking as an energy-efficient mode of long-range traversal. Still, it can serve as a useful mobility primitive for overcoming obstacles, terrain discontinuities, slopes, and gaps that would otherwise be untraversable [13]. In low gravity, such maneuvers are especially attractive because relatively moderate launch velocities can produce extended ballistic flight phases [12].

At the same time, lunar jumping imposes additional control and deployment challenges: the controller must demonstrate high robustness, particularly during flight and landing, to avoid crashing onto the surface. Specifically on non-redundant system architectures, FDIR may even require the ability to recover from a mid-flight system reboot. In addition, constraints in computing hardware for aerospace engineering favor the development of a low-complexity controller. Although quadrupedal jumping has been demonstrated in both terrestrial and low-gravity contexts, commanded point-to-point jumping for a quadruped in lunar gravity has not yet been sufficiently investigated. To address this gap, we develop a deployment-lean reinforcement-learning framework for commanded point-to-point jumping in lunar gravity. The key idea is to pair the governing ballistic properties of lunar flight with a multistage control scheme. This provides a versatile training framework to synthesize an end-to-end deep reinforcement learning-based jumping controller within a single multilayer perceptron control policy. The control policy maps onboard-feasible observations to joint-position targets.

papers.title: SatCraft: Agentic Optimization of Scheduling Policies for Satellite-Cellular Edge Services
papers.abstract: Mobile edge services can combine local computation with satellite and cellular access to deliver time-sensitive results in areas with intermittent terrestrial coverage. Meeting their deadlines and quality requirements calls for joint computation and transmission scheduling that accounts for task dependencies, changing link capacity, and shared resource budgets. However, optimizing resource allocations or tuning parameters within a fixed policy structure offers limited scope to correct failures rooted in the scheduling logic. We propose SatCraft, a framework in which a large language model (LLM) agent uses execution feedback to revise the code of joint scheduling policies. Each revision undergoes policy checks and complete-run evaluation to assess its validity, runtime, and effects on service completion. Because policy performance varies with access conditions, SatCraft retains valid alternatives in a policy library and selects one for each episode using initial access observations and the known resource configuration. Experiments using Starlink and cellular measurement data show that SatCraft improves cumulative completed-service value by 3.61%-16.89% over baselines, including recent state-of-the-art scheduling methods ADPRL, EdgeOPT, and TF-DDRL. It achieves the highest completed-service value in all four resource profiles and averages 25.02 ms per scheduling call. These results demonstrate how LLM-guided policy optimization can improve complete service delivery under the computing, communication, and quality constraints of satellite-cellular networks.

Satellite and cellular connectivity extend the reach of mobile edge services in areas with intermittent terrestrial coverage. Timely delivery requires coordinating computation and communication under shared resource constraints [1, 2]. In field inspection, a vehicle equipped with cameras and an onboard computer continually collects observations for a remote assessment team. When a road anomaly is detected, the team may need both an urgent report and usable image evidence before a deadline. Routine image uploads continue to arrive, competing for the same computing and communication resources. The vehicle can send original observations or process them locally to produce smaller outputs, with satellite and cellular links providing complementary upload paths.

In field inspection, a vehicle equipped with cameras and an onboard computer continually collects observations for a remote assessment team. When a road anomaly is detected, the team may need both an urgent report and usable image evidence before a deadline. Routine image uploads continue to arrive, competing for the same computing and communication resources. The vehicle can send original observations or process them locally to produce smaller outputs, with satellite and cellular links providing complementary upload paths.

These choices create a tradeoff between computing delay and transmission demand [3, 4]. Sending original data avoids local processing delay but requires more transmission capacity; processing first produces a smaller output that becomes ready later. If processing outlasts a period of good link conditions, even a smaller upload may miss its deadline as capacity declines. Competition from other tasks and dependencies between processing stages can introduce further delays [5], while cellular assistance consumes a limited usage budget. An assessment may remain incomplete even when its report arrives on time if the required evidence is missing or unusable. Meeting these requirements calls for joint computation and transmission scheduling that coordinates processing choices, task priorities, and cellular use to deliver complete, acceptable services on time. Fig. 1 illustrates this setting and a possible timing conflict.

Recent research provides important foundations for such joint decisions. Fan et al. optimize inference offloading and resource allocation in satellite–ground networks [6]; SLICE coordinates layer-wise computation across satellite and ground resources [4]; and Shisher et al. co-schedule feature generation and transmission for timely multi-task inference [7]. These approaches establish the value of coordinating computation and communication. For a continuing stream of services, however, a scheduling policy must also translate task progress, result dependencies, and remaining budgets into decisions that remain effective as access conditions change. Execution traces can reveal why an urgent service failed: a processing choice delayed its output, a priority rule postponed required evidence, or premature cellular activation depleted its allowance. Improving such behavior requires revisiting the decision logic and assessing its consequences throughout service execution. Constructing and adapting executable joint scheduling policies is thus a practical challenge alongside resource optimization.

Large language model (LLM) agents offer a way to connect such execution failures to changes in scheduling logic. By interpreting service requirements, policy code, and execution feedback together, an agent can propose changes to the conditions and priorities that govern computation and transmission. Work on program search, reflective heuristic evolution, and tool-assisted scheduler development demonstrates the potential of this approach [8, 9, 10]. For satellite–cellular services, failures such as delayed evidence or premature cellular activation can guide revisions that account for output readiness, required products, and remaining budgets. These revisions must be assessed through complete service executions: helping one task can consume resources needed by later arrivals, so an apparently useful local change may reduce overall delivery. Access variability adds a further consideration, since scheduling logic that is effective under one access pattern may be less useful under another. This suggests improving joint scheduling logic through complete-service feedback and retaining alternative policies for selection based on initial access observations and known resource conditions.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • We formulate a dual-access scheduling model around complete service delivery. It jointly represents output timing after local processing, delivered-result quality, task dependencies, and satellite and cellular resource limits. The objective is the cumulative value of services whose acceptance conditions are met before their deadlines, allowing processing and transmission decisions to be assessed by their downstream effects. • We develop an execution-feedback-driven method for optimizing scheduling policies. SatCraft uses an LLM agent to revise policy code according to specified repair directions and execution feedback. Interface checks and complete-run evaluation admit policies that satisfy validity and runtime constraints to a policy library, where changes to load anticipation, link activation, and quality-dependent paths can be evaluated and reused. • We design a mechanism for context-dependent policy selection and execution. A shallow policy selector relates development-set utility to initial dual-access observations and known resource configurations. After the initial access observation period, SatCraft selects one policy, which then adapts its actions to arriving tasks, revealed quality, and remaining resources. • We evaluate SatCraft using measured Starlink and cellular rates and modeled service workloads. papers.title: HETDEX [OII] galaxies at $z \le 0.48$: Growth of structures from power spectrum multipoles
papers.abstract: We use the monopole and quadrupole power spectra of [\ion{O}{2}]-emitting galaxies in the HETDEX Public Data Release 1 to constrain the growth of cosmic structures at $z\le0.48$. We interpret the power spectra using a simulation-based model built from the Mucho-Uchuu-1G $N$-body simulation. The best-fit model reproduces the observed power spectra remarkably well up to $k_\mathrm{max}=0.7~h~\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, and goodness-of-fit tests confirm that the HETDEX [\ion{O}{2}] clustering is consistent with the \textit{Planck} flat $Λ$CDM cosmology. We test the general relativity (GR) prediction for the linear growth index, $γ\simeq 0.55$. When the Alcock-Paczyński parameters are held fixed at their fiducial values, we find consistency with the GR prediction, $γ=0.55\pm 0.05$. And, when the AP parameters are allowed to vary, $γ=0.60\pm 0.07$, which is consistent with both the GR prediction and the suppressed growth rate reported by \citet{Nguyen_2023}. These results establish HETDEX [\ion{O}{2}] galaxies as a competitive, independent low-redshift probe of the growth of structures and motivate future full cosmological inference.

Throughout this paper, we assume a flat Λ\LambdaCDM model following the Planck 2018 CMB measurement [56] when converting redshfit zz to comoving distance in units of h−1​Mpch^{-1}~\mathrm{Mpc}, and applying galaxy’s peculiar velocity along the line of sight (LOS) to the galaxy position in simulations.

papers.title: Microstructural evolution during isothermal tempering of a highly supersaturated metastable austenitic state of a PM high-speed steel
papers.abstract: This study investigates the microstructural evolution of the powder metallurgical high-speed steel PM HS 3-3-4 during isothermal holding within the transformation gap between pearlite and bainite formation. The focus is on the mechanism of carbide spheroidization and the proposed formation of a chemically graded carbide rim. The heat treatments were carried out in a quenching dilatometer, enabling precise control of the thermal cycles and isothermal holding conditions. Spatially resolved analytic microscopy techniques, including scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), Auger electron spectroscopy (AES) and atom probe tomography (APT), image analysis and complementary thermodynamic simulations (MatCalc) were used to characterize the carbide evolution. Isothermal holding increased carbide circularity, carbide volume fraction, and hardness, while MatCalc calculations predict a strong thermodynamic driving force for additional carbide precipitation. The analytic techniques revealed a compositional gradient of approximately 15 nm at the carbide-matrix interface in the isothermally treated condition, compared with a sharp transition of only 2-3 nm in the directly quenched state. This nanometer-scale gradient provides strong evidence for epitaxial, interface-controlled carbide growth and the formation of a chemically graded carbide rim. The associated solute depletion of the surrounding austenite provides a plausible explanation for its reduced stability, reflected by an increase in the martensite start temperature. The combined results demonstrate that isothermal holding promotes interfacial chemical reorganization, offering new insights into carbide spheroidization and providing a basis for tailoring carbide morphology and the resulting mechanical properties through heat treatment.

papers.title: No Frames, Just Frequencies: Bandwidth-Efficient Deployment-Time Adaptation for Smart Glasses
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks deployed on smart glasses must adapt to changes in the distribution of incoming data while adhering to strict privacy and device constraints. We present No Frames, Just Frequencies, a bandwidth-efficient source-assisted adaptation framework that characterizes distribution shifts using compact frequency descriptors computed on-device. Rather than transmitting camera frames, the glasses compute and send frequency descriptors to a host device that contains a replica of the model. The host device maps the received frequency descriptor to a distribution shift operator that synthesizes out-of-distribution data and adapts a model replica using a pre-defined adaptation protocol. We evaluate the framework on mixtures of ImageNet-C corruptions using convolution-based (ConvNeXtV2-Femto), self-attention-based (DeiT-Tiny), and hybrid (TinyViT-5M) vision models, on person classification (Visual Wake Words), and on object detection (MS-COCO). Our results reveal that adaptation driven solely by the transmitted descriptors recovers $93-95\%$ of the supervised oracle adaptation gain on all three architectures, $82\%$ on Visual Wake Words and $94$--$98\%$ on MS-COCO. Notably, adaptation quality degrades gracefully as the descriptor resolution decreases from $224 $ to $28$ pixels, consistently across architectures, enabling bandwidth reductions from $213\times$ to $784\times$ across the frequency descriptors.

Deep neural network (DNN) models deployed at the edge often lack robustness when the input data (Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019) drift from the training data, degrading the model’s prediction quality (Saukh et al., 2023). Practical deployments must additionally cope with dynamic resource constraints (e.g., fluctuating energy budgets and latency requirements), which may require rapid, runtime reconfiguration of the deployed model (Corti et al., 2026).

Smart glasses represent an especially demanding edge setting: they must continuously process video streams within tight latency and power-efficiency budgets while operating in close physical proximity to the user (Karakostas and others, 2024). The motivation for on-device intelligence is therefore dual: local inference minimizes dependence on network connectivity (Zhou et al., 2019), and processing video data on-device reduces the exposure of raw visual content, which on smart glasses may contain sensitive information (e.g., faces, screens, locations) that should not leave the device.

Privacy is not the only constraint: smart glasses also operate under severe hardware resource limitations. While edge-designed convolutional architectures such as MobileNets (Howard et al., 2017) and EfficientNet (Tan and Le, 2019) have made inference practical on edge devices, adaptation remains the bottleneck for both convolution- and attention-based models (Lin et al., 2023b), since gradient-based methods must store intermediate activations and optimizer states, substantially increasing the memory footprint beyond inference alone (Slamanig et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2022). As a wearable camera moves through heterogeneous environments, the visual stream experiences rapid changes in illumination and motion blur, producing non-stationary shifts over time (Quiñonero-Candela et al., 2008; Yao et al., 2022) that degrade the predictive quality of the deployed model, thus adaptation must operate continuously during deployment.

Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) adapts pre-trained models to changes in data distribution at test time by using each data point once for post-inference adaptation (Sun et al., 2020). Existing TTA methods expose two methodological gaps for resource-constrained edge devices, such as smart glasses. First, popular approaches such as entropy minimization (Wang et al., 2021a) may fail under certain shifts and amplify the model’s prediction errors without safeguards (Press et al., 2024). Second, they assume mini-batches large enough (or an auxiliary cache) to estimate accurate target statistics. Under realistic on-device constraints, where only a few samples may be available, the model’s performance can degrade sharply and may even collapse for online adaptation batches due to unreliable statistics estimation or noisy gradient adaptation (Su et al., 2024; Niu et al., 2023). Prior work mitigates these methodological gaps by emulating larger effective batches with gradient accumulation (Lin et al., 2023a) or by constructing a virtual batch via test-time augmentations (Zhang et al., 2022), which conflicts with strict memory and privacy restrictions when storing or replaying visual samples on smart glasses.

Our approach to bandwidth-efficient deployment-time adaptation satisfies three requirements: (i) it avoids streaming camera frames over the bandwidth-limited uplink by relying on compact, privacy-enhancing distribution-shift frequency descriptors computed on-device; (ii) it offloads the gradient adaptation step to a nearby host device to respect the glasses’ tight compute and memory budgets, restricting the adaptation to a small parameter subset; (iii) it couples adaptation with an explicit characterization of the distribution shift affecting the model’s predictions under non-stationary streams. Concretely, the edge device computes a compact frequency descriptor for each frame and transmits it to a host device (Fig. 1). These descriptors capture only the spectral magnitude, discarding the phase information and aggregating the spectrum into as few as 14 floating-point values, so that the per-frame uplink fits within a low-bandwidth wireless link budget. The host device maps the received descriptor to a four-stage causal corruption directed acyclic graph (DAG), synthesizes adaptation batches from pre-stored in-distribution data, adapts a model replica on a compact subspace via supervised cross-entropy, and transmits the adapted parameters back to the smart glasses, thereby closing the adaptation loop without transmitting camera frames; we term this setting source-assisted adaptation. papers.title: Who Verifies the Agent's Success Claim? Self-Report Leakage in GUI-Agent Completion Judging
papers.abstract: In automation pipelines, a GUI agent's confident success report can let downstream stages proceed even when the recorded execution trace does not show that the agent produced the requested outcome. We call this case a dangerous misreport: an unhedged success claim that the trace does not support as causal accomplishment during the run. We study report--trace auditing, which checks an agent's completion claim against an independently recorded trace. A controlled aware/blind intervention reveals self-report leakage: the agent's own self-report changes how completion is judged. The same judge reads the same task and trace; only that self-report is included or withheld. Withholding it improves trace-only dangerous-misreport recall by 43.4 percentage points with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and 13.3 percentage points with DeepSeek-284B-A13B, with the same trend on held-out Batch 2. This motivates report isolation. The report records what the agent claims, but it must not influence the trace-state judgment. We implement this separation with a structured auditor that separates claim interpretation from claim-blind trace analysis and applies deterministic rules to extracted evidence. Because evidence extraction is separated from the policy that consumes it, the same audit record can be replayed under alternative policies without new model calls. The auditor achieves F1 0.75--0.78 on the 465-record audit-target set and 0.77--0.81 on held-out Batch 2, outperforming claim-aware and prompt-blind controls in recall and F1. Under audit-stage gating, where flag and review both block automatic pass, it blocks 74--90% of dangerous misreports at 45--56% inspection load, or 16--19% of the full in-scope stream after coarse status triage.

papers.intro:
LLM-driven GUI agents are increasingly used inside mobile testing and regression workflows [1, 2, 3, 4], where task outcomes may be consumed by downstream harnesses or review pipelines. Consider a run that ends with “Done—the duplicates were removed.” The harness records the task as pass, downstream stages proceed, and the resulting device state enters the pipeline as if the requested operation had succeeded. But the trace may show a different execution: the agent inspected an empty list, acted on the wrong screen, or failed to save the requested change. No exception is thrown. The failure remains silent because the agent under audit supplies its own success report.

We study report–trace auditing. Given a completed run, the agent reports completion and the audit checks whether the independently recorded trace supports that report. A dangerous misreport occurs when the report claims success but the trace does not show causal accomplishment, meaning that it does not show the agent itself producing the task-relevant outcome during the run. Final-screen compatibility alone is insufficient, because pre-existing goal states, empty target lists, proxy screens, and unsaved edits can all make a failed run appear successful [5, 6]. Such cases are dangerous because they can be recorded as silent false pass outcomes.

Because task-specific success checks are costly to author across heterogeneous GUI tasks and human trajectory review is costly, recent agent-evaluation work increasingly uses LLM or agent judges for trajectory success [7, 8, 9, 10]. A common pattern is to ask the judge to read the task, the execution trace, and the agent’s final report in a single prompt, then decide whether the task was completed [11, 12, 13, 10, 14]. The report thereby ceases to be merely a claim to be verified and instead becomes part of the evidence for its own truth, making the evaluation path circular.

Report isolation alone is not sufficient. We therefore build a report-isolated evidence–policy auditor. A prompt-blind judge withholds the report, but it still returns an opaque verdict that is difficult to inspect or reuse under a different completion policy. Our auditor instead separates the problem into evidence extraction and policy enforcement. One component reads the report to identify the claim; a second reads only the task and trace to extract typed evidence of accomplishment. Neither decides completion directly. Deterministic rules consume the extracted evidence and assign each run to pass, flag, or review. This evidence–policy boundary also makes the audit replayable: cached evidence can be evaluated under alternative policies without another model call [15, 16]. The output is not a prompt-level verdict but a software audit record whose evidence fields and policy decisions can be inspected, regression-tested, and replayed.

papers.title: Reliability-Aware Probabilistic Fusion for Multimodal Learning with Incomplete Evidence
papers.abstract: Multimodal inputs may be missing or degraded, raising distinct questions of evidence availability and trust. We introduce a reliability-aware Gaussian Product-of-Experts (PoE) in which an input-dependent reliability weight tempers each modality's latent precision, while missing experts are omitted. We characterize how reliability and availability affect posterior information and expert influence. Across two clinical multimodal tasks, the full framework remains competitive with complete inputs and achieves its clearest mean-AUROC advantage under modality absence, particularly on HAIM-MIMIC-MM. Ablations show a substantial gain from missing-aware training and an additional HAIM improvement from reliability weighting under matched PoE, missing-aware, and consistency training. Unseen test-time corruptions are used diagnostically and reveal modality-dependent reliability-weight and latent-uncertainty responses, including failure under severe degradation. Thus, reliability weighting provides an explicit evidence-control mechanism, while learning dependable quality signals remains an open challenge.

papers.intro:
Multimodal learning combines complementary information from different sources, such as images, physiological signals, structured measurements, and text, and has become increasingly important in biomedical prediction [1, 2]. In practice, however, multimodal inputs are rarely equally available or equally trustworthy. A modality may be entirely missing, but it may also be present yet degraded by noise, acquisition artifacts, or measurement errors. This creates two related but distinct questions: what should a model do when evidence is unavailable, and how much should it trust evidence that is available?

Multimodal learning combines complementary information from different sources, such as images, physiological signals, structured measurements, and text, and has become increasingly important in biomedical prediction [1, 2]. In practice, however, multimodal inputs are rarely equally available or equally trustworthy. A modality may be entirely missing, but it may also be present yet degraded by noise, acquisition artifacts, or measurement errors. This creates two related but distinct questions: what should a model do when evidence is unavailable, and how much should it trust evidence that is available?

Existing work has largely focused on the first question. Modality dropout trains models to tolerate absent inputs [3], while M3Care uses information from similar patients to compensate for missing modalities [4]. More recent methods learn representations or routing mechanisms that adapt to different modality combinations. DrFuse separates shared and modality-specific information [5], MUSE uses graph-based multimodal representations [6], and Flex-MoE routes different availability patterns through specialized experts [7]. These approaches provide effective mechanisms for incomplete inputs, but missingness is only part of the problem. An observed modality may itself contain uncertain or unreliable evidence, and representation-level fusion does not necessarily provide an explicit statistical account of how strongly such evidence should influence the prediction.

Probabilistic fusion provides a natural way to reason about this. Product-of-Experts (PoE) models combine evidence through the precision of individual probabilistic experts [8], and Gaussian PoE has been used to support inference from arbitrary subsets of modalities [9, 10]. Yet precision alone need not reflect trustworthiness. An expert can assign low variance to an observation that is nevertheless corrupted or misleading, and precision miscalibration can therefore distort multimodal aggregation [11, 10]. This motivates separately parameterizing two operational roles:latent uncertainty describes how concentrated an expert’s evidence is, whereas a reliability-interpreted weight controls how strongly that evidence enters fusion.

papers.title: A DIY DPDK Software Router for Networking Education
papers.abstract: High-performance packet processing frameworks, such as the Data Plane Development Kit (DPDK), are widely used in modern network systems, yet they are rarely integrated into networking curricula. As a result, students often lack exposure to the performance considerations and low-level design choices that shape real-world packet processing systems. We describe a semester-long course project in which students implement a do-it-yourself (DIY) software router using DPDK in a master-level computer networking course. The project guides students through the design and implementation of a multithreaded router, the development of a routing table data structure, and the evaluation of forwarding performance using standard benchmarking tools. We present the project structure and the virtualized infrastructure used to support classes of realistic size. Based on several iterations of the course and survey feedback from participating students, we discuss the observed workload, learning outcomes, and challenges of teaching high-performance packet processing. We release the project material and scripts to recreate the infrastructure, enabling reuse and further refinement by the community.

papers.title: remage: a Geant4-based simulation framework for low-background experiments
papers.abstract: Monte Carlo simulations are an essential tool for data modeling and experimental design in low-background physics. These simulations typically demand a considerable effort, with each collaboration developing and maintaining its own complex Geant4 application. In this paper we present the design and validation of remage, which is an open-source framework designed to standardize these simulations and significantly reduce this effort. Its design separates the geometry, built with dedicated Python tools, from the compiled application. It provides a physics list and event generators tuned to radiogenic and cosmogenic backgrounds, output tailored to the most common detector types, and robust validation backed by modern software development practices. The software is distributed ready to use and scales efficiently with the computing resources that demanding simulations require. remage has been primarily developed for the LEGEND experiment, but is applicable to a wide variety of experiments.

Monte Carlo simulations are a crucial tool in high-energy physics, both for predicting experimental outcomes and for planning new experiments. Geant4 is a state-of-the-art particle tracking toolkit for nuclear, leptonic and optical simulations [1, 2, 3], which are ubiquitous in experimental particle physics and other fields such as medical physics. For example, they are used in low-background physics experiments to simulate radioactive and cosmogenic (i.e., induced by cosmic radiation) background sources, for experimental design and data analysis (see for example [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]).

For example, they are used in low-background physics experiments to simulate radioactive and cosmogenic (i.e., induced by cosmic radiation) background sources, for experimental design and data analysis (see for example [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]).

Geant4 is a general toolkit supporting a vast range of uses. For a particular use case it is typically necessary to develop a dedicated Geant4 application. A significant amount of effort goes into the development of these programs. This includes the implementation of specific (often complex) experimental geometries, selection of appropriate physics processes, and implementation of routines to generate primary particles and store output information. Since Geant4 is based on C++, a low-level programming language with a large barrier to entry, this typically implies writing and maintaining large amounts of C++ code, which further increases the effort required. Finally, considerable validation is required to confirm that the application is appropriate for a certain use case, in particular the physics processes selected from such a general toolkit. The development of these Geant4 applications has historically been performed separately by each experiment or research group [11, 5, 12, 13], with sharing limited by the presence of sensitive information in these applications.
