papers.title: Spatially Gated Demographic Steering for Debiasing Multi-Person Text-to-Image Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-Image models reproduce societal stereotypes, and existing mitigation applies one demographic correction to the whole scene. In multi-person scene generation this creates a trade-off: global steering improves aggregate balance only by homogenizing the people within an image. Steering-based methods like Embedding Arithmetic drive the intra-image diversity below the unsteered baseline. Text- and latent-projection approaches shift the aggregate skew with only marginal gains in intra-image diversity. We present Spatially Gated Steering (SGS), which steers the demographics of each person independently by extracting per-person masks from the Diffusion Transformer's (DiT) internal attention maps at a critical denoising timestep and applying a distinct demographic vector within each mask for the remaining steps. SGS needs no fine-tuning, inversion or layout specifications, and uses a lightweight segmentor over frozen DiT attention features to localize subjects at early timesteps. On skewed occupational prompts, SGS reaches high intra-image racial and gender diversity while keeping aggregate balance competitive and image quality near baseline, a result we validate on two architecturally distinct diffusion transformers, FLUX.1-Dev and SD3.5-Large. Codebase and model weights are available at https://github.com/cvims/spatially-gated-steering
papers.intro:
Text-to-Image (T2I) generation has transformed digital content creation, yet foundational models such as FLUX [24] and Stable Diffusion [10] systematically reproduce societal stereotypes [9]. Gender-neutral prompts like a carpenter yield predominantly male-presenting images; a nurse yields predominantly female-presenting images [28]. Studies show these outputs shift user beliefs about real-world distributions [14], making fairness mitigation essential for responsible deployment.

Text-to-Image (T2I) generation has transformed digital content creation, yet foundational models such as FLUX [24] and Stable Diffusion [10] systematically reproduce societal stereotypes [9]. Gender-neutral prompts like a carpenter yield predominantly male-presenting images; a nurse yields predominantly female-presenting images [28]. Studies show these outputs shift user beliefs about real-world distributions [14], making fairness mitigation essential for responsible deployment.

Several mitigation strategies have been proposed and they operate at different levels of the diffusion pipeline [37]: They modify the text embeddings [39, 6, 43, 22] or fine-tune model weights [13, 36] to shift the aggregate output distribution. While effective for scenes with a single person, global mitigation methods share a fundamental limitation: They apply identical steering to every person in a scene. A prompt like ”a group of nurses” receives one demographic vector, pushing all the persons in the image in the same direction and failing to diversify individuals independently.

While effective for scenes with a single person, global mitigation methods share a fundamental limitation: They apply identical steering to every person in a scene. A prompt like ”a group of nurses” receives one demographic vector, pushing all the persons in the image in the same direction and failing to diversify individuals independently.

This limitation is not merely theoretical: Wan and Chang [41] show that multi-person prompts expose a distinct, compounding class of bias that single-subject evaluations cannot capture. Co-occurring subjects amplify stereotypes even when the same model behaves anti-stereotypically on single-person prompts.

Attempts to address this gap remain limited. Existing approaches either rewrite the generation prompt with a single corrective signal applied to the whole scene [41, 8], optimize demographic distributions at the aggregate level without per-instance control [18], or require an explicit spatial layout as input [7]. To the best of our knowledge, no existing method localizes individuals from the model’s own internal representations and applies independent demographic steering, to achieve intra-image diversity. Figure 1 illustrates this gap: while global mitigation shifts all persons uniformly toward a single demographic mode, our approach steers each individual independently through their spatial mask, reaching distinct attractors within pdatap_{\text{data}} in a single denoising pass.

SGS operates by 1) Identifying and generating the masks of instances of people during the intermediate denoising steps using a lightweight detector, 2) Steering the demographics of the detected individuals, while also maintaining concept coherence.

SGS operates by 1) Identifying and generating the masks of instances of people during the intermediate denoising steps using a lightweight detector, 2) Steering the demographics of the detected individuals, while also maintaining concept coherence.

Our contributions are as follows:

• A trade-off in multi-person fairness. Global mitigation faces an inherent tension: improving aggregate balance requires collapsing intra-image diversity, sometimes below the unsteered baseline. Since any per-instance diversification trivially raises intra-image entropy, the meaningful result is high entropy at a competitive aggregate balance. SGS reaches high intra-image diversity with a competitive aggregate balance by steering per-instance without fine-tuning, flow-inversion or layout. • Instance segmentation from DiT features. We show that self-attention maps of DiTs at a critical denoising timestep encode spatially separable person instances, and train a lightweight DETR-style [4] segmentor on these frozen features that isolates individuals across crowd sizes and scene complexities. • Benchmark and analysis. We introduce a benchmark measuring fairness along both intra-image diversity and aggregate deviation, surfacing the homogenization failure mode of global methods and showing SGS is strong on both axes, on both FLUX.1-Dev and SD3.5-Large.

papers.title: Continuity of Furstenberg entropy on Bowen Poisson bundles
papers.abstract: We provide a sufficient criterion for continuity of the Furstenberg entropy of Bowen Poisson bundles, jointly in the random walk measure and the underlying invariant random subgroup. The criterion applies in particular for tree-like Poisson bundles of a free group and for intersectional invariant random subgroups on lamplighter groups. It also provides continuity of the boundary entropy spectrum of powers of prime measured groups.

papers.title: Zero-group-velocity modes in textured steel plates: experiments and elastic modeling
papers.abstract: Zero-group-velocity (ZGV) resonances are investigated as a non-contact ultrasonic probe of elastic anisotropy in textured steel plates. Directional laser-ultrasonic measurements were performed on 70% cold-rolled Ti-stabilized interstitial-free steel plates in the full-hard and recrystallized condition. Experimental results were compared with predictions based on effective elastic stiffness tensors derived from X-ray diffraction measurements. Classical Voigt-Reuss-Hill estimates and microstructure-resolved finite-element homogenization reproduce the measured angular dependence of the ZGV frequencies well for both states, with the finite-element KUBC/SUBC bounds considerably narrower than the classical Voigt-Reuss bounds. For the full-hard state, agreement with the texture-based model is obtained only after a recovery treatment. This indicates that dislocations present in the full-hard material contribute to its elastic response, an interpretation that is further supported by theoretical estimations. An identifiability analysis shows that the directional ZGV measurements provide access to at least three independently observable combinations of the stiffness tensor components, and concluding suggestions for application in recrystallization monitoring are provided.

papers.intro:
The elastic properties of engineering metals are strongly influenced by their polycrystalline microstructure. In addition to the single-crystal elastic properties, the crystallographic orientations and spatial morphology of the grains affect the macroscopic response [1]. Forming processes such as rolling commonly generate preferred crystallographic textures rather than uniform orientation distributions [2, 3, 4, 5]. The collective response of many grains can then be described by effective macroscopic material properties that account for texture-induced anisotropy. Within the framework of linear elasticity, this behavior is represented by an effective stiffness tensor, which may be estimated from the single-crystal stiffness tensor and the orientation distribution function (ODF).

In the production of steel sheet, control of the crystallographic texture is of considerable technological importance, as it strongly influences the material’s formability and, consequently, its suitability for subsequent manufacturing operations such as deep drawing. During recrystallization of cold-rolled steel sheets, the elongated grains generated by rolling are replaced by a new population of approximately equiaxed grains. This microstructural transformation is typically accompanied by a significant evolution of the crystallographic texture, ultimately determining the effective elastic and plastic properties of the final product [2, 6].

The present work investigates advanced ultrasonic methods for probing the effective elastic behavior of textured sheet metals, with the long-term objective of providing process feedback during recrystallization. Unlike conventional ultrasonic techniques, which often reduce the elastic response to one or a few wave velocities, guided-wave and zero-group-velocity (ZGV) measurements provide a rich set of observables that are sensitive to elastic anisotropy. As a first step, we focus on the fundamental relationship between crystallographic texture and these ultrasonic observables. Experimental results are compared with predictions based on ODF-derived effective stiffness tensors, allowing the sensitivity of the measured resonances and dispersion characteristics to texture-induced anisotropy to be assessed.

Beyond assessing texture-induced anisotropy, the comparison may reveal to what extent the material behavior is adequately described by the homogenized elastic tensor alone. Deviations between measured and predicted resonances could indicate the influence of additional factors that are not explicitly included in the model, such as residual stresses, dislocation density, or other aspects of the microstructure.

Classical mean-field estimates are provided by the Voigt and Reuss models, which assume uniform strain and uniform stress throughout the aggregate, respectively. In the Voigt approach, the stiffness tensor of each grain is first rotated into the sample coordinate system according to its crystallographic orientation, and the effective stiffness is obtained by averaging these rotated stiffness tensors over the orientation distribution. In contrast, the Reuss model averages the correspondingly rotated compliance tensors and subsequently inverts the result to obtain the effective stiffness tensor. These assumptions generally yield upper and lower energetic estimates of the effective stiffness, whereas the Voigt–Reuss–Hill approximation uses their arithmetic mean as a practical intermediate estimate. More advanced self-consistent schemes account approximately for elastic interactions between differently oriented grains by embedding each grain in an effective medium whose properties are determined iteratively. These analytical approaches provide efficient estimates of the homogenized elastic tensor, but they do not explicitly resolve the spatial grain arrangement or local intragranular fields. [7, 8]

Microstructure-resolved finite-element (FE) homogenization [9, 10] avoids the uniform-field assumptions by solving the heterogeneous elastic boundary-value problem directly. For a finite statistical volume element, the apparent elastic response depends on the applied boundary conditions. Kinematically uniform boundary conditions (KUBC) prescribe an affine displacement field at the boundary and produce the stiffer apparent response, whereas statically uniform boundary conditions (SUBC) prescribe uniform macroscopic tractions and produce the more compliant response. Their difference decreases as the considered volume becomes increasingly representative of the material [11]. While it is also possible to simulate a dynamic response with FE in synthetic polycrystals [12], we restrict this report on static models, as good agreement with experiments was found.

Ultrasonic techniques are well established for determining anisotropic elastic stiffness tensors when measurements can be performed along several propagation and polarization directions. Dever [13] determined the three independent elastic constants of single-crystalline α\alpha-iron in a broad temperature range. Measurements and theoretical Voigt–Reuss–Hill-averaged values of the stiffness tensor for textured low-carbon steel were reported by Spalthoff et al. [14]. Such approaches require access to suitable acoustic propagation paths and may involve specially oriented specimens, multiple specimen cuts, or several measurement configurations. These requirements limit their applicability in quality-control settings, where characterization may need to be performed non-destructively on a single component.

papers.title: SWE-DIVE: Multi-Turn Coding Agent Evaluation with Dynamic User Simulation
papers.abstract: Coding agents are typically evaluated using one-shot, well-formulated prompts. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench use existing GitHub issues as input for a coding agent and evaluate whether the agent successfully solves the task. However, in real-world use cases, prompts are often not as well-formulated or structured as existing GitHub issues. Additionally, a coding agent session is not limited to a single prompt; it typically involves a multi-turn interaction in which the user iteratively adds new tasks and requirements that the agent must fulfill. To benchmark these abilities, we developed SWE-DIVE, a dynamic, interactive validation and evaluation framework for benchmarking coding agents in a multi-turn environment. To achieve this, we introduce a user simulator that can simulate different behavioral patterns and communicate with the coding agent. We also introduce a conversation validator that evaluates the user simulator's outputs to determine whether they fulfill the initial requirements and guide the agent toward successfully solving the task. The entire framework is embedded in a Harbor environment, which orchestrates the coding agent, user simulator, and conversation validator, and executes the test environment to determine whether the agent successfully solves the task. Our results and source code are available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/lorenzbrehme/swe-dive_usersim).

papers.intro:
Agents are typically evaluated on benchmarks collected from GitHub issues or crafted for a certain task, like SWE-bench (Jimenez et al.,, 2024). However, the input format of a complete, detailed github issue is not how users normally interact with agents – users often give a high-level prompt that is lacking detail and iterate on the prototype until it’s complete (Baumann et al.,, 2026). In other words, agent prompting is a process of iteratively defining the problem rather than a one-shot attempt.

However, the input format of a complete, detailed github issue is not how users normally interact with agents – users often give a high-level prompt that is lacking detail and iterate on the prototype until it’s complete (Baumann et al.,, 2026). In other words, agent prompting is a process of iteratively defining the problem rather than a one-shot attempt.

Baumann et al., (2026) investigated the behavior of humans using a coding agent and found that the agent is used in multi-turn interactions, where different roles emerge, such as the expert nitpicker or the ambiguous programmer. These multi-turn behaviors are already studied in benchmarks such as CodeFlowBench (Wang et al.,, 2026) and CodeGen (Nijkamp et al.,, 2023), which evaluate coding agents in multi-turn settings. In these benchmarks, tasks typically involve iteratively adding new features, requiring the agent to continually adapt and find solutions. Additionally, AmbigSWE-bench explores the ambiguous behavior of users by providing ambiguous instructions and allowing the agent to ask clarification questions in order to resolve this ambiguity (Vijayvargiya et al.,, 2025). These multi-turn benchmarks follow a predefined process and do not adapt depending on what the agents ask. Baumann et al., (2026) demonstrates that 41% of the turns were pushbacks, indicating that the agent did not perform as the user expected and that clarification was needed. In addition, Vijayvargiya et al., (2025) shows that the agent is still prompted with the full task list, whereas a more realistic setup involves users providing very nitpicky and vague instructions, iteratively adding new tasks in a multi-turn conversation.

papers.title: OMAR: Open-World Multi-Attribute Reasoning for Scene-Conditioned Shelf Organization
papers.abstract: With the advent of foundation models, robots are increasingly capable of understanding and executing explicitly specified human tasks. Extending these capabilities to open-ended tasks, however, requires robots to infer appropriate actions from the observed scene. Household organization exemplifies this challenge, as robots must often act without detailed instructions, predefined object vocabularies, or known object-receptacle associations. While robots may follow instructions or learn organization preferences from demonstrations, inferring the latent organization of an occasionally changing scene and placing a novel object consistently with it remains challenging. We propose an open-world multi-attribute reasoning pipeline that grounds unknown objects across views and constructs an instance-level 3D scene graph for placement reasoning. First, a vision-language model proposes labels together with attributes such as content and packaging type, which are grounded through segmentation, depth, and multi-view association. Then, an LLM reasons over this representation to infer the latent shelf organization and rank scene-consistent object placements without explicitly user-provided preferences. The resulting placement rankings guide subsequent geometric and kinematic feasibility checks for execution. Our experimental evaluation shows that our approach leads to improved instance mapping and placement coherence over single-view language-grounding and geometry-only baselines, enabling autonomous placement of previously unseen objects without predefined object-receptacle mappings or class-specific retraining.

To effectively organize objects in such environments, service robots must act beyond explicitly specified tasks. Multi-view grounding provides this object-level context by associating instances across views and revealing occluded objects.

papers.title: An experimental evaluation of static k-center clustering algorithms on graphs
papers.abstract: The $k$-center problem is one of the most fundamental clustering problems and has applications in a wide range of areas, including facility location, network design, data mining, and machine learning. Given a set of objects together with a distance measure, the goal is to select $k$ centers such that the maximum distance from any object to its closest center is minimized. The $k$-center problem has been studied extensively from a theoretical perspective, both in metric spaces and on graphs. While there have been experimental studies for $k$-center clustering in metric spaces, a comprehensive experimental comparison of graph-based $k$-center algorithms on large-scale graphs is still lacking. In this paper, we bridge this gap by evaluating a set of algorithms ranging from classical approaches such as Gonzalez's greedy algorithm [TCS 1985], an algorithm based on the framework established by Hochbaum and Shmoys [Math. Oper. Res. 1985], to more recent methods, including algorithms by Thorup [SICOMP 2001] and Abboud et al. [SOSA 2023]. Our study considers both running time, solution quality and the effects of parallelism on a variety of synthetic and real-world datasets. Our goal is to provide a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art $k$-center algorithms on graphs and identify the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches in practice.

papers.intro:
Analyzing the structure of large-scale networks is a fundamental problem in many fields. One important task is to partition the underlying data into meaningful subgroups. This process is naturally captured by clustering problems. These problems have been extensively studied in data mining and machine learning [31, 3, 32]. The goal of clustering problems is to group input data together in structures called clusters such that similar data ends up in the same cluster. Among the many clustering objectives, kk-clustering methods represent each cluster by one of kk centers and each data point is assigned to the cluster of its closest center. The kk-center problem is concerned with selecting its centers such that the maximum distance of every data point to its closest center is minimized. Formally, this is an optimization problem of the following form: Given a metric space M=(P,dist)M=(P,\mathrm{dist}) and an integer k≥1k\geq 1, the objective is to compute a set of centers C⊆PC\subseteq P with |C|=k|C|=k minimizing fM​(C)=maxp∈P⁡dist⁡(p,C)f_{M}(C)=\max_{p\in P}\mathrm{dist}(p,C), where dist⁡(p,C)=minq∈C⁡dist⁡(p,q)\mathrm{dist}(p,C)=\min_{q\in C}\mathrm{dist}(p,q).

Formally, this is an optimization problem of the following form: Given a metric space M=(P,dist)M=(P,\mathrm{dist}) and an integer k≥1k\geq 1, the objective is to compute a set of centers C⊆PC\subseteq P with |C|=k|C|=k minimizing fM​(C)=maxp∈P⁡dist⁡(p,C)f_{M}(C)=\max_{p\in P}\mathrm{dist}(p,C), where dist⁡(p,C)=minq∈C⁡dist⁡(p,q)\mathrm{dist}(p,C)=\min_{q\in C}\mathrm{dist}(p,q).

This problem is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-hard [30] and thus TCS research generally focuses on finding efficient approximation algorithms [24, 29, 41, 19]. The kk-center problem is commonly defined on arbitrary metric spaces. In this general setting, often called ‘metric kk-center’ or ‘vertex kk-center’, it is usually assumed that the distances are given to the algorithm explicitly as part of the input or that distances can be queried upon request. However, in transportation, communication, social and web network analysis, data is often inherently represented as a graph, where distances correspond to shortest-path lengths rather than explicitly given pairwise distances. Consequently, the graph kk-center problem has been studied alongside its metric counterpart from theoretical and algorithmic perspectives [49, 1, 21]. Although graph metrics satisfy the triangle inequality and therefore constitute a special case of metric spaces, they introduce a fundamental algorithmic difference. As a result, the practical performance of graph kk-center algorithms depends not only on the quality of the approximation algorithm itself, but also on how efficiently shortest-path computations are performed. Despite recurring progress of theoretical research on graph kk-center there is comparatively little empirical work evaluating these algorithms on modern large-scale graph datasets. This paper aims to fill this gap by providing a comprehensive experimental study of state-of-the-art graph kk-center algorithms on graphs.

papers.title: Consistent Modeling of SEI Growth via Electron Diffusion Validated Across Diverse Cell Specifications and Operating Conditions in LFP/Graphite Cells
papers.abstract: Understanding and predicting degradation in lithium-ion batteries is critical for their widespread deployment. The continuous growth of the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) remains a dominant aging pathway, yet accurately modeling its kinetics across diverse cell specifications and operating conditions remains a significant challenge. Here, we present and validate a physically grounded SEI growth model mediated by the electron diffusion mechanism. This framework intrinsically captures the state of charge (SOC) dependence of degradation through the impact of the anode potential on the electron concentration, which governs the rate of SEI growth. The presented model explicitly accounts for variations in electrolyte salt, anode material, temperature, and cycling rate. Validation against experimental aging data for LFP/graphite cells demonstrates high predictive accuracy across a broad range of cell specifications and cycling conditions, including confined SOC windows, electrolyte salts (LiFSI, LiPF6), artificial graphites (AGC, AGD), temperatures (40-70°C), and C-rates (C/20-1C). Remarkably, a single, consistent set of parameters is applied to simulate the capacity fade for all experiments without recalibration. While quantitative overestimations occur during high-SOC storage periods, the framework consistently captures the observed degradation trends. Our findings underscore that lower SOC operation mitigates degradation, establishing a physics-based model for predicting long-term lithium-ion battery aging.

Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have established an indispensable role in modern energy storage applications [30, 18]. Within this landscape, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry is gaining increasing relevance due to its favorable cost and material abundance [8]. However, regardless of the specific chemistry, battery degradation manifests through a variety of mechanisms [13, 12, 9, 21, 4]. Consequently, understanding and mitigating these degradation pathways remains a critical challenge for virtually all battery deployments, particularly for LFP-based systems, which are increasingly utilized as large-scale stationary energy storage solutions.

Within this landscape, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry is gaining increasing relevance due to its favorable cost and material abundance [8]. However, regardless of the specific chemistry, battery degradation manifests through a variety of mechanisms [13, 12, 9, 21, 4]. Consequently, understanding and mitigating these degradation pathways remains a critical challenge for virtually all battery deployments, particularly for LFP-based systems, which are increasingly utilized as large-scale stationary energy storage solutions.

Among the various degradation mechanisms, the continuous growth of the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) is widely recognized as the dominant aging pathway [22, 25, 6]. During storage, SEI formation typically follows a square-root-of-time dependence [1, 7, 24, 28, 27] and exhibits a pronounced dependence on the state of charge (SOC), as evidenced by experimental studies [15, 14, 20]. Building on these observations, we previously introduced and evaluated a physically grounded SEI growth model based on electron diffusion, which accurately captures the SOC-dependent capacity fade during storage periods [23, 16]. Crucially, our comparative analysis demonstrated the superiority of the electron diffusion mechanism over traditional solvent-diffusion-mediated models [16]. The electron diffusion mechanism has since received independent experimental validation through cyclic voltammetry measurements [17]. Beyond storage conditions, studies on SEI evolution during cycling revealed that electron diffusion dominates the SEI growth over electron migration until late stages of battery aging [26, 27]. Notably, recent experimental findings continue to underscore a strong SOC dependence during cycling, particularly when operation is confined to specific SOC windows [32]. The investigation was supported by the observation of larger heat flows due to SEI reactions at the graphite anode at higher SOC, implying a higher reactivity of the anode at lower potentials [32].

The investigation was supported by the observation of larger heat flows due to SEI reactions at the graphite anode at higher SOC, implying a higher reactivity of the anode at lower potentials [32].

In addition to the SOC dependence, SEI growth is critically sensitive to cell design and operating conditions. The selection of anode materials (e.g., a specific artificial graphite), electrolyte composition (including solvent systems, salts, and functional additives), and operating temperature profoundly influence degradation rates [5, 19, 3]. At extended timescales and elevated temperatures, iron dissolution from the cathode can become significant, leading to accelerated, non-square-root SEI growth profiles [5]. However, for cells cycled under moderate conditions, such non-linear contributions remain negligible at early and intermediate aging periods and are expected to emerge only at advanced states of aging [5].

In this paper, we present our physically derived SEI growth model mediated by the electron diffusion mechanism and compare the model predictions to experimental data across a broad spectrum of cell specifications and operating conditions. Our work was significantly motivated by the systematic experimental data showing clear SOC-dependence during cycling presented in Ref. [32], which we herein analyze and explain using our SEI growth model. Therefore, this work distinguishes from our previous SEI growth modeling publications [23, 16, 26, 27] in modeling and analyzing systematic cycling data in confined SOC regions and including variations in electrolyte salt, anode material, temperature, and cycling rate. By analyzing both published datasets and newly generated experimental results, we demonstrate that our model reproduces the observed capacity fade under diverse cycling protocols, temperatures, electrolyte salts, and artificial graphites. Our model remains simple in use and highly adaptable, allowing straightforward parameterization for new cell configurations. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section II details the mathematical formulation of our model and the parameterization variables. Section III outlines the experimental cell specifications as well as the testing protocols. Section IV presents a comprehensive validation of the model against experimental aging data for a wide range of cycling in confined SOC windows for different electrolyte salts, artificial graphites, and temperatures, as well as different cycling protocols. Finally, Section V summarizes the key findings and outlines directions for future research.

papers.title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
papers.abstract: Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference. The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future. We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.

papers.title: Cyclic group tensors and the volume ratio of projective tensor products
papers.abstract: We revisit the problem of estimating the norm of the natural embedding from the Euclidean space $\ell_2^{n^3}$ into the projective tensor product $\ell_p^n\otimes_π\ell_q^n\otimes_π\ell_r^n$ in the range $1\le p\le q\le 2\le r\le\infty$, studied by Giladi, Prochno, Schütt, Tomczak-Jaegermann and Werner [J. Funct. Anal. 273 (2017), 471-495]. Using convolution on finite cyclic groups, we establish new lower bounds that improve their estimates and determine the exact asymptotic order of the embedding norm whenever $1/p+1/q+1/r\ge 2$. We then apply an estimate of Boedihardjo for the injective norm of random tensors to a randomly signed cyclic convolution tensor and use multilinear interpolation to determine the optimal exponent throughout the entire parameter range, up to logarithmic factors. As consequences, we obtain corresponding improvements and asymptotically sharp estimates, up to logarithmic factors, for the volume ratio of these projective tensor products.

papers.title: Feedback That Backfires in Games: Do LLM Players Repeat the Move They Just Watched Fail?
papers.abstract: When an LLM agent's move fails, the harness writes the move and the failure message into the transcript and asks again. In tool calling, this record makes small models more likely to repeat the failed action. We test whether the same holds in games (Sokoban, Connect Four, Othello), where a move can fail by being illegal or by being legal but losing, both verified exactly. On fixed probe items built by perturbing a correct move, the record backfires: pooled over 8 instruction-tuned models (135M-1.7B) it makes the failed move more likely (corrective gain G = -1.38 nats per token), through the move's surface form, for illegal moves but not for losing ones, and not for every model. An exploratory analysis shows what sets the sign: after the record, the failed move's log-probability barely depends on how likely it was before (slope 0.18). Moves the model would not have played become more likely, and greedy decoding starts to produce them; moves it was about to play become less likely, but greedy decoding still repeats 38% of them. A description of the failure that omits the move string keeps the model's preference instead. Along the OLMo 2 1B post-training ladder the inversion is present in the base model and largely removed at the DPO stage. RAGEN's default models invert in RAGEN's own Sokoban format before any RL. A "do not repeat" instruction does nothing, a clean retry is the worst harness, and a decoder ban stops exact repeats but not illegal play. All measurements ran in float32 on a free Colab GPU, which first reproduced the original paper's number.

papers.intro:
When an LLM plays a game through a harness, some of its moves fail. The harness then does what agent harnesses do with a failed tool call: it writes the move into the transcript, adds the referee’s message (Illegal move: that column is already full.) and asks for another move. The message is ground truth, and a player that reads it should not try the same move again. Yet LLM players are known to get stuck repeating rejected moves; in XiangqiBench, rejected moves make up a third of all calls in failed trials of one protocol (Chai et al., 2026).

The message is ground truth, and a player that reads it should not try the same move again. Yet LLM players are known to get stuck repeating rejected moves; in XiangqiBench, rejected moves make up a third of all calls in failed trials of one protocol (Chai et al., 2026).

In earlier work we measured what such a failure record does to a small model’s next action in tool calling and program repair (Gumaan, 2026). Defining the corrective gain GG of the record as the drop in log-probability of re-emitting the failed action, we found it negative for every instruction-tuned model we tested: the record made the failed call more likely, mostly because the call’s surface form was now in the context. This paper asks whether that holds for game play, where the setting allows three things tool calling did not.

This paper asks whether that holds for game play, where the setting allows three things tool calling did not.

First, a move can fail in two ways: it can be illegal, or legal but losing, and both can be verified exactly (a one-ply check in Connect Four, an exhaustive search for Sokoban deadlocks). Second, the same move can be written in different notations, which varies the surface form while holding the decision fixed. Third, a completion format lets us probe base models, so the measurement can follow one model through the stages of post-training. papers.title: Domain models of turbulent magnetic fields and the spectral shape of ensemble averaged axion-photon conversion
papers.abstract: Axion-like particles are light pseudoscalars that appear in many extensions of the Standard Model and are candidates for dark matter. Through their mixing with photons, they imprint energy dependent modulations on the spectra of astrophysical sources shining through magnetised media. When a distant source shines through the turbulent magnetic field of an intervening galaxy cluster, these modulations are stochastic. It has recently been shown that averaging over an ensemble of such sources instead produces a smooth absorption-like feature. In this work we derive the analytic form of this ensemble averaged signal, previously known only numerically. We further relate the index $a$ of the magnetic field energy spectrum to the index $β$ of the domain size distribution that simulations use to describe the turbulent field. For $1<a<2$ the two indices obey the simple analytic relation $β=3-a$. Any distribution with $β<1$ instead mimics the spectral index $a=2$, which the sharp domain walls impose. For Kolmogorov turbulence, relevant for galaxy clusters, the relation gives $β=4/3$.

Galaxy clusters host μ\muG-scale magnetic fields coherent over kiloparsec scales along sightlines of megaparsec length Carilli and Taylor (2002); Feretti et al. (2012); Murgia et al. (2004); Bonafede et al. (2010). X-ray and gamma ray spectra of active galactic nuclei (AGN) located in or behind clusters have therefore been used extensively to constrain the ALP–photon coupling Wouters and Brun (2013); Conlon et al. (2017); Marsh et al. (2017); Malyshev et al. (2018); Reynolds et al. (2020); Matthews et al. (2022); Sisk-Reynés et al. (2022). Because the cluster field is turbulent, each sightline realises a different random modulation pattern. Constraints from individual sources must therefore be marginalised over many realisations of the magnetic field, which complicates the searches and weakens the derived limits. Refs. Malyshev et al. (2025b); Malyshev et al. (2025a) addressed this obstacle by averaging the conversion probability over many independent sightlines towards an ensemble of background AGN. The stochastic modulations then reduce to a smooth, step-like suppression of the stacked spectrum, whose shape can be predicted for a given model of the field.

papers.title: CulturalRiddles: A Multicultural Benchmark of Riddles
papers.abstract: As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.

papers.title: Scalar-Longitudinal Modes of Extended Electrodynamics in Perfectly Conducting Waveguides and Divergence Cleaning Interpretation
papers.abstract: Extended electrodynamics keeps the scalar combination $C=\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A}+μ_0\varepsilon_0\partialΦ/\partial t$ as a dynamical field rather than imposing the Lorenz gauge condition, and this scalar adds a scalar-longitudinal (SL) family to the TE, TM and TEM modes. With $C=0$ on the wall of a closed perfectly conducting waveguide, the classical modes are unchanged. The SL modes have $\mathbf{B}=0$ and an electric field along $\nabla C$, and their cutoffs are the Dirichlet eigenvalues of the cross-section, the same as the TM cutoffs, with no coaxial TEM counterpart. Charge-conserving sources with zero scalar data do not excite them. Matching at a conductor described by its constitutive laws gives $\partial C/\partial n=0$ instead and couples the scalar-bearing modes to the Maxwell field. The results belong to the $C=0$ problem, the condition that separates the sectors and the one divergence cleaning uses, with benchmarks for the rectangular, circular cylinder, coaxial and L-shaped guides.

papers.title: Reading the Room: Scale-ambiguous Semantic Registration of Sparse VSLAM Maps to Floor Plans in Partially Built Environments
papers.abstract: Many robotic construction applications, such as progress tracking, require registering a sensor trajectory to a prior 2D floor plan. Visual capture is attractive for its low cost and availability, but aligning a visual simultaneous localization and mapping (VSLAM) map to a floor plan is difficult; VSLAM recovers geometry only up to an unknown similarity transform, the sparse point cloud is cross-modal to the symbolic floor plan, sites are only partially built during capture, and construction sites are visually repetitive, degrading map quality while removing distinctive features. Existing methods address at most two of these challenges. We thus introduce Reading the Room(RR), a global-local approach to register scale-ambiguous, sparse, semantic VSLAM maps to partially built floor plans. Our key idea is to define a single robust, differentiable, class-balanced semantic-geometric energy function that governs all stages of the pipeline. We develop two global initialization schemes, leveraging a single inaccurate user-provided correspondence if provided, or estimating the initialization globally using a cross-modal matching network. Both schemes are designed to find initial candidates with respect to the energy function, which is then directly optimized for local refinement. We evaluate RR on 33 sequences across three active construction sites against classical and learning-based baselines, achieving a 4.5x improvement in mean absolute trajectory error over the strongest baseline in the general unconstrained setting, which increases to 7.6x when an anchor is provided.

papers.intro:
Autonomous robots and perception technologies have the potential to transform modern construction. Tracking construction progress against design intent is one of the most direct levers to reduce project delays and cost overruns [1]. However, doing so requires registering a sensor trajectory captured by a robot or site operator to a prior 2D floor plan. To this end, camera-based capture is an especially attractive sensing solution given its vast availability, low cost, weight, and energy consumption, as well as providing visual fidelity and human interpretability. While several works investigate registering dense LiDAR-based reconstruction to floor plans [2, 3, 4], the visual counterpart remains less explored.

To this end, camera-based capture is an especially attractive sensing solution given its vast availability, low cost, weight, and energy consumption, as well as providing visual fidelity and human interpretability. While several works investigate registering dense LiDAR-based reconstruction to floor plans [2, 3, 4], the visual counterpart remains less explored.

In this work, we study the task of aligning a sparse, scale-ambiguous 3D map, as recovered by a monocular VSLAM system [5, 6], to the floor plan of a site under active construction. Multiple properties compound to make this setting unusually difficult, as shown in Fig. 1. First, monocular VSLAM recovers geometry only up to an unknown similarity transform, since scale is not observable without auxiliary sensing. Second, the two representations are highly cross-modal, as VSLAM outputs a sparse, noisy 3D point cloud while the floor plan is a symbolic drawing of design intent. Third, construction sites are only partially built during capture, so large parts of the plan may not yet physically exist, making it an unreliable prior. Lastly, such sites are often visually repetitive, consisting mostly of walls, columns, and voids, which both degrades VSLAM quality and removes the distinctive features registration typically relies on.

Existing approaches address at most one or two of these challenges. Cross-view indoor localization methods [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14] generally assume known metric scale and a fully built environment. Methods embedding a floor plan directly into the SLAM pipeline [15, 16] similarly assume a known, already-built environment and a metric-range sensor such as LiDAR. Map-alignment methods such as region decomposition [2] and graph matching [4] require dense metric reconstructions a sparse VSLAM map cannot easily supply. Recent sparse VSLAM methods instead by-pass dense reconstruction by detecting manually placed visual markers with positions marked a-priori in the floor plan [17]. Learning-based cross-modal matchers [18, 19] can generalize across visually dissimilar modalities [20, 21], but have never been evaluated on this domain. Thus, no existing method jointly handles unknown scale, sparse representations, the cross-modality gap, and partial construction.

papers.title: Microscopic origin of field-induced multiferroicity in Ni3TeO6
papers.abstract: The continued demand for smaller, faster, and more energy-efficient technologies has driven condensed-matter research towards materials combining multiple responses within a single phase. Particularly interesting examples are multiferroic materials featuring cross-couplings between order parameters. Ni3TeO6 is a prominent member of this material class, exhibiting a hysteresis-free transition under magnetic field which simultaneously affects the magnetic structure, electric polarization, and phonon frequencies. Here, we uncover the microscopic origin of this multiferroic transition using a combination of neutron scattering techniques. We establish the presence of a finite Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya exchange term giving rise to non-reciprocal, chiral spin waves which soften in magnetic field. Their condensation alters the magnetic structure which controls the electric polarization and drives an ionic displacement, thereby coupling the magnetic, electric, and lattice degrees of freedom. Our study demonstrates that neutron scattering is a powerful technique to elucidate microscopic interactions in multiferroic materials, informing the design of next-generation electronic devices.

papers.title: Loopholing All the Way: Language Modeling with pure Self-Conditioning
papers.abstract: Recent Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) use Self-Conditioning (SC), or Loopholing, to improve their performance. While SC is traditionally seen as an auxiliary heuristic, its empirical success raises the question: can a continuous generative model be based purely on Self-Conditioning? We answer affirmatively with LAW (``Loopholing All the Way''), which propagates the Expected Embedding under the denoiser's prediction across steps, decoding the tokens once, at the end. On Sudoku, LAW outperforms previous Discrete and Continuous Diffusion Models, including Loopholing Discrete Diffusion. On Maze, LAW is the most accurate from 2 to 64 NFE. After training on TinyGSM and sampling at temperature 1 with 1024 NFE, LAW solves 42.2% of GSM8K problems against 34.5% for uniform Loopholing Discrete Diffusion. Additionally, fine-tuning a pre-trained Uniform Diffusion Model (Duo) with LAW increases its accuracy from 17.2% to 48.1%. Finally, on OpenWebText, LAW pushes the Pareto frontier and approaches Autoregressive Models (ARMs) with 64 NFE. Find our code at https://github.com/ilievanadezhda/law.

papers.intro:
Although Autoregressive Models (ARMs) dominate language modeling (Vaswani et al., 2017; Kaplan et al., 2020; Gemini Team et al., 2023; Grattafiori et al., 2024), their generation process is sequential and their left-to-right factorization can be limiting for tasks that need bidirectional context (Kitouni et al., 2024; Papadopoulos et al., 2024; Nagarajan et al., 2025). Discrete Diffusion Models (DDMs) (Austin et al., 2021; Campbell et al., 2022; Lou et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Ou et al., 2025; Sahoo et al., 2025; Schiff et al., 2025; von Rütte et al., 2025), the most common Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), instead use a bidirectional architecture and can refine tokens in parallel. For tractability, DDMs sample each position independently and discard the denoiser’s prediction after each step. This causes two problems. First, factorized, parallel sampling hurts the sample quality in few-step generation (Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2024; Feng et al., 2025). Second, discarding previous predictions means that the associated uncertainty is lost (information collapse; Jo et al., 2026).

papers.title: Poisson Clustering and Seed Effect of PBHs: Implications for Microlensing, Gravitational Waves, Little Red Dots and Ultra-Faint Dwarf Galaxies
papers.abstract: The existence of primordial black holes (PBHs) could have significant effects on the formation of cosmic structures through both the seed effect and the Poisson effect. For an extended PBH mass function, this should lead to dark virialised bound clusters of black holes with modest mass, together with central black holes of larger mass. We consider the combination of three effects: the inevitable gravitational binding of small-scale inhomogeneities due to Poisson and seed fluctuations; the dilution through dynamical heating of all clusters smaller than around $10^{6}\,M_{\odot}$; the survival of clusters in the outer Galactic halo (i.e. towards the Magellanic Clouds) but their destruction in the central halo region through tidal disruption and collisions. We examine the implications of this for the constraints on the fraction of dark matter in PBHs from microlensing surveys and gravitational-wave events. Although the clustering of PBHs with the expected mass and radius is unlikely to relax the microlensing limits, the decline of the Galactic rotation curve might do so, allowing much of the dark matter to be in solar-mass PBHs formed at the quantum chromodynamics transition. We also emphasise that binary merger rates must be revised: binaries formed in PBH clusters can dominate the merger rate, which may be compatible with the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA gravitational-wave limits if PBHs provide the dark matter. More positively, Ultra-Faint Dwarf Galaxies and Little Red Dots might arise through a combination of the seed and Poisson effects. Our conclusions could be modified for PBHs produced from primordial fluctuations with exponential non-Gaussian tails, since the clustering would then exceed the Poissonian prediction, opening up new possibilities to explain dark matter with solar-mass PBHs.

The possibility that primordial black holes (PBHs) might make up the dark matter goes back 50 years and is a natural consequence of the realisation that Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) implies that the dark matter could not be baryonic [1]. This is because, unlike astrophysical black holes, PBHs would originate in the radiation-dominated period before BBN. Until recently, most dark matter theorists have favoured hypothetical non-baryonic elementary particles but there is still no evidence for this from either direct searches or collider experiments. On the other hand, PBHs are also non-baryonic and share many features of particle ‘cold dark matter’ (CDM).

On the other hand, PBHs are also non-baryonic and share many features of particle ‘cold dark matter’ (CDM).

Historically, three events have stimulated interest in PBHs. The first was the 1996 detection by the MACHO collaboration [2] of microlensing of stars in the Magellanic Clouds by objects in the Galactic halo. Although they found a large excess of stellar-mass lenses, they ultimately concluded that the population of unidentified lenses was insufficient to make up the expected dark matter content of the halo [3]. However, we will argue below that this conclusion may be invalidated in the light of modern measurements of the kinematics of the Galaxy and the effects of an extended PBH mass function. The second event was the 2016 detection of gravitational waves from merging black holes with somewhat larger masses than expected and subsequently there have been around three hundred similar events. Although the mainstream view is that these are associated with stellar black holes, there are reasons to believe that at least some — notably those in the low and high mass gaps where stellar black holes should not arise — may be PBHs. The third event was the recent discovery by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) that supermassive black holes formed at the centres of the first galaxies much earlier than expected in the standard CDM picture without PBHs [4, 5], leading to the suggestion that massive PBHs may play a rôle in seeding them.

A major difference between dark matter particles and PBHs comes from the larger mass of the latter. This implies that PBHs can be a significant source of density fluctuations on some scales via two effects: (1) the Poisson effect, associated with the N\sqrt{N} fluctuation in the number of black holes; (2) the seed effect, associated with the Coulomb attraction of a single black hole. The Poisson effect was first pointed out by Mészáros [12], although he overestimated the size of the effect [13], and in the following years several other authors investigated this [14, 15, 16, 17]. On the other hand, they may lead to the formation of bound cosmological structures (e.g. dwarf galaxies) at a much earlier epoch than expected in the standard CDM model [20]. This may be supported by the recent discovery of “little red dots” (LRDs) at high redshift [21, 22, 23]. papers.title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.

Many modern systems browse the web, execute code, call typed tools, and implement enterprise workflows (Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2024). With this shift in the deployment of LLMs, there is a corresponding shift in the meaning of their “safety”. That is, a tool-enabled agent can cause harm through its actions in the environment, not only by emitting an unsafe sentence as measured in text-based settings.

That is, tool-enabled prompts suppress the activation of the refusal direction at the decision token in most models, and a lower activation predicts the unsafe call in all five models (AUC 0.76–0.86). Nonetheless, when we restore the refusal signal to its no-tool level, we find that for most models only a minority of unsafe calls revert, and most of those that do revert by emitting no tool call rather than a safer one. papers.title: Ab Initio Approach for Quantum Magnets with Coupled Cluster and Transcorrelation
papers.abstract: The nearest-neighbour exchange coupling $J_1$ is the simplest ingredient of model Hamiltonians used to understand magnetism in real materials. Nevertheless, its ab initio determination requires a high-level correlation treatment and a large basis for wave function expansion. Here we compute $J_1$ for five oxygen-bridged spin-1/2 quantum magnets --- Sr$_2$CuO$_3$, La$_2$CuO$_4$, NdNiO$_2$, ZnCu$_3$(OH)$_6$Cl$_2$, and Li$_2$CuO$_2$ --- spanning bridging angles from 180$^\circ$ to 94$^\circ$ and the crossover from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic coupling, using embedded-cluster methodology. To describe the open-shell singlets we use 2-determinant coupled cluster with single and double excitations, which recovers the orbital-breathing enhancement of superexchange from a minimal reference. Basis-set errors are found to be large: extrapolation to the complete basis-set (CBS) limit shifts $J_1$ by up to 50 meV from bases of double-$ζ$ quality. Transcorrelated Hamiltonians reproduce the CBS estimates with modest basis set sizes, yielding an excellent accuracy against experiment at highly affordable cost. These results are the first application of transcorrelated methods in strongly correlated solid-state systems, and establish transcorrelation as a powerful theory in computational research of materials.

papers.intro:
Materials that have low-dimensional, strongly correlated magnetic sublattices are a rich source of exotic physics and widely studied for their use as a platform for new theory and technological applications. Especially materials with oxygen-mediated exchange between magnetic sites, i.e., with superexchange, have been of much interest. Among other phenomena, they show Mott and charge-transfer insulating states, can achieve high-temperature superconducting phases via doping, and frustrated magnetic sublattices can host complex spin liquid state [1, 2, 3]. A complete description of correlated oxide materials remains out of reach, and even making the connection between experimental measurements and theoretical results is not a trivial task.

In cuprate Mott insulators with 3d9 configuration, transition-metal ions carry a single hole in the x2−y2x^{2}\!-\!y^{2} orbital, and the half-filled lattice can remain insulating due to the large on-site Coulomb repulsion UU. Virtual electron hopping with amplitude tt between neighbouring sites with antiparallel spins — forbidden for parallel spins by the Pauli principle — yields an energy gain of order 4​t2/U4t^{2}/U, defining an antiferromagnetic (AFM) exchange coupling J1>0J_{1}>0. Well-known Goodenough-Kanamori rules [4, 5] state that this superexchange is strongest for a straight 180∘ Cu–O–Cu (or Ni–O–Ni) bridge; as the bridge bends towards 90∘, symmetry suppresses the ligand-mediated hopping, and a ferromagnetic (FM) channel driven by Hund’s coupling on the bridging ligand emerges in its place, leading to J1<0J_{1}<0 [6]. The understanding of exotic phases of matter is in large part built on model Hamiltonians, such as the Hubbard Hamiltonian. However, the choice of model and the determination of the corresponding parameters is often a nontrivial task. In particular, some model parameters may not be related to experimental results in a simple way. Their values depend on the amount of physics explicitly built into the model, and the physics not included explicitly should ideally be included implicitly by using renormalized parameters. Ab initio calculations can give guidance in the choice of an appropriate model and can help establishing relations between model parameters and experimental results. Systematically improvable wave-function-based quantum chemistry methods are very useful in this context. They are applicable to strong correlation and can be used both to construct model Hamiltonians and to perform full ab initio calculations [9, 10, 11]. These methods are, however, computationally demanding and their cost grows steeply with system size.

Embedded-cluster quantum chemistry thus has a long record in the determination of exchange couplings in cuprates and nickelates: La2CuO4, Sr2CuO3, and NdNiO2, for example, have been studied with different methods with reasonable accuracy against experiment [16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 11, 21]. There are, however, fewer studies of how the magnetic coupling changes with the bridging angle, including the sign change from AFM to the FM phase [22]; benchmarks of how robust ab initio methods are in these regimes remain scarce. Furthermore, the nickelates that have been discovered relatively recently, have only a few studies with wave function methods [19, 20].

It has been recently shown [18] that describing superexchange requires the inclusion of the so-called orbital breathing effects into the description of the system. The breathing emerges from the on-site virtual 3d–4d interaction of the magnetic sites, effectively extending the 3d orbitals. This reduces the effective UU from about 28 eV deduced from a Cu Coulomb integral to about 8-10 eV in cuprates [23, 24, 25, 26] and simultaneously increases the effective hopping between the Cu atoms [27]. These two effects are crucial in increasing the magnitude of JJ. In establishing these results, however, it was found necessary to use large active-space solvers, augmented with perturbation theory, which clearly has the disadvantage of being computationally expensive and difficult to scale to larger systems.

First, we refine our understanding of orbital-breathing enhanced correlation in these materials, and use the insight to demonstrate that computationally affordable 2-determinant coupled cluster [28] (2det-CC) and its distinguishable cluster (2det-DC) variant [29] (2det-CCSD and 2det-DCSD in this work, since we do not include excitations beyond doubles) are well suited for evaluating J1J_{1} without having to resort to large active space solvers. With this method, we reach larger basis sets than – to our knowledge – used before with wave-function methods in these systems, allowing us to compute complete basis set limit (CBS) estimates of J1J_{1}. Our study shows that basis sets used in previous studies, where a low level of basis was considered sufficient [10, 30, 31], are at least with the coupled cluster method not enough to eliminate the finite-basis error. Second, we apply transcorrelation (TC) theory, for the first time, to these strongly correlated solids, demonstrating that accurate J1J_{1}’s can be obtained in relatively small basis sets, thanks to the drastic acceleration of basis-set convergence of the TC method.

papers.title: A Transfer Learning-Driven Methodology for Efficient and Sustainable Indoor Localization Using VLC
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things enables seamless collaboration among connected devices, making indoor localization a critical component of industrial automation. However, conventional localization techniques struggle in dynamic environments. These methods depend on extensive, frequent data collection and environment-specific calibration, limiting scalability, interoperability, and effective use of prior research while imposing significant energy penalties that hinder practical deployment. To address these challenges, we propose an energy-efficient transfer learning (TL) based approach for visible light communication based indoor localization. Our method leverages TL to tackle environmental variability, including lighting fluctuations and physical obstacles that typically degrade localization performance, while simultaneously reducing computational overhead and energy consumption compared to conventional approaches. We also introduce a novel model efficiency (ME) metric, designed to integrate localization accuracy, energy efficiency, data efficiency, and transfer gain into a single evaluative measure for comprehensive optimization. Evaluations on a real-world dataset collected from a BOSCH factory demonstrate that our model achieves a 47% improvement in localization accuracy compared to a conventional model that does not utilize TL, and achieves up to 67.5% ME with TL models, compared to only 10.4% in conventional models under high-noise conditions. These results underscore the potential of our approach to deliver a highly efficient and scalable indoor localization system suitable for energy-constrained industrial applications.

As manufacturing and logistics environments grow increasingly complex with autonomous mobile robots [3], digital twin implementations [4], and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven process automation [5], the need for precise, reliable and efficient indoor localization system has become critical. This rising demand is driving innovations in location-based services (LBS), transforming industrial operations through enhanced asset tracking, real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and streamlined workflow automation [6].

Despite significant technological advancements, current indoor localization systems face critical performance challenges. These include accuracy, energy consumption, computational complexity, data efficiency, and adaptability to changing environments. These factors have become the primary bottleneck, fundamentally constraining scalability and industrial adoption. For example, energy-intensive algorithms are impractical for battery-powered sensor nodes, and high-speed production lines cannot accommodate lengthy data collection or retraining phases [7]—even if such systems offer high accuracy [8, 9]. Wi-Fi-based systems offer relatively low power consumption [10], but their performance is highly susceptible to environmental interference, resulting in degraded accuracy under dynamic conditions [11]. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) improves energy efficiency further by consuming as little as 10.1 µA in sleep mode and extending device runtime significantly compared to Wi-Fi [12]—but suffers from limited range and poor signal stability in changing environments [13, 14]. Both Wi-Fi and BLE require dense deployment of access points or battery-powered beacons, leading to high installation and maintenance costs [15]. Ultra-Wideband (UWB) technology, while delivering high accuracy, faces energy challenges [16], high device costs, and limited adaptability to environmental changes [17]. Radio frequency (RF) systems are further hindered by electromagnetic interference (EMI) from industrial machinery, which can cause signal attenuation exceeding 15 dBm and necessitate increased transmission power to maintain connectivity [18].

These challenges highlight the need for localization solutions that deliver both high accuracy and operational efficiency, while leveraging cost-effective infrastructure. Visible Light Communication (VLC) has emerged as a promising candidate, utilizing existing Light-Emitting Diode (LED) lighting for both communication and localization. VLC offers centimeter-level precision and can reduce energy consumption by up to 60% compared to dedicated RF systems [19, 20]. The technology is inherently immune to EMI, eliminating the energy penalties associated with increased transmission power in industrial environments [21, 22], and its short-wavelength, line-of-sight (LOS) nature keeps computational demands low [23]. Nevertheless, VLC systems face their own environmental adaptability challenges, distinct from those of RF-based solutions. While RF systems struggle with unpredictable EMI and multipath fading, VLC contends with more deterministic optical issues: ambient light interference, LOS dependencies, and varying lighting conditions [24, 25, 26]. However, these optical challenges are generally more predictable and manageable than the chaotic interference often encountered by RF systems in industrial settings [27, 28].

However, these optical challenges are generally more predictable and manageable than the chaotic interference often encountered by RF systems in industrial settings [27, 28].

To address these challenges and enhance VLC-based localization, machine learning (ML) models have been increasingly adopted to capture complex signal patterns [29]. Yet, many existing ML models rely on assumptions that limit their real-world applicability: they often require large, labeled datasets for offline training and assume the resulting model will remain effective across different times and deployment contexts [6]. In dynamic industrial environments, where lighting and layouts frequently change, these assumptions break down, leading to rapid degradation in model performance. Several adaptive ML strategies have been proposed to overcome these limitations. Federated Learning (FL) enables decentralized model training across multiple devices, preserving data privacy and capturing diverse conditions [30], but requires frequent updates in highly dynamic settings. Continuous Learning (CL) supports incremental adaptation over time [31, 32], but is vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting and depends on costly, labor-intensive labeled data collection. Transfer Learning (TL) offers rapid adaptation to new conditions without extensive retraining or system downtime [33, 34]; however, in existing literature TL has been widely applied in RF-based localization, and has seen limited adaptation to VLC systems, with domain-specific noise and environmental variability still insufficiently addressed.

papers.title: Confirmation of complex non-collinear Fe(II) spin ordering in the iron oxychalcogenide La$_2$O$_2$Fe$_2$OSe$_2$ by broad range $^{139}$La-NQR
papers.abstract: The transition metal oxychalcogenide La$_2$O$_2$Fe$_2$OSe$_2$ exhibits a non-collinear spin-ice like antiferromagnetic ordering below $T_N \approx $ 90 K due to complex magnetic exchange interactions and axial single-ion anisotropy of Fe$^{2+}$ spins. The magnetic structure was deduced/determined from combined $^{57}$Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy and $^{139}$La-NMR on polycrystalline specimen. In this work, we present zero-field $^{139}$La-NQR investigations on polycrystalline La$_2$O$_2$Fe$_2$OSe$_2$ in a broad frequency and temperature range between 2.8 - 20 MHz and 4.2 - 100 K. The measured resonances at $ν_Q$, $2 \, ν_Q$, and $3 \, ν_Q$ are fully consistent with the previous NMR studies and also with the magnetic structure. A substantial modification of the electric field gradient at the La-position below $T_N$ is inconsistent with the current investigations.

papers.intro:
The physics of altermagnets forms one of the most vibrant areas in solid state magnetism research in recent years [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Altermagnets offer a new perspective for Terahertz spintronics applications of compensated antiferromagnets, since they exhibit electronic band structures with large spin-splitting in the eV\mathrm{eV} range in a zero net magnetization system. The spin-split character of the electron bands relies on a non-relativistic effect, namely an anisotropic electron hopping within the two spin sublattices [6], which is caused by the combination of time-reversal-symmetry breaking and spatial rotation between the spin sublattices. Tetragonal systems with the in-plane Lieb-lattice structural motive like KV2Se2O are inherently proposed candidates for altermagnetic properties with d-wave symmetry [7]. D-wave altermagnets are particularly interesting for applications due to their large 90∘ anisotropy of the spin-split electronic band structure.

In 2021 Hussain et al. reported a zero external magnetic field 139La-NQR study on La2O2Fe2OSe2 [17]. The 139La NMR spectra for polycrystalline La2O2Fe2OSe2 show rather broad resonance lines due to the continuous distribution of relative angles formed by the external magnetic field and the principle axes of the local electric field gradient [9]. Those broad lines collapse to discrete lines in the 139La NQR spectra. Below TNT_{\mathrm{N}} the discrete NQR resonances are expected to shift due to the internal transferred magnetic hyperfine field. For one, referred to La 1, the frequency is constant from above TNT_{\mathrm{N}} down to lowest temperature. The frequency of the second subspectrum, assigned as La 2, rises abruptly at TNT_{\mathrm{N}} and shows a strong temperature dependence. At 60 K, the La 2 signal crosses the resonance line of La 1 that is fixed in frequency. Below 30 K, also the La 2 spectrum saturates and becomes temperature independent. papers.title: Cross-Area Transfer Learning for VLC-based Indoor Localization with a Transfer Efficiency Score
papers.abstract: Indoor localization systems are critical for Industry-4.0 applications. Visible Light Communication (VLC)-based systems offer advantages such as immunity to electromagnetic interference, high accuracy, and energy efficiency, but their performance is hindered by environmental variability across deployment areas. This paper presents a transfer learning (TL) framework for VLC-based indoor localization that enhances cross-area robustness while reducing data requirements. Using real-world measurements from four distinct areas of a Bosch manufacturing facility, we show that fine-tuning a deep neural network (DNN) pre-trained on source area data with only 40% of target-area measurements recovers 97% of full-data performance, thereby reducing the amount of target data needed. We further introduce the Transfer Efficiency Score (TES), a composite metric that identifies the most effective source models for transfer without exhaustive evaluation. Guided by TES, the framework selects the best source model, yielding localization errors as low as 40.9 cm with success rates above 86%. Validation on an unseen area confirms its generalization capability, with a 3.28 cm mean error achieved using the TES-selected source model. Overall, the proposed framework provides a scalable and data-efficient pathway for industrial VLC localization, substantially reducing deployment costs and computational burden while maintaining high accuracy in diverse and dynamic environments.

Unplanned downtime from misplaced or untraceable assets remains a major contributor to production delays and operational inefficiencies, underscoring the critical need for robust indoor-positioning solutions in Industry 4.0 environments [1, 2]. Modern factories are increasingly transformed by AI-driven automation and digital-twin workflows, with real-time location-based services (LBS), power asset tracking, process optimization, and coordinated robotics [3, 4]. In this context, indoor localization has evolved from an auxiliary feature into a critical infrastructure that underpins next-generation industrial automation [5].

Despite advances, three core challenges prevent large-scale deployment of indoor localization. First, cross-area robustness, where models trained in one area often degrade significantly when deployed in a different layout or building area [6]. Second, data inefficiency, which means collecting and labeling comprehensive datasets can require days of downtime per area, contradicting the high-cycle production demands [7, 8]. Third, energy and cost constraints, as many radio frequency (RF) based systems consume excessive power or rely on dense beacon infrastructures, driving up maintenance costs and reducing battery lifespan in IoT deployments [9, 10].

While several indoor localization technologies are widely used in industrial environments, each presents its own set of trade-offs relative to the core challenges. Wi‑Fi localization offers moderate power consumption [11] but suffers severe accuracy drops under electromagnetic interference (EMI) from metal machinery and dynamic layouts, which affects both robustness and maintenance demands [12]. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) reduces power consumption in sleep-mode to as little as 10.1 µA [13] but is limited by short range and environmental variability, making it costly to scale and sensitive to changes across deployment areas [10, 14]. Both BLE and Wi-Fi solutions depend on dense infrastructure, often requiring a large number of access points or beacons, which introduces high installation and ongoing maintenance costs [15, 16]. Ultra‑Wideband (UWB) systems achieve higher accuracy, but come with higher hardware costs and power requirements. Like all RF-based approaches, UWB also remains vulnerable to signal degradation from EMI and dynamic industrial layouts [17, 18, 19]. These trade-offs highlight the need for a localization approach that blends high accuracy with an efficient and minimal infrastructure.

Visible Light Communication (VLC) localization emerges as a compelling alternative that leverages light-emitting diode (LED) lighting infrastructures to enable communication and positioning. Compared to RF technologies, VLC achieves centimeter-level accuracy and up to 60% lower energy consumption, while being inherently immune to EMI [20, 21, 22]. Because VLC relies on unobstructed optical paths, its line‑of‑sight, short‑range nature reduces multipath effects and simplifies the signal‑processing pipeline [23]. At the same time, this reliance on direct optical paths makes VLC systems sensitive to changes in ambient lighting, temporary blockages, and uneven surface reflections commonly found in industrial environments [24, 25, 26]. Although these optical challenges can affect performance, they follow consistent physical laws and environmental patterns. For example, ambient lighting often changes gradually or follows known schedules (such as day/night cycles or factory lighting controls); occlusions occur when objects block the line of sight, and their effects can be estimated using geometry or motion sensors; and surface reflectance depends on material properties (e.g., metal or plastic), which influence light reflection in predictable ways. This predictability allows them to be effectively addressed through model-based correction and area-specific adaptation [27, 28].
