Federated Learning (FL) preserves privacy by distributing model training across edge devices [30], but it requires periodic exchange of gradient updates over potentially unreliable factory wireless links, introducing latency in highly dynamic or resource‑constrained settings. Continuous Learning (CL) enables incremental adaptation [31], yet suffers from catastrophic forgetting and depends on continual access to new labeled data, which is costly and labor-intensive. Despite its success in RF-based localization, TL has seen limited application in VLC systems because fundamental propagation differences create unique adaptation challenges. Unlike RF, which is dominated by EMI and multipath fading, VLC is governed by illumination geometry and line-of-sight dependence. VLC systems therefore face environmental factors such as ambient-light interference (e.g., from fluorescent lamps or welding), geometry-dependent multipath scattering from reflective surfaces, and occlusion patterns that critically affect signal visibility. These VLC-specific characteristics require TL strategies that account for optical propagation properties, ambient lighting conditions, and the inherent directional nature of VLC.

papers.title: Model Predictive Control: Systematic Design Tailored to Nonholonomic Systems
papers.abstract: Nonholonomic systems are ubiquitous in applications such as transportation and robotics, yet their control remains challenging. In order to achieve asymptotic stability of a desired equilibrium, model predictive control (MPC) schemes without stabilizing terminal conditions have recently been proposed for nonholonomic kinematic systems. However, this approach still required lengthy system-specific calculations. This paper eliminates the need for these auxiliary calculations, as we propose a streamlined systematic design for MPC stage costs tailored to nonholonomic systems, utilizing the concepts of privileged coordinates and nonholonomic weights. Furthermore, the proposed design methodology is extended beyond purely kinematic models to a wider class of systems with non-negligible dynamics, and we highlight the geometric meaning of the resulting MPC stage costs. The systematic procedure is demonstrated using an articulated vehicle as an example.

Nonholonomic systems arise naturally in many engineering applications and are characterized by non-integrable constraints on their velocities, see, e.g., [1, 2]. Although such systems are ubiquitous in practice, see, e.g., [3, 4], their control remains challenging. In general, linearization does not preserve controllability and violation of Brockett’s necessary condition [5] rules out the existence of Lipschitz-continuous, time-invariant asymptotically stabilizing state feedback laws for nonholonomic systems [6, 7]. These fundamental challenges have motivated the development of sophisticated setpoint control strategies over the past decades [3, 8], proposing either time-varying [9, 10, 11, 12] or discontinuous but time-invariant feedback laws [13, 14]. These works include also recent contributions, e.g., to obtain uniform exponential convergence for the prototypical Brockett integrator with a discontinuous state feedback [14], or to obtain bounded controls for finite-time regulation of one nonholonomic system [12].

This motivates the use of optimization-based control schemes such as model predictive control (MPC), where the system dynamics and actuation constraints can be incorporated directly into the controller design. Deriving provably stabilizing MPC schemes for nonholonomic systems is, however, far from straightforward. In MPC, asymptotic stability is often established through stabilizing terminal conditions, which are commonly constructed based on the system’s linearization [15], an approach that does, in general, not work for nonholonomic systems as shown in [16]. Hence, the construction of terminal conditions is significantly more intricate for nonholonomic systems. Whereas stabilizing terminal conditions have been developed for nonholonomic systems, see, e.g., [17, 18, 19], they are tailored to specific systems and usually rely on hand-designed terminal controllers and associated terminal sets. Proposed terminal sets are then usually not only hand-crafted per system but also, compared to terminal sets for holonomic systems, quite unusual in the sense that they are commonly nonconvex and may not even contain the setpoint in the interior, encompassing instead states from which specific steering commands are known that steer the system to the setpoint. These difficulties motivate the study of MPC schemes without stabilizing terminal ingredients, see, e.g., [20], simplifying and robustifying numerical solution as no (additional) state constraints are introduced. However, for nonholonomic systems, conventional quadratic stage costs generally do not guarantee asymptotic stability of the resulting MPC closed loop, see [21, 22]. For the differential-drive robot, arguably the most prominent wheeled mobile robot, non-quadratic stage costs have been constructed explicitly to establish suitable growth bounds on the value function and, as a consequence, a relaxed Lyapunov inequality to show asymptotic stability of the MPC closed loop [23, 24]. The works [25, 26] provide a mechanical interpretation of the resulting mixed-exponents cost. Control directions directly accessible through the system inputs are penalized less strongly close to the desired steady state than directions that can only be generated through Lie brackets. This insight has subsequently led to the development of tailored mixed-exponents stage costs for MPC-based setpoint control of nonholonomic systems without terminal ingredients [22, 27], building upon results for homogeneous control systems [28]. However, the overall procedure requires the construction of a homogeneous approximation of the nonholonomic kinematics and several auxiliary quantities, which is rather technical and lengthy.

The present paper eliminates the need for these lengthy intermediate constructions and, as its main contribution, provides a compact and systematic design procedure for model predictive controllers without terminal ingredients for nonholonomic systems. The resulting MPC scheme ensures local asymptotical stability of the closed-loop system. To this end, tools from sub-Riemannian geometry are employed to express the system in privileged coordinates, cf. [29, 8]. Based on this representation, it is rigorously shown that a homogeneous approximation can always be obtained for the system class with the associated homogeneity parameters coinciding with the so-called nonholonomic weights. These weights constitute intrinsic geometric characteristics of the nonholonomic system and can be determined in a straightforward manner. As a further novelty, we not only consider nonholonomic kinematics described by driftless control-affine systems but also treat kinematic systems with a so-called dynamic extension. In particular, we extend the ideas of [27] from constant to configuration-dependent dynamic extensions and generalize the corresponding MPC design procedure, including stability guarantees, to this broader system class.

papers.title: Investigating the Impact of Learner Errors on Social Bias in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Existing social bias benchmarks evaluate large language models mostly on fluent, well-formed English, reflecting native speaker usage and leaving non-native writers unrepresented. To address this gap, we investigate how grammatical errors by non-native writers affect social bias. We develop a controlled framework that injects common learner errors into prompts and apply it to three bias benchmarks covering stereotype alignment and demographic preference across gender, race, and religion. We find that grammatical errors increase bias, and the effect grows with the error rate. Among the four common error types we consider, preposition errors produce the largest and most consistent increase in stereotype alignment. Our analysis suggests that errors increase bias when they are more likely to interfere with comprehension. Finally, fine-tuning on erroneous texts reduces the bias increase caused by grammatical errors. Our findings show that bias evaluations based exclusively on well-formed prompts may underestimate the bias experienced by users whose English contains grammatical errors.

papers.intro:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to exhibit social biases such as the reproduction of societal stereotypes and demographic discrimination, which may reflect biases encoded in their training data (Bolukbasi et al., 2016). For example, in coreference resolution an LLM may be more likely to associate a doctor with the masculine pronoun “he”, reflecting a gender stereotype about the profession. Such biases can manifest across downstream tasks and have been extensively studied across social dimensions including gender, race, and religion (Gallegos et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2018; Parrish et al., 2022; Tamkin et al., 2023).

RQ2: How do error types and their location in the prompt affect the increase in social bias exhibited by LLMs? RQ3: Can error-aware fine-tuning mitigate the effects of L2 errors on social bias in LLMs?

papers.title: Orbitol: Crystal Generation on Wyckoff Orbits
papers.abstract: Generative models propose crystalline materials by learning composition and geometry, but unconditional sampling gives no direct control over the space group, which constrains whether responses such as piezoelectricity are symmetry-allowed. We present Orbitol, a crystal generator built on the Crystalite diffusion Transformer that replaces atom tokens with Wyckoff-orbit tokens. Given a space group and a collection of occupied Wyckoff positions, Orbitol generates the atom type and free coordinates of each orbit together with a compatible lattice, so every valid structure is invariant under the operations of the requested group. It generates structures two to three orders of magnitude faster than the symmetry-aware baselines at the evaluated settings. On MP-20, 13.8% of Orbitol's attempts yielded stable or metastable, unique and novel structures that retained the requested space group after relaxation, compared with 10.8% for SGFM, the next best model. We also introduce SPARC, a score that combines retention of the raw detected space group with agreement between the retained-group and training distributions. Finally, we used Orbitol to generate candidates in piezoelectric crystal classes. Of the structures selected by internal screening, 89% passed our density functional theory checks, and 79% also matched no Materials Project or Alexandria entry with the same space group. Their median figure of merit was nine times that of the piezoelectric materials computed in the Materials Project, and 24% of the new candidates ranked in that set's top 10%.
papers.intro:
Generative models such as MatterGen and Crystalite propose new crystals by learning composition and geometry from known materials [1, 2]. Many of them treat a crystal as a set of atoms, and their outputs can overrepresent low-symmetry space groups relative to the training data. The space group P1, which contains only lattice translations [3], accounts for 1.7% of the MP-20 training set, yet DiffCSP, MatterGen and our Crystalite reproduction produce 28.3%, 26.4% and 21.5% P1 structures after relaxation.

Many of them treat a crystal as a set of atoms, and their outputs can overrepresent low-symmetry space groups relative to the training data. The space group P1, which contains only lattice translations [3], accounts for 1.7% of the MP-20 training set, yet DiffCSP, MatterGen and our Crystalite reproduction produce 28.3%, 26.4% and 21.5% P1 structures after relaxation.

Symmetry also constrains which responses a crystal can show. Bulk piezoelectricity is allowed only in the noncentrosymmetric crystal classes other than 432, and pyroelectricity and conventional ferroelectricity require a polar class [3]. Targeting such responses therefore requires choosing the space group of the generated structure. Unconditional generators cannot control the space group. A group label can guide a conditioned model, but the label alone does not guarantee that the generated structure is invariant under the group’s operations [1]. Other generators build the operations into generation: CrystalFormer generates Wyckoff assignments, DiffCSP++ uses supplied ones, and SymADiT and UFO-MGen model orbit representations [4, 5, 6, 7]. We study how to impose these operations during generation, and how much of the requested symmetry is retained after unconstrained relaxation.

papers.title: Fast Bayesian Optimization Through Linear Models
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is typically used only for problems where the underlying function is deemed "expensive" (e.g. in time or money), with the speed of the BO algorithm being of little importance. In the real world, however, problems span a continuous range of values, going from cheap to expensive. In this paper, we present BO algorithms through the lens of a speed-performance Pareto frontier: we compare BO against faster algorithms like CMA-ES, and highlight how certain regions of the Pareto frontier are currently empty. As a solution, we propose a new set of fast BO methods that exploit the linear structure in existing BO algorithms, for both continuous and combinatorial inputs (from ~10 to 6000+ dimensions). Our methods achieve performance similar to state-of-the-art BO, while being more than $10^2\times$ to $10^3\times$ faster, opening the field of BO to an entirely new class of problems.
papers.intro:
Black-box optimization, i.e. optimization of a function that is only observable through evaluations (e.g. a simulator or physical experiment), has been studied since Box and Wilson, (1951). Over the past 75 years, different techniques and approaches have been proposed, ranging from direct search (Nelder and Mead,, 1965) and local surrogates (Powell,, 2009) to evolutionary algorithms (Holland,, 1975; Hansen and Ostermeier,, 2001). Among these, Bayesian optimization (Mockus,, 1975; Jones et al.,, 1998) became known for its sample efficiency, and is now often the default black-box optimizer for certain applications (Snoek et al.,, 2012, e.g. hyperparameter optimization in machine learning;). Nevertheless, until recently, BO was still mostly constrained to low-dimensional continuous spaces (i.e. below 20 dimensions), with a fairly limited number of observations (Frazier,, 2018).

Nevertheless, until recently, BO was still mostly constrained to low-dimensional continuous spaces (i.e. below 20 dimensions), with a fairly limited number of observations (Frazier,, 2018).

In the last decade, a growing body of literature has focused on extending the method to a larger set of problems — such as combinatorial spaces (Doumont et al.,, 2025) or higher dimensions (Hvarfner et al.,, 2024) — enabling BO to spread to new application areas (Moss et al.,, 2025; Fan et al.,, 2026). However, one major limiting factor is still largely unaddressed: BO methods are typically much slower than other black-box optimizers (see Figure 1). For example, current state-of-the-art BO methods can take multiple minutes to choose the next acquisition. If evaluating the black-box function is cheaper than this overhead, then the BO algorithm itself becomes the main cost (Shahriari et al.,, 2016), leading practitioners to instead turn to faster but less sample-efficient black-box optimizers, such as CMA-ES (Hansen and Ostermeier,, 2001; Raponi et al.,, 2025).

However, as demonstrated in Figure 1, their method is still as slow as standard BO methods, primarily due to gradient-based techniques used for (i) fitting hyperparameters, and (ii) optimizing acquisition functions. Instead, in this paper, we show how the structure of this spherical-linear model can be exploited for both tasks, leading to speedups of several orders of magnitude with little to no loss in performance.

papers.title: SkillEval: Learning Interpretable Ability Profiles of LLMs via Cognitive Diagnosis Models
papers.abstract: Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score. This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets. To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross-model, skill-level analysis. The framework integrates advances from two areas: (1) it leverages the meta-cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and (2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities of LLMs. We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval). Compared to the traditional average-based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items. We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks: (1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and (2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM. Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction-tuned models differ from their base models.

papers.intro:
Benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) have rapidly proliferated in recent years. While this creates new opportunities, it also raises a key challenge: how to effectively leverage a large collection of benchmarks for comprehensive LLM evaluation? Current evaluation practices remain quite raw. The common approach is to evaluate a model on all items in a benchmark and then report the average score. This naive statistical way collapses performance across items into a single number, which obscures fine-grained capability differences (Cui et al., 2026a). For example, two LLMs with similar overall accuracy on a math benchmark (0.63 vs. 0.65) may exhibit very different profiles across sub-skills such as algebra and geometry. This leads to a natural question: Given a set of test items, how can we go beyond a scalar score to a more informative, human-understandable capability estimate?

To answer this, we develop a new evaluation framework that aims to assess the latent abilities underlying observed item scores, and represents them as fine-grained skill profiles of LLMs. This problem has long been studied in psychometrics and the education community using various latent variable models. IRT models are also increasingly used in machine learning, but typically for data-centric tasks such as dataset analysis or distillation (Kipnis et al., 2025; Maia Polo et al., 2024; Zouhar et al., 2025; Rodriguez et al., 2021; Cui et al., 2026b), and less often for LLM evaluation as it still produces a scalar overall ability score that suffers from capability collapse. Some recent work explores multidimensional-IRT (Reckase, 2006) and its neural variants that learn ability vectors (Chen et al., 2025; Cui and Sachan, 2025; Song et al., 2025; Gor et al., 2024). papers.title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion
papers.abstract: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.

papers.intro:
X-ray and neutron scattering are central to structural characterization in condensed-matter physics and materials science [3, 64]. Since scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, recovering the underlying structure can lead to non-unique or only weakly constrained inverse problems. Distinct structures or parameter combinations can therefore yield similar scattering patterns, so a single best-fitting structure may conceal alternative solutions that remain compatible with the data. Two distinct strategies address this ambiguity. First, probabilistic inversion uses Bayesian inference to characterize a posterior distribution over structural and instrumental parameters rather than returning a single structure. Second, measurements with complementary sensitivities can be combined so that parameters weakly identified by one observation may be constrained by another.

Two distinct strategies address this ambiguity. First, probabilistic inversion uses Bayesian inference to characterize a posterior distribution over structural and instrumental parameters rather than returning a single structure. Second, measurements with complementary sensitivities can be combined so that parameters weakly identified by one observation may be constrained by another.

Posteriors arising from scattering inverse problems can be strongly correlated, non-Gaussian or multimodal, and joint inference enlarges the parameter space by introducing both quantities shared across measurements and quantities specific to an individual contrast, probe or instrument. These characteristics motivate flexible posterior approximations that can represent complex uncertainty across a range of possible observations. Simulation-based inference (SBI) [16] provides such an approach by training neural networks on simulated parameter–observation pairs to approximate posterior distributions. In the amortized setting, the main computational burden is incurred during training, after which inference for new measurements can be performed rapidly. This makes SBI attractive for repeated or high-throughput analysis in experimental science, including at X-ray and neutron facilities.

Amortized posterior estimators are nevertheless typically trained for a fixed observation model, and a network trained for one simulator cannot in general be combined directly with a network trained for another. Training a new joint model for every number and combination of measurements would undermine the modularity and computational reuse offered by amortization. Compositional SBI provides a foundation for combining posterior information from multiple observations at inference time [22, 41]. Many joint inversion problems, however, require an additional structure of shared and local parameters. Some parameters describe a common physical system and must be shared across observations, whereas others describe a particular contrast, probe or instrument and remain local to an individual measurement. A modular multi-measurement framework must therefore combine separately trained estimators in a common parameter space while correcting the repeated contribution of the shared prior.

It trains a time-dependent vector field that transports samples from a simple base distribution to the target distribution along a prescribed probability path. Flow matching posterior estimation (FMPE) has been shown to be a competitive and scalable SBI method [67]. For the probability path used here, the learned vector field also determines a posterior score, which enables the information supplied by separately trained posterior estimators to be composed during sampling.

Specular X-ray and neutron reflectometry are indispensable techniques for resolving the depth-dependent structure and properties of thin films, multilayers and buried interfaces [17, 5]. Beyond its broad experimental relevance, reflectometry presents a demanding setting for this modular inference framework because it spans different probes, acquisition modes and observation structures. X-ray reflectometry (XRR) is sensitive to the electronic scattering length density (SLD), neutron reflectometry (NR) is sensitive to the nuclear SLD and can exploit isotope-dependent contrast, and polarized neutron reflectometry (PNR) further extends this sensitivity to magnetic properties through the spin dependence of the neutron interaction [47, 11]. Joint analysis of such measurements can constrain parameters that are weakly identified by an individual observation. The information gained nevertheless depends on the experimental design, measurement strategy, contrast engineering and model parameterization [66, 50, 19, 33]. In practical reflectometry analysis, prior knowledge about plausible thickness ranges, expected material SLDs or instrumental conditions further constrains the solution space.

XRR is performed at synchrotron light sources [59, 28] or laboratory sources, whereas NR uses monochromatic or time-of-flight (TOF) reflectometers [9]. Energy-dispersive XRR and rotating-sample XRR geometries further illustrate the move towards rapid and parallel acquisition [38, 44]. Such developments increase the relevance of amortized analysis for in situ and time-resolved scattering experiments [58, 39]. PNR additionally requires polarization components such as polarizers, spin flippers and, depending on the experimental configuration, spin analyzers. In full spin-resolved PNR, four reflectivity cross sections are distinguished: the non–spin-flip channels R↑⁣↑R^{\uparrow\uparrow} and R↓⁣↓R^{\downarrow\downarrow}, and the spin-flip channels R↑⁣↓R^{\uparrow\downarrow} and R↓⁣↑R^{\downarrow\uparrow}, where the first and second arrows denote the incident and reflected neutron-spin states, respectively. Magnetization components parallel to the neutron-spin quantization axis contribute to the non–spin-flip channels, whereas components transverse to this axis couple the two spin states and generate spin-flip scattering. When the incident neutron polarization is selected but the reflected spin state is not resolved, the two measured intensities sum over the possible reflected spin states, such that R↑=R↑⁣↑+R↑⁣↓R^{\uparrow}=R^{\uparrow\uparrow}+R^{\uparrow\downarrow} and R↓=R↓⁣↓+R↓⁣↑R^{\downarrow}=R^{\downarrow\downarrow}+R^{\downarrow\uparrow}. For magnetization collinear with the neutron-spin quantization axis, the spin-flip cross sections vanish, and the measured intensities reduce to R↑=R↑⁣↑R^{\uparrow}=R^{\uparrow\uparrow} and R↓=R↓⁣↓R^{\downarrow}=R^{\downarrow\downarrow}, as assumed by the two-channel PNR model used for the experimental co-refinement examples in this work. Because these channels have fixed physical labels and ordering, they are treated as a single multichannel observation rather than as separate observations combined through compositional inference.

papers.title: A paintbox characterization of labeled partitions
papers.abstract: We study pairs of labeled random partitions $(Π,τ)$ with a finite label set $E$, which can be thought of as a random mutation and coalescence mechanism of a countable number of blocks. Labeled exchangeable partition probability functions (LEPPFs) are defined via labeled analogues of Kingman's paintbox partitions. They satisfy normalization, symmetry and consistency in a multivariate sense. Under an equivariance condition, a representation for $(Π,τ)$ in terms of labeled paintbox partitions is derived, leading to a full characterization of LEPPFs by a unique probability measure $G$. This representation is extended to jointly exchangeable and consistent transition pairs using a product measure $F \otimes G$. These results yield a one-to-one correspondence between distributions of jointly exchangeable and consistent transition pairs and pairs of exchangeable distributions and LEPPFs.
papers.intro:
Exchangeable random partitions have been studied extensively in the literature, see, for example, [9]. They arise naturally in single-type coalescent theory. The distribution of an exchangeable random partition is uniquely described either by its exchangeable partition probability function (EPPF) or by a probability measure on the infinite simplex Δ\Delta, or by random variables P1,P2,…P_{1},P_{2},\ldots, called limiting relative frequencies. See, for example, [8]. In [10], the theory of exchangeable random partitions is used extensively to obtain a characterization of certain coalescent processes in terms of a single measure Ξ\Xi.

The distribution of an exchangeable random partition is uniquely described either by its exchangeable partition probability function (EPPF) or by a probability measure on the infinite simplex Δ\Delta, or by random variables P1,P2,…P_{1},P_{2},\ldots, called limiting relative frequencies. See, for example, [8]. In [10], the theory of exchangeable random partitions is used extensively to obtain a characterization of certain coalescent processes in terms of a single measure Ξ\Xi.

We aim to generalize these results to random labeled partitions, supplementing the results of Kallenberg [7, Section 7.8]. It turns out to be useful to consider certain transition pairs (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau) of random labeled partitions satisfying a joint exchangeability or equivariance condition. One may think of τ\tau as a random initial state consisting entirely of singletons and of Π\Pi as the result of applying random mutation and coalescence mechanisms to that state. We introduce labeled paintbox partitions and show that each labeled paintbox partition possesses a labeled analogue of limiting relative frequencies. Next, we derive a representation for equivariant transition pairs in the flavor of Kallenberg [7, Theorem 7.38 and Corollary 7.40]. This representation is then used to obtain a full characterization of LEPPFs and, under the additional assumption of consistency, a full characterization of jointly exchangeable transition pairs in terms of LEPPFs and exchangeable distributions. Our results have applications in multitype coalescent theory, where consistent coalescent processes are studied, which satisfy a multitype analogue of exchangeability and have an exchangeable initial state. See, for example, [5], where a special case of these processes with asynchronous mergers is studied, or [3], where these processes arise as limits of certain multitype Cannings models.

These results lead to a one-to-one correspondence between jointly exchangeable and consistent transition pairs and pairs consisting of exchangeable distributions and LEPPFs.

papers.title: Extended vs. thin screen approximation in astrophysical settings
papers.abstract: Context: In the context of radio wave propagation through plasma concentrations and for gravitational lensing, the thin screen approximation often provides a suitable approximation for scattering and deflections caused by three-dimensional spatial structures. For scattering of electromagnetic waves from an extended medium, stochastic theories provide analytical bounds on ensemble averaged quantities, such as the scintillation index. If neither the conditions for a stochastic treatment nor the thin screen approximation are fulfilled, fully numerical methods are required. Aims: For an extended structure, the applicability of the thin screen approximation needs to be verified by comparing it with the fully three-dimensional scattering solution. We discuss various exact solutions to simple lensing geometries and provide numerical results for the propagation in the branched-flow regime, which is also of relevance in astrophysical applications. Methods: We transfer several analytical results obtained in quantum mechanical scattering theory to astrophysical settings and complement them with different numerical methods to quantify the deviations of thin screen theories from an extended medium results. Results: We provide the analytical results for spherical waves scattered by a point source and show the emergence of branchef flow in the intermediate regime between thin screen physics and stochastic media results.

papers.intro:
Lensing of distant astronomical objects by a foreground object provides a natural magnifying glass for studying the properties of both the distant objects and the intervening ones. For typical astrophysical applications of lensing to distant objects such as pulsars, Kirchhoff-Fresnel diffraction theory or geometric optics provide a well-established tool to calculate the intensity distributions and the time delays of signals at arriving at an observer. In weak gravitational lensing, Fermat’s principle is often used in combination with the lens equation (Schneider et al. 1992; Wambsganss 1998). In addition, the Kirchhoff-Fresnel diffraction integral can be solved numerically using Fourier methods (Grillo & Cordes 2018), or with Picard-Lefschetz methods for a 1/r1/r-potential and the rational lens (Feldbrugge & Turok 2020; Jow et al. 2023). papers.title: BatchBench: Benchmarking AI Robustness to Batch Effects and Domain Shift in Biomedical Images - A JUMP Cell Painting Leaderboard
papers.abstract: Despite recent advances, current AI systems remain highly susceptible to domain shifts, particularly in biomedical imaging, where images are usually acquired under substantially different experimental conditions. Although recent domain adaptation methods have made substantial progress, significant performance gaps under domain shift persist. To measure progress in this regard, we introduce BatchBench, a leaderboard that evaluates and compares the robustness of AI systems on biomedical images from unseen experimental batches and data sources. BatchBench is built on JUMP-CP, one of the largest publicly available biomedical imaging datasets. Generated using the Cell Painting assay, JUMP-CP exhibits pronounced batch effects and domain shifts, making it a challenging testbed for evaluating robustness to distributional changes.

papers.intro:
Deep learning methods often assume that training and test data are sampled from the same underlying distribution. However, in practice, biological images are acquired across experimental batches, plates, and sites, which introduces non-biological variation known as batch effects. These effects shift the distribution of the input images, such that a model that performs well on its training distribution can fail on images from a new experimental batch or laboratory. This limits the use of AI in applications such as drug discovery, where new data are generated continuously and under changing conditions.

papers.title: Electronic Screening as a Design Lever in La-Doped BaTiO$_3$: Coupled Polarization, Dielectric Response, and Optical Anisotropy
papers.abstract: Donor substitution can tune the coupled ferroelectric, dielectric, electronic, and optical properties of perovskite oxides by modifying lattice distortions and electronic screening. We investigate these effects in La-doped BaTiO3 using density functional theory, density-functional perturbation theory, and the Berry-phase formalism for polarization. For a model with 12.5% La substitution at the Ba site, La incorporation induces anisotropic lattice contraction, reduces tetragonality and Ti off-centering, and weakens the energetic stabilization of the tetragonal ferroelectric phase. The accompanying reduction in polarization is associated with enhanced electronic screening and reduced anomalous Born effective charges. Phonon calculations indicate that the relaxed doped structure is dynamically stable, while hardening of a low-frequency polar mode is consistent with weakened ferroelectricity. The high-frequency dielectric response increases moderately, whereas the static dielectric response decreases as the lattice contribution is suppressed. Electronic-structure calculations show a Fermi-level shift toward the conduction band without mid-gap defect states. The optical spectra exhibit an absorption-edge shift consistent with a Burstein-Moss-type mechanism, enhanced near-edge transparency, and reduced birefringence. Together, these results suggest a microscopic connection between donor-induced screening, polar-mode hardening, reduced dynamical charges, polarization suppression, and decreased optical anisotropy. The conclusions apply to the investigated 12.5% composition; calculations at additional concentrations are needed to establish quantitative doping trends.

papers.title: Enhancing IoT Network Reliability through Antenna Diversity in Real-World Scenarios
papers.abstract: Antenna diversity in Internet of Things (IoT) devices is explored to address challenges associated with fixed device orientation and interference from nearby metallic objects, which can degrade wireless network performance. Integrating multiple antennas with different polarizations can significantly enhance signal quality and network reliability. Experiments demonstrated significant improvements in link quality, with gains exceeding 30 dB in received signal strength for specific scenarios. Already the addition of a second PCB-based antenna alone, resulted in a 17 dB improvement. These findings suggest that the added complexity in hardware and software to incorporate antenna diversity could well be justified by the resulting enhancements in network stability for real-world applications.

Evaluating and improving wireless communication reliability has been the subject of a lot of research, with antenna diversity, being one of the prominent hardware-oriented strategies [3, 5, 4]. Previous studies have explored theoretical aspects of antenna diversity, such as the mathematical modeling of signal propagation and polarization effects [6, 7, 8]. In contrast, this paper explores the practical potential of incorporating multiple simple antennas with different polarizations into the devices, to enhance the performance and reliability of wireless links within the IoT network in real-world scenarios and confirm these with measurements.

papers.title: A Hybrid Neural Network Emulator for M1 Neutrino Reaction Rates in Binary Neutron Star Merger Simulations
papers.abstract: We present a neural network emulator for the bns_nurates library, which computes neutrino reaction rates used in binary neutron star merger simulations. Following a hybrid strategy, we emulate only the computationally dominant two-dimensional reactions---pair processes, bremsstrahlung, and inelastic neutrino-electron scattering---while evaluating the inexpensive one-dimensional processes still with bns_nurates. We find that the emulator reproduces the opacities to within a few percent across the relevant thermodynamic conditions and accelerates their evaluation by roughly an order of magnitude. When deployed in a global Athenak binary neutron star merger simulation, it recovers the remnant structure, neutrino luminosities, and ejecta composition of a reference run using the full bns_nurates library, at approximately half the overall cost

papers.intro:
Binary neutron star (BNS) mergers are among the most energetic and informative events accessible to modern astrophysical observations [6]. The landmark event GW170817 [3] simultaneously revealed gravitational wave (GW) emission, a short gamma-ray burst (GRB 170817A), and a kilonova (AT2017gfo) [2, 4, 48, 17], confirming BNS mergers both as central engines for relativistic jets and as sites of rapid neutron capture (r-process) nucleosynthesis, and opening a new chapter in multi-messenger astrophysics [38, 41, 71, 72, 36, 55, 63, 53]. The merger evolution is governed by coupled physical processes, including general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics and neutrino transport [24]. In particular, neutrinos play a decisive role in setting the electron fraction YeY_{e} of the outflows through their interactions with the surrounding matter, and in redistributing energy and momentum within the remnant [49, 33, 40, 50, 51].

In particular, the gray two-moment (M1) scheme, which evolves the energy-integrated zeroth and first moments of the neutrino distribution function and closes the resulting system of equations with an analytic closure, is widely used due to its balance between accuracy and computational cost.

In moment schemes, the coupling between matter and radiation is set by gray neutrino reaction rates. These rates are supplied by either pre-computed tables [45, 43] or by libraries that evaluate reaction kernels on the fly. One such state-of-the-art library is bns_nurates [14], which takes the local thermodynamic and radiation quantities to construct the neutrino distributions, integrates over energy and angle, and returns the gray emissivities and opacities used in global simulations. On-the-fly rate calculations offer several advantages, including the absence of interpolation errors and the possibility of taking into account the actual neutrino spectrum from the neutrino transport [14]. However, physical accuracy comes at the expense of higher computational cost and the need for real-time feasibility in actual simulations often forces a compromise on physical fidelity. bns_nurates models several of the demanding two-dimensional (two neutrino phase space) kernels: neutrino pair processes, nucleon-nucleon bremsstrahlung and the often-neglected neutrino-electron/positron scattering (NEPS), all of which contribute substantially to the heavy-lepton neutrino opacities [13, 56, 22]. Within widely used approximations, evaluating these kernels is far more expensive than the simpler beta processes, making them challenging to include efficiently in production simulations [62, 21, 20].

This is the first application of neural networks to modeling neutrino reaction rates, although related emulators have been developed for nuclear equations of state [42], for turbulence modeling [35, 15], for subgrid modeling of small-scale feedback on large-scale dynamics [9], and for neutrino flavor oscillations [1, 57, 11]. The central challenge in applying NN emulators to neutrino opacities is the multi-scale nature of the problem: the opacity varies over many orders of magnitude across the thermodynamic phase space of BNS conditions, with sharp gradients near the extreme cases [67]. papers.title: PBR sensitivity to boosted dark matter explanation for the KM3-230213A event
papers.abstract: POEMMA-Balloon with Radio (PBR) is a hybrid fluorescence and optical Cherenkov telescope that is a pathfinder instrument for a future Probe Of Extreme Multi-Messenger Astrophysics (POEMMA), together with a radio instrument, to be flown on a super pressure balloon in Spring 2028. One of its science objectives is follow up of astrophysical event alerts via signals of tau decays in the atmosphere, sourced by Earth-skimming tau neutrinos. The recent report of the KM3NeT Collaboration's muon event with $ E_μ=120^{+110}_{-60}$ PeV sparked searches for beyond the standard model (BSM) physics explanations. Using a specific, boosted dark matter scenario which together with the KM3NeT observation, sets a scale for the fluence of boosted dark matter in this energy range, we assess the capabilities of PBR to constrain or discover such a source for a boosted dark matter energy spectrum above $\sim 10^8$ GeV. PBR has discovery potential for dark matter energies above $10^9$ GeV, and depending on BSM input parameters, to dark matter energies as low as $1.5\times 10^8$ GeV. While the analysis is focused on one BSM example, the methodology is applicable to any BSM physics that affects tau production in the Earth.

papers.intro:
Very high energy neutrino astronomy, as part of a multimessenger program to understand the most powerful accelerators in the Universe, has made significant advances in recent years [1, 2]. With the discovery of the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux [3] and more recent associations of neutrino events with astrophysical transients [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], neutrino telescopes are pushing the frontiers of high-energy and ultrahigh-energy neutrino detection. Until recently, it has been the IceCube Neutrino Observatory [9] that detected the highest energy neutrinos via through-going muons expected to originate from muon neutrinos in the 1−101-10 PeV energy range [10] and a shower with visible energy 6.05±0.726.05\pm 0.72 PeV that likely originates from an incident ν¯e\bar{\nu}_{e} of similar energy [11]. The observation on February 13, 2023 of a nearly horizontal muon track, with a reconstructed energy of Eμ=120−60+110​PeVE_{\mu}=120^{+110}_{-60}\,\mathrm{PeV} [12] by KM3NeT/ARCA detector [13, 14], designated as KM3-230213A, may have been sourced by a muon neutrino of even higher energy, in which case it represents the highest energy neutrino event in a neutrino telescope. However, diffuse flux limits from other experiments and the absence of a clear association with a transient source [12] make the interpretation of KM3-230213A challenging. Instruments with pointing capabilities that are sensitive to neutrino sources in this energy range can facilitate the study such extreme energy events and potentially reveal their origins. Part of the Joint Exploratory Missions for an Extreme Universe Observatory (JEM-EUSO) program [15], the upcoming POEMMA-Balloon with Radio (PBR) mission [16, 17] will be poised to make these observations or establish new limits on transient neutrino sources.

The PBR mission is a stratospheric balloon-based pathfinder for future satellite-based instruments such as the Probe of Multi-Messenger Astrophysics (POEMMA) [18] and M-EUSO [15]. Scheduled to fly on a NASA Super Pressure Ballon (SPB), PBR will be launched from Wanaka, New Zealand in Spring 2028 and circle the Southern Ocean. A mission time of at least 20 days is anticipated. During the flight, science goals will be to observe high-altitude horizontal air showers [19], make first measurements of fluorescence emission from ultra-high-energy cosmic ray (UHECR) air showers from above [20], and most important to this discussion, search for Target-of-Opportunity (ToO) neutrino sources [21]. Multi-messenger event alerts will direct the schedule of instrument pointing for ToO searches [22].

PBR will have a hybrid focal surface comprising a 1.1 m Schmidt telescope with a Fluorescence Camera (FC) and Cherenkov Camera (CC) as a pathfinder instrument for POEMMA. Overall, the field of view (FoV) will be 36∘ (vertical) by 24∘ (horizontal). The CC uses silicon photomultipliers with a pixel size of 3 mm ×\times 3 mm and pixel instantaneous FoV of 0.2∘0.2^{\circ} by 0.2∘0.2^{\circ}. With 2048 pixels, the CC has a total FoV of 6∘6^{\circ} (vertical) by 12∘12^{\circ} (horizontal), 10 ns integration time and a wavelength range of 320−900320-900 nm. The CC can capture ultra-fast pulses from optical Cherenkov light from up-going extensive air showers (EAS) sourced by Earth-skimming neutrinos [23] with estimated neutrino energy thresholds of ≳10\gtrsim 10 PeV [24, 17]. With a NASA-supplied azimuthal rotator and a custom-designed tilt system, the instrument will be pointed to optimize ToO searches. Typical astrophysical ToO events remain in the CC FoV for more than 20 minutes without active tracking [22]. The FC and CC designs for PBR build on experience from prior missions: EUSO-SPB1 [25] and EUSO-SPB2 [26, 27, 28], and from the POEMMA design study [18].

papers.title: Hyperspherical Simplex Representations for Backward-Compatible Retrieval
papers.abstract: Training modern AI models has become increasingly expensive, and updating deployed models can alter their internal feature representations, affecting applications built upon them. In retrieval systems, such updates often require complete gallery re-indexing, a computationally expensive process at scale. Existing backward-compatibility methods enable direct comparison of representations from updated and earlier models, avoiding re-indexing. However, they typically require compatibility-specific training, learned mapping functions, or architectural modifications, and often depend explicitly on the previous model. We propose hyperspherical simplex representations derived from softmax outputs and logits for backward-compatible retrieval across independently trained models. They leverage the simplex structure induced by softmax cross-entropy training with one-hot labels as a common geometric reference across model updates. Since this reference depends on the number of classes, adding new ones expands the simplex, misaligning existing class prototypes with their earlier counterparts. We therefore derive a deterministic linear transformation to restore their alignment. Our theoretical analysis of the formal backward-compatibility definition identifies two geometric conditions under which its inequalities hold in expectation, assuming von Mises--Fisher class distributions with increasing concentration across updates. Aligned regular-simplex representations satisfy these conditions, providing a theoretical basis for the proposed representations under the stated assumptions. Without using additional compatibility-specific losses, learned mappings, or architectural modifications, the proposed representations achieve competitive results on standard compatibility benchmarks, including expanded class sets, more expressive architectures, and independently trained models from public repositories.

papers.intro:
Training modern AI models has become increasingly expensive, limiting accessibility to a few well-resourced organizations (Radford et al., 2021; Dubey et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2023; Anthropic, 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026). Despite reductions in model parameters and computing costs (Dubey et al., 2024), training from scratch, fine-tuning, and inference remain economically challenging (Wang et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2024). As a result, models are increasingly released through public repositories (Marcel & Rodriguez, 2010; Wolf et al., 2019; Wightman, 2019) or provided as services through APIs, simplifying application development and enabling widespread adoption across domains.

Despite reductions in model parameters and computing costs (Dubey et al., 2024), training from scratch, fine-tuning, and inference remain economically challenging (Wang et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2024). As a result, models are increasingly released through public repositories (Marcel & Rodriguez, 2010; Wolf et al., 2019; Wightman, 2019) or provided as services through APIs, simplifying application development and enabling widespread adoption across domains.

As these models become more integrated into real-world systems, the need to update them is also growing. This demand is driven by several factors (Raffel, 2023; Yadav et al., 2025), including evolving training strategies (Biondi et al., 2026; Biondi et al., 2024; Echterhoff et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2020), advancements in model architectures (Touvron et al., 2023; Kaplan et al., 2020), the availability of higher-quality datasets (Gunasekar et al., 2023), the expansion of training classes, or extended training periods (Biderman et al., 2023; Raffel, 2023). Such updates not only improve performance but also bring the rapid progress of the field into deployed models, simplifying their adoption despite the continued growth in the scale and complexity of models, datasets, and infrastructures (Bommasani et al., 2021; Sorscher et al., 2022).

Such updates not only improve performance but also bring the rapid progress of the field into deployed models, simplifying their adoption despite the continued growth in the scale and complexity of models, datasets, and infrastructures (Bommasani et al., 2021; Sorscher et al., 2022).

However, a significant drawback of model updates is that they can compromise compatibility with earlier versions, altering the behavior of applications or services built upon them (Raffel, 2023). For example, image retrieval services might experience unexpected changes in image rankings following a model update, forcing users to adapt when previously top-ranked images no longer appear first (Shen et al., 2020). Similarly, end users, such as drivers of semi-autonomous cars, often develop a mental model of the machine learning system’s capabilities (Bansal et al., 2019a). When updates modify system behavior, users must adjust their mental model of the system’s functionality, a task that can be challenging, dissatisfying, and even unsafe (Bansal et al., 2019b; Templeton, 2019). Recent observations have highlighted similar issues with large language models (LLMs) (Echterhoff et al., 2024; Goswami et al., 2026), raising concerns about AI safety and alignment. This is particularly critical when decisions and textual outputs from these agents are translated into actions (Amodei et al., 2016; Ngo et al., 2024). In such settings, it is essential that the predictions of the updated model mimic those of the old model for any correct classification (Milani Fard et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2021; Ricci et al., 2026b).

This is particularly critical when decisions and textual outputs from these agents are translated into actions (Amodei et al., 2016; Ngo et al., 2024). In such settings, it is essential that the predictions of the updated model mimic those of the old model for any correct classification (Milani Fard et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2021; Ricci et al., 2026b).

Updating a model while ensuring compatibility with its earlier versions has been explored along three complementary dimensions: 1) Weights-level, which explores the merging of model parameters under the assumption of linear mode connectivity, to unify multiple versions into a single, robust model (Frankle et al., 2020; Wortsman et al., 2022; Ainsworth et al., 2023); 2) Representation-level, which seeks to learn backward-compatible representations that are comparable across model updates, so they can be used interchangeably over time (Shen et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2021; Biondi et al., 2026); and 3) Classifier decision-level, which ensures that the updated model preserves the correct predictions of the old model, preventing negative flips (Milani Fard et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2024). They target distinct notions of compatibility and accordingly differ in their objectives, mechanisms, and evaluation criteria.

They target distinct notions of compatibility and accordingly differ in their objectives, mechanisms, and evaluation criteria.

Among these paradigms, we focus on representation-level compatibility, which is particularly relevant to retrieval systems, where feature representations produced by different model versions must remain directly comparable. Backward-compatibility training, introduced by Shen et al. (2020) to avoid image re-indexing of the gallery set, has been established as a standard training paradigm to achieve backward-compatibility between model representations. However, most existing studies on backward-compatibility require training a new model using the old model as a reference (Shen et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2021; Duggal et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023). This approach has become increasingly challenging due to restricted access to old model architectures and weights—often limited by proprietary constraints and non-disclosure policies—as well as the high computational costs associated with training large-scale modern AI models. Recent studies (Biondi et al., 2023a; Biondi et al., 2024; Biondi et al., 2026) have addressed this limitation by learning compatible representations without explicitly using the previous model as a reference. However, these approaches require all parties to agree in advance on a shared, pre-allocated fixed classifier (Pernici et al., 2019; Pernici et al., 2021a; Zhu et al., 2021).

papers.title: Macroscopic Poincaré Inequalities and Weak-Type Characterizations of $p$-Energy Forms
papers.abstract: For a class of regular strongly local $p$-energy forms on complete doubling metric measure spaces, $1<p<\infty$, we derive a macroscopic Poincaré inequality from a Poincaré inequality and a capacity upper bound at a doubling scale $Ψ$. The macroscopic inequality compares $L^p$-oscillations at any two scales and yields a uniform two-scale comparison $J_s\lesssim J_r$, $0<r<s$, for the Korevaar-Schoen functionals, strengthening their usual weak monotonicity property. Conversely, under a density assumption on compactly supported functions, the macroscopic inequality yields a regular strongly local Korevaar-Schoen $p$-energy satisfying a $Ψ$-Poincaré inequality. We also show that the macroscopic inequality forces lower $p$-scaling of $Ψ$ on scales not exceeding $\mathrm{diam} X$; together with doubling, this gives two-sided power bounds. Finally, we establish a weak-type characterization of the energy domain of Brezis-Van Schaftingen-Yung type.

papers.intro:
Poincaré inequalities are a basic principle of first-order analysis: the oscillation of a function on a ball is controlled by its energy near that ball. On metric measure spaces they provide a way to study Sobolev functions without using coordinates or derivatives, see [22]. A macroscopic Poincaré inequality expresses a related principle using only oscillations: variation at a given scale is controlled by averaged variation at any smaller scale. Hytönen and Korte recently established such an inequality on doubling Poincaré spaces, comparing an L1L^{1}-mean oscillation with an LpL^{p}-average of smaller-scale oscillations, normalized by the usual power scale rpr^{p} [23, Theorem 3.4]. This raises the question of whether the same principle holds for energies and geometries whose natural scale is different from rpr^{p}.

Regular strongly local pp-energy forms provide a robust newly developed framework for this question. For 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, such a form (ℰ,ℱ)(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F}) consists of a Sobolev domain ℱ\mathcal{F} and a pp-energy ℰ\mathcal{E}; see [26, 27, 41]. This framework includes the usual gradient energies on Riemannian manifolds and Carnot groups, as well as energies on fractals. In the classical examples the natural scale is Ψ⁡(r)=rp\Psi(r)=r^{p}, whereas on fractals it may be a different power or even a nonpower function. Moreover, an energy measure may be singular with respect to the underlying measure, so that there need not be a gradient density to integrate. These features make it useful to formulate Poincaré inequalities directly in terms of energy measures and a scale function Ψ\Psi.

papers.title: On the strict approximation of currents and space-time trajectories
papers.abstract: This work establishes a wide variety of strict approximation results for space-time trajectories, a class of space-time currents that are used to model the evolution of dislocations in crystalline materials. In particular, we introduce a strict-type notion of convergence which respects quantities associated with geometric transport phenomena and prove approximation results in this topology. These results build on the classical strict approximation results for normal and integral currents developed by Federer and Fleming, which we also review and refine.

Approximation results have occupied a central place in the development of the theory of currents over the past six decades. Already in their seminal paper [17], Federer and Fleming proved three results concerning the approximation of normal and integral currents by polyhedral chains; since then, a wide range of results have been obtained by varying the class of currents to be approximated, the class of approximants, and the topology of the approximation (see, for example, [12, 2, 29, 18, 19]).

papers.title: Asymmetry Tunneling Beyond Adaptive Equivariance Relaxation
papers.abstract: Equivariant neural networks encode prescribed symmetries as powerful inductive biases, yet real-world data may exhibit symmetry-breaking structure that these priors cannot fully capture. Prior work has largely addressed this challenge through model-side equivariance relaxation, seeking an appropriate level of equivariance for the data. This raises a complementary question: must equivariance relaxation be adaptively controlled? To investigate this question, we introduce a residual path alongside a strictly equivariant model and deliberately restrict their interface to examine the transmission of task-relevant structure. Across five benchmarks, we observe both residual collapse and survival despite these restrictions; we call the latter phenomenon asymmetry tunneling. We further characterize this phenomenon through four complementary diagnostics. Our results suggest that adaptive control of equivariance relaxation is not a prerequisite for capturing potential symmetry-breaking structure.

papers.intro:
Equivariant neural networks (Cohen & Welling, 2016; Ravanbakhsh et al., 2017; Kondor & Trivedi, 2018), which encode prescribed symmetries to improve sample efficiency and generalization (Chen et al., 2020; Bietti & Mairal, 2019), have been widely applied in computer vision (Cohen & Welling, 2017), graph learning (Gilmer et al., 2017), and 3D modeling (Schütt et al., 2017). However, real-world data can contain structure that is not fully captured by a strictly equivariant prior (Smidt et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023), due to noise, measurement bias, chirality, local interactions, or other symmetry-breaking effects. To address imperfect symmetries in real-world data, prior work has explored soft equivariance priors, relaxed equivariant architectures, theoretical analyses of approximation–generalization trade-offs, and data-driven adaptation (Finzi et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022; Petrache & Trivedi, 2023; Manolache et al., 2025). These works examine model-side equivariance relaxation, reflecting the view that model equivariance should be adapted to an appropriate level for the data.

This pursuit of an appropriate level of equivariance raises a complementary diagnostic question: must equivariance relaxation be adaptively controlled to capture symmetry-breaking structure? To investigate this question, we use a strictly equivariant model as a reference anchor and introduce an expressive residual path through a deliberately restricted interface. We then test whether this restricted residual path can transmit task-relevant contributions. The residual path is designed with ample expressive capacity to represent potential symmetry-breaking structure, while the restricted interface uses stop-gradient, scalar gating, and a single additive fusion to limit residual–anchor interaction and transmission. Empirically, the restricted residual exhibits two regimes: collapse and survival. We call residual survival despite these restrictions asymmetry tunneling. To characterize this phenomenon, we employ four complementary empirical diagnostics: residual survival, measured relative to the anchor; anchor-relative geometry, by comparing the residual with local variation in anchor representations; physical localization, by tracing its concentration in physical structure; and task relevance, through held-out performance. Our contributions are as follows: 1. We identify asymmetry tunneling as residual survival despite a restricted interface with a strictly equivariant anchor, implemented through stop-gradient, scalar gating, and a single additive fusion. Across tasks, we observe both residual survival and collapse. 2. We characterize these patterns through complementary empirical diagnostics of residual survival, anchor-relative geometry, physical localization, and task relevance to probe potential symmetry-breaking structure.

papers.title: Discovery of a Broad-Line Active Galactic Nucleus at $z = 9.98$
papers.abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has uncovered a previously unexplored population of faint active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in the early Universe. We present MoM-BL-z10 at $z=9.9837\pm0.0009$, identified through a systematic search for broad-line AGNs at $z\geq6$ using public JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectra from the DAWN JWST Archive. The PRISM spectrum exhibits a broad component in H$β$ at 5.35 microns. A narrow+broad Gaussian fit yields a broad H$β$ detection at S/N = 3.87, with FWHM = $3480^{+2040}_{-950}$ km s$^{-1}$ and $L_{{\rm H}β,{\rm broad}}=1.25^{+0.33}_{-0.31}\times10^{42}$ erg s$^{-1}$. The detection of [Ne III] $\lambda3870$ and the high [Ne III]/[O II] and [O III]/H$β$ ratios further support the AGN interpretation. Its rest-frame UV and optical continuum slopes, compact NIRCam morphology, and a tentative MIRI F770W detection suggest similarities to Little Red Dots (LRDs). The broad H$β$ detection enables the first virial SMBH mass estimate at $z\sim10$. We derive $M_{\rm BH}=3.6^{+5.8}_{-1.7}\times10^7 M_\odot$ and $λ_{\rm Edd}=0.11^{+0.10}_{-0.07}$ using the standard single-epoch virial calibration and quasar bolometric correction. We also consider an alternative scenario adopting the LRD-specific bolometric correction and assuming $λ_{\rm Edd}=1$, which yields $M_{\rm BH}=2.1^{+0.6}_{-0.5}\times10^6 M_\odot$. Under either scenario, the inferred SMBH mass at a cosmic age of only 470 Myr highlights the challenge of rapid BH growth in the early Universe, suggesting super-Eddington accretion from a stellar-mass seed or a more massive seed. As the highest-redshift broad-line AGN identified to date, MoM-BL-z10 provides a new observational benchmark for understanding the early growth of supermassive black holes.

papers.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
papers.abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).
papers.intro:
Recent advances in frontier coding agents are turning automated research into an executable workflow: agents can read papers and repositories, modify implementations, run experiments, interpret quantitative feedback, and iterate. A growing body of recent work suggests a common recipe for this vision: cast research as a feedback loop in which an agent operates in a workspace, pursues a measurable objective, and improves through experimentation [50, 38, 28, 62, 23]. Yet most demonstrations so far assume well-structured codebases [19, 36, 61], operate in single-task settings [50, 38, 23], and are heavily skewed toward computer science domains [40, 56, 13]. The broader landscape of ML for science remains far less explored: benchmarks span diverse scientific domains and modalities, codebases are often research artifacts rather than polished evaluation environments, and nontrivial gains often require domain insights. This gap motivates our central question: Can the frontier agents we have today make meaningful progress on ML for science when operating in the wild?

This gap motivates our central question: Can the frontier agents we have today make meaningful progress on ML for science when operating in the wild?

We instantiate this question as automated scientific hill-climbing (Figure 1). In this setting, an agent is given a scientific ML benchmark, its paper, codebase, data, and target metric. Starting from the best available model in the benchmark, the agent works under a fixed resource budget to improve the metrics through code changes and experiments. However, our pilot study shows that this natural setup is fragile. Across 12 tasks from 5 NeurIPS 2025 benchmarks, 5 tasks exhibit severe evaluation-gaming behaviors, including selective reporting, test-set contamination, metric manipulation, and even direct hardcoding. This aligns with recent work showing that coding agents succeed in well-structured evaluation settings but degrade sharply on real-world code and evaluations [10]. These failures motivate a testbed that preserves the in-the-wild nature of scientific tasks, makes meaningful progress measurable, and guards against evaluation gaming.

To address this challenge, we construct Agent4Sci, a testbed for evaluating automated scientific hill-climbing across 20 ML-for-science benchmarks, 25 tasks, and 11 scientific domains spanning the physical sciences, life sciences, Earth and environmental sciences, and scientific engineering. We first standardize each benchmark through human-verified baseline reproductions, repaired data splits, reduced runtime bottlenecks, and isolated environments. On top of this foundation, each run follows the Agent4Sci evaluation protocol. The hill-climbing agent receives the standardized environment with access only to training and validation data, then submits artifacts such as code changes, checkpoints, logs, and outputs. A separate evaluation agent runs the submitted artifacts on the held-out test set, and an auditing agent inspects the trajectory for academic misconduct.

papers.title: Second-Order Nonlinear Microresonators on Thin-Film Lithium Tantalate
papers.abstract: Nonlinear frequency conversion enables coherent light generation in spectral regions that conventional lasers cannot reach directly and is foundational to the generation of squeezed states and correlated photon pairs. Implementing these nonlinear processes in microresonators lowers the required optical power by orders of magnitude but requires two conditions to be met simultaneously across wide optical bandwidths: phase matching between the interacting fields, and an appropriate coupling condition to the resonator both in the fundamental and second harmonic band. While the former can be addressed by quasi-phase matching through periodic poling, coupling two widely separated spectral bands to the resonator is nontrivial because of the wavelength dependence of mode overlap. Here, we demonstrate parametric oscillation and efficient second-harmonic generation in periodically poled racetracks on thin-film lithium tantalate on insulator. The proposed resonators feature bus-ring coupling engineered independently in the two spectral bands via a long synchronous directional coupler. Quasi-phase matching is achieved using sidewall poling that is also wavelength-calibrated and locally adapted to compensate for thickness nonuniformities. Together, these two design elements enable second-order parametric oscillation with an on-chip threshold of 181 uW and 9.8% conversion efficiency, with signal and idler tunable over tens of nanometers by a few hundred megahertz of pump detuning. Our design strategy can be flexibly applied to efficient second-harmonic generation, reaching 25% absolute conversion efficiency at milliwatt pump powers. These results show how the coupling condition is a design variable in second-order nonlinear resonators and establish thin-film lithium tantalate as a competitive platform for efficient and low-power frequency conversion.

papers.title: Depth Separation for Neural Networks under Gaussian Measure
papers.abstract: We revisit the problem of depth separation for neural networks, as studied by Eldan and Shamir, Daniely, and others. Specifically, we consider the natural setting of $L^2$ approximation of radial functions under the standard Gaussian measure in $d$ dimensions. We show that there is a radial function in $L^2$ under the standard Gaussian measure that can be approximated to a fixed sufficiently small $L^2$ error by a depth-3 ReLU neural network of polynomial size in $d$ but can only be approximated by depth-2 networks with subexponentially bounded weights if their size is at least exponential in $d$. For that, we prove a general result showing that if a radial function has substantial mass in the high frequencies of its Hermite expansion, then it cannot be well approximated by a depth-2 neural network with small width and bounded weights. All theorems, lemmas, propositions, and corollaries are verified in Lean~4.

papers.title: A Matroidal Framework for Random Access in Linear Codes
papers.abstract: We study random access in linear codes when codeword symbols are sampled independently and uniformly with replacement. A code is recovery balanced if the expected number of samples required to recover a codeword coordinate is the same for every coordinate. We express the recovery expectations in terms of the associated matroid and derive a coordinatewise identity relating these values for a code and its dual. This proves that a linear code is recovery balanced if and only if its dual is recovery balanced, establishing a conjecture of Gruica et al. We further define the recovery balance for arbitrary matroids and show that asymptotically almost every sparse paving matroid is not recovery balanced.

In the full-recovery setting, the entire information vector must be reconstructed. Work in this direction includes exact recovery-time formulas, optimality results for specific code families, and the analysis of random linear codes [1, 8, 9]. papers.title: Development of a Prototype Superconducting Radio-Frequency Multicell Cavity for Compact, Conduction-Cooled Accelerators
papers.abstract: Jefferson Lab and General Atomics are jointly advancing compact, high-power irradiation systems capable of delivering electron-beam powers in the hundreds of kilowatts based on superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) technology. A critical step toward deploying SRF accelerators in industrial environments is replacing traditional liquid-helium cryogenic systems with conduction-cooled cryomodules powered by commercial cryocoolers. This paper reports recent progress in the design, fabrication, and testing of a prototype three-cell SRF cavity developed at Jefferson Lab and evaluated in a dedicated horizontal test cryostat at General Atomics. Peak surface magnetic fields up to 18.4\,mT, corresponding to accelerating gradients of approximately 4.3\,MV/m, were achieved in one of the cells. The results provide key insights into cavity preparation, thin-film coating, mechanical robustness, and cryogenic integration, offering guidance for the continued maturation of compact, conduction-cooled SRF accelerators for industrial irradiation applications.

papers.intro:
There is a rapidly growing industrial demand for high-power electron and X-ray irradiation systems. Many applications require substantially higher beam power than is available from conventional normal-conducting accelerators. In large research facilities, superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) technology, based on bulk niobium (Nb) cavities operated in liquid helium at 2 K, has become the standard solution for achieving high duty-factor, high-efficiency acceleration. Interest in alternative superconducting materials emerged as early as the 1980s, when the intermetallic compound niobium-tin (Nb3Sn) was investigated as a potential replacement for pure niobium [1]. Although early efforts did not surpass the performance of bulk Nb and struggled with higher losses at higher gradients, renewed development in the late 2000s at Cornell University demonstrated that thin Nb3Sn films grown on Nb substrates could achieve comparable RF losses at roughly twice the operating temperature [2] for usable field gradients. In practical terms, Nb3Sn enables similar accelerating gradients at about 4 K that would otherwise require 2 K operation with pure Nb. This higher operating temperature opens the door to a fundamentally different cryogenic approach: cryogen-free conduction cooling using commercial cryocoolers. Integrating SRF cavities into compact cryomodules cooled solely by conduction offers a transformative upgrade path for industrial accelerators, enabling substantially higher beam power without the complexity of liquid-helium systems.

Jefferson Lab and General Atomics (GA) have been at the forefront of this development, beginning with the conceptual design of a 1 MeV, 1 MW conduction-cooled accelerator based on a single-cell resonator [3]. To reach output energies up to 10 MeV—suitable for a broader range of industrial applications, including deep electron penetration and X-ray generation at 7 - 7.5 MeV—the focus has shifted to multi-cell SRF structures. Energies beyond 10 MeV are generally avoided due to the onset of neutron activation in water, which complicates industrial deployment [4].

To date, only limited demonstrations of conduction-cooled multi-cell SRF operation exist. The Institute of Modern Physics in China has reported a five-cell, 650 MHz conduction-cooled cavity operating with beam, but achieving only 1.57 MeV in continuous-wave mode [5]. The present work describes the approach taken by Jefferson Lab and GA to prepare, coat, and test a three-cell Nb3Sn coated cavity in conduction-cooled operation. The target performance for this demonstration was a quality factor of 1×1010\times 10^{10} at an accelerating gradient of 10 - 12 MV/m, consistent with the design goals for a compact 10 MeV system [6].
