By shielding dense cloud cores from UV photons, dust enables the buildup of key molecules required for star formation (Péroux and Howk, 2020; Schneider and Maiolino, 2024); in particular, the formation of H2 primarily ocurrs on the surfaces of dust grains (Hollenbach and McKee, 1979, e.g.,).

The dominant dust seed producers are asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars and supernovae (SNe) (Draine, 2011; Gall et al., 2011; Micelotta et al., 2018, e.g.,), tightly linking dust content to stellar evolution. Observationally, dust attenuation has been shown to correlate with stellar mass (e.g., Shivaei et al. 2020; Shapley et al. 2022; Woodrum et al. 2025; Maheson et al. 2025), SFR (e.g., Salim and Narayanan 2020; Maheson et al. 2025), the UV-optical slope of the dust attenuation curve (e.g., Salim and Narayanan 2020; Shivaei et al. 2025; Markov et al. 2025a), and galaxy inclination (Chevallard et al., 2013, e.g.,), among others.

One of the most prominent features of dust extinction and attenuation curves is the 2175 Å UV bump (Stecher, 1965). This broad absorption feature is present along many lines of sight in the Milky Way and the Large Magellanic Cloud, but is weak or absent in the Small Magellanic Cloud (Salim and Narayanan 2020). The bump has also been detected up to z∼7z\sim 7 (Witstok et al., 2023; Markov et al., 2023; Ormerod et al., 2025, e.g.,). The UV bump strength has been found to correlate with several galaxy properties, including stellar mass (Shivaei et al., 2022, e.g.,), metallicity (Shivaei et al., 2020; Markov et al., 2025a, e.g.,), slope of the dust attenuation curve (Kriek and Conroy, 2013, e.g.,), specific star formation rate (Battisti et al., 2025, sSFR; e.g.,), and galaxy inclination (Wild et al., 2011; Battisti et al., 2017, e.g.,).

Despite its prominence and connection with other properties, the physical origin of the UV bump remains uncertain. The prevailing view is that the bump originates from graphitic carbon (Draine and Lee, 1984). Other possibilities include UV-processed hydrogenated amorphous carbon (HAC) particles (Mennella et al., 1998) and hyperfullerene carbon particles (Wada et al., 1999). However, these candidates cannot fully explain variations in bump width (Draine and Malhotra, 1993), and the feature is widely thought to arise predominantly, if not entirely, from a mixture of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) molecules (Tielens, 2008; Li, 2020; Lin et al., 2025).

PAH molecules are complex carbonaceous particles that absorb individual UV photons and re-emit them by fluorescence in the mid-IR (Allamandola et al., 1985; Draine, 2003; Tielens, 2008). They are primarily produced in AGB stars (Galliano et al., 2018; Li, 2020), but may also form in supernova ejecta (Otaki et al., 2026), Wolf–Rayet winds (Marchenko and Moffat, 2017; Endo et al., 2022), or intermediate-luminosity red transients (Rose et al., 2025). papers.title: Enhanced Mass Transfer from Extended Shock-Supported Stellar Chromospheres
papers.abstract: Mass transfer (MT) in binary systems is a crucial and complex process. Even before the donor's photosphere fills its Roche lobe, matter from its outer atmosphere can reach the inner Lagrange point, thus initiating interaction in the so-called optically thin phase. Most existing models account for a very tenuous atmosphere supported by thermal gas pressure, thus predicting very little MT until the donor fills its Roche lobe. However, recent hydrodynamic simulations of giant stars suggest that shock-driven outflows can create substantially thicker "chromospheres'' extending to a few stellar radii. In this work, we derive a simple analytic model for a shock-supported chromosphere in a binary potential and calculate the corresponding MT rate. We also implement our prescription in the stellar evolution code MESA. We show that chromospheric MT rates can be orders of magnitude higher than prior estimates for optically thin MT, especially for stars high on the red giant or asymptotic giant branch. This allows for substantial accretion before Roche lobe overflow, both for systems that undergo stable mass transfer and for systems that go through common envelope evolution. Thus, for a given initial binary configuration, this may alter the final period and component masses compared to those predicted classically. Our model is similar to Wind Roche-lobe Overflow, but it is physically rather than empirically motivated. We discuss implications for various post-interaction binaries that can be tested with population synthesis studies and observed binary populations. Additionally, we have identified an inaccuracy in the current implementation of the optically-thin Ritter 1988 prescription in MESA, which we correct.

papers.intro:
Mass transfer is a crucial phenomenon in binary systems which can dramatically alter the evolution of the stars [43, 71]. This occurs when the matter in the outer layers of one of the stars, called the donor, comes close to the inner Lagrange point (L1) of the binary system. This matter gets channeled through the L1 nozzle and accreted onto the companion star, called the accretor. Mass transfer is often triggered as the donor star evolves off the main sequence, expands into a red giant, and starts to fill its Roche lobe. This reduces the potential difference between the stellar photosphere and the L1 point, thus enabling the flow of matter from the donor star to the nozzle.

This occurs when the matter in the outer layers of one of the stars, called the donor, comes close to the inner Lagrange point (L1) of the binary system. This matter gets channeled through the L1 nozzle and accreted onto the companion star, called the accretor. Mass transfer is often triggered as the donor star evolves off the main sequence, expands into a red giant, and starts to fill its Roche lobe. This reduces the potential difference between the stellar photosphere and the L1 point, thus enabling the flow of matter from the donor star to the nozzle.

The outcomes of mass transfer can be diverse. The process can be stable, where the donor stays mostly contained within its Roche lobe. On the other hand, mass transfer from highly evolved convective donors, like asymptotic giant branch (AGB) or red-supergiant (RSG) stars, often leads to instability and common envelope (CE) evolution (CEE) [27]. This leads to substantial mass ejection and orbital shrinkage. The products include systems like hot subdwarfs (e.g. Han et al. 22), short-period binaries with a white dwarf (WD, e.g. Rebassa-Mansergas et al. 57, Sun and Arras 67, Li et al. 37, Jones 33), cataclysmic variables (e.g. Meyer and Meyer-Hofmeister 46), and double compact objects [72].

More recently, [28] combined the optically thin and thick phases into a uniform formalism and also experimented with five different atmospheric models. Both works found M˙\dot{M} to differ by factors of ≈\approx2−42-4 from the 59 prescription, depending on the atmospheric model assumed. Numerical simulations of giant stars, however, suggest otherwise. A combination of coherent stellar pulsations and stochastic convection drives shock waves which elevate matter above the stellar photosphere. This expands the stellar atmosphere [24] and creates a dense “chromosphere” of gravitationally bound, optically thin material above the photosphere. Several subsequent numerical hydrodynamical simulations of AGB and RSG stars have confirmed this scenario [15, 16, 40, for example,]. The chromospheres in all these studies are much denser and more extended than thermally supported atmospheres.

This is expected to significantly affect binary interaction. The extended chromosphere can reach the L1 point at much lower photospheric Roche filling factors of the donor. This will greatly enhance the mass transfer rate compared to that given by 59, potentially modifying the outcome. Consequently, the binary components can interact at larger separations compared to those allowed by the classical 59 prescription – two stars not supposed to interact in the classical formalism can exchange a substantial amount of mass when the extended chromospheres are taken into account.

There is observational evidence on multiple fronts already suggesting enhanced mass transfer at low Roche filling factors. For example, in several known actively mass transferring systems (e.g., symbiotic systems), the M˙\dot{M} values suggested by observations are much larger than those expected from the classical prescriptions at the donors’ Roche fill factor [48, 18]. Several post-mass transfer binaries, e.g., Blue Lurkers [36] and Blue Straggler Stars [42], have long orbital periods where the donors could not have filled their Roche lobes, even in their giant phases. Other post-mass transfer systems such as Barium stars suggest total transferred masses much in excess of what 59-like prescriptions can supply [61]. Chromospheric mass transfer can potentially address these observational puzzles.

papers.title: OGLE-2013-BLG-1125/MOA-2013-BLG-584: Discovery of a gas giant orbiting an M dwarf
papers.abstract: We report the discovery and characterization of a planetary system in the microlensing event OGLE-2013-BLG-1125/MOA-2013-BLG-584. We analyze photometric data from OGLE and MOA surveys, as well as LCO, $μ$FUN, and Mindstep follow-up telescopes to model the microlensing light curve. We also used data from the Keck II telescope collected in 2018 to obtain additional constraints on the lensing system. We found a Saturn-mass planet of mass $M_{\rm p}=105\pm13 \ M_\oplus$ orbiting a low-mass host star $M_{\rm L}=0.139\pm0.011 \ M_\odot$ at $1.00\pm0.08$ kpc from Earth. This discovery adds to the small sample of giant planets orbiting low-mass stars and provides constraints on planet formation theories.

papers.intro:
Gravitational microlensing is sensitive to planets with masses down to Earth-mass. This technique offers several advantages compared to other detection methods. First, it can detect host stars located several kiloparsecs away from Earth (Mao and Paczynski, 1991; Gould and Loeb, 1992) and therefore helps us to understand the planet and stellar formation throughout our Galaxy (Snodgrass et al., 2004; Gaudi et al., 2002; Gould et al., 2010; Sumi, 2010; Sumi et al., 2011; Cassan et al., 2012; Suzuki et al., 2016; Tsapras et al., 2016; Bennett and Rhie, 1996; Zang et al., 2025). Second, microlensing events arise from the chance alignment of a lens and a source star, implying that host stars are sampled approximately in proportion to their Galactic abundance. Consequently, M dwarfs are expected to constitute at least 50%\% of the host population (Henry et al., 2006; Reylé et al., 2021). These microlensing detections therefore contribute to our astrophysical understanding of “planetary” systems orbiting low-mass hosts (Miyazaki et al., 2018; Jung et al., 2018), which potentially include brown dwarfs (Hoy et al., 2026). This is because gravitational microlensing does not require light from the host object to be detected. Indeed, observable light comes only from the more distant source star and is deflected when traversing the planetary system, which acts as the gravitational lens. Because the observed magnification depends on the exact alignment between lens, source, and observer, as well as the configuration of the lens itself, the mass ratio between the components of the lens and the projected orbital separation can lead to distinct observable features in an otherwise symmetric light curve.

papers.title: The Pandora SmallSat: Target Selection and Early Science
papers.abstract: The Pandora spacecraft is a smallsat selected in NASA's inaugural class of Pioneers missions. The aim of the Pandora mission is to disentangle stellar activity signals from exoplanet atmospheric transmission spectroscopy measurements. Pandora accomplishes this goal with its combined visible photometry and NIR spectroscopy that observe each target in the prime mission for 10 separate transit observations, each spanning 24 hours at a time. Targets were carefully selected for the Pandora prime mission. Pandora is specifically studying planets around low-mass stellar hosts (K and M dwarf stars) spanning a range of rotation periods and activity levels. The planets range in size from 1.5 - 15 Earth radii and orbital periods ranging from 1.7 - 11.5 days. In addition to the 10 transit visits planned for each of the 20 prime mission targets, Pandora is observing a number of auxiliary targets encompassing a variety of science topics. This includes topics such as stellar activity and young systems, transit timing variations of exoplanets, brown dwarf compositions, exoplanet phase curves, etc. We will discuss the selection of these targets, how they have been scheduled to fill in gaps in prime mission operations, and early science results. If the mission is extended, there is further opportunity for accomplishing additional science. Here we will discuss the possible options for extended mission operations and science.

The field of exoplanets has evolved significantly since the discoveries of the very first planets outside of our own Solar System [16, 10]. Early exoplanet detections focused on individual systems and primarily measured either planet mass or radius. Over time, technology and techniques advanced, and we were able to measure both mass and radius for many known exoplanets. This enabled us to measure bulk densities for individual planets, allowing astronomers to better understand planetary compositions (namely, e.g. is this planet rocky or gaseous?) and assess planet formation models.

Understanding atmospheric composition provides valuable insight into how planets form and evolve, thus moving us closer to the goal of understanding which planets might be habitable. In particular, carbon and oxygen molecules in planet atmospheres are key tracers of a planet’s formation and evolutionary history[12].

JWST, which launched in 2022, has significantly advanced our ability to study planet atmospheres. With JWST, we have shown that carbon species (e.g., carbon dioxide and methane) are common in exoplanet atmospheres. JWST is limited in sensitivity, and thus largely limited to studying planets orbiting low-mass stars where planetary atmospheric signals are detectable. This is challenging because low-mass stars are known to be highly magnetically active for long portions of their lifetimes. Cool spots and bright faculae on stellar surfaces can vary both spatially and temporally, presenting significant challenges when it comes to extracting planetary spectra from transmission spectroscopy observations. Starspots are also cool enough that water molecules can form, thus limiting our ability to study water in planet atmospheres, as it is challenging to determine the source of water signals. Early results from JWST[11, 14, 1] have been plagued with difficulties interpreting results such as these.

papers.title: Quantitative Imaging of Scandium Isotopes with a Long Axial Field-of-View PET/CT
papers.abstract: Objective. $^{43}$Sc and $^{44}$Sc are positron-emitting isotopes of scandium that have attracted growing interest for theranostic applications in conjunction with the therapeutic isotope $^{47}$Sc. Both isotopes are non-pure positron emitters, and the associated prompt-gamma emission together with the high positron energy introduce complexities in achieving precise quantitative imaging. Approach. We evaluated the quantitative imaging performance of $^{44}$Sc and a $^{43/44}$Sc mixture on a long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) PET/CT using a NEMA IEC body phantom. We assessed contrast recovery coefficients, image noise and bias for different numbers of iterations and for absolute versus relative scatter correction, and implemented an isotope-specific point-spread-function (PSF) correction based on FLUKA-simulated positron ranges. Main results. The quantitative imaging performance of both isotopes is comparable to $^{18}$F, and the vendor's prompt-gamma correction effectively suppresses the additional random coincidences and lung error caused by prompt-gamma emission. The isotope-specific PSF correction further improves contrast recovery. While the bias obtained for $^{44}$Sc meets the EARL acceptance criterion for non-standard radionuclides, the bias for the $^{43/44}$Sc mixture exceeds it, which we attribute to the mixture-specific cross-calibration of the dose calibrators rather than to the PET imaging. Significance. Our results support the use of LAFOV PET/CT for quantitative imaging of scandium isotopes and provide practical reconstruction recommendations for clinical protocols.

Scandium isotopes have emerged as ideal theranostic radionuclides with a chemically more coherent alternative to F18{}^{\makebox[7.97226pt][r]{$\scriptstyle 18$}}_{\makebox[7.97226pt][r]{$\scriptstyle$}}\mathrm{F}/Ga68{}^{\makebox[7.97226pt][r]{$\scriptstyle 68$}}_{\makebox[7.97226pt][r]{$\scriptstyle$}}\mathrm{Ga}- and Lu177{}^{\makebox[11.95839pt][r]{$\scriptstyle 177$}}_{\makebox[11.95839pt][r]{$\scriptstyle$}}\mathrm{Lu}- labeled tracers [33, 34, 32, 45, 28]. papers.title: Dynamical low-rank approximations for the optimal control of matrix ODEs
papers.abstract: We consider the open-loop optimal control of a dynamical system whose state is described by a time-dependent matrix $X(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$. Gradient-based optimization methods may incur substantial computational and memory costs, particularly for large-scale systems and fine temporal discretizations. To alleviate this computational burden, we develop a mathematical framework to use Dynamical Low Rank Approximations (DLRA) in optimal control problems. We study two distinct paradigms: the first one, called Optimize-then-Project (OtP), first derives the optimality system and then approximates both the state and adjoint equations using DLRA. The second one, called Project-then-Optimize (PtO), first replaces the state equation with its DLR approximation, and then derives the optimality conditions for the resulting optimization problem. The two approaches differ fundamentally concerning the role of the adjoint variable. In OtP, the adjoint variable evolves on the manifold of fixed rank matrices, whereas in PtO, the adjoint variable belongs to the tangent space to the fixed-rank manifold at the evolving state variable. This latter formulation leads to a covariant ODE describing the dynamics of the adjoint variable as the underlying tangent space evolves in time. For both approaches we establish rigorous error estimates for the approximated gradients, identifying how their accuracy depends on the low-rank approximations of initial and terminal conditions, the components of the state and adjoint vector fields normal to the relevant tangent spaces, the stability properties of the dynamics, and the manifold curvature. PtO further requires tailored time discretization strategies for the adjoint covariant ODE, which we show to be robust against small singular values of the state variable. To illustrate the framework, we apply these methods to the optimal control of a random parabolic PDE.

papers.title: A design concept for the High Resolution Imager on the Habitable Worlds Observatory
papers.abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will be NASA's next flagship astrophysics mission, designed to search for signs of life on planets around nearby stars and conduct transformational science across astrophysics. Its High Resolution Imager (HRI) is not only the observatory's main imaging camera, but also provides grism spectroscopy and sub-microarcsecond astrometry, as well as the observatory's fine guidance, wavefront sensing and pupil imaging. We present a design concept for HRI, developed during concurrent design sessions by flowing down science requirements within the envelope of NASA's EAC-1 telescope architecture. Light from a 3'x2' field is collimated by two mirrors, then divided by a dichroic for simultaneous observations in an ultraviolet-to-visible arm covering 200-900 nm and a near-infrared arm covering 0.9-2.2 um. By minimising the number of reflective surfaces upstream of the dichroic, our optical design maximises throughput and stability, while reducing wavefront error. Readout modes can be chosen in orbit to image the entire field in exposures of at least 10 seconds, or in smaller windows for observations up to 1 kHz. Throughout, we emphasise the interplay between subsystems that couple design choices.

papers.intro:
The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) is the large ultraviolet, optical and infrared space telescope recommended by the most recent US decadal survey (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2021). It is intended to launch around 2040 and, when it does, it will be the most capable telescope ever flown. Its defining goal is the search for signs of life on planets orbiting other stars, but HWO also inherits the role that Hubble and JWST have played for the wider astrophysics and cosmology community. To meet that broad remit, NASA’s 2023–25 Science, Technology and Architecture Review Team (START) assembled 76 science investigations spanning exoplanets, the Solar system, stellar and galactic astrophysics and cosmology (Scowen et al., 2025; Dressing and others, 2026).

The observatory architecture draws on two earlier large mission concept studies, LUVOIR (The LUVOIR Team, 2019) and HabEx (Gaudi and others, 2020). At least three instruments are expected at launch: a coronagraph, a multi-object spectrograph, and a High Resolution Imager (HRI; see Figure 1). HRI is the observatory’s main imaging camera. Several virtual telescope designs known as Engineering Architecture Concepts (EAC) currently exist (Feinberg et al., 2024; Feinberg et al., 2026). The EAC-1 baseline design calls for imaging over a 3′×2′3^{\prime}\times 2^{\prime} field with more than fifty filters spanning the ultraviolet to the near-infrared, several grisms for slitless spectroscopy, and an astrometric capability at the sub-microarcsecond level (Liu et al., 2026). It is required by 33 of the 76 investigations, more than any other instrument. A broad summary of the science that motivates the HRI instrument described here, together with the interests of the community that assembled this study, is given by Van Eylen et al. (2025).

Three observatory-level roles add to HRI’s requirements and design. It should supply telescope fine guidance (from continuous, rapid measurements of astrometry of bright guide stars) to keep the telescope pointed at its science target; wavefront sensing to maintain the phasing and alignment of HWO’s segmented primary mirror; and pupil plane imaging to acquire ‘selfie’ images of that mirror, to monitor micrometeorite or other damage. Together these mean that HRI is not simply the instrument that produces the mission’s imaging data, which potentially has the broadest impact; it is a piece of observatory infrastructure. Unlike other instruments it cannot be deferred to a servicing mission, because without it the telescope cannot be pointed or aligned.

This paper describes a concept study for HRI carried out by a UK-led consortium with a French partner responsible for the astrometric channel. The study was funded by the UK Space Agency and executed largely through two intensive sessions at a Concurrent Design Facility (CDF), with daily contact with NASA staff so that the design could track the mission architecture as it evolved. The work was baselined against NASA’s EAC-1, a 6 m off-axis segmented telescope with a room temperature optical train, an ff-number of 20.4 at the focal plane, and an orbit at the second Earth–Sun Lagrange point L2. Several other candidate architectures, EACs 2-6, are being considered and the next phase of this study will adopt some of these other designs.

HRI comprises an Imager, itself split into an ultraviolet–visible (UVIS) channel and a near-infrared (NIR) channel, together with an astrometric channel that also supplies the fine guidance function. The astrometric channel has its own focal plane fed directly by the telescope, with intentionally no foreoptics, to minimise sources of unknown field distortion and to add stability. It is developed by a separate team and is described in detail by Amiaux and others (2025); its scientific rationale, and in particular the measurement of true masses for the potentially habitable planets that the coronagraph will identify, is set out by Malbet and others (2026). We therefore discuss the astrometric channel in this paper only where it shares resources with the Imager. It sits inside the same enclosure, draws on the same power and data processing units, and is the single largest consumer of the instrument’s thermal and power budgets.

We aim to explain the reasoning behind the design rather than to document it exhaustively, because the details will change with further EACs. Section 2 traces the flowdown from science cases to numerical requirements. Section 3 describes the optical design, the argument for keeping the number of reflective surfaces small, and the fine guidance, wavefront sensing and pupil imaging functions that the same optics provide for the observatory as a whole. Section 4 describes the focal planes and, in particular, the readout modes that let one piece of hardware behave as several different instruments. Sections 5 to 7 cover the thermal, mechanical and electronic architectures. Section 8 draws out the couplings between these subsystems, which we regard as the most important result of the study, and Section 9 sets out what needs to happen next.

papers.title: Early versus Late RGB-Infrared Fusion for Counter-UAV Detection: A Comparative Study
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel strategy for UAV detection through visible (RGB) and infrared (IR) fusion, in order to improve accuracy and precision in harsh environments and weather conditions. In this research, two opposite approaches have been studied and implemented: the first concerns image-level (early) fusion, which merges two different spectra into a single image to which one detector is applied. On the other hand, the second approach, called decision-level (late) fusion, focuses on blending together the output bounding boxes of two different detection pipelines, aiming to create a common result that can be applied to both spectra simultaneously. Both strategies have been extensively tested in a dedicated environment, which included alternating low and high brightness scenes, different backgrounds (sky and ground), distances (5, 25 and 60 m), altitudes and zoom levels (1X, 2X and 4X). These tests allowed for the assessment of actual detection capabilities and system reliability in real-world applications. Furthermore, the two fusion strategies were evaluated and compared over a set of aligned images in order to highlight the better approach of the two. The results indicate that early fusion achieves better raw performance, since it incorporates the thermal information from the beginning of the training process. However, late fusion presents an innovative and useful detection workflow that can be applied in cases of sensor or frame misalignment. Both positive and negative aspects have also been pointed out and discussed, in order to give a more comprehensive overview. Finally, the paper outlines implementation considerations and practical recommendations based on operational priorities. Overall, the findings contribute to the research in RGB-IR fusion modalities, with the goal of enhancing UAV detection capabilities.

papers.intro:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are becoming increasingly common in military and civilian applications. They can be used in surveillance, mapping and transporting materials. However, there are safety and security concerns which have to be taken into consideration, since modern UAVs might be able to operate in varied environments and evade traditional surveillance methods. In order to reduce these weaknesses, many advanced sensors are used in current scenarios. For example, visible light (RGB) cameras are widely adopted, as they offer excellent spatial resolutions and reduced costs [1]. However, they have problems in low light, adverse weather conditions [2] and crowded backgrounds. Concerning this particular aspect, the terrain texture may be difficult to separate from the drone’s surface, since UAVs are usually made from composite and camouflaged materials. On the other hand, infrared (IR) cameras work effectively in low light situations and night scenes. Nevertheless, they have reduced thermal and spatial resolution and are expensive. Therefore, this research focuses on fused solutions for UAV detection, aiming to combine the strengths of both sensors [3]. There are some studies in Computer Vision which have explored the capabilities of sensor fusion strategies in object detection systems [4]. However, the Counter-UAV setting still remains an underexplored research area for fusion. Most of the existing approaches require significant adjustments and fixes to the sensors before fusion can be applied. In this paper, the following innovative fusion pipelines for YOLO-based Counter-UAV detection have been adopted and evaluated: • An image-level (early) fusion that composes synchronized and aligned RGB and IR inputs into a unified representation for a single detector. • A decision-level (late) fusion that processes RGB and IR streams independently and merges their detections post-inference.

papers.title: Data-driven calibration of a two-dimensional traffic flow model: Dimension reduction and optimization strategies
papers.abstract: We study the data-driven calibration of a two-dimensional first-order macroscopic traffic flow model, in which the movement along and across the road is described by a three-parameter flux model. The calibration is based on three real-world datasets, ranging from microscopic drone trajectories on German highways to aggregated urban sensor measurements. We recall the well-posedness of the underlying scalar conservation law and derive structural properties of the flux model. In particular, one parameter enters linearly and can be eliminated analytically, which reduces the non-linear least-squares problem from three to two dimensions. We solve the full and reduced calibration problem with two local optimization methods, Nelder-Mead and L-BFGS-B, and three global population-based methods Differential Evolution, Consensus-Based Optimization, and its deterministic variant Quasi-Monte Carlo consensus based optimization. In addition to accuracy and computational cost, we examine how sensitive the objective is to the parameters and how robust the algorithms are with respect to randomness and initialization. The reduced formulation is considerably cheaper and less sensitive to the choice of optimizer. The local methods are the most efficient when suitably initialized, whereas the global methods are more robust.

papers.title: Multi-Objective Protein Optimization via Modular Diffusion Steering
papers.abstract: Protein engineering often requires improving several properties simultaneously, motivating the search for high-performing sequences that represent useful fitness tradeoffs. Discovering these sequences is challenging because the design space is combinatorially large and experimental campaigns often permit only a few rounds of batched measurements. We introduce \textit{MODS}, a modular framework for multi-objective protein optimization via inference-time diffusion steering. For each proposal, MODS samples augmented Chebyshev scalarization weights and a fitness-surrogate ensemble member to define a scalar steering reward. Varying the weights directs generation toward different objective tradeoffs, while varying ensemble members diversifies the predictions used for guidance. Because MODS expresses multi-objective acquisition through scalar rewards, it can be paired with different diffusion models and compatible steering procedures. After each evaluation batch, MODS updates the surrogates without retraining the generative model. We evaluate MODS on six protein optimization tasks using predictive oracles trained on experimental assay data, with two diffusion models and two steering procedures. MODS achieves competitive final hypervolume across all six tasks with both diffusion models, and substantially outperforms the best evaluated baseline on several tasks. Our results demonstrate a flexible and effective approach to multi-objective protein optimization with limited feedback.

papers.title: First-principles modeling of ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys
papers.abstract: The atomic ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys strongly influences their magnetic properties and mechanical behavior. While general features of long-range atomic ordering are known from the experimentally established phase diagram in this composition range, detailed atomic configurations and driving forces behind them remain speculative. Here, we address this gap by using effective cluster interactions (ECI) obtained from density functional theory (DFT) calculations and subsequent statistical thermodynamics modeling to unravel the interplay between magnetism, composition, and temperature in body-centered cubic (bcc) Fe-Si alloys up to 20 at% Si. Our analysis reveals that the ordering behavior is governed by a strong coupling between magnetic order, lattice expansion, and Si concentration, with specific ECI shells switching sign or magnitude as the magnetic state changes, which is reflected in the phase equilibria and ordering behavior of Fe-Si alloys. In particular, we demonstrate that D0$_3$ ordering is, in fact, primary in the totally ordered ferromagnetic state, while the B2 type of ordering is promoted in the paramagnetic state at elevated temperatures. The temperature-dependent evolution of these ordering patterns, obtained from Monte Carlo simulations based on the magnetically resolved ECIs, reproduces the experimentally observed phase equilibria and short-range order characteristics. By explicitly linking the magnetic state with the effective interactions and macroscopic phase behavior, this work establishes a predictive framework for an ab initio-based description of ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys and highlights the decisive role of magnetism in ordering phenomena in this system.

papers.intro:
The unique electromagnetic properties of Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys make them a perfect choice for the production of transformers and electric motors. These so-called electrical steels have improved energy efficiency due to reduced core losses and enhanced magnetic permeability. These are bcc random alloys with a Si content usually below 12 at%. At the same time, a large body of experimental data suggests that the origin of these magnetic properties is related to a specific B2-type atomic short-range order (SRO), i.e., the existence of pairs of Si atoms at the second coordination shell of the bcc lattice (see, for instance, [11, 12]). If Si content exceeds 6 wt% or 12 at%, these alloys suffer from significantly reduced ductility, preventing the development of steels with more advanced properties. The origin of brittleness in such high-Si electrical steels is also attributed to atomic ordering, namely, a precipitation of the Fe3Si-D03 ordered phase, which, according to the existing phase diagrams should occur at temperatures below around 800800 K at this concentration [32, 19, 8]. This means that knowing the details of the atomic ordering phenomena in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys and understanding their origin is of prime importance for the scientifically guided development of electrical steels.

Several experimental investigations of atomic SRO in random Fe–Si alloys with compositions corresponding to electrical steels have been reported (see, in particular, [6, 12]). Although detailed information on the atomic SRO is limited due to experimental restrictions for dilute alloys, the prevailing consensus is that a B2-type SRO dominates in alloys with Si content below 8 at%, whereas a D03-type SRO emerges at higher Si concentrations. At the same time, theoretical studies of atomic ordering in these alloys remain scarce, likely due to the complex nature of interatomic interactions driven by magnetism, which is extremely challenging to model accurately in ab initio calculations. In fact, there exists only one ab initio investigation of effective interactions and atomic SRO in Fe–(4–10) at% Si by Gorbatov et al. [15]. As demonstrated in that work, increasing magnetic order promotes D03-type atomic ordering; that is, only the B2-type SRO exists in the paramagnetic state, while upon lowering the temperature, the D03-type SRO appears in the ferromagnetic state, consistent with experimental observations.

papers.title: S-PASS: Star-Topology Pinching-Antenna Systems with Pipelined Antenna Pre-Positioning
papers.abstract: Pinching-antenna systems (PASS) flexibly reconfigure the wireless channel by positioning dielectric antennas along a waveguide near each user. Releasing and re-attaching an antenna, however, is a mechanical operation orders of magnitude slower than electronic switching, wasting much transmission time. Existing designs generally assume instant reconfiguration, neglect the mechanical latency, or keep the antenna fixed. This paper proposes S-PASS, a star architecture of waveguides sharing one radio-frequency chain through a switch, and pipelined antenna pre-positioning (PAP), a time-division protocol in which idle waveguides pre-position their antennas for their next users while one transmits. It derives in closed form the scheduling efficiency, the number of waveguides beyond which the latency costs no transmission time, and the latency up to which PAP outperforms fixed placement. Analytical and numerical results show that this latency grows with each added waveguide, and users at the outer ends of the waveguides gain most.

papers.intro:
Pinching-antenna systems (PASS) [1, 2, 3] apply a dielectric particle, a “pinch”, to a waveguide to create a radiation point, a pinching antenna (PA), within meters of a user. Large-scale path loss and line-of-sight blockage become design variables. For multi-user service on a single waveguide, re-pinching, i.e., releasing the pinch and re-attaching it at the next user’s position, enables time-division multiple access (TDMA) with every user served from the point on the waveguide closest to it. In the symmetric-rate two-user example of [4], such re-pinched TDMA needs less transmit power than fixed-placement power-domain non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), because a fixed placement penalizes the user farthest from the pinch. This advantage assumes that re-pinching takes no time. In practice, releasing the pinch and re-attaching it elsewhere is a mechanical cycle that can take milliseconds to seconds. A recent survey of reconfigurable antennas names the mismatch between that timescale and the much faster scheduling loop “a key unresolved issue” [5]. A re-pinch of tens of milliseconds can leave the channel idle for many slots. Re-pinched TDMA incurs this overhead between slots requiring different PA positions, whereas fixed-placement NOMA avoids it.

Existing designs treat reconfiguration latency in different ways. Waveguide switching and multiplexing studies [6], the access protocols of segmented waveguide-enabled PASS (SWAN) [7, 8], and a switched-feed design that routes one radio-frequency (RF) chain among star-arranged waveguide segments to reduce terahertz in-guide loss [9] model at most the electronic switching time, not the mechanical latency. On a single waveguide, the latency of re-pinched TDMA has been modeled as a guard interval [10], and antenna roaming accepts a finite moving speed and lets the antenna transmit while it travels [11]. Movable-antenna designs trade movement time against transmission time [12], and electronically reconfigurable pinching avoids movement but radiates only where elements were installed [13]. None of them lets an idle PA move while another waveguide transmits, the case analyzed in this paper.

On these arms, pipelined antenna pre-positioning (PAP), a TDMA protocol, moves the antennas of the idle arms to their next users while one arm transmits, so that motion and transmission overlap as in a processor pipeline. The S in S-PASS stands for both features, the star topology and the scheduling it enables. Both features set S-PASS apart from center-fed PASS (C-PASS) [14], which splits the power at the center of a single waveguide so that both halves radiate at once, and which does not consider antenna movement time. PAP absorbs the latency completely once enough arms share a balanced load and partly otherwise, and it reduces to conventional TDMA as the latency vanishes. The main contributions are as follows. • We propose the S-PASS architecture and the PAP protocol. S-PASS feeds all arms at the central hub, where one RF chain reaches them through a switch, whereas SWAN feeds its segments at remote points along the waveguide, which requires cabling to each feed. An isolated arm failure removes only its own sector. Each arm carries a single PA, so the pre-positioned antennas leave the uplink free of the inter-antenna radiation (IAR) that couples several active pinches on one waveguide [7]. • We derive the scheduling efficiency of PAP, the fraction of the frame that carries payload, over finite frames in closed form for its interleaved and burst schedules, the number of arms beyond which the latency costs no transmission time, and the latency up to which PAP outperforms the fixed-placement NOMA reference and fixed-placement TDMA. papers.title: DewHand: Direct Metric World-Space Hand Motion Reconstruction from Egocentric Videos
papers.abstract: Recovering metric world-space hand motion from egocentric video supports understanding human interactions and transferring them to embodied agents. Three challenges complicate this task: multi-stage pipelines propagate errors from independently estimated hand and camera motion; monocular observations leave physical scale ambiguous; and occlusion and out-of-view hands admit multiple plausible motion trajectories. We present DewHand, a unified model for direct joint reconstruction of world-space hand and camera motion. To avoid compounding errors from multi-stage estimation, DewHand jointly predicts hand and camera motion in a shared world coordinate system within a single-stage pipeline. To resolve metric-scale ambiguity, it combines scene-level geometric features from VGGT-$Ω$ with metric-space supervision, while hand-specific features preserve fine-grained articulation. To handle occlusion and out-of-view hands, we formulate reconstruction as conditional motion generation with flow matching. Under the same architecture, this generative formulation outperforms direct regression in both accuracy and temporal smoothness with only two sampling steps. Experiments on HOT3D and ARCTIC demonstrate improved world-space accuracy and temporal consistency over state-of-the-art methods. DewHand reduces rigid-aligned world-space error relative to StableHand from 32.9 to 28.4 mm on HOT3D and from 76.2 to 36.2 mm on ARCTIC. It also recovers camera scale within 10% on two thirds of HOT3D clips, versus about a quarter for SLAM. Moreover, in zero-shot evaluations on HoloAssist, H2O, and TACO, captured with different devices, DewHand achieves the lowest rigid-aligned world-space error (WA-MPJPE) on each dataset.

Consider a wearer reaching for an object while turning their head. In camera coordinates, even a stationary hand appears to move with the camera; conversely, camera motion can hide or amplify the hand’s motion in the image. A useful reconstruction must separate these effects and preserve the hand’s position relative to the surrounding scene throughout the interaction.

Three challenges motivate our formulation. First, accurate local hand reconstruction does not by itself ensure a consistent world-space trajectory. Despite strong per-frame estimators (Pavlakos et al., 2024; Potamias et al., 2025), existing world-space pipelines typically estimate hands and camera motion separately, compose their outputs, and optionally apply temporal optimization or motion-prior refinement (Zhang et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026). Camera drift and mismatches between these estimates can therefore propagate into the reconstructed hand motion. Second, monocular video provides projective observations rather than direct metric measurements, leaving physical scale ambiguous even when local articulation is accurately recovered. Third, self-occlusion, hand-object interactions, motion blur, and frequent exits from the field of view make hand observations incomplete. The visible evidence may be consistent with multiple motion trajectories, motivating a conditional distribution over hand and camera motion.

papers.title: Geometry-Conditioned Target Speaker Extraction based on spatial features incorporating acoustic propagation principles
papers.abstract: Recently, spatially selective non-linear filter (SSF) was proposed for target speaker extraction, utilizing the direction-of-arrival (DOA) of the target speaker as a spatial cue. To overcome its dependency on a fixed microphone array geometry, geometry-conditioned SSF (GCSSF) was proposed, which maps the target DOA and the microphone positions into abstract high-dimensional embeddings using positional encoding. As an alternative to these high-dimensional embeddings, in this paper we propose utilizing two spatial features incorporating acoustic propagation principles for geometry conditioning: 1) the steering vector of the target speaker, which captures inter-microphone phase differences, and 2) a spatial mask based on GCC-PHAT, which quantifies presence of the target speaker per time-frequency bin. These features are used as input to a geometry-conditioning encoder and integrated via a FiLM layer into the GCSSF system. Experimental results on circular and random arrays demonstrate that conditioning with spatial features improves target extraction performance compared to abstract high-dimensional embeddings, maintaining a clear performance advantage across a wide range of target DOA errors.

papers.intro:
Extracting a target speaker from a mixture of speakers and background noise remains a fundamental challenge in acoustic signal processing [28]. To discriminate the target speaker from interfering sources, various cues have been proposed, such as enrollment utterances [27, 20], visual information [12], and spatial features [4, 24, 8, 19]. In this paper, we focus on the spatially selective non-linear filter (SSF) proposed in [24]. The SSF utilizes the target direction-of-arrival (DOA) as a spatial cue and uses Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layers to estimate a complex-valued mask that is applied to the reference microphone signal to extract the target speaker.

Despite its effectiveness, a limitation of the standard SSF is its inherent dependency on the fixed microphone array geometry considered during training. Recently, geometry-agnostic systems have been proposed for noise reduction [7, 22, 26, 10], blind speaker separation [11], and target speaker extraction [23, 9]. While the system in [23] is restricted to a fixed look direction, the geometry-conditioned SSF (GCSSF) system in [9] allows for arbitrary DOA-steered extraction. The GCSSF system utilizes microphone positional encoding (MPE) [2] to map the target DOA and microphone positions into abstract high-dimensional sinusoidal embeddings.

Similar to the MPE features in [9], these features are used as input to the geometry-conditioning branch of the GCSSF, which includes an encoder and a Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) layer [14]. In the experimental evaluation, the proposed GCSSF systems using the proposed spatial features as well as the baseline SSF and the GCSSF-MPE system are trained on random arrays and evaluated on both circular and random arrays. Experimental results demonstrate that conditioning the network with explicit spatial features consistently outperforms the baselines across all evaluated metrics, with the TSV feature yielding the best performance. Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis demonstrates that the proposed systems maintain better target speaker extraction performance than the baseline systems for target DOA errors up to 20∘20^{\circ}.

papers.title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Realistic Scenarios Through Representation Engineering
papers.abstract: Reward hacking is a major problem in current production machine learning systems, resulting in costly and dangerous failures. Here we study how to monitor for and mitigate reward hacking in realistic settings, including tool calls and long contexts. We apply a dynamic intervention to steering directions obtained by three different methods: difference-in-means vectors from labeled rollouts, gradient optimization-based vectors, and vectors extracted when models reference an anti-reward-hacking model spec. This dynamic intervention perturbs model representations less than uniform steering vector addition to the residual stream, allowing for more precise edits. We find that we are able to cheaply and significantly reduce reward hacking without correspondingly significant costs to model coherence or capability, and that steering vectors originally extracted from coding environments also generalize to reducing reward hacking in other domains. Our results pave the way towards latent space monitoring and control over realistic production systems.

papers.intro:
Reward hacking is a well known failure mode in machine learning systems, where models learn to increase reward on a proxy objective in ways that model developers don’t intend. This can lead to many safety issues when those models go into downstream production (MacDiarmid et al., 2025). This is no longer a theoretical concern. Recent events involving an agent swarm penetrating HuggingFace’s infrastructure were due in large part to misconfigured training environments which the agent hacked to increase its reward (METR, 2026). As agents continue to grow in prevalence and capability, this failure mode will correspondingly become much more important than its current state. We propose inference time techniques for monitoring and mitigating reward hacking in realistic agentic coding environments over long contexts.

We propose inference time techniques for monitoring and mitigating reward hacking in realistic agentic coding environments over long contexts.

Inference time interventions work well only when the behavior can be cheaply detected and mitigated against. We find that this is the case in our setting. A small number of labeled rollouts is sufficient to identify a direction that is useful not only for monitoring, but also for dynamic steering via representation engineering (Turner et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023). We use activation capping from Lu et al. (2026) to suppress reward hacking by intervening only when activations exceed some threshold along the hacking direction, minimizing collateral effects on other capabilities. This allows model developers to be more confident in applying this technique, as it will minimally alter representations and only in a small, predictable fraction of a model’s rollouts.

papers.title: Revealing Hidden Failure Modes in Chest X-ray Classification via Spectral Domain Analysis
papers.abstract: Deep learning models for chest X-ray anomaly detection remain vulnerable to subtle distributional shifts (e.g., acquisition technique, patient-related factors, and preprocessing). Traditional error analysis often relies on semantic metadata or model embeddings, which can mask low-level signal variations that degrade performance. In this work, we propose a data-centric framework for automated failure mode discovery using spectral analysis. We project images into the frequency domain and extract a compact profile summarizing the distribution of signal energy across frequency bands. By performing unsupervised clustering on these spectral profiles, we demonstrate that model failures are not randomly distributed, but are strongly concentrated within specific spectral clusters. This method effectively isolates "blind spots", enabling the prediction of model reliability and the discovery of performance-degrading data slices without requiring ground-truth failure annotations.

Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in the interpretation of chest X-rays (CXRs), where algorithms now frequently match or exceed radiologist performance in controlled settings Katzman et al. (2024); Bettinger et al. (2024). However, in the context of clinical deployment, models often fail to generalize to data that deviates statistically from their training distribution, resulting in significant and unanticipated performance degradation Zech et al. (2018); Yu et al. (2022). Ensuring the reliability of these systems requires the ability to anticipate and identify failure modes before they impact patient care.

papers.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Detecting Satirical Code-Mixed Sentences
papers.abstract: Code-switching is a natural linguistic phenomenon, yet its impact on high-level reasoning tasks remains largely unexplored in under-resourced languages like Romanian. Natural language processing tasks, such as satire detection, rely heavily on nuanced cultural and syntactic cues that large language models struggle to capture. In this paper, we investigate four methods (i.e., random replacement, phrase translation, dependency parsing, and large language models) for generating synthetic code-mixed Romanian sentences with English, German, French, and Italian. We start with an existing dataset for satire detection, compiled from Romanian news articles and annotated at the sentence level by humans, and augment it with over 600k samples, namely CS-SeLeRoSa. We provide an in-depth analysis of the dataset generation process. Then, we evaluate several multilingual large language models across zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and fine-tuning regimes on both the synthetic corpus and a human-adjudicated gold benchmark, namely CS-SeLeRoSa-Gold. While older open models suffer substantial degradation (dropping to 37%-55% macro-F1), newer models like Gemma 4 31B achieve 68.1% zero-shot, rivaling frontier models like GPT-5 mini (69.5%). Furthermore, fine-tuning significantly reduces formatting errors and improves the results, increasing Gemma 4 31B to 77.5% on CS-SeLeRoSa and 72.6% on the gold standard, outperforming frontier zero-shot baselines.

papers.intro:
Code-switching or code-mixing is a common phenomenon in multilingual communities in which speakers alternate between two or more languages within the same sentence Guzmán et al. (2017). While early natural language processing (NLP) and linguistic studies primarily mapped constraints on widely spoken pairs, the structural behavior of code-switching shifts significantly when applied to morphologically rich languages Myers-Scotton (1993).

Code-switching was previously explored in the context of satire, irony, and humor detection, but primarily in other combinations, such as Hindi-English Bansal et al. (2020); Aggarwal et al. (2020); Mazumder et al. (2025) or Spanish-English. For example, Bansal et al. (2020) investigated Hindi-English code-mixed tweets for detecting humor, sarcasm, and hate speech, arguing that code-mixing can be used to emphasize these phenomena. They also show that it can improve the model’s performance on downstream tasks. Belani and Flanigan (2023) proposed a dataset generated from transcribing day-by-day conversations for Spanish-English with various labels, including usage of code-mixing for jokes. Pant and Dadu (2020) proposed mapping the code-switched text to a higher-resource language through transliteration and showing improved performance for sarcasm and hate speech detection. However, this remains an underexplored area due to data scarcity. Consequently, many studies, including ours, rely on synthetic generation. This practice has positively spurred the community to develop diverse generation techniques, even though most evaluations continue to focus on downstream tasks using existing, naturally code-mixed text Aguilar et al. (2020); Sheth et al. (2025).

papers.title: Auditing Conformal Prediction for Language Models Under Inference-Time Model Shift
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) for language models is typically evaluated under a matched protocol, in which calibration and deployment use the same post-training inference configuration, such as quantization mode and inference temperature. In deployment, these choices often differ from those used at calibration to meet memory or throughput constraints or serving policies. We argue that this exposes a limitation in current CP evaluation protocols for language models. We formalize the underlying phenomenon as inference-time model shift: a change in the conformal score distribution induced by inference configuration rather than by the input--label distribution, and theoretically characterize how it breaks split-conformal exchangeability even when the task distribution and trained model are unchanged. We then evaluate its consequences across 8 language models, 4 finite-label benchmarks, and 12 inference configurations. We find that matched evaluation can substantially overstate deployment-time coverage, and that the effect is heterogeneous across models and datasets. We argue that inference configuration should be reported as a first-class experimental axis in CP evaluations for language-model systems.

papers.intro:
Conformal prediction (CP) is a distribution-free framework for uncertainty quantification: given a trained predictor and a held-out calibration set, it returns a prediction set guaranteed to contain the true label with a user-specified probability 1−α1-\alpha in finite samples Vovk et al. (2005); Angelopoulos and Bates (2023). The guarantee is obtained by calibrating a threshold on nonconformity scores, which are real-valued scores of disagreement between the predictor’s output and a candidate label, and rests on an important assumption: that calibration and test scores are exchangeable. A substantial literature studies how this assumption fails when the data-generating distribution shifts, including covariate shift, label shift, online drift, and other forms of non-exchangeability Tibshirani et al. (2019); Gibbs and Candès (2021); Oliveira et al. (2024). In each case, the source of failure is a change in the joint distribution PX​YP_{XY} between calibration and deployment.

papers.title: Integrating Flow Matching and Model Predictive Control for Safe Robot Navigation
papers.abstract: Learning-based path planners based on diffusion and flow matching can generate diverse trajectories from demonstrations but typically lack mechanisms for constraint satisfaction and collision avoidance during deployment. This work proposes a framework that combines flow-matching-based path planning with model predictive path-following control to integrate data-driven path generation with real-time, constraint-aware execution. The flow-matching model captures multimodal path distributions, while the predictive controller adapts motion online to satisfy state and input constraints and avoid obstacles using updated local sensor information. An event-triggered re-planning scheme incorporates predictive control solutions into subsequent path generation, promoting collision-free navigation in environments with previously unseen obstacles. Simulation results for mobile robot navigation demonstrate robust performance across cluttered environments. The framework provides a systematic approach to combining flow matching with predictive control for adaptive, data-driven navigation.

papers.title: Certified Neural Approximation of Robust Nonlinear Model Predictive Control
papers.abstract: Model predictive control is a high-performance control method, but it incurs comparatively high online computational costs across many control tasks and is challenging to realize in low-level hardware settings. To address this, we present a framework for generating neural network controllers that provably inherit the safety and stability guarantees of a robust model predictive policy. In contrast to approaches based on post-verification or additional online safety filters, our method provides constructive, a priori design conditions that ensure preservation of recursive feasibility and stability before deployment. We treat the approximation error as a bounded input disturbance, which is addressed in the MPC design. This allows the neural network controller to directly inherit robustness from the underlying model predictive controller, which enables the transfer of guarantees to the approximation. The design process is an offline, constructive synthesis pipeline and can be implemented once Lipschitz bounds are specified. We further demonstrate in simulation that the learned controller reproduces the closed-loop behavior of the original controller while reducing online computation.

papers.title: Unlocking Spatial Grounding in Flow-Matching Models via SNR Tuning
papers.abstract: Despite the success of foundation models in image synthesis, achieving fine-grained spatial control remains a significant challenge, typically requiring auxiliary structural adapters or complex inference-time steering. While modern vision-language (VLM) text encoders possess the latent capacity to represent spatial coordinates, generative models often fail to leverage this information. We demonstrate that the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution is a critical determinant of spatial grounding in flow-matching models. Using a novel synthetic benchmark of geometric primitives, we isolate structural mechanics from textural complexity inherent in natural imagery and introduce a rigorous color-aware layout metric to quantify spatial fidelity. We show that training on a centered SNR distribution results in poor layout adherence (25.9%). Instead, we identify high-noise regimes as a "critical learning phase" for spatial grounding. Shifting the training focus toward these stages increases layout adherence to 80.8%, effectively reaching the 83.6% reconstruction ceiling of the underlying variational autoencoder. We find that the necessity for this shift scales with resolution and aspect ratio variance, and that the conservative noise schedules employed by models like FLUX.1 are insufficient for precise layout adherence. Finally, we show that these findings translate to real-world imagery via the COCO dataset (1.0 vs. 57.3 Average Precision), where state-of-the-art layout adherence is unlocked through distribution tuning alone, without architectural modifications.

papers.title: Optimized Compressor Parameterization for Produced Music in Hearing Aids
papers.abstract: Hearing aid compression is typically designed for speech, yet music demands different trade-offs due to its narrower dynamic range (DR) and impulsive transients. This paper investigates whether music fitting benefits from being signal-aware, both in mapping compression demand across signal-audiogram conditions and in tuning its parameters to these combinations rather than inheriting them from speech-derived prescriptions. Compression demand is characterized across eight audiometric profiles, three residual DR severities, and three produced music signals under linear gain. Signal dynamics emerge as a first-order factor: production-compressed music fits the residual DR of the mild-to-moderate profiles evaluated, while dynamically rich recordings challenge even moderate hearing loss. Per-signal optimization of single- and multi-band wide dynamic range compression is then applied to two profiles with the highest compression demand. This optimization improves the Hearing Aid Audio Quality Index over gain-optimized NAL-NL2 baselines while also improving audibility, indicating substantial headroom for music-specific fitting.
papers.intro:
Music listening is an important use case for hearing aids, yet hearing aid design and evaluation remain focused on speech intelligibility [20]. Produced (i.e., mixed and mastered) music differs from speech in ways relevant to hearing aid processing: it typically exhibits a narrower dynamic range (DR) [14] and is often listened to at higher levels [5, 19]. These properties place demands on wide dynamic range compression (WDRC) that speech-oriented designs are not optimized to meet.

Produced (i.e., mixed and mastered) music differs from speech in ways relevant to hearing aid processing: it typically exhibits a narrower dynamic range (DR) [14] and is often listened to at higher levels [5, 19]. These properties place demands on wide dynamic range compression (WDRC) that speech-oriented designs are not optimized to meet.

Commercial hearing aids often offer dedicated music programs, typically with slower compression and reduced noise reduction [20, 17]. However, evidence for their effectiveness is inconclusive [9, 10]. Objective-function-driven optimization of insertion gains and compression thresholds has been explored for speech intelligibility [8], but direct optimization of compressor parameterization for music remains unexplored.

However, evidence for their effectiveness is inconclusive [9, 10]. Objective-function-driven optimization of insertion gains and compression thresholds has been explored for speech intelligibility [8], but direct optimization of compressor parameterization for music remains unexplored.

A key factor in compression demand may be the listener’s residual DR, the range between hearing threshold (HTL) and uncomfortable loudness level (UCL). Sensorineural hearing loss (HL) often reduces this range through loudness recruitment and, with hyperacusis, through lowered UCLs [16]. Hearing aid users generally prefer reduced or no compression for music [14, 4], but whether this is possible without sacrificing audibility likely depends on residual DR. As hearing loss becomes more severe, compression becomes more strongly indicated, yet also more detrimental to music quality [14]. How compression demand varies across audiogram shape and residual DR severity has not been systematically characterized, and commercially released recordings already undergo multi-stage compression [14], potentially reducing the need for further processing.

This paper addresses two questions: how compression demand varies across HL profile, residual DR, and music signal dynamics; and whether per-signal parameter optimization improves objective compression quality beyond fixed clinical fittings. The contributions are: (1) a continuous characterization of compression demand across eight HL profiles with three residual DR classes each, showing that signal dynamics is a first-order factor comparable to residual DR severity; and (2) per-signal optimization of 1-, 7-, and 20-channel WDRC for two audiograms with strong compression demand, revealing a quality–audibility trade-off shaped by audiogram and signal dynamics, with multi-band architectures improving HAAQI relative to gain-optimized NAL-NL2 baselines [13].

papers.title: Recent upgrades to the CRIS Decay Spectroscopy Station: Accessing $β$- and $γ$-ray spectroscopy on pure isomeric beams
papers.abstract: The Decay Spectroscopy Station (DSS) of the Collinear Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy (CRIS) experiment at ISOLDE-CERN has been upgraded to perform isomer-selective $β$- and $γ$-ray spectroscopy, including a new tape system to perform spectroscopy, free from residual activity. The baseplate of the detection chamber was redesigned to incorporate the tape, a MicroTOF detector for beam diagnostics, and a custom-made, high-vacuum-compatible plastic scintillator. The vacuum operation reached a stable pressure of $10^{-7}$ mbar in the detection chamber, overcoming vacuum issues from the previous design. Around the detection chamber, up to three high-purity germanium (HPGe) detectors and four LaBr detectors can be installed, giving a total photopeak efficiency of the HPGe detectors of 7% at 200 keV. The implementation of a 24-channel digital DAQ system combines the detection array with the CRIS setup to perform laser-assisted $β$- and $γ$-ray spectroscopy. A commissioning experiment with isomeric beams of $^{106g,106m}$In, purified by narrow-band laser resonance ionization, showed complete removal of activity from the $β$ detector and full separation of the ground and isomeric state of $^{106}$In. An average $β$-detection efficiency of 19(2)% was determined from the experiment.

papers.intro:
Decay spectroscopy is a long-standing method to study the nuclear states of radioactive isotopes and stable isotopes. It allows measurements of, for example, the half-lives, branching ratios, and excitation energies of nuclear states populated by radioactive decays. Additionally, spins and parities can be assigned based on the multipolarities of the γ\gamma rays, conversion electron coefficients, and the underlying selection rules of the different decay channels Krane and Halliday (1987).

It allows measurements of, for example, the half-lives, branching ratios, and excitation energies of nuclear states populated by radioactive decays. Additionally, spins and parities can be assigned based on the multipolarities of the γ\gamma rays, conversion electron coefficients, and the underlying selection rules of the different decay channels Krane and Halliday (1987).

Despite the large variety of information accessible, decay spectroscopy measurements at radioactive ion beam facilities regularly deal with isobaric or isomeric contaminants, creating difficulties in disentangling the decay of interest. For example, close-lying isomers with similar half-lives and hyperfine structure (hfs) cannot be resolved, which can lead to erroneous interpretations van den Borne et al. (2025); Olaizola et al. (2025), such as wrong spin/parity assignments. In decay spectroscopy measurements, in-source resonance ionization spectroscopy Fedosseev et al. (2017) can be utilized to increase the purity of the isotope of interest in the delivered ion beam Andel et al. (2026). Here, the atomic structure, a unique fingerprint for each isotope, is probed with lasers to purify the mix of different elements that is extracted from ISOLDE targets. However, the limited resolution of in-source laser spectroscopy (FWHM of several GHz) restricts its application to selectively ionizing different isotopes where the hfs is well separated. In several cases, as in the example hfs of 106In shown in Fig. 1, the overlap between the hfs of two nuclear states does not enable suppression of isomeric contamination by in-source laser spectroscopy.

The DSS 2 added a new 1010 cm×10\times 10 cm×25\times 25 cm Al chamber containing an APIPS and a PIPS detector in line with the beam axis. The windmill design was replaced with a ladder design containing two carbon foils and a copper plate, used as a Faraday cup for beam tuning. A linear actuator was used to switch between the foils and the copper plate. papers.title: pplx-embed-v2-late Technical Report
papers.abstract: In this report, we introduce pplx-embed-v2-late, a pair of 0.6B and 9B multilingual and multimodal late-interaction models. Both models achieve state-of-the-art results within their respective size classes across a range of text, image, and visual document retrieval benchmarks. On visual document retrieval tasks, pplx-embed-v2-late-0.6b is competitive with models several times larger than itself. The models are trained via representation distillation from an 18B teacher. Consequently, they share an embedding space that supports asymmetric deployment: documents can be indexed with the 9B model and queried with the low-latency 0.6B model. Both models are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/perplexity-ai/pplx-embed-v2.

papers.intro:
Retrieval systems face a trade-off between efficiency and the depth of interaction between queries and documents. Dense embeddings interact via cheap inner products, which allow for efficient approximate nearest neighbor search. At the other extreme, cross-encoders process the query and document together, enabling richer interaction but requiring a separate forward pass for every ranked candidate. Late-interaction models (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) occupy the space between the two. Documents are indexed offline and represented as bags of embedding vectors. These document vectors interact with query vectors via the MaxSim rule, allowing richer interaction than dense embeddings (Jayaram, 2026). Late-interaction models have shown especially strong performance in out-of-domain settings (Santhanam et al., 2022; Clavié, 2024), long-context retrieval (Warner et al., 2025; Chaffin, 2025a; Takehi et al., 2025), agentic search (Chaffin, 2026; Mixedbread Team, 2026), and visual document retrieval (VDR) (Faysse et al., 2025; Günther et al., 2025).

In this report, we introduce pplx-embed-v2-late, a pair of 0.6B and 9B multimodal and multilingual late-interaction models. Both models are distilled at the representation level from a contrastively trained 18B teacher. We find that representation distillation outperforms contrastive training alone, especially at smaller model scales. Since the 0.6B and 9B models are trained to match the same teacher, the two encoders are interchangeable: a query embedded by the 0.6B model can be scored directly against an index built by the 9B model, and vice versa. This allows for hybrid deployment options where the latency-critical query path can be served by the fast 0.6B model while documents are indexed offline via the stronger 9B model, with the cost of indexing amortized over the lifetime of the index. Both models individually achieve state-of-the-art performance on a range of text, image, and VDR benchmarks, including ViDoRe-V3 (Loison et al., 2026). In concurrent work, Liu et al. (2026) study representation-level distillation in late-interaction models to produce small query encoders. Our work distills query and document token representations into compact multimodal late-interaction models that can serve as both query and document encoders.

papers.title: An Eco-Friendly Tourism Trip Planner Driven by Z-Number Uncertainty: Evidence from Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul
papers.abstract: Deployed tourism trip planners ingest travel times and ratings as exact numbers, although routing services return travel times that vary with the hour of departure and a platform rating may rest on a handful of reviews or on hundreds of thousands. We present an eco-friendly trip planner that represents both quantities as Z-numbers, which pair a fuzzy restriction on a value with a fuzzy reliability on the evidence behind it, and that constructs them directly from routing-service observations at six departure hours and from platform review counts rather than from linguistic elicitation. A hybrid loss combines score, carbon, travel-time, and reliability terms, and an adaptive large neighborhood search returns single-day itineraries through a conversational front end. We compare the planner with a crisp-mean baseline under an identical optimizer in Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul, with fifteen points of interest and thirty seeds per city, and we evaluate the selected itineraries on their trip carbon and their total travel time. Pooled over 150 seed-paired runs, the planner lowers trip carbon from 3.24 to 2.61 kg (19.3%, Wilcoxon p = 0.017; city-clustered bootstrap interval 6.4% to 26.7%) and travel time from 123 to 109 minutes per trip (11.5%, p = 2.8e-10; interval 5.0% to 18.2%). The travel-time reductions survive a Holm correction in Baku, Istanbul, and Abu Dhabi; the carbon reduction is significant in Baku and large but uncertain in the dispersed catalogs of Dubai and Abu Dhabi; and neither metric changes in Tashkent. Review counts are estimates of at least 3,000 for every point of interest, so rating reliability does not vary, and with a single baseline, the results establish feasibility and direction rather than a general advantage. Code, routing caches, frozen routing tables, and per-seed results are openly released.

Digital technology has reshaped how travelers discover, evaluate, and sequence the attractions of a destination, and the itinerary that a tourist actually follows is now, to a considerable degree, the output of an information system rather than of a guidebook. The day-trip design problem, in which a tourist arriving in an unfamiliar city must select a sequence of points of interest (POIs) and the transport options that connect them so as to balance experiential, monetary, temporal, and environmental criteria, has accordingly become one of the canonical applications of multi-criteria optimization (Gavalas et al., 2014; Vansteenwegen et al., 2011). Commercial planners such as TripAdvisor itineraries, Google Maps multi-stop routing, Sygic Travel, and Wanderlog, together with academic prototypes such as P-Tour (Maruyama et al., 2004), CT-Planner5 (Kurata et al., 2015), and PersTour (Lim et al., 2018), address this task with considerable sophistication. What they do not address is the uncertainty in the data on which every such planner relies.

What they do not address is the uncertainty in the data on which every such planner relies.

That uncertainty has two sources. Routing services supply travel times that depend on the departure hour, the transport mode, and the recent traffic pattern, so that a single origin-destination-mode triple yields estimates that differ by a factor of two or more across the tourist-active day on congested corridors. Ratings carry uncertainty of a different kind: a POI with a mean of four and a half stars from five reviews carries less information than one with the same mean from five thousand, yet existing planners treat the two identically. A planner that ingests this evidence as crisp numbers discards the dimension of reliability that the evidence itself supplies. The Z-number formalism of Zadeh (2011) represents an uncertain quantity as an ordered pair of fuzzy numbers, a restriction on the value and a reliability on the assertion, and so separates by construction the magnitude of an estimate from the sufficiency of the evidence on which it rests. Z-number arithmetic and ranking have been developed in depth (Aliev et al., 2016b; Aliev et al., 2016a), but Z-numbers have rarely served as the substrate of a working trip planner whose parameters come from operational data rather than from linguistic judgments.

The contributions of the paper are three. First, we specify data-driven construction operators that map routing observations and review counts to trapezoidal Z-numbers, a hybrid loss that combines them with crisp carbon and cost terms, and a two-step treatment of soft constraints, and we document a working implementation in sufficient detail for reproduction.
