papers.title: Data-Driven Glyph Positioning for Handwritten Music Synthesis
papers.abstract: Synthesised data is a common strategy to address the lack of annotated handwritten music scores in Optical Music Recognition (OMR). Smashcima is a recent synthesis framework that assembles pages of handwritten scores by sampling glyph images from MUSCIMA++ and positioning them with hard-coded rules. In this work we ask whether these rules are grounded empirically and whether a learned model for context-dependent positioning can further improve synthesis quality. We extract inter-glyph distributions from around 285 thousand annotated relationships across MUSCIMA++ and OmniOMR, finding that several key parameters deviate systematically from real handwriting. Replacing these constants with empirical means reduces positioning RMSE by up to 60%. We then train a Graph Neural Network (GNN) on the Music Notation Graph structure to predict context-dependent offsets, achieving an additional 50 to 85% RMSE reduction on stems and beams by modelling how neighbouring glyphs constrain placement. Cross-dataset analysis shows that spacing differences between the two corpora are explained by note density (3.3), not style, and that duration-proportional spacing does not hold in handwriting (R2 = 0.001). In downstream evaluation, a YOLOv8 detector pretrained on GNN-positioned synthetic data achieves +30% mAP50 over the baseline and +11% over empirical means when fine-tuned on 200 real handwritten staves, showing that positioning accuracy matters for downstream OMR.

papers.intro:
An OMR system’s performance highly depends on the availability of training data. Manually annotating handwritten scores is labour-intensive and there are only a few relatively small such datasets for the purpose of training deep learning models. To address this there are synthesis frameworks which generate realistic training images from symbolic music representations. However, recent work has identified a “glass ceiling” on the effectiveness of synthetic training data [1], where increasing the volume of synthetic data yields diminishing returns. Understanding what this ceiling is made of and how to get past it requires decomposing the synthetic-to-real domain gap into its main factors such as symbol appearance, paper texture, and spatial layout.

In this paper, we focus on the layout component. Smashcima [10] is an open-source synthesis tool that takes a MusicXML file and produces rastered images of handwritten music together with pixel-level annotations by sampling real glyph images from MUSCIMA++ [11] and positioning them according to a set of rules. However, the numerical parameters of these rules (stem length, accidental offset, beam angle, inter-note spacing) are constants chosen by visual inspection rather than measured from data. Moreover, these rules treat each relationship independently, they cannot model how the position of one glyph constrains its neighbours.

papers.title: Constrained Tagging for Span Labeling
papers.abstract: Generative LLMs can label spans without task-specific training, but their output is not tied to positions in the input: a returned span may be absent from the input or occur several times. We present constrained tagging, a training-free method in which the model reproduces the input and wraps each span in labeled inline markup. A logits processor using a byte-level token trie and a finite-state machine admits only tokens that continue the input verbatim or form a valid tag, so the output reproduces the input exactly with labels from the given set, and spans may begin or end at any character boundary, even inside a token. Two-phase decoding lets reasoning models reason before the constraint engages. On six datasets and six open-weight models, the guarantee holds in all but 0.022% of 255,312 constrained generations, each failure a reasoning model exhausting its token budget or never closing its reasoning, and the constraint adds no measurable cost. Unlike context-based prompting, which loses 8.5% of its spans, constrained tagging locates every span it proposes on every dataset; it is as accurate on two datasets, and on the other four its errors lie in which spans the model chooses, not where they are.

papers.intro:
Classifying text spans is a fundamental problem in NLP, with applications ranging from named entity recognition and extractive question answering to grammatical error correction, toxic language detection, and other information extraction tasks. Traditionally, this problem has been addressed with encoder-only models such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), which directly produce token-level predictions. These models need a large annotated dataset for every task, and they must be retrained whenever the label set changes. Generative large language models (LLMs), which have grown far larger and more capable and can now reason before they answer, offer a different paradigm: they can perform span labeling in a zero-shot setting through prompting alone, which makes them attractive when labeled data are scarce or the label set changes.

Classifying text spans is a fundamental problem in NLP, with applications ranging from named entity recognition and extractive question answering to grammatical error correction, toxic language detection, and other information extraction tasks. Traditionally, this problem has been addressed with encoder-only models such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), which directly produce token-level predictions. These models need a large annotated dataset for every task, and they must be retrained whenever the label set changes. Generative large language models (LLMs), which have grown far larger and more capable and can now reason before they answer, offer a different paradigm: they can perform span labeling in a zero-shot setting through prompting alone, which makes them attractive when labeled data are scarce or the label set changes.

Applying generative LLMs to span labeling, however, introduces a challenge encoders do not face: once the model identifies a span of interest, how do we locate it precisely within the original input text? Generative LLMs operate auto-regressively, producing output tokens without any inherent correspondence to positions in the source text. This creates a fundamental localization problem, which is particularly acute when the same surface form appears several times: simply extracting “Charles” from the model output provides no information about which occurrence was identified or where in the text it is located (Fig. 1). Generative models may also fail to copy text faithfully, producing spans that cannot be aligned to the source at all.

In this paper, we use a constrained decoding approach to span labeling. We classify spans with a tagging mechanism: the model reproduces the input text and tags each span inline, wrapping it in markup that assigns it a label (Fig. 1). A logits processor, guided by a byte-level token trie (Fredkin, 1960) and a finite-state machine, restricts the generation at every step to tokens that either continue the input verbatim or form a valid tag with a label from the given label set. papers.title: Post-Pruning vs. Early Stopping: Which Works Better for Link Prediction with AnyBurl?
papers.abstract: Rule-based link prediction combines symbolic and statistical artificial intelligence methods by inductively learning a set of rules from a knowledge graph (KG), with the aim of completing the graph when a query cannot be answered from the KG alone. Several systems have been proposed, and while they perform well on classical benchmarks, even compared with embedding-based systems, many of them produce a large number of rules. This compromises scalability in the query-answering phase, especially under strong hardware constraints. In this work, we investigate the behavior of AnyBurl, a state-of-the-art rule learner for link prediction, to determine whether running it for a given time and then pruning the learned rules yields better query-answering performance at test time than a simpler approach that stops rule generation earlier.
papers.intro:
Knowledge Graphs (KGs) [19] have attracted increasing attention in recent years. For our purposes, a KG can be regarded as a large collection of subject-relation-object triplets, for instance (Bob,lives,London)(\texttt{Bob},\texttt{lives},\texttt{London}); well-known examples include FreeBase [7], DBPedia [3], Microsoft Satori [33], and YAGO [40]. Although a KG typically gathers a large number of facts (triplets), it is nonetheless assumed to be often incomplete [11]: entities, relations between entities, or both may be missing. This observation raises the question of whether a graph can be completed. The problem has been capturing the interest of several communities, with applications in intelligent question answering [20], recommender systems [43] and network security systems [21]. Concretely, given a KG 𝒢\mathcal{G}, a completion task amounts to filling gaps such as (Einstein, bornIn, ?) or (?, worksAt, Apple). The most widespread approaches rely on graph embeddings [2, 34, 35] or, more recently, on large language models [38]. A parallel line of work instead learns symbolic representations [13, 12, 29, 30, 14]: rules are induced from the data and link prediction queries are then answered by applying these rules over the knowledge graph, treated as a set of facts. Closely related are neuro-symbolic methods, which come in various forms. One such form injects logical knowledge (e.g. Description Logics) into an embedding space by encoding constraints directly in the objective function, as done in [23, 1, 16, 27].

More generally, pruning AI systems after training is a well-established practice. In particular, a variety of approaches have been proposed for pruning neural networks, both at the level of individual weights (unstructured pruning) and at the level of entire neurons, channels or layers (structured pruning) [9]. In this area, one of the most widely used heuristics is magnitude pruning, which discards the weights with smallest absolute value. As in that setting, our goal is to retain only a small fraction of the model while preserving predictive performance. The difference lies in the units being pruned: ours are logical rules, rather than weights, which are not individually interpretable. Therefore, post-training rule pruning could be considered as the symbolic counterpart of magnitude pruning and model compression.

papers.title: On finite-dimensional attractor to 2D incompressible fluid with stress-diffusion
papers.abstract: We consider incompressible visco-elastic rate-type fluid flow, with the Cauchy stress defined in terms of positive-definite symmetric tensor $B$. The tensor $B$ obeys an evolution equation, combining Oldroyd-B and Giesekus model, and, crucially, a diffusion term. Restricting ourselves to the 2D periodic problem, we show existence of a finite-dimensional global attractor. We also estimate its dimension explicitely in terms of the equation parameters.

papers.title: Hitting time for loose Hamilton cycles in the random hypergraph process
papers.abstract: The random hypergraph process starts with an empty hypergraph on $n$ vertices and adds a uniformly chosen missing edge at each step. For even $n$, we prove that, with high probability, a $3$-uniform loose Hamilton cycle appears when the last isolated vertex disappears. The approach developed here adapts arguments from Kahn's work on perfect matchings. It can also be extended to obtain the corresponding hitting-time theorems for $r=2$ and every fixed $r\ge4$ satisfying $(r-1)\mid n$. Furthermore, it can be used to estimate the numbers of loose Hamilton cycles at these hitting times for every fixed $r\ge2$, up to a factor of $\exp\{o(n)\}$.

papers.title: Silent Alignment in Two-Layer Linear Networks: A High-Dimensional Perspective
papers.abstract: We study gradient flow in a two-layer linear network in the high-dimensional regime where the input, inner and output dimensions diverge proportionally. Under whitened inputs and isotropic imbalance, we combine a closed-form solution of the dynamics with prior random matrix theory results to derive a high-dimensional limit for the dynamics. Our method yields exact asymptotic spectral distributions for the weight matrices at all times and characterizes the evolution of the learned subspace. In the small-initialization limit, we identify a silent alignment phenomenon: the singular directions of the network align on an order-one timescale, while the singular values and empirical loss remain at their initial values. Visible learning occurs later, on a logarithmic timescale, as singular values progressively escape zero and the loss decreases. This phase is characterized by a saddle-to-saddle dynamics, which becomes a continuous process of spectral learning in the high-dimensional limit.

papers.title: A combined HST and JWST analysis of the stellar population in Draco II
papers.abstract: Draco II (Dra II) is one of the faintest and most metal-poor Milky Way satellites known, yet its nature as either an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy or an extended globular cluster remains debated. We perform a photometric analysis of the stellar population of Dra II reducing deep multi-band observations from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). We select Dra II member stars based on their proper motions and photometric quality criteria. For the first time, optical and infrared photometry are combined to produce a stellar catalogue reaching 50 percent completeness at $F814W = 26.5$ mag (corresponding to the absolute magnitude $M_{F814W} = 10.1$ mag). The colour-magnitude diagram confirms that Dra II hosts an old stellar population with an age of $13.5_{-1.5}^{+1.7}$ Gyr at a distance of $19.2\pm0.9$ kpc. We measure an $α$-enhanced stellar population with a low mean metallicity of $[\rm Fe/H]_{CaHK} = -2.38 \pm 0.17$ dex and confirm the presence of an intrinsic metallicity spread of $σ_{[\rm Fe/H]} = 0.85 \pm 0.13$ dex. We identify 10 unresolved main-sequence binary stars in the HST catalogue with mass ratios $q > 0.5$ in the mass range $0.43<M_1/M_\odot<0.71$, corresponding to a binary fraction of $f_{bin}^{q>0.5} = 0.21 \pm 0.07$. This value is higher than those typically observed in globular clusters and lies near the upper range measured in open clusters. The stellar mass function is best modelled by a single power law with a slope of $1.53\pm0.26$ over the mass range $0.13$--$0.77\ M_\odot$. We find no evidence of mass segregation. Consistent results are obtained independently from the JWST catalogue. Combining these findings strongly suggests that Draco II is best classified as an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy rather than a globular cluster.

Large sky surveys like the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (York et al., 2000, SDSS;), the Dark Energy Survey (Dark Energy Survey Collaboration, 2005, DES;) or the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System 1 3π\pi survey11 1 https://outerspace.stsci.edu/display/PANSTARRS/ (Chambers et al., 2016, Pan-STARRS 1 3π\pi;) uncovered an abundance of elusive Milky Way satellites (Willman et al., 2005; Belokurov et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2015). Among these systems, ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (Simon, 2019, UFDs;) are particularly important to study galaxy formation and dark matter. UFDs are extreme environments: they are the oldest, most dark-matter dominated, most metal-poor, and least chemically evolved stellar systems known (Simon, 2019), making them valuable laboratories for understanding the early stages of galaxy formation and chemical enrichment in the Universe (Kroupa et al., 2010; Bullock and Boylan-Kolchin, 2017). Indeed, as dwarf galaxies (DG) are embedded in dark matter halos (Kauffmann et al., 1993; Strigari et al., 2008; Tolstoy et al., 2009; Willman and Strader, 2012) they provide key constraints on the nature of dark matter and the low-mass end of galaxy formation within Λ\LambdaCDM cosmology (Strigari, 2018; Simon, 2019).

Characterising the stellar population of UFDs remains difficult due to their extremely low luminosities and sparse stellar populations. Deep photometric observations with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have therefore become essential to resolve their stellar populations and constrain their star formation histories, metallicity distributions, and stellar mass functions (Geha et al., 2013; Weisz and Boylan-Kolchin, 2017; Simon, 2019; Fu et al., 2023; Milone et al., 2023a). papers.title: FEAST: Spatially Resolved Star Formation History of the NGC 4485/NGC 4490 System and its Tidal Bridge from JWST/NIRCam Color Magnitude Diagrams
papers.abstract: We present the spatially resolved star formation history (SFH) of the interacting, low-mass, gas-rich galaxy pair NGC 4485/NGC 4490, based on deep JWST/NIRCam imaging obtained as part of the FEAST program. Using resolved stars' near-infrared color-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) and the SFERA 2.0 CMD fitting code, we reconstruct the SFH of the system, including the tidal bridge connecting the two galaxies. We find that recent star formation is widespread across the system, extending beyond the main bodies of the galaxies into the tidal bridge and other off-center areas. In particular, a significant fraction of the recent star formation in NGC 4485 occurs outside its central region. All major regions of the system exhibit two prominent episodes of enhanced star formation, occurring around 0.5-1 Gyr and 10-30 Myr ago, with the tidal bridge showing the largest increase relative to its average star formation rate. These peaks in star formation activity occur a few hundred million years after the epochs of the first and second pericenter passages predicted by independent dynamical models, supporting a scenario in which repeated tidal interactions triggered the observed bursts through gas redistribution and compression. Our results place direct observational constraints on the formation history of NGC 4485/NGC 4490 and provide evidence for the important role of galaxy interactions in driving spatially extended, bursty star formation in low-mass galaxies.

papers.intro:
Understanding how galaxy interactions and mergers regulate the conversion of gas into stars remains a fundamental challenge in the field of galaxy formation and evolution. Within the hierarchical framework of the Lambda-cold dark matter (Λ\LambdaCDM) cosmological model, galaxies are predicted to grow through accretion of smaller satellites [161, 129, 162, 26, 25]. Interactions and mergers are therefore expected to play a key role in shaping galaxy evolution across a wide range of masses. They can alter galaxy morphology and kinematics, redistribute angular momentum, drive gas inflows, increase gas densities, and trigger enhanced episodes of star formation [see e.g., 10, 11, 121, 99, 22, 58, 126, 124, 88, 149, 122, 21, among others]. While the impact of interactions and mergers has been extensively studied in the Milky Way and other massive galaxies [86, 14, 111, 110, 48, 115], the role of these processes in the low-mass dwarf galaxy regime (M⋆≲109​M⊙\mathrm{M_{\star}\lesssim 10^{9}\,M_{\odot}}) has historically been investigated primarily through individual systems [121, see e.g.,], while only in the past decade have dedicated observational surveys enabled a systematic exploration of interacting dwarf galaxy populations [145, 29, 81, 146, 124, 2, 139, 43, 147, 100, see, e.g.,].

Observations of isolated low-mass galaxy pairs have revealed systematically elevated star formation rates relative to those of isolated dwarfs, with the enhancement becoming stronger as the separation between the galaxies decreases [145]. Unlike mergers involving massive galaxies, where star formation is often concentrated in the nuclear regions as tidal torques funnel gas toward the center [6, 117, 11, 59, 84, 83, 149, 75], interacting dwarf galaxies frequently exhibit spatially extended and clumpy star formation distributed throughout their disks and tidal structures [145, 146, 132, 124, 106, 44, 20]. This suggests that the response of the interstellar medium to tidal interactions depends strongly on galaxy mass, with low-mass systems being highly susceptible to efficient gas stripping and structural transformation, while higher-mass galaxies predominantly exhibit gas redistribution and tidally induced morphological features rather than large-scale gas removal [63, 130, 78].

Lahén et al. These bursts of star formation are predicted to be several times stronger than the average SFR, enough to leave strong and observable traces in the stellar populations of such systems.

In this scenario, interacting low-mass galaxies in the nearby Universe (i.e., within ∼20\sim 20 Mpc from us) provide a unique opportunity to investigate these processes at high spatial resolutions. At such distances, individual stars and star clusters can be resolved with modern space-based facilities [150, 113, 160, 4, 159, 142], enabling the reconstruction of spatially resolved star formation histories (SFHs) from deep color–magnitude diagrams (CMDs, see Cignoni and Tosi 37 and references therein). Because resolved stellar populations retain a fossil record of the past star formation activity, they provide a direct means of probing how interactions influence star formation across the entire merger history. These nearby systems therefore serve as fundamental laboratories for understanding galaxy assembly in the early Universe, when interactions and mergers were more common and hierarchical growth proceeded more rapidly [41], but where comparable spatial resolution cannot be achieved.

One of the best nearby laboratories for studying low-mass, gas-rich galaxy interaction is the NGC 4485/4490 system (Arp 269). NGC 4485 and NGC 4490 form a pair of interacting galaxies with stellar masses of ∼3.2×108​M⊙\sim 3.2\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}} and ∼2.5×109​M⊙\sim 2.5\times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}, respectively. The system is located at a distance of ∼7.4\sim 7.4 Mpc [28, 135], and the galaxy centers are separated by ∼7.5\sim 7.5 kpc in projection. They exhibit a prograde motion and a velocity difference of approximately 30​km​s−130\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} [127]. NGC 4490 has an oxygen abundance of 12+log⁡(O/H)=8.37\mathrm{12+\log(O/H)=8.37} derived from HII regions [131]. The pair is also relatively isolated, with the nearest massive galaxy, NGC 4369, located at a projected distance of ∼300\sim 300 kpc and differing in radial velocity by more than 400​km​s−1400\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} [126, 127]. These properties make NGC 4485/NGC 4490 particularly interesting, as it is one of the nearby systems in which individual stars can be resolved across a tidally induced, actively star-forming bridge (Bortolini et al. 20, see also Figure 1). Indeed, although a similar bridge can be studied in greater detail between the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, disentangling the effects of their mutual interaction from those induced by the gravitational influence of the Milky Way remains challenging [12, 17, 65, 27].

papers.title: MAPS: Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning for Regulating Search Momentum in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by retrieving external knowledge. Recently, some RAG methods interleave reasoning and retrieval, enabling LLMs to progressively generate sub-queries and retrieve external knowledge. However, these methods may suffer from redundant or ineffective sub-queries and insufficiently diverse query exploration. Moreover, due to the tightly interleaved nature of reasoning and retrieval, it remains unclear how the evolving reasoning process influences query intent. To characterize the evolution of query intent during reasoning, we introduce search momentum, which captures the accumulated retrieval tendency induced by historical changes in generated sub-queries along the reasoning trajectory. Through momentum-based analysis, we find that the query generation process tends to continuously evolve along existing retrieval trajectories. Based on this observation, we propose MAPS, a Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning framework for regulating search momentum and mitigating query-intent drift. MAPS first retains the retrieved knowledge and a refined reasoning state, thereby reducing the influence of historical reasoning trajectories on subsequent sub-query generation. Subsequently, MAPS extends the conventional sequential reasoning process into a parallel reasoning paradigm. At each iteration, MAPS identifies complementary retrieval directions, generates corresponding sub-queries for parallel retrieval, and consolidates the retrieved evidence to update the knowledge and reasoning states. Experiments on six question-answering benchmarks demonstrate that MAPS consistently outperforms representative RAG methods across different backbone models. All code and resources are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/MAPS.

Large Language Models (LLMs) (Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in knowledge-intensive question answering and complex reasoning. However, they remain susceptible to hallucinations (Jiang et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2023), leading to factually incorrect or unsupported responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020; Izacard et al., 2023) addresses this issue by enabling LLMs to access external knowledge during inference, thereby improving the factuality and reliability of their responses. However, for multi-hop queries (Yang et al., 2018), the required evidence is often distributed across multiple documents and interconnected through dependencies, making single-step retrieval insufficient to comprehensively acquire the information needed to answer the query (Fang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026).

Large Language Models (LLMs) (Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in knowledge-intensive question answering and complex reasoning. However, they remain susceptible to hallucinations (Jiang et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2023), leading to factually incorrect or unsupported responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020; Izacard et al., 2023) addresses this issue by enabling LLMs to access external knowledge during inference, thereby improving the factuality and reliability of their responses. However, for multi-hop queries (Yang et al., 2018), the required evidence is often distributed across multiple documents and interconnected through dependencies, making single-step retrieval insufficient to comprehensively acquire the information needed to answer the query (Fang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026).

To address this limitation, recent RAG approaches have explored leveraging the reasoning capabilities of LLMs to adaptively acquire external evidence. These methods (Li et al., 2025a; Jin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025) interleave reasoning and retrieval, allowing LLMs to identify missing information, generate sub-queries, and retrieve relevant documents to progressively support the original query. Specifically, an LLM is prompted to generate sub-queries when additional knowledge is necessary, retrieve relevant documents, and incorporate the retrieved evidence into subsequent reasoning. However, as reasoning and retrieval proceed iteratively, these methods can suffer from redundant or ineffective sub-queries, excessively long retrieval chains, or insufficient exploration diversity (Ji et al., 2025; Martinez et al., 2025), ultimately degrading retrieval and downstream reasoning performance. Due to the tightly interleaved nature of reasoning and retrieval, it remains unclear how the evolving reasoning process influences the search direction, particularly when comprehensive evidence requires exploration beyond the current retrieval trajectory.

To characterize how search intentions evolve throughout the reasoning process, we introduce search momentum, which captures the accumulated retrieval tendency induced by historical changes in generated sub-queries along the reasoning trajectory. At each step, we update the search momentum by aggregating the current sub-query with the accumulated momentum through a stepwise learnable weight. We learn these weights by using the updated momentum to predict the query-intent drift at the current step. By analyzing the resulting search momentum across reasoning steps, we observe that the deviation directions of subsequent sub-queries become increasingly aligned with the accumulated search momentum as retrieval proceeds deeper. This finding suggests that query generation tends to follow the existing retrieval trajectory, rather than correcting or escaping accumulated deviations through subsequent reasoning (Guo et al., 2025). Such momentum-driven behavior can progressively amplify early search deviations, causing the retrieval process to drift away from the original information need. This motivates us to regulate the accumulation of search momentum and preserve alignment between the evolving retrieval process and the original query intent.

Specifically, MAPS identifies multiple complementary retrieval directions from the current reasoning state and generates corresponding sub-queries in parallel to explore these directions. The resulting evidence is consolidated to update the accumulated knowledge and refined reasoning state, which serves as the basis for the next reasoning iteration.

Our experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that MAPS achieves significant improvements over all baseline methods across different backbone models, highlighting its strong generalization ability and robustness. Further analyses show that MAPS effectively regulates the evolution of search momentum, preventing it from being dominated by a single retrieval direction. Our experiments further demonstrate that MAPS effectively mitigates query intent drift and maintains stronger relevance between generated sub-queries and supporting evidence throughout iterative reasoning. Moreover, MAPS enables the model to acquire the prerequisite knowledge required for reasoning at an earlier stage, while reducing unnecessary retrieval iterations.

papers.title: A relative Schinzel-Zassenhaus bound for the polynomial $T^2 - 1$
papers.abstract: For $f(T) = T^2 - 1$, we establish a lower bound for the relative dynamical house of wandering algebraic integers. This bound depends on the degree over the maximal abelian extension of the rationals. Our proof follows Dimitrov's approach to the Schinzel-Zassenhaus Conjecture and its generalization by Habegger-Schmidt.

papers.title: CRAFT-ε: A Conformer-Resolved Atom- and Fragment-based Theory for the Static Relative Permittivity of Pure Organic Liquids
papers.abstract: The static relative permittivity is an important property in thermodynamic modeling, electrochemistry, and solvent design, but predicting it directly from molecular structure remains challenging because both electronic polarization and molecular dipole orientation contribute to the measured response. Here, we introduce CRAFT-ε (Conformer-Resolved Atom- and Fragment-based Theory for ε), a conformer-resolved molecular descriptor model for predicting the static relative permittivity of neutral pure liquids. Conformer free energies, molecular dipoles, and atom-resolved polarizabilities are obtained from a GFN2-xTB/ALPB 10 workflow. The molecular dipole is decomposed into chemically defined polar-fragment vectors, allowing fitted corrections to retain both the magnitude and relative orientation of local dipolar contributions. Electronic and orientational polarization are combined with a group-contribution molar volume in the Onsager-Kirkwood-Fröhlich relation. A staged parameterization with 41 parameters is applied to nonpolar, polar, and hydrogen-bonding compounds. For 1393 liquids with permittivities between 1.5 and 183, CRAFT-ε reaches a five-fold cross-validated average absolute deviation of 2.40 ({R^2} = 0.93). Conformational averaging 15 is essential for liquids with several polar groups. Compared with an established fragment-based model with 139 parameters, it reaches a similar cross-validated RMSE (3.65 versus 3.41) with about a quarter of the parameters and applies to every liquid of the dataset. The resulting framework provides a computationally inexpensive route from molecular structure to liquid dielectric response and forms a basis for later application to solvent mixtures and electrolyte systems.

The static relative permittivity, εr\varepsilon_{r}, is one of the fundamental macroscopic properties connecting molecular-scale electrostatics with the behavior of condensed phases. It determines the screening of electrostatic interactions and consequently enters descriptions of solvation, electrolyte thermodynamics, reaction media, phase equilibria, and electrochemical systems. Reliable values are therefore required both as experimental material properties and as input quantities for predictive thermodynamic models.

The static relative permittivity, εr\varepsilon_{r}, is one of the fundamental macroscopic properties connecting molecular-scale electrostatics with the behavior of condensed phases. It determines the screening of electrostatic interactions and consequently enters descriptions of solvation, electrolyte thermodynamics, reaction media, phase equilibria, and electrochemical systems. Reliable values are therefore required both as experimental material properties and as input quantities for predictive thermodynamic models.

For electrolyte systems in particular, the relative permittivity directly affects long-range electrostatic contributions such as Debye–Hückel-type terms as well as Born-type descriptions of ionic solvation. Predictions of ionic activity coefficients and phase equilibria can consequently be highly sensitive to the dielectric model employed. In practical applications, experimental dielectric constants or empirical correlations are therefore frequently supplied externally to thermodynamic models. This limits predictivity when new solvents or solvent mixtures are considered.

Predicting εr\varepsilon_{r} from molecular structure is challenging because the static dielectric response contains physically distinct contributions. The rapid electronic response is related primarily to molecular polarizability, while the usually larger low-frequency contribution of polar liquids originates from molecular reorientation. The latter depends not only on the isolated-molecule dipole moment but also on molecular conformation, local liquid structure, intermolecular association, and dipole–dipole correlations. Classical dielectric theories relate both contributions to molecular properties: the Clausius–Mossotti relation connects the electronic polarizability with the high-frequency response, whereas the theories of Onsager, Kirkwood and Fröhlich add the orientational polarization of permanent dipoles [bottcher_theory_1973, onsager_electric_1936, noauthor_dielectric_1939, frohlich_theory_1958]. Their direct use as predictive models is nevertheless difficult, because effective liquid-phase dipoles, local-field effects and orientational correlations are generally not known from molecular structure alone, and a single optimized gas-phase geometry discards conformational information that can be relevant in the liquid.

Classical dielectric theories relate both contributions to molecular properties: the Clausius–Mossotti relation connects the electronic polarizability with the high-frequency response, whereas the theories of Onsager, Kirkwood and Fröhlich add the orientational polarization of permanent dipoles [bottcher_theory_1973, onsager_electric_1936, noauthor_dielectric_1939, frohlich_theory_1958]. Their direct use as predictive models is nevertheless difficult, because effective liquid-phase dipoles, local-field effects and orientational correlations are generally not known from molecular structure alone, and a single optimized gas-phase geometry discards conformational information that can be relevant in the liquid.

An alternative is to retain these physically motivated dielectric relations while representing the missing condensed-phase effects through transferable molecular descriptors and a limited number of fitted parameters. Such an approach occupies an intermediate position between simple empirical structure–property correlations and explicit molecular simulation. It may therefore be particularly useful for high-throughput applications, where large numbers of candidate molecules must be evaluated at a computational cost that precludes explicit condensed-phase sampling.

papers.title: Quantum Interference Enhanced Rectification in Mesoscopic Nanowires
papers.abstract: Nanoscale nonreciprocal elements are needed to control signal flow in scalable quantum technologies, but existing nonreciprocal components are often bulky. Here, we show that a strongly nonreciprocal current-voltage relation can arise entirely from coherent elastic scattering in a mesoscopic Rashba nanowire with gate-defined scatterers. We first identify the symmetry constraints that enforce reciprocal transmission in a phase coherent conductor even when inversion and time-reversal symmetry are broken. We then show how gates that are capacitively coupled to the leads, together with a magnetic scatterer or transverse subband mixing, can remove these constraints. In the weak-scattering regime, nonreciprocal conductance originates from interference between distinct backscattering paths. In the strong-scattering regime, nonreciprocity can be resonantly enhanced by the hybridization of the transmitting channel with bound states that arise from a higher transverse subband or spin-split band. In this regime, we find that a bias-induced change in the gate potentials of about one percent can produce an order-unity diode response, i.e., electrons are transmitted almost as in a clean wire for one bias polarity, whereas for the other polarity the current is strongly suppressed.

papers.title: Open-Vocabulary Models and Label Propagation for Uncertainty-aware Pseudo-Labeling of Object Detection Datasets
papers.abstract: Object detection models rely on large-scale annotated datasets that require substantial manual annotation effort. The labeling costs further increase when annotation uncertainty is captured through soft labels, as multiple annotations must be collected for each object. We address this challenge by introducing a semi-supervised framework for the uncertainty-aware annotation of object detection datasets. Our approach leverages open-vocabulary object detectors to generate region proposals and semantically meaningful object representations. Based on these representations, we construct an object-level similarity graph and propagate probabilistic label information. Our framework assigns soft labels to previously unlabeled objects, quantifying both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. We evaluate our method on four object detection benchmarks with soft-label annotations and demonstrate that high-quality annotations can be obtained with only a small fraction of manually labeled objects. Furthermore, we show that detectors trained on semi-automatically annotated data achieve performance comparable to models trained on fully manually annotated data. We achieve state-of-the-art downstream detection performance for the task of semi-supervised object detection on the COCO dataset, with 40.5% AP virtually matching the performance of the model trained on fully manually constructed data (40.9%) at only 1% of labeling costs. These results highlight the potential of open-vocabulary models and graph-based label propagation for efficient, accurate and uncertainty-aware pseudo-labeling.

papers.intro:
Modern object detectors rely on large-scale annotated datasets, whose creation requires substantial manual effort. In contrast to image classification, object detection annotations must specify the location and category of every object, making dataset construction particularly time-consuming. Furthermore, existing object detection benchmarks generally treat annotations as deterministic, despite the fact that ambiguity is inherent to many detection tasks due to occlusions, unclear object boundaries, blurring, and semantic uncertainty. Recently, object detection datasets that capture semantic uncertainty were proposed [1, 2]. Annotation uncertainty is captured through multiple independent annotations, often more than ten human evaluations per object. While such approaches provide valuable information about human uncertainty, their annotation costs may limit scalability. This motivates the development of semi-automated methods that can efficiently propagate label information and capture semantic uncertainty. While graph-based semi-supervised techniques proved to be effective in image classification [3, 4, 5], similar methods for uncertainty-aware annotation in object detection remain unexplored.

In this work, we develop graph-based semi-supervised learning in the domain of object detection by leveraging powerful open-vocabulary object detectors such as Grounding DINO [6] to generate initial region proposals and semantically meaningful object representations. With these object representations, we construct a similarity graph over which label information is propagated (Figure 1). To propagate label information, we rely on probabilistic label spreading [5] which generalizes classical label spreading [3] to the domain of soft labels and accounts for aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. This way, our method propagates (potentially noisy) label information obtained for few objects to other localized but yet unlabeled objects. This enables the uncertainty-aware, semi-automated annotation of object detection datasets. As a result, all detected objects are equipped with a soft label that reflects the individual class probabilities, including the background class. Soft labels generalize conventional labels and reflect the aleatoric uncertainty associated with label assignments [7]. They allow for uncertainty-aware training [8] and thorough assessment of model uncertainty [2]. Creating soft labels manually requires the repeated evaluation of instances by multiple annotators so that datasets with soft labels are rare [5, 2].

papers.title: Free-XOR TFHE via Lazy Bootstrapping
papers.abstract: Gate bootstrapping (GB) is a widely used technique in FHEW-like fully homomorphic encryption schemes, such as TFHE,for evaluating Boolean gates while simultaneously reducing the noise of the resulting ciphertext. However, the computational cost of GB is typically dominated by an expensive blind rotation (BR). [8] proposed a gate bootstrapping framework in which XOR gates can be evaluated simply by adding the two input ciphertexts, resulting in what they call freeXOR. To obtain a functionally complete set of operations, they further designed a GB procedure for evaluating AND gates using two lightweight blind rotations. In this work, we propose a similar gate bootstrapping framework that supports free evaluation of XOR gates while evaluating all symmetric binary Boolean gates, i.e., the 8 gates whose output is identical for the inputs (0,1)and (1,0), using two blind rotations. In addition to providing broader gate support, our construction is substantially simpler than that of [8], both conceptually and in terms of implementation. As a proof of concept, we implemented our approach and compared it with standard TFHE, measuring speedups of about 30% for AES and 34% for SHA.

papers.intro:
Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) allows computation directly on encrypted data without decrypting it. Among FHE schemes, TFHE (Chillotti et al., 2020) is widely used for Boolean circuits. In the conventional TFHE approach, each bit is encrypted independently as an LWE ciphertext, and each gate is evaluated through programmable bootstrapping (PBS), which computes a function on the encrypted value while refreshing the ciphertext to control noise accumulation. PBS is one of the most expensive operations in TFHE, so the cost of evaluating a circuit is strongly influenced by the number of bootstrappings it requires.

In conventional TFHE, every gate, including XOR gates, is evaluated via PBS. Chen et al. (Chen et al., 2024) proposed an approach called free-XOR, which allows XOR gates to be evaluated without PBS. This is possible because XOR corresponds to addition modulo 22, which can be implemented directly using lightweight homomorphic addition. Therefore, circuits containing many XOR gates, such as those arising in symmetric cryptography and arithmetic, can benefit significantly from this technique.

Our main ideas are as follows. • Two-bit encoding with the Free-XOR property. We encode each bit as an element of ℤ4\mathbb{Z}_{4}, with the least significant bit representing the encoded Boolean value. Addition modulo 44 therefore computes the XOR of the underlying bits without requiring a programmable bootstrapping (PBS). The most significant bit acts as a redundant component that can be eliminated through bootstrapping when necessary. As in conventional TFHE constructions, we also reserve a padding bit to support non-negacyclic functions during programmable bootstrapping. Additionally, we introduce headroom into the encoding to accommodate multiple consecutive XOR additions over the integers without carrying into the padding bit. papers.title: Conformer diversity over quantity in COSMO-RS-based LLE predictions
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of phase equilibria is essential for chemical process design, particularly in systems characterized by complex intermolecular interactions. This work investigates the influence of conformer selection and sigma-profile characteristics on COSMO-RS predictions of liquid-liquid equilibria (LLE), using the tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol (THFA)-methyl isobutyl ketone (MIBK)-water system as a case study. Calculations were performed at the TZVP and TZVPD-FINE levels of theory. While TZVP failed to capture the experimentally observed phase behavior, TZVPD-FINE provided substantially improved predictions. The differences are attributed to the relative importance assigned to less-polar conformers and more-polar conformers capable of hydrogen bonding. Although the TZVPD-FINE calculations reproduced the main experimental trends, the predicted organic-phase composition showed a mean percentage deviation of 5.27%, slightly exceeding the adopted 5% agreement threshold. Investigations using individual conformers demonstrated that predictions can be strongly influenced by conformer selection and that representative conformer ensembles are necessary for reliable results. Further analysis showed that diversity in sigma profiles is more important for predictive accuracy than the total number of conformers. These findings emphasize the importance of carefully selecting conformers when applying COSMO-RS to liquid-liquid equilibria involving phases of contrasting polarity.

papers.title: In search of the third dimension in Compton X-ray polarimeters
papers.abstract: Compton polarimeters are typically designed to be sensitive only to the azimuthal angle of the scattered photon, ignoring the scattering angle. Such a 2-dimensional reconstruction of the event is pursued for both simplicity and because the polarization of the incident photon influences only the azimuthal response of the instrument. While this is true for on-axis sources, when the source starts to be off-axis of several degrees the azimuthal response of the instrument is effectively a convolution of the azimuthal and polar scattering angles: measuring the latter would provide a better sensitivity and smaller systematic effects. In this contribution, we will present a design which allows to estimate the scattering angle in a Compton polarimeter through the read-out of the light signal at the two ends of scintillator bars. Such a design is being tested with a representative set-up and first results on the performance are presented.

papers.intro:
The measurement of the polarization of the emission from astronomical sources at high energy has known a rapid development in the last years. The launch of the NASA-ASI Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer mission (IXPE[26]) in December 2021 finally has paved the way to measurements in the 2–8 keV energy range for a number of sources belonging to essentially all the classes of X-ray cosmic sources. The outstanding results of this mission on both galactic[14, 20, 27] and extra-galactic[15, 16] sources confirmed the long expectation that a significant polarization was to be found in the majority of high energy cosmic sources, and its detection would have provide us unique insights in the emission mechanism and geometry of these sources. With a planned launch in 2027, the Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI[22]) is another small-explorer mission bound to carry out imaging, spectroscopy and polarimetry of astrophysical sources in the energy band 0.2–5 MeV. Beyond these (relatively) large missions, a number of instruments have been designed or adapted as a secondary priority to measure polarization. They either targeted specific cosmic sources on-board, e.g., scientific balloons or CubeSats, or bright transient sources like Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs). Just to name a few of them, there are PolarLight [7], PoGO+[9], POLAR/POLAR-2[13, 4], Astrosat[25] or X-Calibur [1].

A possible implementation of a “classical” design for Compton polarimeters working in the hard X-rays is shown in Figure 1a. The polarimeter comprises of an array of bars made of some scintillator material arranged parallel to the instrument axis and read-out from the bottom; inner bars are used to Compton-scatter the incident photon, while the external ones are designed to absorb it after the interaction. The former are usually made of a plastic material, so that scattering becomes dominant over photoelectric absorption above 20 keV and the instrument can reach a lower energy threshold; the latter can either be identical to simplify the design or they can be made of an inorganic crystal to have a higher stopping power and spectral resolution. The line which connects the centers of the two hit bars provides the best approximation of the azimuthal angle φ\varphi, which provides the azimuthal response of the instrument; the histogram of the scattering directions, called modulation curve, shows a cosine square modulation in case of linearly polarized photons and a statistically–flat distribution for unpolarized radiation. papers.title: On optimal (v,5,3,1) optical orthogonal codes
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish a tight upper bound for the size of a $(v,5,3,1)$ optical orthogonal code (OOC) and call such a code optimal when it achieves this upper bound. In addition, if an optimal OOC has the property that all non-identity elements of $\mathbb{Z}_v$ are covered by the list of differences of its codeword-sets then it is called perfect. In this paper, we present direct and recursive constructions for infinite classes of optimal and perfect $(v,5,3,1)$-OOCs.

papers.title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
papers.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

Reinforcement learning (RL) (Sutton and Barto, 1998) and multi-agent RL (MARL) (Albrecht et al., 2024) have gradually become the basis of a new modelling paradigm for simulating the behaviour of agents in economics and finance. Reinforcement learning (RL) (Sutton and Barto, 1998) and multi-agent RL (MARL) (Albrecht et al., 2024) have gradually become the basis of a new modelling paradigm for simulating the behaviour of agents in economics and finance. In RL, agents learn to maximise their rewards through repeated interaction with the economy they inhabit, so that MARL becomes a principled way of populating a simulated economy with many diverse decision makers, each optimising a reasonable objective.

The adoption of this approach was pioneered in finance, where RL and MARL are now commonly used to represent trading, hedging or market-making agents across a range of markets (Karpe et al., 2020; Ardon et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2023; Mascioli et al., 2024; Evans and Ganesh, 2024; Bacaloni et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), or within multi-agent market simulators supported by a growing ecosystem of open-source platforms (Amrouni et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Ardon et al., 2023; Frey et al., 2023). In macroeconomics and structural macro-financial modelling, adoption has been comparatively slower. Indeed, in spite of a growing body of specialised research in the field, from stylised economies (Zheng et al., 2022; Cook and Palmer, 2025; Brusatin et al., 2024), to proofs of concept in monetary policy (Chen et al., 2025; Hinterlang and Tänzer, 2021), and tax design (Curry et al., 2023; Mi et al., 2024; Dwarakanath et al., 2024a; Agrawal et al., 2025), the methodology has not entered the toolkit of policymakers and practitioners.

In macroeconomics and structural macro-financial modelling, adoption has been comparatively slower. Indeed, in spite of a growing body of specialised research in the field, from stylised economies (Zheng et al., 2022; Cook and Palmer, 2025; Brusatin et al., 2024), to proofs of concept in monetary policy (Chen et al., 2025; Hinterlang and Tänzer, 2021), and tax design (Curry et al., 2023; Mi et al., 2024; Dwarakanath et al., 2024a; Agrawal et al., 2025), the methodology has not entered the toolkit of policymakers and practitioners.

In our view, the reason is twofold. On the one hand, this is due to scepticism and resistance towards alternative modelling methodologies, from a community that is long accustomed to a specific way of building models based on the dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) approach. This resistance is understandable, as the DSGE approach provides a shared frame of reference that keeps modelling out of the “wilderness of bounded rationality” (Farmer, 2024), where infinitely many deviations from optimality become available. On the other hand, this is due to the considerably higher computational cost of training RL or MARL systems, whereas a typical DSGE model can be specified and solved in seconds. A shared framework and fast solvers, in turn, make these models practical to use, and explain the remarkable success of specialised modelling software such as Dynare (Adjemian et al., 2011; Villemot, 2011).

JAX has often been proposed as a viable way to lower RL training times by allowing environment, policy and optimiser to live inside a single compiled program directly on the accelerator (Lu et al., 2022; Rutherford et al., 2024; Pretorius et al., 2021). papers.title: Simply Logical -- The First Three Decades
papers.abstract: This paper charts the evolution of the Prolog textbook Simply Logical -- Intelligent Reasoning by Example from print with runnable programmes on a 3.5-inch diskette published in 1994, via various intermediate online versions, to the fully interactive online edition available today. Our aim is to investigate -- from both the writer's and the reader's perspectives -- the potential impact of technology on educational materials. The three authors of this paper present three distinct and complementary points of view, which come together to shape an interactive online book that offers an immersive learning experience. Peter describes the philosophy behind the original book and experiences teaching from it. Jan demonstrates how contemporary web programming has enabled a fully interactive realisation of the book's philosophy. Kacper reports how different technologies can be adopted to build a versatile authoring toolkit that underpins the interactive online edition of the book. Collating these distinct yet coherent perspectives allows us to reflect on future opportunities for interactive Prolog teaching materials arising from the continuous development of web technologies. The insights we offer should be of interest to teachers of Prolog as well as those wanting to find out about the latest educational technologies.

papers.title: Evaluating Visual Language Models on Visual Grounding for Visually Impaired People
papers.abstract: Visual grounding (VG) in visual question answering (VQA) is a fundamental capability of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), enabling the detection of the most relevant region in an image to answer the question. This reflects the model's capability of multimodal comprehension, which is crucial when interacting with visually impaired people (VIP). Indeed, visual grounding, when applied to assistive scenarios, is not merely a technical feature, but rather a trust and safety requirement. In this work, we study visual grounding in VLMs for visually impaired people. To this end, we assess open-source VLMs on visual grounding using the VizWiz-VQA-Grounding dataset and challenge, which contains real-life images taken by VIP. We propose VG-SHAP, which extends an existing explainability framework to provide visual grounding explanations, allowing the evaluation of black-box VLMs. Our results on the VizWiz-VQA-Grounding challenge show that despite generating correct answers, VLMs struggle to ground in the proper region in the image. However, these results are constrained by the quality of the segmentation model of our explainability framework and further research is necessary.

papers.intro:
Grounding, the collaborative process by which speakers establish and maintain mutual understanding, is crucial in human communication (Clark and Schaefer, 1989). Visual grounding (Nagaraja et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2016; Mao et al., 2016) in VQA describes a model’s ability to localize the relevant region in the image to answer the question. Despite its importance, recent VLMs tend to answer with self-confidence(Shaikh et al., 2024) rather than grounding their responses. When it comes to assisting visually impaired people (VIP), visual grounding is essential to clearly communicate uncertainties and to correct misunderstandings. Particularly, in critical assistive scenarios, such as verifying the name of a medication, the dosage on a label, or the expiration date on a food package, where the VIP must be able to trust that the VLM’s answer is derived from the correct part of the image and whenever the model is uncertain, it should explicitly convey it.

Particularly, in critical assistive scenarios, such as verifying the name of a medication, the dosage on a label, or the expiration date on a food package, where the VIP must be able to trust that the VLM’s answer is derived from the correct part of the image and whenever the model is uncertain, it should explicitly convey it.

VLMs have recently achieved remarkable progress across a wide range of multimodal tasks, particularly in VQA, where models generate natural language responses conditioned on both image and textual inputs (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Antol et al., 2015). These advances have enabled practical applications such as assistive systems for visually impaired people (VIPs), where users rely on visual models in their day-to-day tasks (Liu et al., 2024a). One of the most important aspects of this use-case is visual grounding, which will ensure safety and reliability for the VIPs. However, most modern large-scale VLMs are evaluated primarily on textual correctness, and their grounding capabilities on images taken by VIPs remain largely underexplored. Furthermore, many state-of-the-art models operate as black boxes and do not expose internal attention maps, making it difficult to directly assess their visual reasoning processes.

In this work, our contribution is two-fold. First, we extend an existing explainability framework (Cafagna et al., 2023) to generate visual grounding explanations, and we integrate recent state-of-the-art segmentation models into it. Second, we assess the visual grounding capabilities of open-source VLMs on the VizWiz-VQA-Grounding dataset and compare them to the baselines reported in the challenge of the same name (Chen et al., 2022). Our preliminary results show that although VLMs tend to generate the correct answer, they do not correctly ground in the proper region in the image, suggesting they lack visual grounding. However, because our evaluation relies on external segmentation models, the results are subject to uncertainty and require further investigation before drawing definitive conclusions about the reliability and trustworthiness of VLMs.

papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning Assistance for Resilient Haptic Teleoperation over a 5G Network
papers.abstract: Haptic teleoperation requires low-latency and reliable communication to preserve stable and responsive interaction between a human operator and a remote environment. However, network congestion can strongly degrade teleoperation performance, particularly when haptic traffic competes with other data flows for limited radio resources. This work investigates a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-assisted teleoperation framework over an Ericsson 5G standalone (SA) testbed under different congestion and quality-of-service (QoS) configurations. In the evaluated task, a human operator uses a haptic device to steer a spaceship through a remote virtual game. The DRL agent runs inside the remote environment, hosted at the network edge, and assists the operator by blending its own actions with the operator's commands received over the 5G network. This placement gives the agent direct access to the current state of the environment, unaffected by network delay. Experimental results show that DRL assistance improves task performance under all network conditions, with the largest benefit under congestion, where it reduces mean task completion time by 20.6%. Under congestion, assisted operation even outperforms unassisted operation with QoS prioritisation, which restores latency close to the uncongested baseline.
papers.intro:
The Tactile Internet extends network-mediated teleoperation beyond audio and video by allowing a human operator to interact physically with a remote environment [1]. The human operator sends control commands and receives haptic feedback, forming a closed loop over the network [2]. This makes teleoperation highly sensitive not only to average latency, but also to how latency evolves during the task [3]. A delayed or inconsistent response can reduce task precision, degrade the human operator’s control transparency, and eventually affect the stability of the interaction.

A delayed or inconsistent response can reduce task precision, degrade the human operator’s control transparency, and eventually affect the stability of the interaction.

This becomes particularly challenging over a shared mobile network, where delay is not constant. Wireless channel conditions vary over time, users compete for resources, and sustained traffic can create queues that grow during operation. Studies of teleoperation under delay often isolate the control problem by injecting fixed or stochastic latency into an otherwise ideal connection [4]. This is useful for evaluating the effect of delay, but it treats the network as an external parameter. In a typical cellular system, the evolution of delay during task execution exposes the human operator to changing communication conditions. Measuring network behaviour alongside task outcomes is therefore necessary to examine how these variations relate to teleoperation performance.

Existing work addresses this problem from three directions. On the network side, quality-of-service (QoS) mechanisms and network slicing prioritise latency-sensitive traffic, shaping the delivered latency and throughput [5], and learned resource allocation can adapt this prioritisation dynamically [6, 7]. At the signal level, learning-based haptic signal prediction estimates delayed or lost haptic samples at the receiver, relaxing the delay bound that the network must satisfy [8, 9], and feature-attribution methods improve the robustness of such predictors [10, 11]. At the endpoint, shared autonomy blends the operator’s command with an autonomous policy to support them when the control loop degrades [12, 13, 14], including in teleoperation under delay [4, 15].

These strategies are well established but usually studied in isolation. Network studies characterise congestion and QoS through network metrics such as latency, jitter, and throughput, without linking them to task-level metrics such as completion time and accuracy. Signal prediction is typically evaluated through prediction error on recorded haptic traces, and learning-based assistance under injected delay only. Congestion in real networks, however, produces latency that is uncertain and fluctuates during the task. It therefore remains unclear whether assistance still benefits the human operator over a live network, and how it interacts with QoS prioritisation, in which the network schedules the teleoperation traffic ahead of competing traffic to preserve its latency.

The task is a virtual navigation game in which the human operator steers a spaceship with a haptic device while avoiding a penalty region, the water-zone. The water-zone is invisible to the operator and is perceived only through haptic feedback. Its high viscosity reduces the spaceship’s maximum speed and produces a drag force that opposes motion, making the spaceship slower and harder to steer, while a restoring force pushes the spaceship towards the empty space, outside of the water-zone. The agent is pretrained offline in the same virtual environment, with haptic feedback as its observation, so that it responds to the same contact forces the human operator perceives.

papers.title: Stability analysis of boundary element methods for the wave equation: The weakly singular operator in $1d$
papers.abstract: We discuss the construction of stable discrete pairs of trial and test spaces for the wave equation. Building on a general abstract operator-theoretic framework, we show how optimal pairings can be derived for a one-dimensional boundary element formulation of the wave equation with prescribed Dirichlet data, based on an indirect single layer potential ansatz. In this setting, the optimal test space can be computed analytically and has a physical interpretation, reflecting the non-local nature of the underlying operator.
papers.intro:
Recent work on time-domain boundary integral equations for the wave equation has shown that their variational formulations are continuous and inf-sup stable [13], and only occasionally elliptic [1, 14]. Therefore, the discrete stability of their discretization via space-time boundary element methods (BEM) relies on finding pairs of discrete test and trial spaces such that the discrete inf-sup condition holds independently of mesh refinement.

papers.title: Rethinking Video Storage for AI Training: Breaking Cross-Frame Dependencies for Efficient Random Access
papers.abstract: Large-scale AI training increasingly relies on massive video datasets with random temporal sampling patterns. However, existing video storage paradigms are optimized for sequential playback and employ sophisticated inter-frame reference structures to maximize compression efficiency. When applied to the random-sampling workloads of AI training, these paradigms face substantial decoding-efficiency bottlenecks. Workarounds such as independent JPEG frames and short groups of pictures (GOPs) reduce decoding work at the cost of larger storage and transfer volumes. In this paper, we identify two sources of decode amplification: sequential reconstruction of unrelated frames and reconstruction of the reference chains required by sampled targets. We address both sources by co-designing the decoding schedule and video reference structure. Dependency-aware sparse decoding reconstructs only requested frames and their required references, skipping unrelated reconstruction without transcoding the source videos. Optional offline Dependency-Decoupled Random Access (DDRA) encoding further reduces reference reconstruction by restricting each interior frame to two bounding intra-coded anchors. Together, sparse decoding and DDRA retain inter-frame prediction while bounding reconstruction to at most three frames per requested target, independent of the intra period. Experiments on a large-scale robotics corpus show that, at comparable reconstruction quality, our method achieves $1.45\times$ the loading throughput of LeRobot v3 with 58.7% less media payload.

papers.title: The medium is the message: How neurometabolic entanglement generates conscious experience
papers.abstract: Most neuroscientific accounts of consciousness assume that conscious experience is constituted by the information conveyed between neurons. The physical-chemical details of the metabolic and physiological processes that convey this information are correspondingly presumed to be relevant only insofar as they support the organization of information processes. We describe an alternative perspective that denies this presumed independence of the processing of neural information and the metabolic-physiological details of these processes. We call this alternative paradigm the theory of neuro-metabolic entanglement (NME). NME proposes that mental experience exemplifies the inseparability of the organization of neural information processes from the constraints imposed by the material-energetic properties of the neural medium itself. Central to this account is a recursive, Möbius-like loop of neural connections that entangles patterns of forebrain information processing with midbrain regulatory systems that modulate forebrain metabolism. This enables patterns of neural activity to indirectly modify the global distribution of metabolic resources underlying these information processes. It also constitutes a bottleneck that integrates diverse neural processes into an adaptively relevant unitary experience organized in terms of the global redistribution of metabolic support. Computational models of neural function cannot treat energy supply as a fixed background parameter; our proposed Möbius-like loop of neuro-metabolic entanglement offers a framework for future models in which neural activity is dynamically and recursively modulated by the network's own metabolism. Recognizing this entanglement is a first step toward dissolving the explanatory gap highlighted by the so-called "hard problem" of consciousness.

papers.title: PHD-Hand: A Printable Humanoid Dexterous Hand with Linkage-Driven 3-DOA Digits
papers.abstract: Currently, dexterous humanoid robot hands are widely considered the final hardware bottleneck that hampers generalist robots from physically assisting people at home and work. As conventional tendon-driven designs suffer from high cost, demanding maintenance, poor reliability, and short durability, alternative linkage-driven designs have increasingly gained attention. Despite their potential to avoid the weaknesses of tendon-driven hands, integrating multiple degrees of actuation (DOA) in a single digit with linkage drivetrains is a challenge for design and fabrication. Only a few studies have managed to present functional humanoid hands that are completely linkage-driven and have at least three DOAs per digit without compromising actuator placement and other design preferences. Our work introduces a new linkage-driven hand featuring a unique flexure hinge. Together with elastic drive rods made of spring steel, the linkage drivetrains are significantly simplified. Unlike other linkage-driven designs of similar dexterity, our design does not require many miniature moving parts. As a result, the hand can be fabricated easily with a budget 3D printer. This not only significantly lowers the barrier to entry for using and developing dexterous humanoid robot hand functions, but also allows the hands to be sized much closer to regular human hands. The design offers desirable kinematic advantages as well. A prototype is evaluated for grasping and object manipulation. In addition, this paper presents our latest findings on kinematics and control of the hand.

Instead, we have found “degrees of actuation (DOA)” to be a more precise term. per digit. The “root joint” of a digit should have two DOAs for tilting, while the “upper two joints’’33 3 For a finger, the root joint is an MCP joint, and the upper two joints include a PIP joint and a DIP joint. For the thumb, the root joint is a CMC joint, and the upper two joints include an MCP joint and an IP joint. To keep the narrative concise and friendly to a broader audience, instead of the anatomical terminology, we use the terms “root joint” and “upper two joints” in this paper. almost always flex/extend together and share a single DOA44 4 The thumb actually moves differently from the fingers, though the difference is not that significant. .

A straightforward way to build such a digit is to place the actuators inside or on the digits to drive the joints “locally” with a structure similar to serial robot manipulators (e.g., [1, 2, 3, 4]). This results in a dilemma of the digit either having weak actuation or being oversize and overweight. It is therefore desirable to have the actuators placed off the digits, which requires additional drivetrain(s) to deliver actuation to the upper two joints. The most common solution is to use tendon drives. The design is largely inspired by human anatomy and has been the mainstream choice of dexterous robot hands [5]. However, without self-healing, the complex tendon systems required for dexterity wear out and loosen up quickly, which leads to demanding maintenance and short life span [6]. Performance of tendon-driven hands is often jeopardized by cable fraying, knot slippage, and tension drift [7][8]. In particular, cable rupture is the top failure mode [8]. In addition, tendon-driven bidirectional actuation requires either two actuators per DOA (leads to sizing problems) or closed-loop tendon routing (prone to loosening and slacking) [9]. The absence of bidirectional actuation excludes the hand from performing certain skills.

Some designs use geared drivetrains to transmit actuation from actuators placed off the digit to the upper two joints. [11] shows a representative design in this category. Each of its digits has a 2-DOA root joint and 1-DOA coupled upper two joints. Actuation is transmitted to the upper two joints using a bevel gear drive coaxially located with the drive shafts of the root joint. Other than the fabrication hassle and inevitable backlash, complexity of the design results in a hand size significantly larger than human hands.

Alternatively, linkage-driven designs have the potential to avoid the weaknesses of tendon and gear-based designs [12]. However, integrating three DOAs with linkage drivetrains in one digit (while keeping the actuators off the digit) poses a great challenge for design and fabrication. There are only a few presentations [13, 14, 15, 16, 17], which share similar designs and have only emerged over recent years. Among them, the design presented in [13] is both pioneering and most ready for practical use. It adopts a novel 5-joint linkage drivetrain to deliver actuation to the upper two joints through the root joint (Fig. 1-a, the portion circled in red). As impressive as the prototype and demonstration are, the nontrivial number of miniature parts (Fig. 1-b) require serious fabrication capability and make it challenging to balance between durability, size, and cost. The prototype in [13] has a hand length around 218 mm which is 13% larger than average male human hands. The design is replicated in [14] and improved in [15] with hand lengths of 255 mm and 219 mm respectively. In addition, the kinematics of the root joint and upper two joints is partially coupled, which complicates the control. Our work aims at developing a dexterous humanoid robot hand that • Has five digits with three DOAs per digit (two for the root joint, one for the coupled upper two joints); • Has each DOA bidirectionally actuated with a decent strength, good backdrivability, and minimal backlash; • Can be fabricated at a size very close to human hands with minimal costs using a budget 3D printer; • Has long-lasting durability and requires minimal maintenance. papers.title: Spatial preferential attachment models: robustness revisited
papers.abstract: We investigate robustness under percolation in the degree-driven spatial preferential attachment model. Consider a profile that is regularly varying with exponent $-δ$, where $δ>1$, and an attachment rule with asymptotic slope $γ\in(0,1)$. Jacob and Mörters (Ann. Probab. 45 (2017)) proved robustness when $$ δ\left(\frac1γ-1\right)<1. $$ We prove the converse in the strict regime: if $$ δ\left(\frac1γ-1\right)>1, $$ then sufficiently strong Bernoulli vertex thinning destroys the giant component. In particular, the strict robustness boundary coincides with that of the age-dependent random connection model.

papers.intro:
Spatial preferential attachment provides a setting in which power-law degree distributions coexist with geometric clustering. In the model introduced by Jacob and Mörters [11], vertices are born in space-time, and a new vertex links to older vertices with probabilities depending on distance and on the current degree of the older endpoint. An asymptotically linear attachment rule with slope γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) produces a degree distribution with power-law exponent τ=1+1/γ\tau=1+1/\gamma, while the spatial profile controls the probability of long edges. The positive limiting average clustering coefficient distinguishes these graphs from the locally tree-like models for which branching-process approximations have been very effective.

A central question is robustness, that is, whether a giant component survives independent vertex thinning for every positive retention probability.
