papers.title: A linear, second-order, unconditionally energy-stable scalar-auxiliary-variable scheme for the CHQ viscoelastic phase-separation model
papers.abstract: The CHQ model describes viscoelastic phase separation in a polymer--solvent mixture: a Cahn--Hilliard equation for the polymer volume fraction $φ$ is two-way coupled, through a phase-dependent cross-diffusion flux, to a damped relaxation equation for a scalar bulk elastic stress $q$. We propose a scalar-auxiliary-variable (SAV) time discretisation of this system, combining the SAV reformulation of the double-well potential with a second-order backward differentiation formula (BDF2) and a second-order extrapolation of all phase-dependent mobilities: a linear, computationally cheaper complement to the reference scheme's fully nonlinear Newton solve. The resulting method is (i) linear at every time step, with a coupling structure we prove has exactly one solution at every step, for every choice of time-step size; (ii) mass conserving, exactly, as an algebraic identity of the discrete equations themselves (the only drift ever seen numerically traces to the finite tolerance of the iterative linear solver, not a failure of the conservation property); and (iii) unconditionally stable for a modified discrete energy, via an exact one-step energy--dissipation identity. We show the energy identity extends to this filtered variant as well, with two explicit extra non-negative terms. Hence, the scheme actually producing the physics results is itself provably stable for the same energy. A Fourier--Galerkin implementation verifies that the energy identity holds at every time step to within floating-point round-off. It also confirms second-order temporal accuracy, including in the steep-interface regime, and agreement with an independently implemented nonlinear Newton--BDF2 solver. Compared with that independent nonlinear Newton--BDF2 solver, at equal grid resolution, the SAV method uses $2.5$--$3.0\times$ fewer linear-solver iterations and $1.7$--$2.0\times$ less wall-clock time.

papers.intro:
Phase separation in polymer solutions and melts is frequently accompanied by a pronounced viscoelastic response: the slower-relaxing polymer network resists deformation on the timescale of demixing, and the resulting elastic stress can dramatically alter, and in some cases arrest, the coarsening process compared to a simple binary fluid. The same coupling between phase separation and viscoelasticity is central to biomolecular condensates in living cells [1]. Condensates themselves age into viscoelastic, Maxwell-fluid-like materials rather than remaining simple liquids [2], and the surrounding chromatin network has been shown experimentally to slow the coalescence of nucleolar droplets by orders of magnitude relative to isolated liquid droplets, an arrest effect closely analogous to the elastic suppression of coarsening studied here [3]. More directly still, recent experiments show that tuning the viscoelastic properties of a nucleus-mimicking compartment controls the dynamics and liquid-to-solid transition of protein condensates [4]. This phenomenon, reviewed by Tanaka [5] and modelled by a hierarchy of increasingly reduced continuum descriptions, couples a Cahn–Hilliard-type phase-field equation to an evolution equation for the elastic stress through a cross-diffusion flux. This structure is numerically delicate: energy-stable schemes for the uncoupled Cahn–Hilliard equation do not automatically extend to the coupled system, and the reference discretisation for exactly this reduced model [6] requires a nonlinear solve at every time step. This paper shows that a linear scheme can retain the same unconditional energy stability.

papers.title: The MIni-Halos in MIni-Clusters (MIMIC) project: New insights into the origin of mini-halos from a LOFAR, uGMRT, and MeerKAT study of diffuse radio emission in Abell 496 and ZwCl 235
papers.abstract: We aim at investigating the presence of diffuse radio emission in low-mass (M$_{500}\leq3\times10^{14}$ M$_{\odot}$), relaxed galaxy clusters. We present a pilot study for the MIMIC (MIni-halos in MIni-Clusters) project, focusing on Abell 496 and ZwCl 235, using LOFAR (54, 144 MHz), uGMRT (400, 650 MHz), and MeerKAT (1.28 GHz) data, as well as Chandra X-ray data. We detect diffuse radio emission in the central 100 kpc of both Abell 496 and ZwCl 235, spatially confined within sloshing-induced cold fronts seen in X-ray images. The diffuse sources satisfy the classification criteria for radio mini-halos and represent the least powerful known to date, with 1.4 GHz radio powers of $(2.2\pm0.2)\times10^{22}$ W/Hz in Abell 496 and $(1.3\pm0.3)\times10^{22}$ W/Hz in ZwCl 235. The mini-halos have steep spectra ($-1.9\leqα\leq-1.4$), and in Abell 496 we find outward steepening of the spectral index. In both clusters, the radio and X-ray surface brightness are correlated over the diffuse source extent, with sub-linear or nearly linear slopes depending on frequency. Separately, we present the properties of two extended (>200 kpc) tailed radio galaxies in both clusters. The steep spectra, sub-linear radio-X-ray correlations, and confinement within cold fronts suggest that contribution from fossil plasma advected from the central radio galaxy and plausible turbulent re-acceleration are at play in Abell 496 and ZwCl 235. These two systems allow us to extend mini-halo scaling relations toward the low-power regime. We confirm a strong correlation between the mini-halo radio power and the cool core X-ray luminosity, with $P_{1.4} \propto L_{X,70}^{1.5\pm0.2}$. We find, for the first time, tentative indications that mini-halos with steeper radio spectra may preferentially be associated with lower core X-ray luminosities and lower radio power. (abridged)

papers.intro:
In recent years, increasing attention has been devoted to diffuse radio emission in galaxy clusters, thanks to sensitive radio telescopes that revealed a growing number of cluster-scale diffuse sources (e.g., van Weeren et al. 2019; Knowles et al. 2022; Botteon et al. 2022). The origin of diffuse radio emission extending for hundreds of kpc remains an open question. The synchrotron cooling timescale of the electrons (∼107−8\sim 10^{7-8} yr) is shorter than the typical particle transport timescales (∼\sim108-9 yr) and, as such, diffusion processes alone would fail to explain the 100s kpc – Mpc size of diffuse sources (e.g., Jaffe 1977; Bagchi et al. 2002). Potential solutions to this “slow diffusion problem” involve additional mechanisms – such as turbulent reacceleration of particles or in-situ (hadronic) production of electrons (e.g., Brunetti and Jones 2014 for a review). These mechanisms have been extensively investigated in massive galaxy clusters (with M500⪆5×1014{}_{500}\gtrapprox 5\times 10^{14} M⊙), which satisfy the conditions to produce and sustain diffuse synchrotron radio sources (e.g., Giacintucci et al. 2017; van Weeren et al. 2019; Knowles et al. 2019). In the case of unrelaxed galaxy clusters, energetic mergers are known to be the origin of diffuse radio sources – most notably radio halos and radio relics (van Weeren et al., 2019); in these cases shock and turbulent reacceleration are thought to be the dominant mechanisms. Similarly, relaxed galaxy clusters can show diffuse radio emission. The dense “cool-core” at the center of these systems is likely to host radio mini-halos (80% of relaxed clusters with M500≥6×1014{}_{500}\geq 6\times 10^{14} M⊙, see Giacintucci et al. 2017), that are diffuse radio sources surrounding the central brightest cluster galaxy (BCG), with sizes of ∼100−500\sim 100-500 kpc (e.g., Gitti et al. 2002; Giacintucci et al. 2014; Giacintucci et al. 2017; Giacintucci et al. 2019; Trehaeven et al. 2023). Mini-halos are typically confined within sloshing-induced cold fronts (e.g., Giacintucci et al. 2017), which supports their connection with weak turbulence in the central regions, and therefore a turbulent re-acceleration scenario for their origin (see Bravi et al. 2016). At the same time, the radio surface brightness profiles are typically more peaked than the X-ray surface brightness ones, supporting an hadronic origin of the relativistic particles (Ignesti et al., 2020). Therefore, their origin is still debated. The active galactic nucleus (AGN) in the BCG may also contribute to the origin of mini-halos by injecting electrons into the intracluster medium (ICM). These particles could be advected by gas motions and provide a reservoir of seed electrons for re-acceleration (ZuHone et al., 2021; Vazza and Botteon, 2024; Domínguez-Fernández et al., 2024), while AGN-driven jets and bubbles may also generate turbulence in the cluster core (Sotira et al., 2025; Bellomi et al., 2025). In addition, the AGN may supply cosmic-ray protons relevant for hadronic scenarios (Pfrommer and Enßlin, 2004). In connection to this point, an open question on mini-halos is related to whether their radio powers scale with cluster mass (e.g., Kolokythas et al. 2025). Literature studies have found contrasting evidence of such a scaling (see e.g., Giacintucci et al. 2019; Richard-Laferrière et al. 2020), and rather pointed to the connection of mini-halo power with the global or core cluster X-ray luminosities (Gitti et al. 2002; Gitti et al. 2004; Bravi et al. 2016; Gitti et al. 2018; Giacintucci et al. 2019; Richard-Laferrière et al. 2020). For radio halos in unrelaxed clusters, the observed scaling of radio power with mass and dynamics is consistent with turbulent re-acceleration models (e.g., Cassano et al. 2013; Balboni et al. 2025). Whether giant radio halos and mini-halos share similar scalings (and thus, origin of the relativistic particles) remains debated (e.g., Cassano et al. 2008; Biava et al. 2024). A potential source of uncertainty in establishing the existence of a radio power – mass relation for mini-halos is that most known mini-halos are hosted in clusters with M500≥5×1014M_{500}\geq 5\times 10^{14} M⊙; only a few are known for M500∼3−5×1014M_{500}\sim 3-5\times 10^{14} M⊙ (Giacintucci et al., 2019; Richard-Laferrière et al., 2020; Kolokythas et al., 2025), and evidence for mini-halos at lower cluster masses is still unclear11 1 The mini-halo cluster 2A 0335+096 lies slightly above or below 3×10143\times 10^{14} M⊙ depending on the reference (3.4×10143.4\times 10^{14} M⊙, Piffaretti et al. 2011, or 2.3×10142.3\times 10^{14} M⊙, Planck Collaboration et al. 2016). (see also Kolokythas et al. 2025). papers.title: Connected Coloring Games on Corona Products of Graphs
papers.abstract: We study the connected coloring game on corona products of graphs. For connected graphs $G$ and $H$, we prove the sharp upper bound $χ_{cg}(G\circ H)\leq\max\{Δ(G),Δ(H)+1\}+1$ and establish a further bound using the Bob-start ordinary coloring game on the second factor. We show that the difference between the Alice-start and Bob-start connected game chromatic numbers can be arbitrarily large in either direction. We further prove that a connected subgraph may have arbitrarily larger connected game chromatic number than its ambient connected graph, and that $χ_{cg}(G\circ H)$ cannot be bounded in terms of $χ_{cg}(G)$ and $χ_{cg}(H)$ alone, even when both factors have connected game chromatic number $2$. We also obtain corona products for which the difference $χ_g-χ_{cg}$ is arbitrarily large and construct infinitely many connected graphs with $χ_g<χ_{cg}$. Finally, for corona products of trees, we prove the universal upper bound $5$, characterize those attaining the value $3$, give structural sufficient conditions for the value $4$, and exhibit a broad family attaining the value $5$.

papers.intro:
The graph coloring game is a two-player game in which the first player’s goal is to produce a proper vertex coloring of the entire graph, while the second player’s goal is to prevent this from happening. The game was introduced by Steven Brams in the context of map coloring; it was presented by Gardner in 1981 and later discussed in a graph-theoretic framework by Bodlaender (Gardner, 1981; Bodlaender, 1991). Given a graph GG and a fixed set of colors, two players, named Alice and Bob, alternately take turns coloring previously uncolored vertices, always maintaining a proper coloring. Alice wins if the entire graph is eventually colored, while Bob wins if it becomes impossible to color some uncolored vertex. The least number of colors for which Alice has a winning strategy is the game chromatic number, denoted by χg​(G)\chi_{g}(G).

The game chromatic number has been extensively studied for many classes of graphs. A result of Faigle, Kern, Kierstead and Trotter states that every forest FF satisfies χg​(F)≤4\chi_{g}(F)\leq 4 (Faigle et al., 1993). Further work considers exact values and bounds on the game chromatic numbers of planar and outerplanar graphs, partial kk-trees, and other sparse graph classes (Kierstead and Trotter, 1994; Dinski and Zhu, 1999; Guan and Zhu, 1999; Zhu, 1999; Zhu, 2000; Kierstead, 2000; Zhu, 2008b). Costa et al. (2020) showed that the game is also computationally difficult, more precisely, that the corresponding decision problem is PSPACE-complete. For the main results concerning the classical map-coloring game, as well as for fundamental techniques in this field, see Bartnicki et al. (2007).

(2020) introduced the connected coloring game, which is played according to the rules of the ordinary coloring game, with the additional requirement that the colored vertices at each stage of the game induce a connected subgraph. The minimum number of colors for which Alice has a winning strategy in this game is the connected game chromatic number, denoted by χc​g​(G)\chi_{cg}(G). Finally, it was proved that both the Alice-start and Bob-start versions of the connected coloring game are PSPACE-complete (Lima et al., 2022).

papers.title: Lasting mEMRIs: Signatures of Multiple Black Hole Extreme Mass Ratio Inspirals from AGN discs
papers.abstract: Encounters of stellar-mass black holes (sBH) in active galactic nuclei discs naturally form mean-motion resonances of sBH pairs. These mean-motion resonances can be broken close to the central supermassive black hole when gravitational-wave emission dominates over gas torques. We derive a simple condition that depends only on the sBH mass ratio and the resonance index for which a pair of sBH in a mean-motion resonance will remain intact and can be detectable as a multiple Extreme-Mass-Ratio-Inspirals (mEMRIs) in the LISA band. We present for the first time the gravitational-wave strain signatures of a pair of co-migrating sBH in mean-motion resonance, including additional gravitational-wave harmonics associated with orbital conjunctions of the individual EMRIs. The frequency evolution and the associated chirp mass is degenerate with isolated EMRIs of different masses. However, the mEMRI mass ratio is quantised by the resonance order and is larger than the true mass ratio. The degeneracy can be broken if the true sBH mass ratio can be inferred from individual strain amplitudes. We argue that mEMRIs should be common if disc driven EMRIs are to be detected by LISA, with $\sim 10$ mEMRIs per year in the local universe ($z \lesssim 0.2$), highlighting the need to model mEMRI systems in future LISA data analysis.

papers.intro:
The accretion discs of active galactic nuclei (AGN) are among the most dynamically rich environments in the Universe for compact objects. These include the central supermassive black hole (SMBH) and stellar-mass black holes (sBHs), which are either captured from the surrounding nuclear star cluster (Bartos et al., 2017; Tagawa et al., 2020) or formed in situ in the disc’s self-gravitating outer regions (Stone et al., 2017; Gilbaum & Stone, 2022). Gas drag drives sBHs onto nearly circular, coplanar orbits (Generozov & Perets, 2023; Wang et al., 2024), after which disc torques cause them to migrate inward (Bellovary et al., 2016; Grishin et al., 2024). The dense gas also leads to sBH–sBH binary formation through dynamical encounters at low relative velocities (Rowan et al., 2023; Moncrieff et al., 2026), making AGN discs a prolific channel for gravitational-wave (GW) mergers detectable by LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA (LVK) (McKernan et al., 2020; Tagawa et al., 2020).

In the absence of migration traps, whose locations depend on the AGN disc profile and sBH masses, sBHs may migrate close enough to the central SMBH for GW emission to drive a merger within the AGN lifetime (Pan & Yang, 2021; Gilbaum et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025). The final inspiral produces an extreme mass-ratio inspiral (EMRI), potentially detectable by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) (Amaro-Seoane et al., 2023) or Tianqin (Li et al., 2025). The imprint of the AGN environment on the EMRI waveform, through gas drag, nearby perturbers, and relativistic precession, offers a unique probe of disc physics and the SMBH spacetime (Barausse et al., 2007; Kocsis et al., 2011). Moreover, combining the GW-inferred luminosity distance with an electromagnetic redshift enables a standard-siren measurement of the Hubble constant (Laghi et al., 2021).

Most studies of BH dynamics in AGN discs incorporate simplified 1D prescriptions for the interaction of sBHs during encounters (Tagawa et al., 2020; Vaccaro et al., 2026, e.g.,, although see Rowan & Pessah, 2026 for a recent hybrid 3D N-body simulations). However, N-body simulations coupled with semi-analytic prescriptions for gas torques show that differential migration naturally leads to the formation of mean motion resonances (Secunda et al., 2019; Lott et al., 2025; Moncrieff et al., 2026; Gonglewski et al., 2026, MMRs, ). MMRs maintain the period ratio of two orbiting objects at a simple integer ratio, preventing further differential migration, close encounters, and binary formation. These MMRs have been shown to be important in determining the expected population properties of sBH mergers in AGN discs (Moncrieff et al., 2026; Epstein-Martin et al., 2025; Gonglewski et al., 2026), and can remain stable until very close to the central SMBH (Peng & Chen, 2023; Peng et al., 2024). A detection of a sBH pair in MMR with LISA and/or Tianqin could lead to unique observational signatures.

We begin in Section 2 by overviewing sBH dynamics in AGN discs and our numerical setup. We derive a simple criterion for MMR stability against differential GW-induced migration and verity it with numerical examples of MMR formation, break-up and retention in the relativistic limit. In Section 3 we study the relativistic effects on the evolution of the stable mEMRI on apsidal anti-alignment, eccentricity growth and offset from exact resonance. In Section 4 we analyse the GW signal from a fiducial mEMRI system, showing unique signatures. In Section 5 we discuss the impact of mEMRIs on LISA data analysis, degeneracies and characteristics. In Section 6, we discuss the the astrophysical implications, rates, comparison to past work, caveats and future prospects. Finally, we summarise our main results in Section 7.

papers.title: Temporal Exploration and Rendezvous via Weisfeiler-Leman Colorings
papers.abstract: Temporal graphs are graphs whose edge relation changes in discrete time steps. The Temporal Exploration Problem (TEXP) asks for a temporal walk that visits all vertices. We show that every connected temporal graph with $n$ vertices can be explored in $O(qn\log^3(n))$ time steps, where $q$ is the number of vertex color classes induced by the 2-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (2-WL) coloring. For small $q$, our bound substantially improves on the known worst-case bound of $Θ(n^2)$ in general connected temporal graphs. A corresponding walk can be constructed in deterministic polynomial time. The upper bound is complemented by lower bounds of $Ω(n\log(n))$ when $q$ is constant and $Ω(qn)$ when $1 \leq q \leq n$. We also apply our techniques to the Temporal Rendezvous Problem (TRP), in which two agents that do not communicate have to meet on a vertex of the temporal graph. Our exploration algorithm yields that, with only polynomial-time computational power, the agents can meet in $O(n\log^3(n))$ time steps, leaving a gap of only $\log^2(n)$ to the known lower bound. Dogeas, Erlebach, Kammer, Meintrup, and Moses Jr. [ICALP'24] have shown an $O(rn^{1+ε})$ bound for TEXP, for every fixed $ε> 0$, where $r$ is the number of orbits, and an $O(n^{1+ε})$ bound for TRP. Both results require superpolynomial computation time. Our contribution improves upon these results in several ways. First, the dependence on $n$ in the upper bounds on the number of time steps is decreased from $n^{1+ε}$ to $n\log^3(n)$ for both TEXP and TRP. Second, for TEXP, we bound the number of time steps linearly by the parameter q, which is efficiently computable and upper bounded by $r$. Third, we provide novel deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for both TEXP and TRP.

papers.intro:
Temporal graphs are graphs whose edge sets change over discrete time steps. For surveys and background, see [28, 75]. Formally, a temporal graph 𝒢=(G1,…,GL)\mathcal{G}=(G_{1},\ldots,G_{L}) with lifetime LL is a sequence of graphs, called snapshots, on a common vertex set VV. The graph obtained by the union over all snapshots is called the underlying graph. In each time step, a temporal walk either stays at the current vertex or traverses an edge present in the current snapshot. One of the most prominent research directions regarding temporal graphs is the study of problems involving temporal walks. Examples include temporal reachability [3, 30, 39, 46, 85, 86], temporal connected components [17, 19, 33], temporal spanners [29, 31, 71], and Temporal Exploration (TEXP), which was first introduced by Michail and Spirakis [76].

The lower-bound results have motivated extensive work on identifying restricted settings in which the quadratic barrier can be broken. Subquadratic upper bounds are known for connected temporal graphs with bounded-degree snapshots [44, 41, 18], planar underlying graphs and underlying graphs of bounded pathwidth or treewidth, and cycles with few chords [2, 21, 45]. Despite extensive progress, temporal exploration in connected temporal graphs is still far from well understood. While many natural restrictions are known to admit subquadratic exploration, the best upper and lower bounds often remain widely separated. For instance, for bounded-degree snapshots, bounded-degree underlying graphs, planar underlying graphs, and snapshots being cycles, the best lower bound is still only Ω⁡(n​log⁡n)\Omega(n\log n) [45], whereas the best upper bounds remain around n3/2n^{3/2} (up to logarithmic factors) [18]. Even highly structured cases are not completely settled: for temporal graphs whose underlying graph is a (2×k)(2\times k)-grid, the known bounds still differ by a polylogarithmic factor [45]. Thus, while the quadratic barrier can be broken in many settings, the fine-grained behavior of temporal exploration remains open for several fundamental graph classes.

papers.title: Plausible but Unimplantable: A Trustworthiness Audit of Shape Completion Foundation Models for Cranial Defect Reconstruction
papers.abstract: A patient who has lost part of the skull vault needs an implant that fits the defect exactly, and such implants are still drawn by hand in CAD by specialists, which makes each case slow and expensive. The task can be considered as a shape completion problem, so pretrained completion models, and now the first shape completion foundation models, look like a way to remove that manual step. We audited three publicly released pretrained shape completion models, two of them foundation models, applied zero-shot to 239 cranial defects, some carved from public skull datasets and some real post-craniectomy cases. Each output was compared with simply returning the patient's own remaining bone, and tested for whether the predicted material could be placed without intersecting the bone that is still there. On the 210 carved defects none of the three improved on doing nothing, and on the 29 real cases only one did so beyond chance. Yet not one output, from any model in any configuration, was implantable: none managed both to stay clear of the bone the patient still has and to place more material than doing nothing, where a task-specific volumetric model, trained for this task and selected on these cases, was implantable on all but one. The output that most convincingly resembles a skull is no more placeable than the rest, and at these point densities implant thickness cannot be read off the emitted points at all, which is a property of the output representation rather than of any one model. On this evidence the shape completion foundation models we could obtain cannot be trusted and, used as released, are not usable in clinical practice. Substantial research towards trustworthy foundation models for shape completion is still needed.

papers.intro:
After a decompressive craniectomy, a head injury or a tumour resection that takes bone, a patient is left with an opening in the skull vault, closed with an implant shaped to that patient’s anatomy [11, 9]. The implant should protect the brain and restore the original shape of the skull, and whether it fits is settled in the operating room [10, 12].

The implant should protect the brain and restore the original shape of the skull, and whether it fits is settled in the operating room [10, 12].

Such implants are designed by hand, in CAD, by specialists, which makes each case slow and expensive and limits how many patients can be offered one. Automation has been pursued for a decade, mostly as volumetric completion of the missing bone, and networks trained for that task now do well on public benchmarks [11, 9, 12], most recently point-cloud diffusion and flow matching [5, 8, 7]. Every one of them has to be trained on data for the task, and that is the cost a foundation model promises to remove.

Completion models are judged by how closely the completed shape resembles a reference, and that resemblance is not what a surgeon needs to know: it cannot say whether the model added anything the patient’s own bone did not already supply, nor whether what it predicted could physically be placed in that patient [16, 15, 24].

Contribution: We audit three publicly released pretrained shape completion models, applied zero-shot to cranial defects, and judge them by what the clinic needs rather than by what a benchmark reports. First, we score every output against an explicit do-nothing baseline, the patient’s own retained bone. Second, we introduce a physical acceptance criterion, under which the predicted material must sit in the defect without intersecting the bone that remains, and we report how many patients could receive each output. Third, we test whether the language conditioning these models advertise carries anatomical information, reading each against its own noise floor. Together they let a completion model be judged on the thing that decides its use: whether what it produced could be put in a patient.

papers.title: Teaching quantum mechanics in secondary schools: A qubit-first learning path to Bell's inequalities
papers.abstract: Teaching quantum mechanics at the secondary school level remains a major educational challenge. Traditional historical approaches often present the theory as a sequence of disconnected phenomena, requiring extensive prior knowledge of classical physics before students can appreciate the conceptual structure of quantum physics. In this work, we present the design, implementation, and evaluation of a curriculum based on the two state (qubit first) approach, in which the fundamental postulates of quantum mechanics are introduced through mathematically accessible two level systems and realized with light polarization. The curriculum integrates theoretical instruction, laboratory activities, a coherent progression grounded in the interactive simulations, and inquiry based learning into a coherent pathway that progresses from quantum states and superposition to entanglement and the experimental violation of Bell's inequalities. A distinctive feature of the project is the experimental realization of the violation of Bell's inequalities obtained in a newly established quantum optics laboratory in an Italian high school, where students performed, for the first time in Italy, an authentic Bell test using polarization-entangled photons. The same educational framework was adopted for in service teacher professional development courses. Learning outcomes were evaluated through mixed methods. Preliminary analysis indicates significant improvements in conceptual understanding, confidence in using mathematical formalism, and appreciation of the relationship between theory, experimentation, and the foundations of quantum mechanics. The proposed curriculum shows that two-state formalism and supported by real laboratory experiences enables secondary-school students to engage more meaningfully with both the conceptual foundations of quantum mechanics and their experimental verification.

papers.title: On unit groups of purely infinite rings
papers.abstract: We prove that the unit group of any purely infinite, regular, right self-injective ring admits a universal sequence of words (thus has strong distortion), is minimally almost periodic, has finite involution width, is verbally simple and verbally elliptic, and has uncountable uniform strong cofinality. These findings are consequences of more refined structural results, some of which provide concrete cardinal estimates involving the Goodearl--Boyle dimension of the ring. A central ingredient in our results is a comprehensive study of bounded normal generation, in particular with respect to certain classes of involutions. Along the way, we develop some abstract methods and concepts pertaining to geometric group theory.

papers.intro:

papers.title: The End of Consensus Research?
papers.abstract: Consensus is a fundamental problem in distributed computing and at the core of state machine replication (SMR). Despite decades of active human research, discovering practical low-latency solutions to the problem is still open, as it requires combining protocol knowledge, correctness reasoning, implementation, and experimental evaluation. We report on how AI helped us discover A-greement, a new consensus protocol for geo-replicated state machines that significantly outperforms state-of-the-art solutions. Averaged across six deployments with 5 or 9 replicas, A-greement reduces the mean latency of a geo-distributed key-value store over the fastest baseline by 12.2% and 33.3% on write-heavy and read-heavy workloads, respectively, and matches the fastest baseline on read-only workloads. A-greement combines lease-authorized local reads, direct client learning for leader-ordered writes, and a fast fixed-quorum per-key write path, selected according to network topology and workload. At the heart of our discovery lies AI-greement, an agent harness for the "autonomous" discovery, implementation, experimentation, and verification of candidate protocols. AI-greement integrates (1) a concept-oriented protocol knowledge base, (2) a modular implementation skeleton, and (3) a Lean-based verification framework with reusable safety definitions, reference specifications, and proofs. AI-greement is of independent interest: its Lean formalization uncovers several previously unreported vulnerabilities in existing consensus protocols, and it provides guidelines on how domain-specific harnesses can turn general-purpose coding agents into effective tools for (distributed) computing research. Yet we argue that human consensus experts remain essential before, during, and after the search: agents reshape the researcher's role rather than end consensus research.
papers.intro:
In SMR (SMR) [37, 65], a universal paradigm to build highly-available computing systems, consensus enables replicas to agree on a common sequence of client commands, maintaining consistent state despite concurrent requests and failures. Consensus is a fundamental building block of modern distributed systems, underpinning replicated databases [17, 71, 30], storage systems [6], cloud coordination services [10] and blockchain infrastructures [8, 81]. Consensus has been an active research area for over four decades. However, designing and implementing consensus protocols that are both correct and practically efficient remains an exceptionally challenging task [12, 55]. Protocol decisions involving ordering, quorums, recovery, and execution are tightly coupled: an optimization that shortens the common-case path may complicate recovery or introduce subtle correctness violations [12, 70, 64], as we also find for the optimizations of EPaxos Revisited [75] (§ 8). Translating a protocol design into a working system further requires preserving its safety properties throughout implementation optimizations [25, 79, 68], as well as demonstrating performance improvements across diverse network topologies and workloads. Advancing the state of the art in consensus therefore requires tightly integrating protocol knowledge, correctness reasoning, implementation and experimental evaluation.

The overall question we address in this paper is whether, just like in other fields of computing, AI could help “crack” the consensus problem. More specifically, we aim to come up with a new practically effective solution that would, on the one hand, tolerate, besides failures of the processes, failures of the network (i.e., asynchronous periods) and, on the other hand, expedite decisions in common failure-free executions. In particular, we ask whether we can develop a consensus protocol that would yield an SMR scheme in which, in the common case, (a) read-only commands complete at a nearby replica and (b) commands with updates take one round trip to a majority of replicas. This would essentially be optimal. Importantly, and unlike many recent AI-assisted results in mathematics and theoretical computer science, we seek a protocol that is practically useful and hence, besides algorithmic design and proofs, consider the implementation, deployment and evaluation as part of the AI-assisted task.

In short, we show in this paper that the answer is positive. Yet, we highlight the crucial role of the human researcher in the development of an adequate AI agent, the prompting of the agent as well as the certification of the agent’s output. We furthermore argue that this human researcher needs to be a consensus expert to effectively steer and leverage the capabilities of agents.

Recent advances in the capabilities of LLM have indeed enabled coding agents to autonomously perform increasingly complex software engineering tasks [35, 80]. For example, Codex by OpenAI [57], Claude Code by Anthropic [4], and Cursor Agent by Anysphere [5] can navigate repositories, modify code, execute tests, and iteratively refine implementations based on execution feedback. However, these general-purpose capabilities do not necessarily translate into the autonomous discovery of consensus protocols. Existing AI-driven systems research frameworks optimize self-contained policies such as schedulers and load balancers in simulators [54, 14], but do not seem an adequate fit for consensus, whose logic is spread across many communicating, failure-prone nodes [14]. Our preliminary experiment in § 2.3 also suggests that a coding agent combined with a frontier LLM, starting from a single existing consensus codebase, finds only marginal improvements. This gap motivates the need for specific support for consensus research beyond general-purpose coding capabilities.

We present AI-greement, an agent harness that equips general-purpose coding agents with domain-specific support for autonomous consensus research. AI-greement addresses three key challenges in consensus discovery. First, synthesizing new protocols requires understanding and combining mechanisms scattered across the consensus literature. To support this, a concept-oriented protocol knowledge base organizes consensus mechanisms and grounds them in concrete examples from published protocols. Second, translating novel designs into executable implementations is challenging because consensus mechanisms often have complex protocol states and message flows. A modular implementation skeleton structures this scheme through well-defined components and interfaces, allowing the agent to focus on protocol-specific logic. Third, subtle correctness violations can escape conventional testing, which covers only a limited set of message orderings and failure scenarios. Formal verification closes this gap by proving safety for every execution of a protocol model, but writing such models and proofs from scratch for each candidate is too costly. A Lean-based verification framework therefore provides reusable safety definitions, reference specifications, and proof libraries, so the agent can obtain machine-checked evidence that its design, as modeled, is safe. These components work together in an iterative discovery process, where performance measurements and fault-injection results guide the agent toward more efficient and robust designs.

papers.title: Closedness of bounded strength and partition rank loci
papers.abstract: We show the existence of a quartic form of strength $3$ in the closure of the strength at most $2$ locus, answering a question of Ballico--Bik--Oneto--Ventura in the negative. In the analogous setting of partition rank as introduced by Naslund, we further show that the locus of tensors of partition rank at most $2$ is closed, but the locus of tensors of partition rank at most $3$ is not. Together with a suspension lemma, this answers for all $r$ whether the locus of forms/tensors of strength/partition rank at most $r$ is Zariski-closed.

papers.title: Funnel-Precompensated Disturbance Observer for Uncertain Minimum-Phase SISO Linear Systems of Arbitrary Relative Degree
papers.abstract: Disturbance observers (DOBs) recover nominal behavior, but fast filters risk peaking. We propose a funnel-precompensated DOB for uncertain minimum-phase single-input single-output linear systems of known relative degree. A stable-factor residual yields a minimum-phase channel. At relative degree two, gain conditions require positive plant high-frequency gains and one positive common design gain; for higher degrees, the common-design result also uses a plant-gain interval and mismatch condition. Global boundedness, practical nominal-output recovery, and open-funnel initialization are established.
papers.intro:
Disturbance-observer-based (DOB) control augments a nominally stabilizing controller with an inner loop that compensates matched disturbances and model mismatch [1, 2]. Conventional realizations use a low-pass QQ-filter to make the nominal inverse proper; reducing its time scale improves recovery over an admissible uncertainty class but can introduce fast-dynamics peaking [1].

Disturbance-observer-based (DOB) control augments a nominally stabilizing controller with an inner loop that compensates matched disturbances and model mismatch [1, 2]. Conventional realizations use a low-pass QQ-filter to make the nominal inverse proper; reducing its time scale improves recovery over an admissible uncertainty class but can introduce fast-dynamics peaking [1].

Funnel control replaces a fixed high gain by an error-dependent gain near a prescribed boundary. A funnel pre-compensator (FPC) provides an artificial output and its derivatives [3, 4]. For systems of arbitrary relative degree, FPC cascades preserve minimum phase and the original relative degree [5]. High-gain-observer funnel control handles arbitrary relative degree through a sufficiently large fixed observer gain [6]. The methods in [7, 8] target direct tracking; the present work regulates an uncertain DOB residual.

For systems of arbitrary relative degree, FPC cascades preserve minimum phase and the original relative degree [5]. High-gain-observer funnel control handles arbitrary relative degree through a sufficiently large fixed observer gain [6]. The methods in [7, 8] target direct tracking; the present work regulates an uncertain DOB residual.

Stable coprime-factor graph representations describe nominal input–output behavior [9]. We connect arbitrary-relative-degree FPC theory to DOB design through a stable-factor residual. The resulting minimum-phase channel preserves each plant’s relative degree and positive high-frequency gain without requiring nominal stabilization of the actual plant. At relative degree two, plant high-frequency gains and the common design gain need only be positive; from relative degree three, the common-design result also uses a plant-gain interval and mismatch condition. The residual realization shows that the bounded equivalent disturbance enters through the matched input channel required by the FPC result. A stable recovery identity gives nominal-output bounds. Finite-horizon observability bounds the plant and controller realization states and completes the implemented-state boundedness argument. For bounded reciprocal funnels, an admissible stable weighting gives a filtered-estimation-error bound. Open funnels remove residual-channel and FPC initial-domain restrictions. Online implementation uses the residual and, for relative degree at least two, the FPC states.

papers.title: Stability for the adjoint Finner inequality and improved lower bounds on the $k$-plane transform
papers.abstract: We establish stability properties of near-extremisers for the Loomis--Whitney inequality and its adjoint, presenting our results in the general framework of Finner. In particular, we show that a function nearly achieves equality in the adjoint Finner inequality if and only if it is near to being an indicator function of a cartesian product. As an application, we obtain new lower bounds for the classical $k$-plane transform on $L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$, modestly improving those obtained recently by Tao and the first author. We also present an alternative approach to such improvements based on stability in the setting of the Brascamp--Lieb inequality and the theory of fusion frames. We conclude with an interpretation of our $k$-plane transform estimates as adjoint forms of the continuous Brascamp--Lieb inequalities.

papers.title: ReSeg: Retraining-free segmentation of abdominal organs via generalizable semantic representation learning
papers.abstract: Abdominal organ segmentation is essential in modern medical applications. While existing deep learning approaches demonstrate promising performance, their heavy reliance on large-scale image data raises concerns over generalization capability and privacy risks. This motivates the development of generalizable segmentation training paradigms based on domain-randomized image synthesis, facilitating generalization across unseen real image domains. However, existing paradigms either suffer from limited segmentation performance when applied to abdominal organs, or require dataset-specific finetuning. To address these limitations, we propose ReSeg, a novel two-stage retraining-free framework for domain-agnostic zero-shot abdominal organ segmentation. At the first stage, our organ-agnostic synthetic data-driven pretraining approach exploits semantically and visually diverse synthetic images generated by a dedicated data engine to optimize a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet). The network is thereby capable of learning semantic features robust against variations in anatomical structure, imaging contrast, resolution and spatial context, which provide universal representation capabilities that serve as a foundation for segmentation learning. Subsequently, in the second stage, we continue to train an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet), whose encoder is initialized with the pretrained weights. This training process is facilitated by another dedicated data engine, which generates diversified visual images while strictly retaining the inherent spatial layout of abdominal organs. Comprehensive evaluation on seven abdominal organ segmentation datasets across three different modalities including CT, MRI, and PET demonstrates that ReSeg consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods while eliminating the need for real training images.

Abdominal organ segmentation plays a pivotal role in medical imaging by enabling precise organ localization and volumetric analysis, serving as a foundation for computer-aided diagnosis (Chan et al., 2020), therapy planning (Chen et al., 2021), and surgical navigation (Okamoto et al., 2015). For instance, liver segmentation aids focal lesion detection and liver fibrosis staging (Tong et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2023), and kidney segmentation from preoperative scans is a prerequisite for building 3D models that support augmented reality navigation in laparoscopic partial nephrectomy (Zhang et al., 2019). Manual segmentation of abdominal organs is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and error-prone, thus spurring the need for accurate automatic segmentation algorithms.

Automated segmentation of abdominal organs from volumetric medical images is a challenging task. First, soft tissues usually have low contrast characteristic in abdominal imaging, leading to weak boundaries between adjacent anatomical structures (Wang et al., 2019). Second, the abdominal cavity presents a complex background with highly variable morphological structures, whose shapes and sizes exhibit significant heterogeneity among patients (Ma et al., 2021). Third, abdominal images acquired from different clinical settings often vary substantially in terms of field of view (FOV), introducing inconsistencies in the contextual information associated with organs.

Second, the abdominal cavity presents a complex background with highly variable morphological structures, whose shapes and sizes exhibit significant heterogeneity among patients (Ma et al., 2021). The field has witnessed remarkable progress through deep learning approaches to meet the challenges mentioned above (Isensee et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025). This progress has shifted the research focus from dataset-specific models towards universal foundation models, which offer improved performance while enhancing generalization capability. Some studies leverage approaches inspired by Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) (Liu et al., 2023) or Segment Anything Model (SAM) (Du et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024; He et al., 2025) to handle diverse segmentation tasks, while others advance representation learning methods to pretrain networks with powerful feature extraction capability. These include reconstruction-based methods like MAE (He et al., 2022), SimMIM (Xie et al., 2022), and MiM (Zhuang et al., 2025a), as well as contrastive learning approaches such as VoCo (Wu et al., 2024), UAE (Bai et al., 2025), and SuperCL (Zeng et al., 2026). Finetuning these pretrained networks on downstream segmentation datasets has yielded promising results.

Finetuning these pretrained networks on downstream segmentation datasets has yielded promising results.

Despite these advantages, most existing biomedical foundation segmentation methods face a fundamental limitation: they require large amounts of medical image datasets covering multiple domains to achieve excellent generalization performance and inherently have high reliance on real medical images for training (Liu et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024; He et al., 2025). Such reliance introduces not only privacy risks but also modality-specific biases, as significant domain gaps persist with large-scale data (Huang et al., 2025), leading models to learn suboptimal feature representations. This results in limited generalization in real clinical scenarios, particularly when processing images from entirely unseen biomedical scenarios with variant imaging modalities, such as Computed Tomography (CT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and Positron Emission Tomography (PET). Hence, there is an urgent need for a domain-agnostic zero-shot segmentation approach, where the model can segment images from unseen domains with cross-modality discrepancies and intra-modality variations.

Recently, there have been research efforts dedicated to developing generalizable segmentation training paradigms based on domain-randomized image synthesis strategies in brain MR image analysis (Billot et al., 2023; Ayaz et al., 2024; Gopinath et al., 2025). These approaches train Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) exclusively on synthetic images sampled from a generative model conditioned on label maps, eliminating the requirement for real training images. By leveraging a domain randomization strategy, they generate pseudo training images with varying contrasts and resolutions, exposing models to extensive variability during training. This forces the models to learn domain-independent features, enabling effective generalization to real clinical scans across diverse domains during inference. Beyond brain imaging, such a paradigm has also been extended in existing literature to segmentation tasks targeting other anatomical structures, including vascular structures (Chollet et al., 2024) and cellular nuclei (Dey et al., 2024). Building on the domain randomization concept, Anatomix (Dey et al., 2025) further introduced a general-purpose representation learning framework powered by a dedicated data engine, which synthesizes highly variable training samples from compositions of organ shape templates. This enables the pretraining of a network that serves as a strong, dataset-agnostic initialization for finetuning on new segmentation datasets.

Despite significant progress achieved so far, to achieve generalizable segmentation of abdominal organs without access to real training images, several challenges persist. First, most existing approaches are designed for structures with relatively fixed anatomical topology and stable tissue intensity distribution such as the brain (Billot et al., 2023), the vascular structures (Chollet et al., 2024), and the cellular nuclei (Dey et al., 2024), and thus fall short in segmentation performance when applied to abdominal organs (as demonstrated by the experimental results presented in Fig. 1), which exhibit large morphological variations among patients. Second, it is challenging to generate realistic synthetic abdominal data due to the lack of standardized anatomical atlases and refined annotated templates, resulting in severe domain gaps between synthetic and real clinical scans. Third, the existing domain-randomization-based representation learning method Anatomix (Dey et al., 2025) focuses on acquiring appearance-agnostic representations, yet overlooks the contextual consistency in the learned features. This may lead to diminished performance when segmenting images across varying FOVs where contextual information changes. Finally, although the existing representation learning method Anatomix (Dey et al., 2025) enhances domain-agnostic features, additional finetuning on downstream datasets is required for adapting the pretrained network to task-specific segmentation, limiting their applicability in retraining-free settings.

papers.title: UNIVERS: Learning UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis for generalizable one-shot landmark localization
papers.abstract: One-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying fields of view (FOVs) is challenging. While existing self-supervised learning methods have shown promising performance, they rely on contrastive learning built upon augmented views of the same image, which inherently limits their generalization in cross-modality scenarios. This motivates research on cross-modality embedding learning using paired multi-modality images. However, existing methods suffer from not only limited training data, but also the requirement of multi-stage iterative training. To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. Our framework leverages diverse pseudo-data synthesized from organ shape templates, with randomization applied to semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. Coupled with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning, this domain randomization strategy forces the network to disregard domain-specific biases and learn features that are robust against variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Consequently, the trained model enables one-shot landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. In this study, the efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated by applying it to the task of localizing the adrenal glands, which are paired, small, and irregular endocrine organs. In particular, comprehensive experiments are conducted on three challenging adrenal gland datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that UNIVERS consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) one-shot landmark localization approaches, with particularly prominent advantages in cross-modality scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Kendra9999/UNIVERS.

papers.intro:
The adrenal glands are paired, small, irregular endocrine organs located superior to both kidneys [1]. By secreting essential hormones, they play vital roles in regulating stress response, metabolism, electrolyte homeostasis, and sympathetic nervous system [2, 3]. Adrenal disorders, such as adrenal hyperplasia and adrenal tumor, are frequently encountered in routine radiological imaging [4]. Such abnormalities can disrupt hormonal balance, resulting in hypertension and other hormone-related symptoms [5]. Computer-aided interpretation of adrenal imaging offers a noninvasive and effective approach, playing an increasingly critical role in the clinical management of adrenal-related diseases. Due to the extremely small size of the adrenal glands, precise localization of their centers in volumetric medical images becomes an essential preprocessing step for many downstream computer-aided tasks, such as adrenal segmentation [3] and lesion classification [6]. Existing landmark localization methods mostly rely on supervised learning [7, 8], which requires large amounts of manually annotated training data. Unfortunately, annotating medical images is laborious, costly, and requires clinical expertise.

Due to the extremely small size of the adrenal glands, precise localization of their centers in volumetric medical images becomes an essential preprocessing step for many downstream computer-aided tasks, such as adrenal segmentation [3] and lesion classification [6]. Existing landmark localization methods mostly rely on supervised learning [7, 8], which requires large amounts of manually annotated training data. Unfortunately, annotating medical images is laborious, costly, and requires clinical expertise.

To reduce the annotation burden, recent research has shifted towards one-shot landmark localization, which requires only a single annotated support image to identify corresponding landmarks in query images [9, 10, 11, 12]. An emerging paradigm to find such landmark correspondences is achieved by learning discriminative voxel-wise anatomical embeddings. Typically, two augmented, overlapping views are extracted from the same image and fed into a Siamese network to generate voxel-wise embeddings. Then, self-supervised contrastive learning is applied, which encourages corresponding voxels across the two views to have similar embeddings while pushing non-corresponding voxels apart in the embedding space. Given the anatomical structural consistency, the learned embeddings map corresponding landmarks to similar feature representations. Consequently, annotations from a single support image can be transferred to query images via feature similarity matching. Building on this concept, several strategies have been proposed to enhance landmark localization performance, including negative sampling [10], coarse-to-fine architectures [9, 10, 11], and semantic embedding learning [12]. More recently, Universal Anatomical Embedding (UAE-M) [12] has extended this line of work to cross-modality landmark matching between Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). This method learns voxel correspondences across unaligned multi-modality images via an iterative training process.

First, most existing methods [9, 10, 11] build upon the heuristic that corresponding voxels across augmented views of the same image should yield similar embeddings, while their training is restricted to single-modality data. As a result, these methods struggle to match corresponding anatomical structures across multi-modality images. Second, while UAE-M [12] addresses cross-modality landmark matching, it relies on paired multi-modality images of the same subject. Such image pairs are usually unaligned across modalities, necessitating multi-stage iterative training to establish reliable voxel correspondences. More importantly, existing methods [9, 10, 11, 12] rely heavily on real clinical images, yet it is challenging, if not impossible, to collect large-scale multi-modality datasets. Accordingly, networks are exposed to a limited spectrum of domain variations in anatomical structure, imaging contrast, spatial resolution, field of view (FOV), and patient pose. Such insufficient data diversity results in suboptimal feature representations that lack robustness to large domain shifts in real clinical scenarios.

To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis for generalizable one-shot landmark localization. Instead of relying on real training images, our learning process utilizes synthetic data generated from organ shape templates, where randomization is introduced in semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. This strategy exposes the network to a wide range of variability during contrastive learning, forcing it to learn features that are robust to variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Discriminative voxel-wise embedding learning is then achieved via a Cross-domain Discriminative Voxel-wise Contrastive (CDVC) loss, which encourages the voxel-wise discriminability of domain-invariant features amidst contextual variations. During inference, UNIVERS relies exclusively on anatomical structural consistency to distinguish voxels, generating domain-invariant voxel-wise embeddings for real clinical images from multiple domains without retraining or finetuning. UNIVERS achieves superior performance compared with existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods under three one-shot evaluation settings: intra-dataset, cross-dataset intra-modality, cross-dataset cross-modality. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework for learning UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to learn generalizable, discriminative voxel-wise embeddings exclusively from pseudo-data synthesized via domain randomization. • We design a novel Cross-domain Discriminative Voxel-wise Contrastive (CDVC) loss, which operates on multi-domain pseudo-patch quadruplets with multiple positives to drive the network toward learning domain-invariant and discriminative embeddings. • We develop a coarse-to-fine one-shot adrenal gland localization framework built upon a single frozen UNIVERS network, which enables landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. • We conduct comprehensive experiments under three one-shot settings across three distinct datasets. papers.title: Bridge change-of-measure for propagator estimation of diffusions
papers.abstract: The propagator of one-dimensional diffusions has relevant applications in statistical inference and across many disciplines. Yet it is obtained in closed form only for very few simple models. Here we analyze an importance sampling strategy based on a bridge change of measure to estimate propagators: paths are generated under an auxiliary diffusion whose bridge between the two fixed boundary points is easy to generate, and the target propagator is recovered through a Radon-Nikodym derivative or likelihood ratio correction derived from Girsanov's theorem. This method overcomes the main limitations of the crude Monte Carlo estimator, which relies on binning in state space, introducing bias and becoming inefficient with rare transitions. We apply the method to a range of benchmark processes and show that the bridge-based estimator matches the accuracy of crude Monte Carlo with orders of magnitude fewer sample paths. Finally, we elaborate on discretization schemes for the Radon-Nikodym derivative and on approximations to the best-in-class change of measure, both of which increase the efficiency of the method.

This method belongs to the family of importance sampling or change-of-measure techniques and uses change-of-measure methods combined with bridge processes and their propagators.

The structure of the article is the following. In Sec. II, the Crude Monte Carlo propagator estimator is discussed. In Sec. III, the Bridge change-of-measure Monte Carlo estimator (BCMMCE) of the propagator is introduced. Two discretization schemes for the evaluation of a path integral appearing in the BCMMCE are presented in Sec. IV. On the practical side, Sec. V provides the two algorithms of Bridge change-of-measure Monte Carlo propagator estimation: the estimation algorithm with Wiener bridges in Sec. V.1 and the estimation algorithm with arbitrary Markov bridges in Sec. V.2. Then, Sec. VI suggests a parametric approximation to the best-in-class bridge measure. Sec. VII presents the results of the numerical study. Applications of Wiener bridges to the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, Cox-Ingersol-Ross and stochastic logistic target processes are presented in Sec. VII.1. Applications of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck bridges to the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and stochastic logistic target processes are given in Sec. VII.2. The approximation to a parametric best-in-class Ornstein-Uhlenbeck bridge is given in Sec. VII.3 and comparisons of path integral discretizations can be found in Sec. VII.4. Sec. VIII concludes the article.

papers.title: Probing the QPO and spectro-temporal evolution of MAXI J1750-327 with XPoSat during its first detected outburst : Constraints on black-hole mass and spin
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive timing and broadband spectral study of the newly discovered black hole low-mass X-ray binary candidate MAXI J1750-327 during its August 2026 outburst, using 11 continuous observations obtained with the XSPECT instrument onboard XPoSat. During epochs 1-2, we detect prominent type C QPO exhibiting a systematic upward frequency drift, accompanied by a prominent low-frequency noise component, with a clear transition from type-C to type-B, with subsequent disappearance of QPOs after epoch 4. Broadband spectral modeling reveals that this timing transition is directly mirrored by a fundamental restructuring of the accretion geometry. The inner disk temperature abruptly increases before settling into a steady range, accompanied by a steep reduction in disk normalization across the transition from epoch 3 to 4. This behavior signifies an active dynamical inward migration of the thin accretion disk toward the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO). The Comptonized flux declines sharply after the QPO turns off, suggesting a transition from a hard to soft state, through intermediate states. We also observed that the spectro-temporal correlations provide compelling physical support for the Lense-Thirring (LT) precession framework to be the origin of the type-C QPOs. Using a Bayesian framework, we constrain the black hole mass to be $M_{\rm BH}=7.92^{+6.19}_{-3.72} M_{\odot}$ and the dimensionless spin parameter to be $a_*=0.163^{+0.116}_{-0.056}$ by jointly modeling the observed type-C QPO frequencies with the global LT precession model and marginalizing over the uncertainties in distance, inclination, and diskbb normalization.

papers.intro:
Low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) consist of a stellar mass black hole (BH), accreting matter from a low-mass (≲1​M⊙\lesssim 1~M_{\odot}) companion star via Roche-lobe overflow, with the transferred material forming an accretion disk around the compact source [46]. Over the course of an outburst, the source evolves through a well-established sequence of spectral states, canonically described as the hard state, the hard-intermediate state, the soft-intermediate state, and the soft state, each characterized by a distinct combination of energy spectral shape and fast X-ray variability [19, 3]. In the hard state, the energy spectrum is dominated by a Comptonized power law with a photon index of Γ≈1.5\Gamma\approx 1.5–1.71.7 and a high-energy cutoff around 100100–200200 keV, attributed to inverse-Compton scattering of soft disk photons in a hot, optically thin corona, while the accretion disk itself is thought to be truncated at some radius larger than the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), or otherwise only weakly contributing to the observed flux [14, 15]. As the outburst progresses, the source typically softens: the disk component strengthens and its inner radius is inferred to move inward, the coronal photon index steepens toward Γ≈2\Gamma\approx 2–2.52.5, and the source ultimately enters the soft state. This overall evolution is conventionally visualized in a hardness-intensity diagram (HID), in which the source traces out a characteristic hysteresis-like “q”-shaped track: rising in luminosity at roughly constant hardness along the hard-state branch, softening rapidly at high luminosity as it crosses to the soft-state branch, and eventually returning to the hard state at comparatively lower luminosity as the outburst decays [16, 19, 3]. These spectral state transitions are accompanied by systematic changes in the variability of the X-ray flux, most notably in the fractional rms of the broadband noise and the strength of quasi-periodic oscillations [39, 45]. Combined spectral and timing analysis is therefore a key diagnostic of how the accretion geometry, and in particular the innermost regions of the flow, evolves during an outburst [60, 25].

A defining timing signature of BH LMXBs is the appearance of low-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in the power density spectrum, first identified in the early RXTE era [35, 58] and since observed to be ubiquitous during outbursts. These QPOs are conventionally classified into types A, B and C based on their centroid frequency, quality factor, rms amplitude and the strength of the accompanying broadband noise [63, 6]. Type-C QPOs, the most commonly observed variety, appear predominantly in the hard and hard-intermediate states as strong, narrow peaks with frequencies ranging from ∼0.01\sim 0.01–3030 Hz, often accompanied by one or more harmonics, superposed on strong band-limited noise; type-B QPOs are instead confined to the soft-intermediate state near the state transition and are associated with weaker underlying noise; and type-A QPOs are weak, broad features occasionally seen in the soft state [6, 38, 25].

These QPOs are conventionally classified into types A, B and C based on their centroid frequency, quality factor, rms amplitude and the strength of the accompanying broadband noise [63, 6]. Type-C QPOs, the most commonly observed variety, appear predominantly in the hard and hard-intermediate states as strong, narrow peaks with frequencies ranging from ∼0.01\sim 0.01–3030 Hz, often accompanied by one or more harmonics, superposed on strong band-limited noise; type-B QPOs are instead confined to the soft-intermediate state near the state transition and are associated with weaker underlying noise; and type-A QPOs are weak, broad features occasionally seen in the soft state [6, 38, 25].

The physical origin of these low-frequency QPOs remains debated, but the most widely favored explanation for type-C QPOs invokes geometric Lense–Thirring precession of a hot, radially extended inner accretion flow that is misaligned with the BH spin axis [55, 22]. In this relativistic precession model, the entire inner flow precesses rigidly at the nodal precession frequency appropriate to its outer edge, naturally producing the observed correlations between QPO frequency, spectral hardness and characteristic disk/corona radii, and explaining the strong dependence of QPO amplitude on the system’s inclination [22, 38, 25]. Alternative models attribute the oscillation to intrinsic instabilities of the accretion flow itself, such as the accretion-ejection instability driven by spiral density waves at the inner edge of a magnetized disk [48], or to non-linear feedback between the corona and the disk that drives limit-cycle-like oscillations in the Comptonized flux [5, 32].

As the source softens and the inner flow geometry evolves toward a more disk-dominated configuration, the type-C QPO is generally observed to weaken and eventually disappear[44], typically in the soft-intermediate state coincident with, or shortly before, the appearance of a type-B QPO and the transition to the soft state [6, 39]. In the precession framework, this QPO “turn-off” is interpreted as the shrinking of the precessing region as the geometrically thin disk moves inward, so that the characteristic precession frequency increases and the fractional rms of the oscillation drops below detectability [22, 25].

The hard-to-soft transition is frequently accompanied by discrete flaring activity and enhanced variability near the state boundary, along with a marked change in the source’s radio properties: the steady, compact jet associated with the hard state is quenched as the source crosses into the soft state, often preceded by a transient, optically thin radio flare linked to the ejection of discrete jet knots [16, 17]. Tracking the joint evolution of the QPO frequency and amplitude, the broadband X-ray spectrum, and any associated radio flaring therefore provides a comprehensive picture of how the accretion flow reconfigures itself over the course of an outburst [65, 31]. The disappearance of the type-C QPO is therefore especially significant, since it may signal an abrupt restructuring of the precessing inner flow rather than a smooth drift in frequency[44]. Rapid QPO transitions, including the sudden loss of the type-C QPO, have been reported in several BHXRBs and are often accompanied by changes in the broadband noise and the emergence of a type-B QPO [53, 66]. In Swift J1727.8–1613, a brief hard-to-soft excursion saw the type-C QPO vanish together with a marked drop in broadband noise, while a type-B QPO appeared alongside discrete radio-jet ejections evidence for a close link between the breakdown of the precessing inner flow and the accretion–ejection process [27]. Despite this observational progress, the physical trigger for the type-C QPO’s disappearance remains poorly understood.

papers.title: The (missing) gamma-ray counterparts to EP events
papers.abstract: While the connection of Fast X-ray Transients (FXTs) detected by Einstein Probe (EP) with Gamma-ray Bursts (GRBs) is increasingly compelling, most lack gamma-ray counterparts, leaving their relation to GRBs unclear. We performed a systematic search for gamma-ray counterparts to the 72 transients detected by EP in its first year, using targeted searches in Fermi/GBM and Fermi/LAT data, complemented by SVOM/GRM, SVOM/ECLAIRs, Swift/BAT and Konus-Wind. For the visible events without a gamma-ray counterpart, we derived simultaneous $3σ$ flux upper limits in the 10-1000 keV and the 0.1-1 GeV band. We find that 23 events (32%) have a gamma-ray counterpart (seven sub-threshold), while 49 events (68%) have none, despite most being visible. For events with a gamma-ray counterpart, the X-ray flux over the gamma-ray $T_{\rm 90}$ is systematically higher than over the full X-ray duration, with flux ratios $1 \lesssim F_{\rm [10-1000\,keV]}/F_{\rm [0.5-4\,keV]} \lesssim 100$, suggesting that gamma-rays are preferentially detected during the brightest X-ray phases. For events without gamma-ray counterpart, the most stringent Fermi/GBM upper limits imply $E_{\rm peak} \lesssim 30$-100 keV and, for the 14 events with measured redshifts, $L_{\rm iso}\lesssim 10^{48}-9\times10^{51}$ erg/s. If classical GRB correlations hold in this regime, these lower energetics imply lower bulk Lorentz factors ($Γ_0 \lesssim 100$), as confirmed in a few cases by afterglow constraints. No significant GeV emission was detected by Fermi/LAT, yielding $1 \lesssim F_{0.1-1\,{\rm GeV}}/F_{0.5-4\,{\rm keV}} \lesssim 10$, placing the first constraints on a potential synchrotron self-Compton component for this new population. Although individual origins remain uncertain, many EP FXTs could be compatible with the GRB population, extending it toward lower $E_{\rm peak}$, luminosities, and bulk Lorentz factors.

papers.intro:
For more than five decades, gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) have been primarily discovered and characterized through their prompt γ\gamma-ray emission. From their discovery by the Vela satellites (Klebesadel et al. 1973), decades of observations with dedicated γ\gamma-ray instruments, from BATSE to Swift/BAT and Fermi/GBM, have built a rich picture of the GRB phenomenology in the hard X-ray and γ\gamma-ray bands, establishing e.g. the bimodal duration distribution (Kouveliotou et al. 1993), the discovery of their cosmological origin (thanks to rapid X-ray localization, Costa et al. 1997; van Paradijs et al. 1997), the spectral correlations (Yonetoku et al. 2004; Amati, L. et al. 2002), and the connection to their progenitors: the collapse of massive stars for long GRBs (Woosley 2001; Galama et al. 1998, e.g.), and the merger of compact objects for short GRBs (Abbott et al. 2017; Granot et al. 2018; Ascenzi et al. 2021, e.g.).

For more than five decades, gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) have been primarily discovered and characterized through their prompt γ\gamma-ray emission. From their discovery by the Vela satellites (Klebesadel et al. 1973), decades of observations with dedicated γ\gamma-ray instruments, from BATSE to Swift/BAT and Fermi/GBM, have built a rich picture of the GRB phenomenology in the hard X-ray and γ\gamma-ray bands, establishing e.g. the bimodal duration distribution (Kouveliotou et al. 1993), the discovery of their cosmological origin (thanks to rapid X-ray localization, Costa et al. 1997; van Paradijs et al. 1997), the spectral correlations (Yonetoku et al. 2004; Amati, L. et al. 2002), and the connection to their progenitors: the collapse of massive stars for long GRBs (Woosley 2001; Galama et al. 1998, e.g.), and the merger of compact objects for short GRBs (Abbott et al. 2017; Granot et al. 2018; Ascenzi et al. 2021, e.g.).

In contrast, the X-ray band during the prompt phase has remained comparatively underexplored, despite its importance for probing GRB physics, e.g. the central engine activity, the radiative mechanism (Oganesyan et al. 2018, e.g.), and the jet structure, among others. The limited field of view and low-energy sensitivity of past X-ray missions have hindered the systematic exploration of the X-ray transient sky. Among the softest members of the GRB population known to date, X-ray flashes (Heise et al. 2001; Frontera 2004, XRFs;), events whose prompt emission peaks below ∼\sim30 keV, were first identified by BeppoSAX, but have remained under-sampled ever since. Their physical origin is still debated, with proposed scenarios including on-axis weak jets (Lamb et al. 2004, e.g.), off-axis relativistic jets (Yamazaki et al. 2002, e.g.), and relativistic shock breakouts (Wang et al. 2007, e.g.). While Swift/XRT has revolutionised in many ways our understanding of GRBs, including the study of XRF (Sakamoto et al. 2008) and the sampling of the transition between the prompt and early afterglow phases, simultaneous X-ray observations of the beginning of the prompt emission are still rare. As a result, the softest tail of the GRB distribution remains largely inaccessible to systematic studies.

In parallel, several fast X-ray transients (FXTs) have been discovered over the past two decades through archival searches in X-ray catalogs of Chandra and XMM-Newton (Soderberg et al. 2008; Jonker et al. 2013; Bauer et al. 2017; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2023; Alp & Larsson 2020). These searches revealed a class of long-lived (∼\sim few to tens of ks) X-ray flares with no obvious γ\gamma-ray counterparts. Their durations, fluxes, spectra, and temporal properties suggest a connection with relativistic explosions; however, the lack of counterparts at other wavelengths and robust redshift estimates in most cases (despite thorough searches for host galaxies, see Jonker et al. 2021; Eappachen et al. 2022; Eappachen et al. 2023; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2026) has prevented a clear determination of their physical nature. A wide range of progenitor models has therefore been tested, including supernova shock breakouts (Alp & Larsson 2020), compact binary mergers producing long-lived magnetars (Sun et al. 2019; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2024; Xue et al. 2019), off-axis GRBs afterglows (Sarin et al. 2021; Wichern et al. 2024), and tidal disruption events, but their nature remains largely unconstrained. Yet, these discoveries hinted at the existence of a rich and unexplored population of X-ray transients, potentially linked to phenomena traditionally studied in γ\gamma-rays.
