These searches revealed a class of long-lived (∼\sim few to tens of ks) X-ray flares with no obvious γ\gamma-ray counterparts. Their durations, fluxes, spectra, and temporal properties suggest a connection with relativistic explosions; however, the lack of counterparts at other wavelengths and robust redshift estimates in most cases (despite thorough searches for host galaxies, see Jonker et al. 2021; Eappachen et al. 2022; Eappachen et al. 2023; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2026) has prevented a clear determination of their physical nature. A wide range of progenitor models has therefore been tested, including supernova shock breakouts (Alp & Larsson 2020), compact binary mergers producing long-lived magnetars (Sun et al. 2019; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2024; Xue et al. 2019), off-axis GRBs afterglows (Sarin et al. 2021; Wichern et al. 2024), and tidal disruption events, but their nature remains largely unconstrained. Yet, these discoveries hinted at the existence of a rich and unexplored population of X-ray transients, potentially linked to phenomena traditionally studied in γ\gamma-rays.

This observational landscape has changed significantly with the advent of the Einstein Probe mission (EP; Yuan et al. 2022) and, soon after, SVOM (Wei et al. 2023). Thanks to their sensitivity at soft X-ray energies, the Wide-field X-ray Telescope (WXT; 0.5–4 keV) on board EP and the ECLAIRs instrument (4–150 keV) on board SVOM have opened a new window on the poorly explored soft high-energy transient sky. In particular, EP/WXT, employing novel lobster-eye optics, combines a large field of view (∼\sim3600 deg2) with a sensitivity of ∼2.6×10−11\sim 2.6\times 10^{-11} erg cm-2 s-1 in a 1 ks exposure (Yuan et al. 2022), allowing the discovery and rapid localisation of faint X-ray transients. Several of the EP FXTs have been directly associated with GRBs through contemporaneous detections by γ\gamma-ray satellites (Yin et al. 2024; Jiang et al. 2025, e.g.), even at redshift ∼5\sim 5 (Levan et al. 2024a; Liu et al. 2025), while others showed no γ\gamma-ray counterparts (Ravasio & Jonker 2024; Ravasio et al. 2025a; Ravasio et al. 2025b; Zhang et al. 2025, e.g.). Interestingly, despite the lack of γ\gamma-ray detections in many cases, EP transients often exhibit late-time lightcurve properties consistent with those of GRB afterglows, suggesting a potential physical connection even when the prompt gamma-ray emission is not observed (Sun et al. 2025a; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2026; Cotter et al. 2026; Gianfagna et al. 2025). Indeed, among events without a γ\gamma-ray counterpart, many have been linked to the collapsar channel through the emergence of broad-lined Type Ic supernovae (Ic-BL SNe), similar to those accompanying nearby long GRBs (van Dalen et al. 2025; Rastinejad et al. 2025; Li et al. 2025; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2026; van Hoof et al. 2026b, e.g.). The inferred formation rate and luminosity function of FXTs are reported to be consistent with a massive-star progenitor channel (Guo et al. 2025), while O’Connor et al. 2025 found that their redshift distribution is statistically consistent with that of long GRBs. Evidence for an association with compact object mergers remains more elusive, with the exception of EP250207b (Jonker et al. 2026) (later found to be at z=3.2, van Hoof et al., in prep), and EP250704a, which was coincident with a short GRB (Fraija et al. 2026; Li et al. 2026a). Other proposed physical origins for EP FXTs include TDEs, as suggested for GRB 250702B/EP250702a (Neights et al. 2026; Gompertz et al. 2026; Levan et al. 2025b; Oganesyan et al. 2025; Granot et al. 2026; Li et al. 2026b), and supernova shock breakout (SBO), as in the case of EP260321a (Yuan et al. 2026; Martin-Carrillo et al. 2026; Rastinejad et al. 2026; Chen et al. 2026b; O’Connor et al. 2026). The physical nature of a large fraction of EP FXTs without a γ\gamma-ray counterpart remains, however, fundamentally unconstrained.

papers.title: Can we constrain the binary neutron star merger time from kilonova light curves?
papers.abstract: The joint observation of gravitational waves (GWs) from a binary neutron star (BNS) merger (GW170817), together with a short Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB 170817A) and a kilonova (KN, AT2017gfo), marked the birth of multimessenger astronomy with GWs, and demonstrated the informative power of multimessenger observations. More BNS merger and KN detections are expected , thanks to the increasing sensitivity of GW detectors and the advent of new electromagnetic facilities such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. However, the association between a BNS merger and a KN might not be trivial: the detection of a KN might not coincide with the onset of the EM emission, making it difficult to define a temporal window to assess the coincidence with a GW event. In this work we investigate the possibility to constrain the BNS merger time from KN light curves, exploring different observing conditions and with focus on the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. We used different KN models and different inference frameworks to simulate and fit KN light curves. We explored different cadences and wavelength coverages for observations, to investigate how the different observing conditions can affect the capability to recover the BNS merger time. The tests performed also include real data related to AT2017gfo, plus a few GRBs that have been associated to possible KN candidates. We find that, under realistic observing conditions with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the BNS merger time can be recovered with a precision of 5.5 days (90\% CI) with a best-case scenario with an accuracy of 0.18 day and a precision of 0.74 day (90 \% CI). Results can slightly improve (by $\sim$ 5 \%) if the source redshift is available. Upper limits near the merger time can also improve the results, reducing the width of the posterior by $\sim60$ \%. The BNS merger time estimate could also benefit from EM follow-up observations with other telescopes.

papers.intro:
On August 17, 2017, Advanced LIGO (LIGO Scientific Collaboration et al., 2015) and Advanced Virgo (Acernese et al., 2015) observed for the first time a gravitational wave (GW) signal from a binary neutron star (BNS) inspiral (GW170817, Abbott et al., 2017a). Less than two seconds later, a short gamma-ray burst (sGRB), GRB 170817A, was detected by the Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM) onboard Fermi (Goldstein et al., 2017), and the spectrometer anti-coincidence shield (SPI-ACS) onboard INTEGRAL (Savchenko et al., 2017). This joint observation provided the first direct evidence that at least a fraction of sGRBs have a BNS system as progenitor, and marked the birth of multi-messenger astronomy with GWs. The electromagnetic (EM) follow-up campaign that followed this multi-messenger observation led to the discovery of an optical transient (SSS17a/AT 2017gfo) in the host galaxy NGC 4993, also detected in ultraviolet and infrared wavelengths (see Abbott et al., 2017b and references therein). Photometric and spectroscopic observations of the source allowed to identify it as a kilonova (Pian et al., 2017; Smartt et al., 2017): this supports the hypothesis that BNS mergers are sites of r-process nucleosynthesis of heavy elements. A second GW signal from a BNS merger has been observed in 2019, during the third LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) observing run: GW190425 (Abbott et al., 2020). Despite an extensive EM follow-up campaign, no EM counterpart was found in association with this GW event (see, e.g., Hosseinzadeh et al., 2019), mainly due to the poorly constrained sky localisation of the event (of the order of 8000 deg2). No other significant BNS merger has been reported since then (The LIGO Scientific Collaboration et al., 2025; The LIGO Scientific Collaboration et al., 2026). The Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, and KAGRA (Akutsu et al., 2019) detectors concluded the fourth observing run (O4) in November 2025 and are now in a period of upgrades and commissioning. Even before this transition, synergy between LVK and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory was already underway: while Rubin was still in its early-operations phase, prior to the start of sustained LSST observations, it carried out Target-of-Opportunity follow-up of gravitational-wave candidates reported during the final part of O4, such as the sub-solar-mass neutron-star merger candidate S251112cm, for which Rubin observations began about two days later (MacBride et al., 2026). This collaboration is expected to deepen further: the Vera C. Rubin Observatory officially began its ten year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) on 2026 June 30, and a new, LVK six-month observing run, Intermediate Run 1 (IR1), is expected to start in January 2027, during which GW interferometers will operate in closer synergy with Rubin’s now fully operational LSST survey.

In the future, our potential of achieving multi-messenger detections can increase using different, complementary approaches. In fact, aside from EM follow-up of candidate GW signals, other kind of searches can be performed, such as externally triggered searches. In this last scenario, an EM/neutrino transient is detected, and then GW data are analysed offline in detail to look for a possible GW signal in temporal and spatial coincidence with the observed non-GW signal (e.g., a GRB). The scope of these targeted searches is to enhance our ability to detect GW signals in coincidence with non-GW transients with respect to standard, all-sky GW searches. Pipelines used by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration for such searches are X-pipeline (Sutton et al., 2010; Wąs et al., 2012), which performs a search for generic GW signals, and PyGRB (Harry and Fairhurst, 2011; Williamson et al., 2014), that looks for GW signals produced by BNS or NS-BH mergers.

In addition to this, there are online pipelines that perform low-latency searches of coincidences between EM events or neutrino event candidates and GW triggers. Specifically, the Rapid, on-source VOEvent Coincident Monitor (RAVEN) pipeline searches for and analyses coincidences between GW candidates and non-GW events such as, e.g., Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) and neutrinos in low-latency (see Urban, 2016; Piotrzkowski, 2022). RAVEN typically analyses coincidences in real-time, listening to alerts from GRB/low energy neutrino experiments, submitting these to the Gravitational-Wave Candidate Event Database (GraceDB)11 1 https://gracedb.ligo.org/, and then checking whether there are coincident GW candidates already in GraceDB and vice-versa. If a coincidence is found, the significance of the multi-messenger event is determined by computing the overlap between the skymaps of the two events, and generating a resulting joint false alarm rate (FAR).

One crucial aspect of all the above described multi-messenger searches (including EM follow-up of GW events) is the definition of time window for two events to be considered as coincident. For GRBs this is quite straightfoward: the GRB trigger time typically corresponds to the onset of the GRB emission, and theoretical models predict the possible time offset of the GRB emission with respect to GW signal; for instance with PyGRB the search for a GW signal is performed in a time window between -5 s and +1 s from the trigger time of short GRBs (see, e.g., Abbott et al., 2022). papers.title: Radio and high-energy variable emission from a multi-wavelength follow-up of the infant planet-hosting star V1298 Tau
papers.abstract: V1298 Tau is a very young and magnetically active K1V star which hosts a benchmark multi-planetary system to study planet formation and evolutionary history at the earliest stages. Between 2025 and 2026, we conducted a campaign to monitor the variability of V1298 Tau in radio (band C), X-ray, and NUV bands, with the support of publicly available contemporary optical light curve, and to investigate multi-band correlations to link the emission with stellar activity. Radio observations were carried out with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) in band C (4.5--6.5 GHz). X-ray and NUV observations were carried out with the Swift satellite over 20 days, ending one month before the begin of the radio campaign. We analysed the temporal variability of peak (integrated) fluxes in the C-band and of X-ray (NUV) luminosities on various timescales, comparing it with the variability observed in the high-cadence optical light curve collected by the ASAS-SN survey. We observed both radio and high-energy time variable emission. JVLA detected emission in 90\% of the visits, switching between high ($\geq$0.1 mJy/beam) and low flux states in matter of days or hours. The fluxes show moderate correlation with the optical light curve, suggesting modulation with the stellar rotation period. Except for one visit, dynamic spectral analysis does not reveal short-term (minutes) variability, nor is there any evidence of circularly polarised emissions. Overall, the radio observations can be explained as gyrosynchrotron and/or cyclotron emission from the corona, and linked to stellar magnetic activity. At high-energy, we detected significant variability in X-ray luminosity (within the range ~1.2--2.5x10$^{+30}$ erg/s), the decay phase of a stellar flare, and evidence of correlation with the optical flux. Our data confirm that V1298\,Tau follows the near-linear Güdel-Benz relation.

papers.intro:
V1298 Tau is an infant star 20±\pm10 Myr old located at a distance d=108.02±d=108.02\pm0.23 pc which hosts a multi-planetary system, consisting of at least four transiting planets detected by the Kepler/K2 space telescope (David et al., 2019a; David et al., 2019b). It represents a benchmark among new born planetary systems to investigate the formation and evolution of planets within the first hundred Myr. In an attempt to improve the multi-wavelength characterisation of the host star, Damasso et al. (2025) (hereafter D25) reported the first detection of time variable radio emission from V1298 Tau in L (1–2 GHz) and C (4.5–6.5 GHz) bands with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Telescope (JVLA). That study was motivated by the expectation of detectable non-thermal radio emission over a broad range of frequencies, triggered by intense stellar magnetic fields and dense winds which are predicted to characterise infant stars. Just to mention a few notable examples V 830 Tau, a 2 Myr-old T Tauri star at 130.37±\pm0.28 pc, was detected as a radio-bright and variable source thanks to JVLA observations (Bower et al., 2016; Osten and Wolk, 2025, detected emission larger than 1 mJy in band C;), and emission was also recorded from the multi-planetary system AU Mic (age ∼\sim22 Myr old), monitored during an intensive radio campaign with the Australia Telescope Compact Array between 1.1 and 3.1 GHz (Bloot et al., 2024). In general, the increasing survey coverage and sensitivity allow to radio detect many young, nearby stars (Launhardt et al., 2022; Driessen et al., 2024). The radio-monitoring conducted by D25 on V1298 Tau was intended as a pilot targeted follow-up to increase the radio sensitivity with respect to survey-like campaigns, to contribute to a first characterisation of the plasma environment where the planets are embedded, and to probe the strength of the coronal magnetic field and plasma density. With a similar motivation, Maggio et al. (2023) monitored the far-UV and X-ray high-energy emission from this system with the Hubble Space Telescope/Cosmic Origins Spectrograph and XMM-Newton, investigating the time evolution of the irradiation in the UV band, and its effect on the evaporation of the atmosphere of the infant exoplanets at the very early stages.

papers.title: In-orbit anomaly and recovery of IXPE detector 2
papers.abstract: The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) is a joint NASA-ASI mission launched in December 2021 to measure the linear polarization of celestial X-ray sources in the 2-8 keV energy range. The payload comprises three identical telescopes, each combining grazing-incidence X-ray optics with a focal-plane photoelectric polarimeter based on the Gas Pixel Detector technology. On 14 April 2025, the second detector experienced an anomaly that significantly altered the electrical behavior of the ASIC responsible for reading out the photoelectron track images. In this contribution, we describe the effect of the anomaly on the instrumental response and the actions taken to mitigate its effects and recover the scientific observations of the instrument.

papers.intro:
The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) is a small mission jointly developed by NASA and ASI[23]. The mission carries a payload comprising three identical, co-aligned telescopes dedicated to measuring the linear polarization of celestial sources in the soft X-ray band, over the 2–8 keV energy range (see Figure 1). The mission is led by NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center, which also provided the ultra-light grazing-incidence mirror assemblies, achieving a point spread function better than 30 arcsec[15, 16], with a contribution from Nagoya University for thermal filters. The focal plane instrumentation was provided by ASI, INAF, and INFN[20]. The detectors are imaging photoelectric polarimeters based on the Gas Pixel Detector (GPD), developed in Italy since 2001[4, 2, 3]. The GPD operates by imaging the track of the photoelectron emitted following the photoabsorption of an X-ray photon. The former is identified by the ion-electron pairs produced through ionization: the latter are drifted toward a Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) and multiplied before begin collected on the top of a pixillated ASIC developed specifically for X-ray polarimetry. The measured track is analyzed to determine both the absorption point and the initial emission direction of the photoelectron, the latter being correlated with the polarization of the incident radiation. The energy of the absorbed photon is proportional to the total collected charge, while the trigger time provides its arrival time with a precision of a few microseconds. Each GPD is housed in a Detector Unit (DU)[1], which also includes four calibration sources, providing both polarized and unpolarized radiation, as well as a filter for observations of very bright targets[14, 10]. Compared with its few predecessors, IXPE improves the sensitivity to polarization by approximately two orders of magnitude in the observing time required to detect a given polarization signal, while also enabling spatially, spectrally, and temporally resolved polarimetric measurements.

IXPE was launched on 9 December 2021 into a low-equatorial orbit at an altitude of approximately 600 km. Since the start of science operations on 11 January 2022, IXPE has detected X-ray polarization from tens of celestial sources spanning nearly all major classes of X-ray bright astrophysical objects. These observations have demonstrated that X-ray polarization is detectable in approximately two-thirds of the observed sources and provides powerful new observables for discriminating among competing theoretical models[12, 9, 21, 11, 5, 22].

papers.title: Structure-Aware Message Passing on Petri Nets through Directed Walks and Incidence Diffusion
papers.abstract: A common application of the process mining discipline is to connect observed event data with Petri nets, which are bipartite, directed graphical process models with rich formal underpinnings. Recent work learns vector representations of Petri nets to retrieve process models and relate them to event logs, but leaves implicit two key aspects hidden within the net's structure: directed cycles (process loops) and invariants recorded by the net's incidence matrix. We expose both of these to message-passing graph neural networks, through a positional encoding built from return probabilities of directed place-transition walks (PNRWPE), and through same-type messages gated by diffusion kernels of the incidence matrix (DA-PNGNN). Our constructions raise macro balanced accuracy in predicting the generation factors of the 96 Process Discovery Contest 2023 models from 0.751 to 0.796 with PNRWPE, which nearly doubles accuracy on process loops, and to 0.830 with DA-PNGNN, which, without retuning, also improves net-to-tree retrieval top-1 accuracy on the self-supervised ProcRosetta benchmark by 4.1 to 5.9 points.
papers.intro:
Petri nets are a commonly used formal model of discrete-event dynamical systems supporting the analysis of concurrent computation [17]. This has made them popular in the process-mining literature, which constructs, checks, and simulates them routinely [22]. Other process-mining tasks, such as retrieving similar models from a collection or relating a model to the event logs of the same process, can be approached by learning vector representations of the nets themselves. Existing work has learned such representations for retrieval and classification [6], and a recent study [4] has built a multimodal neural model that aligns the process net with the process tree that generated it [22] and the associated event logs.

This has made them popular in the process-mining literature, which constructs, checks, and simulates them routinely [22]. Other process-mining tasks, such as retrieving similar models from a collection or relating a model to the event logs of the same process, can be approached by learning vector representations of the nets themselves. Existing work has learned such representations for retrieval and classification [6], and a recent study [4] has built a multimodal neural model that aligns the process net with the process tree that generated it [22] and the associated event logs.

A Petri net is, stripped to its bare bones, a directed bipartite graph whose two node partitions (or types) have semantic roles, and whose incidence matrix carries an algebra of conservation that Petri net theory has studied for decades [17]. Message passing is the de facto paradigm for learning on graphs [11]. It relies on repeated local aggregation of learned node features along the edges of the graph. It is therefore a natural tool for learning representations of a Petri net, and simple adaptations of message-passing networks have been shown to be beneficial [4]. We argue that current modeling approaches are not making complete use of specific structural inductive biases that a Petri net structure can provide. Concrete examples are notions of where a node sits relative to directed cycles, and whether paths between node partitions that lead to potential token conservation exist. This raises the central question that motivates our work: can the structure that Petri net theory makes explicit improve learned representations of process models?

papers.title: Generalization Bounds via Vector-Valued $L_p$ Correlation $V_α$
papers.abstract: Understanding generalization of randomized learning algorithms remains a central challenge. Mutual-information and total-variation bounds provide complementary ways to quantify data--hypothesis dependence, but they can behave quite differently in high-dimensional regimes. We study a one-parameter family of dependence measures, the vector-valued $L_p$-norm correlation $V_α$, and derive generalization bounds whose dependence terms interpolate between total variation (TV) at $α=1$ and variance and $χ^2$ related behavior at $α=2$. For $α>2$, the Hölder-conjugate loss moment is below two, yielding heavy-tailed specializations that can remain finite even when the loss variance is infinite. A particularly interpretable specialization occurs at $α=2$, where the bound can be expressed in terms of the variability of the algorithm's output density across datasets, $\int \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_S[p(w\mid S)]}~ dw$. We show that the entire $V_α$ family is invariant under smooth bijective reparameterizations of the hypothesis space. We also introduce an adaptive density stability (ADS) condition that implies explicit control of $V_2$, and we verify it for Gibbs-type posteriors under bounded losses (yielding rates that depend on the inverse temperature and sample size). To address scaling, we extend the framework to a conditional formulation using supersamples, analogous in spirit to conditional mutual information (CMI), and discuss evaluations in the output space as a practical surrogate for estimating dependence. Simulations on Bayesian linear regression illustrate how tuning $α$ can change the tightness of the resulting bounds across regimes. Additional supersample experiments on noisy MNIST and on a pretrained ResNet-50 for CIFAR-10 show similar behavior of the projected loss-space bounds beyond the original clean-MNIST setting.

papers.title: Are Joint-Embedding Predictive Objectives Effective for Longitudinal EHRs?
papers.abstract: Masked language modelling (MLM) is the dominant pretraining objective for transformer encoders applied to longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs). However, reconstructing individual events may overemphasise noisy or weakly informative observations and does not explicitly encourage learning higher-level patient states. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) instead learn by predicting representations in latent space and have shown strong performance in a variety of domains. In this paper, we investigate to what extent JEPA can be adapted to EHR sequence representation. Our empirical investigation using MIMIC-IV shows that although all three of our JEPA formulations train stably without representational collapse, they consistently underperform standard MLM. We find that target size, not target heterogeneity, increases prediction error, yet reducing the target size does not recover downstream performance. This suggests that stable latent prediction alone is insufficient for competitive EHR representation learning and highlights the challenge of defining clinically meaningful latent targets for EHR.

Electronic Health Records (EHRs) are longitudinal records of patient-healthcare interactions. Recent work has increasingly focused on EHR foundation models, which aim to learn general-purpose patient representations through self-supervised learning and can be adapted to a range of downstream clinical prediction tasks [19, 17, 18, 15]. Electronic Health Records (EHRs) are longitudinal records of patient-healthcare interactions. Recent work has increasingly focused on EHR foundation models, which aim to learn general-purpose patient representations through self-supervised learning and can be adapted to a range of downstream clinical prediction tasks [19, 17, 18, 15]. Downstream performance therefore hinges on the quality of these representations.

Due to the sequential nature of EHRs, transformer encoders have become a common backbone for EHR representation learning. A dominant objective for pretraining has been BERT-style masked language modelling (MLM), in which the model is trained to reconstruct masked medical events from their surrounding context [11, 10, 16, 14]. However, exact token reconstruction may not provide the ideal learning signal for longitudinal clinical data. EHR sequences contain routine, repeated, administrative, and partially unpredictable events, yet MLM treats reconstruction of each masked token as equally important. This may encourage representations that capture the identity of local events rather than the true patient state.

However, exact token reconstruction may not provide the ideal learning signal for longitudinal clinical data. EHR sequences contain routine, repeated, administrative, and partially unpredictable events, yet MLM treats reconstruction of each masked token as equally important. This may encourage representations that capture the identity of local events rather than the true patient state.

In contrast, clinicians use their medical knowledge to abstract away irrelevant detail and focus on key events, trends, and interactions to form a higher-level representation of the patient state. This motivation is closely aligned with Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), which provide an alternative form of self-supervision [9, 2]. Rather than reconstructing observations in the input space, JEPA trains a predictor to estimate latent representations of unobserved targets from an available context. This approach has shown strong representation-learning performance in vision [2, 3], world modelling [12] and language [8]. Latent prediction is intended to produce semantically meaningful features and avoid unnecessary reconstruction of unpredictable low-level detail. This is particularly appealing for EHRs, where multiple observed event sequences may correspond to similar underlying clinical states and trajectories.

papers.title: Block Diffusion for Longitudinal EHR: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Representation Trade-offs
papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models have proved effective for zero-shot prediction from longitudinal electronic health records, but impose strictly sequential generation on trajectories containing temporally clustered and interdependent clinical events. We investigate block-based masked diffusion (BD) as an alternative on MIMIC-IV under matched tokenisation, context length, model capacity, and evaluation conditions. Across block sizes, BD exhibits a clear quality--efficiency trade-off, with small-block configurations retaining much of the predictive performance of AR while enabling substantially faster inference. A representative $B{=}8$ configuration achieves approximately $1.43\times$ faster evaluation. Although generative rollout remains below AR in most settings, frozen linear probes on BD and AR representations achieve near-identical performance across clinical prediction tasks, indicating that BD learns comparably informative clinical representations. Increasing the denoising budget yields diminishing returns, while alternative decoding strategies provide limited gains. Overall, our results show that block diffusion is a viable and computationally attractive approach to longitudinal EHR modelling, with further improvements in iterative decoding offering a promising route toward closing the remaining generative performance gap.

papers.intro:
Foundation models for structured electronic health record (EHR) data have predominantly adopted autoregressive (AR) sequence modelling. By generating possible future patient trajectories, these models have demonstrated strong zero-shot performance across clinical prediction tasks, in some settings approaching or exceeding task-specific supervised baselines [10, 11, 20, 15]. However, AR modelling imposes a strict left-to-right factorisation with each event generated conditionally on all preceding events before subsequent events can be considered. Longitudinal EHRs are only partly sequential in this sense. Clinical activity often occurs in temporally concentrated bursts, making groups of nearby events a natural target for partially parallel generation (Appendix A.9), and in our MIMIC-IV data, 47.4% of recorded timestamps contain at least eight tokens (Appendix A.4). This strict factorisation also carries an inference cost, as token-by-token decoding limits parallelism and requires sequential computation for each generated event. This motivates generative objectives that relax strict next-token prediction and instead allow groups of clinical events to be modelled jointly.

Discrete diffusion language models provide one such alternative by learning to reconstruct corrupted tokens through iterative denoising [12]. These models have shown strong generative and representation-learning performance in other structured scientific domains, including protein sequence modelling and molecular graph generation [19, 17]. Block diffusion (BD) introduces an AR factorisation across blocks while denoising tokens jointly within each block, enabling partial parallelism while retaining causal conditioning on previously generated context [1]. Prior work has shown a quality–parallelism trade-off: larger blocks allow more parallel generation but generally degrade likelihood and generation quality, whereas smaller blocks more closely approach AR performance. Discrete diffusion has previously been applied to EHRs for synthetic data generation [16, 3], but its behaviour relative to strong AR foundation models for zero-shot clinical prediction remains less well understood.

papers.title: Inhomogeneous random graphs: how heavy tails reshape connectivity
papers.abstract: We study inhomogeneous random graphs on $n$ vertices with independent Pareto weights of parameter $α>0$ and connection probabilities $\min(\varepsilon_n W_iW_j, 1)$. Our main focus is the infinite-mean regime $0<α<1$. Under the scaling $n\varepsilon_n^α=λ$, with $λ>0$ fixed, the global architecture of the graph is entirely governed by the Poisson point process $Π$ of rescaled extreme weights. In particular, the size of the largest component, divided by $n$, converges to a non-degenerate random variable expressed as an explicit functional of $Π$. Through the point process $Π$, we also characterize the exact limiting connectivity probability, uncovering a non-sharp connectivity threshold. The second largest component and the diameter of the largest component are bounded with high probability. The distance between two uniformly chosen vertices in the largest component is at most three with high probability. We also prove convergence of the point process of rescaled degrees and identify the limiting distribution of the maximum degree. For completeness, we obtain expected degree asymptotics, typical degree limits and connectivity regimes for all $α>0$. Due to the failure of classical branching process approximations in the infinite-mean regime, our approach relies fundamentally on analyzing the extreme weight environment $Π$.

papers.title: Passive RF Sensing for People Counting with Dense IoT Networks
papers.abstract: Radio Frequency (RF) convergence, the joint use of radio signals for both communication and sensing, is gaining increasing attention in research and industry, mostly for its potential in Internet of Things (IoT) applications. By using RF signals of opportunity, such as those generate by the wireless networks, RF sensing exploits the effects of human bodies on the electromagnetic waves to detect both people presence and their movements without requiring wearable devices. In this paper, we address the problem of estimating the number of people in a monitored area covered by several RF nodes of a wireless network: to this aim, we propose a composite diffraction-based model, namely C-MAM, to capture the cumulative RF attenuation induced by multiple human bodies. Building on this model, we derive the analytical resolvability bounds that quantify the maximum number of distinguishable individuals based on the layout geometry and other physical characteristics of the wireless network. These bounds allow for the pre-deployment assessment of RF sensing performance under different scenarios.

Radio Frequency (RF) sensing refers to a set of opportunistic techniques designed to detect, locate, and track people within areas covered by ambient RF signals (1). In the context of the Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) paradigm (2), RF sensing systems turn each wireless node into a virtual sensor, enabling simultaneous communication and sensing. Typically operating in the unlicensed 2.4÷62.4\div 6 GHz ISM bands, these systems exploit cm-scale wavelengths to capture body-induced alterations in multipath propagation.

papers.title: Kinetic Fluctuation-Dissipation Relation in collisionless plasmas: a correlated noise source
papers.abstract: We here focus on small-scale dynamics of collisionless plasmas by employing a generalized kinetic Langevin framework driven by a stochastic time-correlated forcing. Our investigation captures the steady-state Fluctuation-Dissipation Relation (FDR) where the energy injection at low frequencies is due to the time-correlated forcing and the small-scale energy conversion occurs via Landau damping, the latter --though formally reversible-- acting as an effective dissipation mechanism. We analytically extract the resulting asymptotic spectral scalings across multiple physical regimes and characterize the velocity-space cascade by decomposing the plasma distribution function with Hermite polynomials. The framework is then generalized to a multi-scale forcing scenario in which correlation rates are distributed according to a power-law distribution. This extension provides closed-form analytical expressions that may serve to interpret spacecraft in-situ observations. All analytical predictions are successfully validated through direct numerical integrations of the underlying kinetic equations.

papers.intro:
The issue of energy conversion and dissipation in nearly collisionless plasmas is a fundamental, long-standing problem in space and astrophysical plasma physics [1, 2, 3]. In these environments, such as the solar wind and the Earth’s magnetosphere, viscous-like dissipation induced by collisional effects is thought to be negligible, as collisional frequencies are way smaller than typical frequencies associated with collisionless phenomena. Therefore, energy conversion at kinetic scales is mediated by nonlinear wave-particle interactions and generally occurs in the entire phase space, frequently driving non-thermal plasma distribution functions.

In these environments, such as the solar wind and the Earth’s magnetosphere, viscous-like dissipation induced by collisional effects is thought to be negligible, as collisional frequencies are way smaller than typical frequencies associated with collisionless phenomena. Therefore, energy conversion at kinetic scales is mediated by nonlinear wave-particle interactions and generally occurs in the entire phase space, frequently driving non-thermal plasma distribution functions.

A common feature of space and astrophysical plasmas is that they are manifestly turbulent [4]. Nonlinear mechanisms transfer energy from large, energy-containing scales to small, kinetic scales at which energy conversion and, eventually, dissipation occur. Moreover, temporal and spatial coherent structures such as vortices and sheets emerge across scales as a result of intermittency. The fundamental turbulent nature of nearly-collisionless space plasmas has paved the way to investigate these systems in the framework of statistical physics of non-equilibrium complex systems [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. In this context, the Fluctuation-Dissipation Relation (FDR) represents a powerful theoretical tool to describe the steady-state balance between the energy injected into the system at large scales and the internal energy conversion and dissipation mechanisms.

In this context, the Fluctuation-Dissipation Relation (FDR) represents a powerful theoretical tool to describe the steady-state balance between the energy injected into the system at large scales and the internal energy conversion and dissipation mechanisms.

Previous theoretical models [12] have made significant progress by treating the turbulent energy injection as a white-noise source within a kinetic Langevin framework. However, this approach intrinsically leaves a knowledge gap, as also evidenced by recent studies based on space plasmas observations [13, 14]. Indeed, by definition, turbulence is characterized by finite spatial and temporal correlations [15, 16, 17], and assuming instantaneous decorrelation (white noise) may oversimplify the turbulent plasma dynamics. Hence, treating turbulent forcing with time-correlated noise is important to accurately model large-scale forcing and, in turn, interpret the plasma behavior and spectral signatures [13, 14].

In this work, we generalize the kinetic framework based on the Langevin phenomenology introduced in Ref. [12], by considering a damped-forced collisionless electrostatic plasma model where plasma response is driven by a stochastic forcing term characterized by a finite correlation time, which mimics the property of plasma turbulence [13]. In this framework, the continuous power injected from larger scales is counterbalanced by collisionless energy conversion mechanisms, as Landau damping. The forcing drives a stationary state where these kinetic processes effectively mediate the energy conversion and, despite their reversible nature, act as an effective dissipation, intended here as a energy transfer from electric field to particle distribution function. This balance ultimately drives the plasma toward a steady-state equilibrium governed by the FDR. We analytically derive the generalized FDR for the system response and extract its asymptotic spectral scalings across several interesting physical regimes. Moreover, to establish a direct connection between theoretical modeling and in-situ spacecraft observations, we extend our analysis to a multi-scale forcing scenario: the stochastic source is modeled as a superposition of noises with different correlation times governed by a power-law distribution [13]. All of our analytical predictions are validated against direct numerical integrations of the underlying kinetic equations.

papers.title: Electric-field tunable spin texture in dual-gated HfS$_2$/graphene van der Waals heterostructures
papers.abstract: Spin-charge interconversion provides the essential link between spin information and electrical signals in spintronic devices. In spin-orbit coupled systems, spin-charge interconversion can contain multiple components associated with different spin-polarization directions, reflecting the underlying spin texture. Tuning this spin texture therefore provides a way to control not only the magnitude of spin-charge interconversion, but also the balance among its different components. Graphene-based van der Waals heterostructures provide an attractive platform for this purpose because interfacial spin-orbit coupling can host multiple spin-charge interconversion channels that couple to different spin-polarization directions. Here, we demonstrate electric-field control of spin texture in a dual-gated HfS$_2$/graphene van der Waals heterostructure, where independent control of carrier density and vertical electric field allows us to disentangle electrostatic doping from electric field-induced spin-orbit effects. Nonlocal spin precession measurements show that near zero vertical electric field, spin-charge interconversion is dominated by a spin Hall component with out-of-plane spins. Increasing the vertical electric field enhances additional in-plane spin components with Rashba-Edelstein-like character, including both parallel and perpendicular to the charge current contributions. These results provide experimental evidence that a vertical electric field can reconfigure the effective spin texture and control the corresponding spin-charge interconversion components, demonstrating electrical tunability of spin-orbit functionalities.

papers.title: On unitary vertex operator algebras
papers.abstract: We prove that a conformal vertex algebra with a non-zero invariant Hermitian form is unitary as soon as it admits a non-zero positive energy module with a positive definite invariant Hermitian form. Using free field realizations, we deduce that the principal simple $W$-algebra $W_k(\mathfrak g)$ of a simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is unitary for central charge $c\ge rank(\mathfrak g)+24\bigl((ρ|ρ^\vee)+\|ρ\|\,\|ρ^\vee\|\bigr)$, and, if $\mathfrak g$ is simply laced, for all $c\ge rank(\mathfrak g)$. Among basic Lie superalgebras which are not Lie algebras, the free field argument applies to $osp(1|2n)$ and $osp(2|2n)$. It shows that $W_k(osp(1|2n))$ is unitary for $c\ge n+\frac12$ and gives an explicit bound for $osp(2|2n)$. Next, we prove that if $\mathfrak s$ is an even $sl_2$-subalgebra of a simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ whose centralizer is not abelian, then the simple $W$-algebra $W_k(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak s)$ is unitary for at most finitely many $k$. We illustrate this on the $W$-algebras of $sl_{qm}$ attached to the nilpotents of Jordan type $q^m$: unitarity is possible only at two levels, and for $q=2$ it does occur at both. For instance, the $W$-algebra of $sl_4$ attached to the partition $2+2$ is unitary only for $k=-2$ and $k=-\frac32$. This fails for Lie superalgebras, as minimal $W$-algebras show, but still holds under stronger assumptions. Finally, we prove that a simple $W$-algebra $W_k(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak s)$ can be unitary for only finitely many $k$ if $\mathfrak g$ is a simple Lie algebra and $\mathfrak s$ is not a distinguished $sl_2$ subalgebra.

papers.title: Germwise singular Fourier--Mukai partnerships
papers.abstract: We study how local behavior on the base controls whether integral transforms induce fully faithful functors or equivalences between singularity categories of proper flat families. By working with étale germs, we show (under mild hypotheses) that the loci where this happens are open and are compatible with étale base change. Moreover, we give examples, exhibit an autoequivalence of the singularity category which detects regularity of the base, and compute these loci for arithmetic families.

papers.title: Building a Nested LADDER for LLM Unstructured Post-Training Pruning
papers.abstract: Non-uniform allocation can improve post-training pruning of large language models, yet quality can still degrade sharply at high sparsity. To control degradation as sparsity increases, we introduce LADDER (Layer-Wise Allocation via Damage-Driven Evaluation and Refinement), which allocates sparsity incrementally. At each step, it evaluates pruning an additional fraction of weights from each eligible layer and commits the layer update that causes the least end-to-end degradation per removed parameter. This process produces non-uniform sparsity profiles and exactly nested masks across multiple budgets. We evaluate LADDER on five OPT, Llama, and Qwen models across 10-90% sparsity, using SparseGPT as its candidate-generation backend and comparing against uniform and adaptive allocation baselines. Results reveal a clear operating-regime trade-off: LADDER is comparable or slightly weaker at benign sparsity but becomes substantially more robust from 70% onward. This high-sparsity advantage largely persists after posterior distillation across four of five models and translates into improved retention of aggregate zero-shot accuracy.

papers.title: Small and Large Quasi-Kernels in General Digraphs
papers.abstract: In a digraph $D$, a set $Q$ of vertices is a quasi-kernel if $Q$ is an independent set and every vertex in $D$ can be reached from $Q$ via at most two edges. The small quasi-kernel conjecture by Erdős and Székely predicts that every source-free $n$-vertex digraph contains a quasi-kernel of size at most $n - n/2$. Chvátal and Lovász' 1974 work implies a bound of $n - \sqrt{n}+1$. In 2024, Sprio shows the bound $n - \frac{1}{4} \sqrt{n \log_2 n}$. We show that there always is a quasi-kernel of size at most $n - \frac{1}{51}n^{2/3} / \ln^{2/3}(n)$. For the related large quasi-kernel conjecture by Spiro, we show that there always is a quasi-kernel $Q$ with $|N^+[Q]| \ge 0.2917 \cdot n^{2/3} / \ln^{2/3}(n)$.

papers.title: Fully Dynamic Triangle and 4-Vertex Subgraph Counting: From Theory to Practice and Back Again
papers.abstract: Counting small patterns is a core primitive in large-scale graph analytics, with numerous applications in data management and network analysis. As modern graphs are massive and continuously evolving, maintaining such counts efficiently under updates is essential. Although specialized dynamic algorithms for patterns with up to four vertices exist, they remain largely theoretical; practitioners instead rely on general-purpose or approximate methods. We present an in-depth study of two dynamic approaches by Eppstein et al. and Hanauer et al. for maintaining counts of triangles and all connected four-vertex subgraph patterns, both based on variants of heavy-light vertex partitioning. We introduce theoretical and practical optimizations and develop hybrid variants that combine complementary strengths of both approaches. Experiments on 56 large real-world and synthetic dynamic graphs show that our optimized algorithms outperform the original methods and strong static and dynamic baselines on nearly all instances, both in total running time and worst-case update time, with speedups of up to several orders of magnitude. We further provide practical guidelines for algorithm selection and tuning. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive empirical study of heavy-light partitioning for dynamic subgraph counting, and our findings may inform other algorithms based on this technique.

papers.title: Constraining Dynamical Dark Energy with Tomographic Galaxy and CMB Weak Lensing Through Higher-Order Statistics
papers.abstract: Tomographic weak gravitational lensing probes cosmic structure growth and geometry, making it a powerful probe of dynamical dark energy. We forecast information beyond the lensing power spectrum from non-Gaussian statistics of tomographic galaxy and CMB lensing convergence maps. Using the $\texttt{DDELenS}$ suite of ray-traced $N$-body simulations, we build Gaussian process emulators for power spectra, Minkowski functionals, moments, peak and minima counts, and the wavelet scattering transform, varying $Ω_m$, $σ_8$, $w_0$, and $w_a$. We consider Rubin-like galaxy lensing and Simons Observatory-like CMB lensing over $15{,}000\,\mathrm{deg}^2$, and validate the analysis using a withheld fiducial cosmology, analytical power-spectrum forecasts, and Gaussian random-field null tests. As an initial step, we neglect baryonic effects and intrinsic alignments and approximate galaxy sources as discrete redshift planes. Using all source redshifts at $z_s=\{0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 1100\}$, combining all five non-Gaussian statistics reduces uncertainties on $w_0$ and $w_a$ by $24.3\%$ and $28.0\%$, and on $Ω_m$ and $σ_8$ by $41.9\%$ and $45.8\%$, relative to the power-spectrum-only baseline. The resulting $w_0$ and $w_a$ uncertainties are $34.7\%$ and $48.7\%$ smaller than current DESI+DES constraints. If the DESI+DES best-fit values remain unchanged, this precision would increase the significance of the departure from $Λ$CDM from $3.0σ$ to $5.2σ$, compared with $3.8σ$ from the power spectrum alone, assuming a Gaussian posterior and unchanged $w_0$--$w_a$ correlation. Minkowski functionals and moments provide comparable constraining power, while combining them with the other summaries gives the strongest constraints. Broad galaxy-lensing redshift coverage is particularly important for dynamical dark energy, while CMB lensing provides complementary information.

papers.intro:
Understanding the physical origin of the accelerated expansion of the Universe remains a central goal of cosmology. In the standard Λ\LambdaCDM model, dark energy is described by a cosmological constant with a time-independent equation of state, w=−1w=-1. Recent measurements from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), including baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) [10, 5, 6] and full-shape galaxy power spectrum measurements [9, 11], have increased interest in models with an evolving dark-energy equation of state. When combined with CMB measurements and Type Ia supernova data from Pantheon+, Union3, or DES [20, 76, 1, 70], these observations show a moderate preference for w0>−1w_{0}>-1 and wa<0w_{a}<0 in the Chevallier–Polarski–Linder (CPL) parametrization [30, 52]. More recently, a joint analysis of supernovae, BAO, weak lensing, and galaxy clustering from the full Dark Energy Survey (DES) dataset reported a preference for dynamical dark energy ranging from 2.2​σ2.2\sigma to 3.0​σ3.0\sigma, depending on the combination of external datasets [2]. Whether these indications reflect genuine new physics or residual systematics in supernova and large-scale-structure measurements remains an open question [43, 36, 24, 27]. Resolving this question will require continued scrutiny of existing datasets, quantitative forecasts of the additional discriminating power that future observations can provide, and the collection of new data with Rubin, Euclid, Roman, DESI, and other surveys.

Weak gravitational lensing is particularly useful in this context because it is sensitive both to the matter distribution along the line of sight and to the distances between the observer, lenses, and sources [7, 50]. Galaxy weak-lensing measurements from DES [3, 4], the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS) [40, 81], and the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC) [64] have already demonstrated the constraining power of cosmic shear and related lensing observables. The next generation of galaxy weak-lensing measurements from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time [31], the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope [15, 77], and Euclid [47] will substantially increase both the survey area and the number of well-measured source galaxies. Dividing these sources into redshift bins provides tomographic information that helps separate the effects of cosmological parameters on the lensing signal [54, 51, 32]. CMB lensing provides a complementary view of the matter distribution, with a source plane at the epoch of recombination and a broad lensing kernel extending beyond the redshift range most directly probed by galaxy lensing [50]. CMB lensing has already been measured at high signal-to-noise with Planck [14, 23], ACT [73, 55], and SPT/SPT-3G [82, 65], while the Simons Observatory will provide substantially improved sensitivity [13, 8]. The overlap between galaxy and CMB lensing in the large-scale structure they trace produces correlations that can provide additional cosmological information and reduce parameter degeneracies [25].

The power spectrum is a natural starting point for extracting cosmological information from these observations. For a Gaussian field, it provides a complete statistical description, but nonlinear gravitational evolution generates non-Gaussian structure that is not fully captured by two-point statistics. Lensing maps can therefore contain additional information in their amplitude distributions, spatial morphology, and higher-order correlations. Several summary statistics have been developed to access this information, including Minkowski functionals and moments [66, 68, 58], peak and minima counts [37, 51, 33], and the wavelet scattering transform [29, 28, 19]. For dynamical dark energy, however, non-Gaussian information alone cannot replace the redshift leverage provided by lensing tomography. A single source plane provides only limited sensitivity to the evolution of the dark-energy equation of state, leaving strong degeneracies among w0w_{0}, waw_{a}, and other cosmological parameters. Combining multiple source redshifts and their cross-correlations is therefore particularly important for constraining dynamical dark energy. The relevant question is then how much additional information non-Gaussian statistics provide once this tomographic information is included. CMB lensing can further contribute by extending the redshift baseline and by constraining parameter combinations that are degenerate in galaxy lensing alone. We therefore separately quantify the gains from increasing the source-redshift coverage and from adding non-Gaussian statistics, and examine how these two sources of information complement one another.

The power spectrum is a natural starting point for extracting cosmological information from these observations. For a Gaussian field, it provides a complete statistical description, but nonlinear gravitational evolution generates non-Gaussian structure that is not fully captured by two-point statistics. Lensing maps can therefore contain additional information in their amplitude distributions, spatial morphology, and higher-order correlations. Several summary statistics have been developed to access this information, including Minkowski functionals and moments [66, 68, 58], peak and minima counts [37, 51, 33], and the wavelet scattering transform [29, 28, 19]. We therefore separately quantify the gains from increasing the source-redshift coverage and from adding non-Gaussian statistics, and examine how these two sources of information complement one another.

In this work, we use the DDELenS simulation suite [25] to forecast constraints on Ωm\Omega_{m}, σ8\sigma_{8}, w0w_{0}, and waw_{a} from tomographic galaxy and CMB lensing. We adopt a Rubin-like galaxy lensing survey and Simons Observatory-like CMB lensing as a concrete case study — though the methodology applies equally to Roman and Euclid — and compare several combinations of source redshifts. Using Gaussian process emulators trained on ray-traced NN-body simulations, we predict the power spectra and five sets of additional summary statistics: Minkowski functionals, moments, peak counts, minima counts, and the wavelet scattering transform. We also examine the contributions of individual Minkowski functionals and moments to identify which components drive their constraining power. For these initial forecasts, we neglect baryonic effects and intrinsic alignments and approximate galaxy source populations as discrete redshift planes, allowing us to assess the statistical potential of the summary statistics within a simplified experimental setup. We will revisit these effects in future work.

papers.title: On the Largest Cardinality Subset Sum
papers.abstract: We study Largest Cardinality Subset Sum (LCSS): given $n$ nonnegative integers and a target $t$, compute a subset summing to $t$ with maximum cardinality. We also consider its all-targets version (ATLCSS), which asks for this maximum for every sum $s\in\{1,\ldots,t\}$. The LCSS problem sits squarely between the subset sum and the knapsack problem. A straightforward dynamic-programming algorithm runs in time $O(nt)$ and solves ATLCSS, and using Jin and Bringmann (both in STOC 2024, independent work) $0$-$1$ knapsack results we achieve a $\widetilde{O}(n + a_{\max}^2)$-time deterministic algorithm for LCSS. Our main result is a randomized $\widetilde{O}(n+\sqrt{n}\,t)$-time algorithm for LCSS. Then, we complement this result with a randomized $\widetilde{O}(n+t^{3/2})$-time algorithm for ATLCSS. Together, our two algorithms give a $\widetilde{O}(n+t\min\{\sqrt{n},\sqrt{t}\})$-time algorithm for LCSS. As an application of ATLCSS, we solve the search version of Projection Subset Sum, introduced by Dutta and Rajasree (SYNSAC 2023), in $\widetilde{O}(n+t^{3/2})$ time for every fixed $\ell_p$ norm with $p\geq 1$. For $\ell_1$, we obtain $\widetilde{O}(n+t)$ time, removing the unique-representation assumption required by their algorithm. Both algorithms output an optimal modified vector and a witnessing subset.

A natural next question is what can be learned about the subsets attaining a given target. We study the maximum size of such a subset. papers.title: ERCLIP: Small-Data Adaptation of CLIP for Free-Length Image-Text Retrieval
papers.abstract: CLIP's 77-token text encoder truncates detailed image descriptions. We present ERCLIP, a small-data adaptation of CLIP for long-caption image--text retrieval. During training, a long caption is split into sentences that the CLIP text encoder encodes independently; the sentence embeddings are fused by mean pooling or a gated residual Transformer scorer and receive their own contrastive loss. At inference ERCLIP is an unmodified CLIP dual encoder: test captions are still read through the 77-token window, and only training sees the full caption. We find that this fine-tuning erodes CLIP's zero-shot classification, most when the fusion output is not a combination of CLIP embeddings, and add a frozen-CLIP preservation loss on the image and short-caption embeddings. With 20k pairs and one epoch, ERCLIP improves long-caption R@1 over CLIP by 6.5--11.2 points, closing 62--77% of the gap to LongCLIP with 2% of its long captions. Preservation recovers 1.5--2.1 ImageNet zero-shot points (30--42% of the loss) and adds up to 2.4 points of COCO image-to-text R@1, at no inference cost.

papers.intro:
CLIP dual encoders align images and text in a shared embedding space and support both retrieval and zero-shot recognition [16]. Their text encoders, however, read at most 77 tokens, so detailed descriptions are truncated and the discarded facts never reach the embedding. Long-context methods extend the positional embeddings, match features across caption lengths, or learn token selection [25, 22, 14, 21]. They rely on large long-caption corpora and rarely report what the adaptation does to the tasks CLIP already solves, a cost documented for classification fine-tuning [20, 7] but not for long-caption retrieval.

papers.title: Isotropy sets of periodic geodesic flows on three dimensional manifolds
papers.abstract: A classical theorem of Wadsley states that if all geodesics on a Riemannian manifold M are periodic, then they have a common period, and the geodesic flow induces an S^1-action on the unit tangent bundle. Moreover, a conjecture of Berger asserts that this action is free whenever M is simply connected. In this paper, we investigate the Berger conjecture in dimension three by studying the isotropy set of the S^1-action induced by the geodesic flow. Using Morse theory for the energy functional on the free loop space of M, we establish two results in this direction. First, we show that all isotropy groups of the geodesic flow have odd order. Second, we prove that the geodesic flow either acts freely on the unit tangent bundle $T^1M$ or has at least two singular orbit types. This paper serves as preparation for the subsequent paper The Berger conjecture for three-dimensional manifolds, in which the conjecture is proved in dimension three.

If γ\gamma is unit speed, then its shortest period is called the length of γ\gamma. Manifolds all of whose geodesics are closed have been objects of special interest for quite a while, mainly since Zoll and Tannery discovered metrics with this property on the sphere that are different from the round metric. The most common examples of manifolds all of whose geodesic are closed are compact symmetric Spaces of rank 11, the so-called CROSSes, namely the spheres equipped with the round metric, the real, complex and quaternionic projective spaces equipped with their Fubini-Study metric and the Cayley plane. A theorem of Wadsley says that if (M,⟨⋅,⋅⟩)(M,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle) is a manifold all of whose geodesics are closed, then all geodesics have a common period. This implies that the geodesic flow induces a smooth 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}-action on the unit tangent bundle T1​MT^{1}M of MM. A conjecture of Berger states that on a simply connected manifold with this property all unit speed geodesics have the same minimal period. This means that the least common period that exists by Wadsley’s theorem is also the smallest period of each single unit speed geodesic. This is the case if and only if the 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}-action of the geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle is free. The conjecture was proven to be true for two-dimensional manifolds by Gromoll and Grove in [3]. Marco Radeschi and Burkhard Wilking were the first to use Morse theory on the free loop space to attack the conjecture. In [7], they showed that the conjecture also holds for topological spheres of dimension greater than or equal to four. In this paper we will sharpen John Olsen’s results about the isotropy set of the geodesic flow. First we show that the order of the isotropy group of each component of the isotropy set of the geodesic flow is odd.

papers.title: Phase-Coherent Multistatic Sensing under Phase Noise in Distributed ISAC
papers.abstract: We investigate phase-coherent multistatic sensing in distributed ISAC systems where spatially separated access points (APs) share a common, non-ideal local oscillator (LO) impaired by phase noise (PN). In the presence of a single transmit AP and multiple receive APs with OFDM transmission, we derive the joint statistics of PN across receive APs and reveal its unique covariance structure that depends on target location through propagation delays of individual bistatic links. Based on this statistical characterization, we carry out a Cramér-Rao bound analysis of three receiver models, namely PN-free, PN-aware and PN-ignorant, for both isotropic and non-isotropic targets. Simulation results verify the location-dependent statistics of PN in shared-LO distributed architectures while demonstrating how transmit power, LO quality, AP deployment and scattering characteristics affect multistatic localization.

papers.intro:
Distributed ISAC (ISAC) extends environmental perception from individual transceivers to a network of cooperating AP [40, 25]. Spatially separated AP observe targets from complementary viewpoints, providing geometric diversity and broader sensing coverage [25]. By fusing sensing information at different levels, ranging from raw measurements to local estimates, distributed ISAC can improve localization accuracy in multistatic configurations relative to conventional monostatic sensing [16]. By leveraging the existing communication infrastructure, it can thus overcome key limitations of single-node sensing and support the demanding sensing requirements envisioned for 6G applications.

A key practical requirement to realize these gains is to maintain inter-AP phase coherence.

papers.title: Forward-Only Learning for Shared-Kernel Wavelet Neural Networks without Backpropagation
papers.abstract: Backpropagation remains the dominant training paradigm, using backward gradients and local updates that can suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients in deep networks. Although the Forward-Forward algorithm avoids conventional backpropagation, it remains mainly local or layer-wise, motivating global whole-network learning using forward evaluations only. For shared-kernel wavelet neural networks, we therefore propose a CMA-ES-based global forward-only learning framework. We further introduce structure-aware parameter decomposition and channel-specific credit assignment, factorizing the search into three subspaces. On BSDS500, our method reduces test MSE from 4.1783 to 4.0130 and improves PSNR from 42.621 to 42.787~dB over Adam/BP without backward propagation. Beyond these gains, training requires only 6 training-set coverages, compared with 1500 epochs for BP. Ablations show that structural decomposition and aligned credit assignment are more important than increasing population size, demonstrating the feasibility of whole-network forward-only learning for compact reconstruction networks. These results suggest a potential route toward forward-only optimization of compact reconstruction models for resource-constrained imaging and edge or near-sensor systems.
papers.intro:
Image reconstruction is a fundamental problem in computational imaging and low-level vision, where neural methods recover high-quality images from degraded or transformed measurements [20, 1, 13]. Practical systems increasingly require not only reconstruction accuracy but also low memory and computational costs. Multiscale and wavelet-inspired architectures are well suited to this goal because they capture image structures across resolutions while introducing structured analysis–synthesis operations [18, 8, 4].

Backpropagation remains the dominant neural-network training paradigm, using local first-order gradient information for iterative parameter updates [14, 10]. Recent backpropagation-free methods, including the Forward-Forward algorithm, avoid conventional backward propagation but remain predominantly based on layer-local objectives [7, 15, 10]. In contrast, evolutionary and derivative-free methods evaluate populations of complete candidate solutions, enabling global exploration without gradients [9, 6]. Here, global refers to population-based search over the complete network parameterization rather than guaranteed convergence to a global optimum. Although such whole-network search is generally impractical for large neural networks, the compact parameterization of shared-kernel wavelet networks makes it tractable.

In this work, we propose a global forward-only learning framework for shared-kernel wavelet neural networks. As illustrated in Fig. 1, conventional BP relies on backward gradient propagation and local gradient-based updates, whereas our approach evaluates complete network candidates through forward reconstruction losses and adapts a population distribution using CMA-ES [6]. Compactness alone, however, does not make naive joint search effective. We therefore introduce structure-aware parameter decomposition and channel-specific credit assignment to align the search with the intrinsic network structure. The resulting framework optimizes the complete network through forward evaluations only, without automatic differentiation or backward propagation.

papers.title: Mitigating Model Collapse through Dreaming Learning
papers.abstract: Training generative models on synthetic data causes loss of diversity and a decrease in performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. We study this degeneration spectrally in a controlled Markov setting. The eigenvalue spectrum of the learned transition operator offers a direct view of the process, since the subdominant eigenvalues set how fast the chain mixes and therefore how much of the state space it continues to explore. We find that sampling at temperature $T_s < 1$ acts on the operator like repeated sharpening, pushing it toward a deterministic system: the subdominant eigenvalues approach the unit circle and the spectral gap narrows. When $T_s < 1$, even data accumulation does not appear to arrest this drift. We then analyze Dreaming Learning, a regulariser that, in parallel with regular training, adds a loss term on the model's own samples drawn at a raised temperature $T_d > 1$. Because high-temperature samples flatten the predicted distribution, training on them keeps the entries of the learned operator from becoming vanishingly small, which in turn keeps the eigenvalues bounded away from the unit circle. Measurements of the spectra over 5000 generations are consistent with this picture, and the mitigation effect persists in more complex settings such as LSTM language models and a 124M-parameter GPT-2.

papers.intro:
As synthetic data is an ever-increasing percentage of online content, generative models are increasingly retrained on data they themselves produced, without being able to distinguish human-made content from machine-made one. This phenomenon lowers diversity and drives learned distributions toward low-entropy distributions, an effect observed across GANs, diffusion models and language models (Shumailov et al., 2024; Dohmatob et al., 2024a; Liu and others, 2022; Yoon et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024). The leading mitigation technique is accumulation: retaining a fraction of real data alongside synthetic data (Gerstgrasser and others, 2024; Seddik et al., 2024). Accumulation bounds test error, but existing analyses fix the sampling temperature used in language modeling experiments at Ts=1T_{s}=1, almost never used during inference (Renze and Guven, 2024), and no consensus exists on real-to-synthetic ratios (Dohmatob et al., 2024b). Furthermore, datasets cannot always be distinguished upfront, risking sub-optimal mitigation.

papers.title: Super-tetragonal ferroelectric barium titanate through anionic overstoichiometry
papers.abstract: Ferroelectric oxides, characterized by an electrical polarization that is switchable with an electric field, are an appealing class of materials for energy-efficient computing, electronics, and photonics. In thin films, the properties of ferroelectrics are commonly tuned using substrate-imposed epitaxial strain, an approach limited to biaxial strain states and a finite number of available substrates. Here, we demonstrate that is is possible to move beyond conventional epitaxial growth by using pulsed laser deposition under highly non-equilibrium conditions. Specifically, we show that this unconventional processing route allows us to stabilize a super-tetragonal phase of ferroelectric $\text{BaTiO}_3$. The key to this stabilization lies in the insertion of surplus oxygen atoms into the unit cell, resulting in peroxide bond formation that give rise to an aspect ratio of as high as 1.08. Notably, this super-tetragonal phase exhibits an enhanced ferroelectric polarization, reduced coercivity, lower leakage currents, and increased cycling endurance compared to conventional bulk-like $\text{BaTiO}_3$ films. These results, thus, showcase the potential of non-equilibrium growth for defect engineering to obtain emergent phases in complex oxides and tune their physical properties in thin films expanding the scope of traditional epitaxy.

papers.title: Comprehensive Acoustic Characterization of a Broadband Lateral MEMS Ultrasonic Transducer by Near-Field Acoustic Holography and Coupled Multiphysics Simulation
papers.abstract: Broadband airborne ultrasonic transducers are attractive for applications such as ranging, echo-location, and acoustic material characterization, where wide bandwidths enable advanced excitation and signal-processing techniques. Recently, a lateral capacitive micromachined ultrasonic transducer (L-CMUT) employing electrostatically actuated in-plane microbeams was introduced as a broadband MEMS transducer concept. However, a comprehensive investigation of its acoustic radiation behavior and quantitative validation of corresponding multiphysics models have not yet been reported. In this work, we present a combined experimental and numerical characterization of a previously reported L-CMUT device operating between 10 kHz and 60 kHz. A coupled electrostatic--structural--thermoviscous finite-element model is combined with an acoustic boundary-element formulation to investigate the complete transduction chain from electrostatic actuation to acoustic radiation. The numerical predictions are validated experimentally using spherical near-field acoustic holography, enabling reconstruction of three-dimensional directivity patterns, radiated acoustic power, and spherical harmonic representations of the radiated sound field. The results show that the broadband behavior originates from strong thermoviscous damping within the narrow beam--stator cavities, resulting in strongly overdamped operation despite a mechanical eigenfrequency near 50 kHz. Good agreement between simulations and measurements is obtained for radiation patterns, radiated sound power, and spherical harmonic content. Furthermore, horn loading primarily redistributes acoustic energy and modifies directivity while only weakly affecting the total radiated acoustic power.

papers.title: Koala: Non-disruptive Reconfiguration for Long-running Stateful Dataflows
papers.abstract: Stateful dataflow systems must decide where state lives relative to the tasks that process it. For long-running applications that require frequent reconfiguration due to changes in resource allocation, partitioning, or task placement, this design choice presents a core trade-off between adaptability and performance. Co-locating state with computation ensures low latency at steady state but makes reconfiguration disruptive, as any change forces state migration. On the other hand, keeping state in an external store makes reconfiguration seamless, but incurs overhead on every access. We present Koala, a reconfiguration protocol for distributed dataflow systems that retains the operational performance of embedded-state architectures while matching the disruption-free adaptability of external-state designs. Unlike prior protocols which relocate all state regardless of whether it will soon be accessed, Koala migrates state in a fine-grained, lazy manner. To achieve that, it employs a lightweight ownership transfer mechanism that safely decouples event routing from state location. We implement Koala in a new streaming dataflow system and evaluate it on real-world and synthetic benchmarks. When compared with the state-of-the-art protocol DRRS, Koala consumes backlog up to 23x faster and transfers 8.7x less state on average during reconfiguration.

papers.title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies. We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance. For SmolVLA, the head on the vision-language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs. We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings. Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs. With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.
