papers.title: Statistics of entries of matrices from the general linear group over a finite field
papers.abstract: Let $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$ be the group of $n\times n$ invertible matrices over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$. How many matrices in $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$ are there with a subset of their entries prescribed? Motivated by the random matrix theory of classical compact groups, we address this question and various variants, with a focus on asymptotic results that are valid as $n$ tends to infinity. Our methods are Fourier-analytic, with the main input being an exponential sum over $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$, evaluated in 1955 by Hodges via elementary methods. Our results turn out to be related to investigations carried out in other fields, including coding theory, universality for $p$-adic matrices and algebraic combinatorics.

papers.title: Signals and Queries: Token-Efficient Agentic Context Discovery
papers.abstract: User-facing LLM agents must identify which behavioral policies apply at each turn, but evaluating every policy with an LLM is costly. We introduce Signals and Queries (S&Q), a lightweight first-stage relevance filter developed for Parlant 4.0 that removes at least 30% of candidate policies before downstream evaluation while preserving high recall. For each policy, an LLM generates activating examples and hard negatives offline. An independent logistic classifier trained on their embeddings then predicts relevance using embeddings and vector dot products, with no per-turn LLM calls. This shifts expensive relevance evaluation to a smaller candidate set, while allowing each policy's classifier to be updated independently. Evaluated against 9,144 LLM-judge relevance labels covering 254 $τ^2$-bench conversation prefixes and 36 airline policies, S&Q achieves higher precision than top-K and cosine-threshold retrieval at every evaluated recall level, with consistent results across two embedding providers. These findings support inexpensive, per-policy classification as a practical first stage for reducing downstream evaluation workload in customer-facing agents.

papers.title: Where AI Vulnerability Discovery Harnesses Go Quiet: Structural False Negatives and Hidden Vulnerabilities
papers.abstract: LLM-based vulnerability discovery harnesses can miss real, reachable vulnerabilities because of how the harness around the model is built. Steps that select code, filter it, and store and merge findings can drop a vulnerability before or after the model runs, independently of the model's capability, and the report usually gives no sign that this happened. These drops come from engineering choices, and errors. They leave vulnerabilities undetected, and an attacker who knows the harness's rules can also use them to hide a vulnerability on purpose. Understanding these drops shows how to build harnesses that fix or disclose them and are harder to evade. Starting from the two harnesses we maintain, Knostic's OpenAnt and raptor, and then examining 10 additional open-source harnesses, we mapped 13 points where such drops occur and organized them into a taxonomy. Using each harness's own code, we show a single file that six harnesses dropped before their model saw its code, five of them without notice. We propose engineering failure patterns mapped to these drops, and relate them to Ptacek and Newsham's work on intrusion detection evasion. The paper also covers content-steered verdicts and prompt injection, and gives design principles and tests for harnesses that report accurately what they analyzed. The reliability findings likely apply to other LLM harnesses, beyond vulnerability research and application security, and the evasion findings apply wherever an attacker can write or influence the code being checked. We also argue that harnesses built to be descriptive can, in effect, be prescriptive. Rules written to describe typical code and typical model replies end up deciding what is analyzed, and anything that does not conform is treated as absent or as "no vulnerability."
papers.intro:
A harness report with no findings can mean three things: the code is clean, the model analyzed the vulnerable code and missed the vulnerability, or the vulnerability never reached the model or was removed after it. The report usually looks the same in all three cases.

papers.title: Region-Aware Multi-View Inspection Using Deep Learning and Domain-Informed Decision Fusion
papers.abstract: Automated optical inspection of precision components with tiny surface defects remains challenging when different regions of the same component exhibit different defect characteristics and, therefore, different acceptance criteria. This paper presents a region-aware, dual-model inspection framework that combines instance segmentation of localized seat-region defects with image-level classification of global shaft-region anomalies. Rather than treating these two model detections as sufficient evidence for component rejection, a deterministic decision fusion layer that formalizes industrial Standard Operating Procedures is applied to the model outputs to make the final component level decision. A PLC-synchronized imaging system acquires 18 seat and 18 shaft images over a full 360-degree rotation to provide multi-view circumferential coverage. The framework was evaluated on 380 automotive fuel injector needles, covering representative operational defect types, using identical model predictions in all configurations. Direct model-output aggregation via simple union logic (where any single-view detection flags a rejection) identified all 104 non-conforming components but produced a component level false rejection rate of 57.6%. Inclusion of a complete decision layer maintained the observed non-conforming (NOK) recall of 100% while reducing the false rejection rate to 10.9%, corresponding to an 81.1% reduction in false-positive component decisions. The results demonstrate that formalized manufacturing acceptance criteria can complement sensitive visual models by translating frame-level detections into practical and traceable component-level decisions.
papers.intro:
High-precision manufacturing of functionally critical components demands reliable quality inspection because small surface flaws may cause a component to violate its specified acceptance criteria. Inspection is particularly challenging for reflective or geometrically complex components because defect appearance can vary with viewpoint and imaging conditions [1, 2], while production deployment also requires reliable synchronization and timely decision transfer [3].

High-precision manufacturing of functionally critical components demands reliable quality inspection because small surface flaws may cause a component to violate its specified acceptance criteria. Inspection is particularly challenging for reflective or geometrically complex components because defect appearance can vary with viewpoint and imaging conditions [1, 2], while production deployment also requires reliable synchronization and timely decision transfer [3].

Deep learning has significantly improved industrial visual inspection by learning discriminative representations for subtle anomalies and enabling defect localization beyond image-level decisions [4, 5]. However, practical deployment in high-throughput manufacturing still faces two recurring issues across many product types. First, highly sensitive detectors can trigger excessive false rejects when visually benign marks are flagged as defects, reducing line efficiency and operator trust [6, 7]. Second, single-view inspection can miss defects that are only observable at certain angles on reflective or curved surfaces [2], motivating multi-view acquisition and fusion [1]. In addition, serial two-stage architectures, in which a segmentation network first localizes potential defects and a subsequent decision network performs image-level defective/non-defective classification, have demonstrated strong surface-defect detection performance [8]. However, such architectures differ from the present framework because both stages analyze the same inspected surface in sequence, whereas the proposed system assigns segmentation and classification to different functional regions and combines their outputs only at the component-decision level.

A key challenge in industrial visual inspection is that detecting a visual irregularity and determining component acceptability are not identical tasks. A sensitive model may identify small surface defects or benign visual patterns, but not every model detection necessarily violates the applicable component acceptance criteria. Its relevance may depend on its location relative to the component boundary, functional region, predicted category, dimensions, and occurrence count.

A sensitive model may identify small surface defects or benign visual patterns, but not every model detection necessarily violates the applicable component acceptance criteria. Its relevance may depend on its location relative to the component boundary, functional region, predicted category, dimensions, and occurrence count.

This distinction is particularly important when multiple functionally critical regions coexist within a single component. Such regions may exhibit different defect morphologies, functional risks, and acceptance conditions. Applying a uniform decision criterion across the entire component can therefore cause small, out-of-region, or functionally permissible detections to propagate into component-level false rejects. At the same time, some defects manifest as global structural anomalies that do not require pixel-level localization but must still be detected reliably. These considerations motivate a region-aware design in which specialized models generate visual detections and a separate decision layer evaluates those detections before component-level aggregation.

papers.title: Deciding Scale Placement in MXFP4 Dot Products with Integer Arithmetic
papers.abstract: The Open Compute Project's microscaling (MX) family includes MXFP4, which stores 32 four-bit elements with a shared power-of-two scale. When lowering a dot-product reduction, a compiler can apply these scales before the reduction, or defer scaling until afterwards. Although equivalent over real numbers, these formulations can produce different IEEE binary32 results through overflow or underflow, with equivalence also depending on the reduction tree. We study the legality of compiler rewrites in either direction by deriving conditions under which the two formulations are bitwise equivalent. To decide rewrite legality, we construct an integer state machine that exploits the finite element alphabet and shared power-of-two scales, modeling overflow, NaN, and subnormal rounding. We prove its faithfulness under bounded scale codes and integer coefficients, yielding an exact encoding of the equivalence query in quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic (QF_LIA). For MXFP4, we derive a closed-form sufficient upper bound on the sum of scale exponents for any fixed binary reduction tree within the supported coefficient range. This bound depends on the size of the largest proper subtree. For four tree shapes at block lengths $k\in\{2,3,4,8,16,32\}$ and two shapes at $k=64$, SMT finds counterexamples when this upper bound is increased by one exponent step. Against the standard direct encoding in quantifier-free floating-point arithmetic (QF_FP), on matched queries cvc5 proves the integer version in seconds but reaches a configured one-CPU-hour limit on the floating-point proof even at $k=2$. The implementation was cross-checked using an independent floating-point encoding, exhaustive and stratified binary32 execution, and GPU replay of counterexamples. An MLIR lowering prototype demonstrates selection between the two formulations using the certified conditions as static or runtime guards.
papers.intro:
As ML models, particularly large language models, continue to grow in size, they require substantial memory and computational resources to store and process their parameters and intermediate activations. Reducing the number of bits used to represent each value can improve throughput and reduce energy use on supporting hardware compared to full 32-bit floating-point arithmetic, by reducing data movement and enabling efficient arithmetic. However, reducing bit width affects precision and dynamic range, and requires care to preserve numerical accuracy and to avoid overflow or underflow.

However, reducing bit width affects precision and dynamic range, and requires care to preserve numerical accuracy and to avoid overflow or underflow.

Block scaling formats like Open Compute Project’s microscaling (MX) formats, which store a tensor as blocks of narrow elements that share one scale [24, 27], extend the dynamic range of the elements while keeping storage costs moderate. These formats have become so important that major vendors have added native support: NVIDIA’s Blackwell tensor cores and AMD’s matrix cores support multiplying block-scaled matrices [23, 5]. On the software end, frameworks like Triton expose the operation as dot_scaled and emulate it on other targets [31], and torchao emulates it by dequantizing to a wide type and calling an ordinary matrix multiply [26].

papers.title: Scalar--Mean Rigidity for Hyperbolic Balls in Dimensions $2\le n\le 5$
papers.abstract: In this paper, we prove the non-spin hyperbolic scalar--mean rigidity theorem in dimensions $2\leq n\leq5$, resolving the corresponding low-dimensional case of a problem of Gromov. The proof combines the Jang deformation with capillary $μ$-bubble dimension reduction. We also establish weighted scalar--mean rigidity for Euclidean ball--torus products in total dimension at most seven and show that its hyperbolic analogue fails.

papers.title: $L^p$-Liouville properties and realizations of Schrödinger operators on incomplete Riemannian manifolds
papers.abstract: The aim of the paper is to highlight and standardize in a self-contained framework the connections between some properties associated with the Laplace-Beltrami operator on possibly incomplete Riemannian manifolds. We present both new and well-known characterizations of the positivity-preserving property, essential self-adjointness, and Liouville-type results for $L^2$-functions, using the latter to establish a clear hierarchy among these properties. Furthermore, we prove the stability of the essential self-adjointness of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on incomplete Riemannian manifolds under the removal of closed (possibly non-compact) subsets from a complete manifold, subject to suitable conditions on their (generalized) Hausdorff measure. With appropriate modifications, this framework is adapted throughout the paper to the general $L^p$-case for $p\in (1,+\infty)$.

papers.title: Examples of absolutely minimal polyhedral chains in maximum norm spaces
papers.abstract: We construct explicit area-minimizing polyhedral disks in $\R^n$ with the maximum norm for $n=2,3,4$. Their boundaries are polygonal images of the geodesic circle of length $2π$, obtained from $n$ distance functions. Piecewise constant calibrations show that these disks minimize mass among Ambrosio--Kirchheim metric currents with the same boundary. The example for $n=4$ gives the lower bound $11π^2/20\approx5.42828$ for Gromov's filling area conjecture. For $n>4$, finite linear programs provide further lower bounds.

papers.title: Extending Doi--Takeuchi correspondence to bimodules and noncommutative covers
papers.abstract: Doi and Takeuchi, and independently Blattner, Cohen and Montgomery, have exhibited a correspondence between cleft extensions of an algebra $U$ by a Hopf algebra $H$ and $H$-measurings on $U$ equipped with a compatible normalized 2-cocycle. Each cleft extension is isomorphic as an algebra, a left $U$-module and a right $H$-comodule to the crossed product algebra constructed from the measuring and the cocycle. Cleft $H$-extensions are a special case of $H$-Hopf-Galois extensions, describing noncommutative principal $H$-bundles with affine total and affine base space. Corings are used to describe noncommutative space covers, allowing a description of possibly nonaffine noncommutative spaces. We propose to describe the total space of a noncommutative $H$-principal bundle by an internal $E$-coring in $H$-comodules where $E$ is an $H$-comodule algebra which is itself $H$-Hopf-Galois. This article focuses on the cleft case. As corings involve bimodules and morphisms of bimodules we extend the Doi--Takeuchi correspondence to bimodule $H$-comodules between cleft extensions on one side and bimodules of $H$-coinvariants equipped with bimodule $H$-measurings compatible with 2-cocycles on the other side. In fact, the correspondences for algebras and for bimodules are parts of a biequivalence of suitable bicategories defined in this article. As a corollary one obtains a correspondence between cleft $H$-extensions of corings and corings equipped with a nonabelian Čech 1-cocycle covalued in $H$.
papers.intro:
In noncommutative algebraic geometry, Hopf algebras are often viewed as a generalization of (the categorically formal duals to) affine algebraic groups. Faithfully flat Hopf-Galois extensions [4, 14] of algebras by Hopf algebras are analogues of torsors (in appropriate flat topology) for affine algebraic groups whose total and base spaces are affine as well. In noncommutative case we can glue pieces using flat localizations [19, 13], ideals [7] or faithfully flat maps [11]. If the pieces are affine, corings supply a formalism [6, 7]; if the pieces themselves are not affine we may need more general comonads [3, 13, 21].

Faithfully flat Hopf-Galois extensions [4, 14] of algebras by Hopf algebras are analogues of torsors (in appropriate flat topology) for affine algebraic groups whose total and base spaces are affine as well. In noncommutative case we can glue pieces using flat localizations [19, 13], ideals [7] or faithfully flat maps [11]. If the pieces are affine, corings supply a formalism [6, 7]; if the pieces themselves are not affine we may need more general comonads [3, 13, 21].

We may also be interested that the affine pieces are in some sense trivial principal bundles [4]. In commutative case, the algebra of functions on trivial principal bundle (when both the base and total space are affine) is the tensor product of the algebra of functions on the base and of the fiber. In noncommutative case the tensor product algebra seems to be too restrictive in major examples and one goes beyond to include either smash product algebras [10, 12] or more generally cocycled crossed product algebras [12, 9] with canonical structure of a comodule over the Hopf algebra. In both cases one should allow also objects which are isomorphic to these products in appropriate sense. For crossed product algebras these appear to be cleft Hopf-Galois extensions. Each class of cleft Hopf-Galois extensions is represented up to isomorphism by a cocycled crossed product algebra. This is the geometric meaning of the Doi–Takeuchi correspondence [1, 9] reviewed in 1.2. The present article globalizes this correspondence to covers presented by corings generalizing an earlier sketch for the smash product case [15]. Technical elements of the present construction involve internalization of corings [2] to the category of comodules over a Hopf algebra, a new (bi)cocycled crossed product construction for bimodules and a bicategorical setup unifying the algebra, bimodule and morphism of bimodules aspects of the correspondence.

papers.abstract: We study the alternating perturbation of Conway's nested recurrence, $C(n)=C(C(n-1))+C(n-C(n-1))+(-1)^n$ for $n\geq 3$, with $C(1)=C(2)=1$. We prove that the sequence is well defined and satisfies $C(n)=ψ^{-3}n+O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$, where $ψ>1$ is the real root of $ψ^3=ψ^2+1$.

papers.title: Energy-fed commitment: a minimal model of random selection followed by reinforcement
papers.abstract: When a symmetric instability is crossed, fluctuations choose one of several equivalent branches. We study a minimal stochastic model of what can then make that choice progressively harder to undo. After selection, the stiffness of the selected state grows in proportion to the energy released each time the structure recovers from a perturbation; in this conservative model that energy equals, up to small and explicitly computed terms, the work absorbed from the perturbing agent. The model is a phenomenological closure with one coupling constant. That energy reinforces a branch already chosen, rather than choosing it, is an assumption of the model, which we state and do not derive. Its consequences are quantitative. The growth of commitment depends on how the structure is driven: geometric under displacement control, linear under energy control and sublinear under force control, so that committed states absorb more work per cycle under displacement control and less under force control. Reinforcement suppresses reversal exponentially; beyond a finite commitment the alternative minimum disappears and reversals become rare crossings of an irreversibility threshold. With unbounded reinforcement a choice is retained forever with positive probability under stated conditions; with saturating reinforcement retention is finite, with a lifetime that grows exponentially with the saturation level. Exact first-passage calculations agree with stochastic simulations; these verify the closure and its analysis but cannot test the physical postulate. We identify the experiments that could: protocols that separate absorbed energy from the number of perturbations, and driven steady states with nonzero housekeeping heat, in which heat and absorbed work differ.
papers.intro:
Open systems driven far from equilibrium form structures through instabilities: convection cells, chemical waves, crystal morphologies, chiral domains [1, 2]. At a symmetric bifurcation with winner-take-all competition only one of the possible branches is realized, and which one is decided largely by chance [3, 4, 5]; the classic demonstration is the random chirality of sodium chlorate crystals [3]. A structure formed in this way may carry traces of its history [1, 6], and a transient perturbation can move a driven system to a different persistent state [7]. This paper asks a narrower question: what simple mechanism could make a randomly selected state progressively harder to reverse, and with what statistics?

At a symmetric bifurcation with winner-take-all competition only one of the possible branches is realized, and which one is decided largely by chance [3, 4, 5]; the classic demonstration is the random chirality of sodium chlorate crystals [3]. A structure formed in this way may carry traces of its history [1, 6], and a transient perturbation can move a driven system to a different persistent state [7]. This paper asks a narrower question: what simple mechanism could make a randomly selected state progressively harder to reverse, and with what statistics?

Several lines of work bear on it. Fluctuation relations for driven systems connect the relative likelihood of outcomes to the heat dissipated in reaching them and to their probability of reverting [8, 9]. Numerical studies of driven multistable networks find that the configurations reached are those that absorb little work from the specific drive [10, 11], and low-rattling arguments predict self-organization towards states with small drive-induced fluctuations [12]. Readings of nonequilibrium selection in terms of entropy production assign dissipation the role of favouring some outcomes over others [13, 7, 4], and the thermodynamics of switching between nonequilibrium steady states has been analysed directly [14]. Driven disordered matter encodes its loading history [15, 16, 17], and in cyclically driven solids a transient rise in dissipation signals the formation of memory [18]. In plasticity, the work-hardening hypothesis makes the yield stress a function of the plastic work dissipated [19]. Positive-feedback loops make cell-fate decisions bistable and effectively irreversible [20]. Flashing and feedback ratchets change the potential in time, the latter according to the measured state [21, 22], and reinforced random processes give general criteria for when a reinforced choice persists [23].

The model studied here combines a random choice with a specific reinforcement rule. A slow variable, the commitment HH, accumulates the energy released when the selected structure recovers from perturbations, and stiffens the selected state [Eq. (4)]. The rule is a constitutive closure, in the spirit of the work-hardening hypothesis [19]; it is not derived from a microscopic model, and it is a feedback-controlled potential whose full thermodynamic accounting, including the information processed by the feedback [24], is not attempted here. Because the commitment starts at zero at the bifurcation, energy in this model can only reinforce a choice made by fluctuations, never make it: this is the model’s working hypothesis, not one of its results. The results are the quantitative consequences of the closure for the growth of commitment and the statistics of reversal, together with the experiments that would test it.

papers.title: A bounded Borel set in the plane none of whose orthogonal projections is Borel
papers.abstract: We construct a bounded Borel set in the plane whose orthogonal projection onto every line is non-Borel. This gives a negative answer to a question of Thierry De Pauw.
papers.intro:
The orthogonal projection of a Borel subset of the plane need not be Borel. Such projections are analytic sets, and the existence of analytic non-Borel sets goes back to Suslin [4]. De Pauw asked whether every Borel subset of the plane nevertheless has a Borel orthogonal projection in at least one direction; see Tristant [5] for this question and related constructions. We answer the question in the negative.

We answer the question in the negative.

There exists a bounded Borel set ℬ⊂ℝ2\mathcal{B}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} whose orthogonal projection onto every line in the plane is not a Borel set.

Our proof begins with a Borel set whose projection onto one coordinate is non-Borel. We encode this projection simultaneously in a family of directions. To keep the copies from interfering, we work in a second plane: a point (x,y)(x,y) represents the line s=x+t​ys=x+ty, so projection in direction tt becomes intersection with the vertical line at tt. We construct a set Σ\Sigma with Cantor vertical sections such that through each point of Σ\Sigma there passes a Cantor family of lines meeting Σ\Sigma at that point only. Finitely many rotated and translated copies then give the result in every direction.

papers.title: Compaction Laundering: Provenance Destruction in Context-Compacting Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents that run long enough must compact their context, summarizing the conversation, discarding the original, and carrying the summary forward as memory. We show that in popular open-source coding agents this step is an exploitable trust boundary. Harnesses that flatten the typed conversation into a single plain string, marking each message with a text label such as [User]:, destroy message provenance in code, before the summarizer runs. An attacker who controls anything the agent reads can forge a user turn that survives compaction as a genuine instruction. Across five flattening harnesses (pi, opencode, Cline, Aider, OpenHands) the forged approval launders into the agent's memory 87-100% of the time, up to a ~908,000-token context window; across four role-typed harnesses (Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Continue) the identical attack succeeds 0% of the time. We follow the attack to executed consequences. A laundered standing approval drives real tool-running agents to execute attacker-controlled curl | sh in a sandbox, and end to end in the live pi TUI at ~50% against a 0% paired clean arm. The same channel reliably steers an agent's plan away from a file an attacker designates off-limits, which can blind a code review to a planted backdoor. Because the provenance is destroyed deterministically in harness code, no prompt-level defense can restore it; we measure a code-level provenance check that catches 77% of laundering while demoting 2% of legitimate summary content. The defect also has a straightforward fix at the serializer, escaping the role labels before flattening; the role-typed harnesses avoid it entirely by keeping messages role-typed.
papers.intro:
An agent that runs for long enough fills its context window and must compress its own memory to continue. It summarizes the conversation so far into a short note, discards the original, and treats that note as its memory from then on. We study popular open-source coding agents, and find that this step is an exploitable trust boundary in a class of them. To build the summary, these harnesses take the conversation, in which every message still records whether it came from the user or from a tool, and flatten it into a single plain string, marking each line with a text label such as [User]: or [Tool result]:. They do not escape those labels when they appear inside untrusted content. An agent that runs for long enough fills its context window and must compress its own memory to continue. It summarizes the conversation so far into a short note, discards the original, and treats that note as its memory from then on. There has been substantial work on memory poisoning and prompt injection in LLM agents [2, 3, 4]. This work contributes:

1. A measurement of compaction laundering across nine released harnesses, with results that divide sharply by whether the harness flattens roles into text labels or keeps them role-typed (E10): 87–100% for the flattening harnesses, 0% for the role-typed ones, the latter serving as a built-in control. 2. The attack carried through to executed consequences (E6, E11, E15): a laundered approval drives real tool-running agents to execute attacker code on all five flattening harnesses, via both insider and external scenarios, and live in the real pi TUI at ~50% against a 0% paired clean arm. Straiker [1] described this consequence without runtime evidence, and Sleeper [3] demonstrated it only in the separate persistent-memory channel. 3. A characterization of what attenuates the attack (E13, E14, E15, E16): whether the forged line reaches the summary is unaffected by the conversation’s size or by the line’s position in it, but whether the agent acts on it is not. Execution tracks how prominently the summary carries the forged line, how inherently suspicious the payload is, and whether the agent’s own pre-compaction audit — its inspection of the fetched artifacts before summarizing — survives into the summary. The first and the last reduce to placement: a line re-delivered just before compaction is both maximally prominent and dated after the audit ran. The audit cannot be forged away, because assistant- and tool-role claims are checkable against the transcript while user-role claims are not. 4. A code-level defense, evaluated against prompt and classifier baselines (E9): a check that compares the summary’s user-attributed claims against the genuine user turns still in the harness’s memory catches 77% of laundering while demoting 2% of legitimate summary content; an in-prompt anti-injection rule of the kind Gemini CLI includes stops 13–25% on the same data, and published classifier defenses report 67% at best. papers.title: Asking a Multimodal LLM Whether Someone Fell: Zero-Shot Screening of Low-Resolution Thermal Video in a Laboratory and an Occupied Home
papers.abstract: Thermal cameras can watch over older people living alone without capturing faces, and multimodal large language models (LLMs) can judge a short video without task-specific training. We evaluate a production multimodal LLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash at temperature 0, as the decision stage of an event-triggered fall screener, used exactly as a deployed prototype uses it: one request per short thermal clip, with its sound track when there is one, and its predecessor Gemini 3.7 Flash on the same requests. On 438 staged falls and 563 non-fall windows that we located by hand in a public 32x24 thermal dataset, the deployed request called 69% of the held-out subjects' falls (67% over all subjects; bed falls excluded) and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying on the floor and getting up. Over 76 h of ordinary life in an occupied room, recorded at 160x120 with sound, it called none of 395 clips a fall (95% upper bound 1.2 false alarms per day) and caught 4 of the 9 staged falls the camera could see. One cautionary sentence in the prompt ("a person who goes out of view ... is not a fall") accounted for many of the misses: removing it raised sensitivity on the held-out subjects from 69% to 83% on 3.8 Flash and from 80% to 92% on Gemini 3.7 Flash, and in the home from 4 to 9 of the 9 visible falls, with no false call in ordinary living but at the price of calling deliberate lie-downs a fall. Sensitivity collapsed at 8x6 pixels (34%); identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows; and when the model called a fall, its explanation placed it within a second of the annotated landing 99% of the time. Two conventional detectors trained on the laboratory data caught nearly every held-out laboratory fall but raised 14.2 and 23.9 false alarms per day in the home. We release the frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset and every model answer on it.
papers.intro:
Falls are a leading cause of injury among older adults, and what happens after the fall matters as much as the fall itself. In a cohort of people over 90, about 80% of those who fell could not get up unaided after at least one fall, three in ten of them lay on the floor for an hour or more, over 80% of falls happened when they were alone, and call alarms, though widely available, went unused in most falls [1]. A system that notices a fall and asks the person whether they are all right could shorten that time. Wearable alarms only help when they are worn and pressed, and cameras are unwelcome in many homes. Thermal sensing sits in between: a low-resolution thermal image shows a warm body and its posture, but not a face or a document [2].

Thermal fall detection has been studied for two decades, almost always by training a classifier on staged falls and testing it on more staged falls from the same setting [3, 4, 5, 6]. Two problems recur. Staged falls by young adults differ from real falls of older people [7, 8], and in a real home the decisive number is how often the system raises an alarm when nothing happened, which laboratory datasets cannot measure. A screener that interrupts a household twice a day is switched off.

Multimodal large language models (LLMs) offer a different route: they can watch a short video with its sound track and answer a question about it without any task-specific training, and they explain their answer in words. This makes them attractive as the decision stage of a screening pipeline. A cheap always-on gate decides that something happened, and the model is asked once about a short clip. But thermal video is far from the visible-light video these models were trained on, and it is not obvious how they behave on a 32×2432\times 24 thermopile array or a 160×120160\times 120 microbolometer, how much the answer depends on how the temperatures are rendered into colours, on a sentence of the prompt, or on the sound, and how stable the answer is when the same question is asked twice.

We measure these things for a production model, Gemini 3.8 Flash, used exactly as a deployed prototype uses it. Our contributions are: • An evaluation of the LLM review stage on two complementary sources: 438 hand-located staged falls and 563 non-fall windows from a public 32×2432\times 24 thermal dataset [6], with held-out subjects; and every clip that an event-triggered pipeline produced over 98.2 camera-hours of continuous radiometric thermal video and audio in one occupied room. • Single-factor ablations of sensor resolution (from 160×120160\times 120 down to 8×68\times 6), colour map, display size, sound, prompt wording and model generation, plus repeated identical requests to measure test–retest stability at temperature 0. • A comparison with conventional detectors (a hand-written descent rule and a gradient-boosted classifier trained on the public data), in the laboratory and transferred to the home. • Practical lessons for anyone using an LLM as a sensor’s judge, including how one cautious sentence in the prompt, which kept false alarms at home near zero, also cost a large share of the visible laboratory falls. We release the frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset, the windows cut from it, every prompt and every model answer on those windows, under CC BY 4.0, at https://senecta.ai/research/thermal-fall-llm-data.zip. The home recordings stay private.

papers.title: On Divisibility Properties of Zipf Law and Relatives
papers.abstract: We describe recursive chance mechanisms and processes involving Zipf's law and relatives, all showing up mixing properties, both geometric and Poisson. Relations to Markov processes are explored.

papers.title: Flowz: When Does Learning Forecast Errors Add Value? Conditional Flow Matching for Financial Price Forecasts
papers.abstract: Learning a forecasting model's errors offers a modular way to improve its predictive distribution while retaining its underlying dynamics. We study this approach with Flowz, a conditional flow model of direct multi-step price-level residuals fitted using random features and ridge regression. Each EWMA, ARIMA, ARFIMA, and structural baseline is compared with a Gaussian residual location-scale control and a conditional Flowz extension. The experiment uses 24 US stocks selected across four liquidity-volatility strata, 104 common forecast origins, horizons of 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, and 160 trading observations, and three fit seeds. Marginal CRPS is the primary score. At farther horizons, Flowz reduces mean CRPS by 30.7% against EWMA and 24.0% against its Gaussian residual control. The EWMA improvement holds at each fit seed and exceeds the Gaussian control for all 24 stocks in the far band. The ARIMA, ARFIMA, and structural extensions worsen both comparators. Conditional residual learning is therefore useful for the drifting EWMA specification in this experiment, with gains concentrated at longer horizons.
papers.intro:
Financial forecasts must describe both future price levels and the uncertainty surrounding them. A forecast can have a useful central estimate but poorly represent the range of subsequent outcomes. Conversely, wide intervals can cover observations while providing little precision. Proper scoring rules evaluate the predictive distribution as a whole [6].

The question of how to improve these distributions is timely. Financial stability analysis highlights the connection between uncertainty, market functioning, and abrupt repricing [13]. At the same time, models such as Chronos illustrate rapid advances in probabilistic time-series forecasting [12]. A complementary statistical route is to retain an existing forecasting model and learn the structure of its errors. This route is attractive when the baseline already captures useful dynamics and can be updated economically as new observations arrive.

Flowz implements this approach by learning joint vectors of future price-level errors conditional on a local market state. A baseline supplies the forecast mean and marginal scales. Historical errors are centered and standardized, and a conditional flow maps Gaussian inputs into residual scenarios. Adding those scenarios to the baseline produces a predictive distribution for future levels. The statistical value of this construction depends on the information remaining in the baseline’s errors.

We ask three research questions: 1. Incremental value: Does conditional residual learning improve the predictive distribution of the same underlying baseline? 2. Value beyond location and scale: Does Flowz improve a Gaussian control with the same training-only residual centering and scaling? 3. Conditions of usefulness: How do these effects vary across forecast horizons, baseline engines, liquidity, and volatility? The working hypothesis is that conditional residual learning improves CRPS, particularly at longer horizons where baseline errors accumulate. We examine this hypothesis through matched comparisons across four baseline engines and a recent stock panel. The experiment is exploratory: all engines and all three fit seeds enter the reported results.

papers.title: Every Alarm Has a Cause: An Open Generator of Telecom Alarm Storms with Exact Root Causes, Bound to NORIA-O, RFC 8632 and TMF642
papers.abstract: Alarm root-cause analysis is studied on data that cannot be shared. Operator logs are confidential, so what the field publishes is a causal graph between alarm types rather than per-incident causes, a fixed scenario set, gated, or never released. Two recent benchmarks carry per-incident root causes at scale; neither states a download location or a licence. We give a generator rather than a dataset. It runs on real backbone topologies from the Internet Topology Zoo and records the exact root cause and the propagation path of every alarm -- a by-product of generation, not a labelling pass. Every emitted field binds to a term in NORIA-O, RFC 8632, RFC 8345 or TMF642, and an unknown term fails the run. We ship fixed configurations, splits, a scorer and nine baselines. A one-line rule -- rank the device that raised the earliest critical alarm -- takes top-1 at 0.650 against 0.575 for our own temporal method, and wins 13 of 15 runs over three backbones and five seeds. An LLM given the same view reaches 0.600, the same model allowed to query the graph 0.625, and the rule wins on real operator alarms too, at 0.773: a property of alarm streams, not of our generator. One fault class separates the table: when a site loses power its PoP reports nothing, so every method that ranks alarmed devices scores 0.000 or near it, while the two that walk the topology to a silent candidate take 1.000 and 0.833.
papers.intro:
A network operations centre sees a storm of alarms and must name the one resource that caused them. Research on this problem is evaluated on data nobody else can obtain, because an operator’s alarm log carries its customers, its topology and its failures. The consequence is not that the work is wrong but that it is incomparable: two methods reporting 0.70.7 on two private logs have not been compared.

papers.title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage
papers.abstract: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and unparseable. We present VX-One, a small multi-head network (100K--10M parameters) with calibrated typed outputs: a binary gate, a closed-set choice with an explicit unknown option where the benchmark supports it (and abstention elsewhere), and an ordinal score. Heads are temperature-calibrated, with 0.7--1.7 ms single-event CPU p50 latency. We evaluate UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, and EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random Forest, MLP, and Kitsune baselines, and measure a Suricata-to-VX-One cascade over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Results are deliberately double-sided: on UNSW the gate ties the best baseline (0.9837+/-0.0002 versus MLP 0.9835+/-0.0013 across three seeds), while VX-One wins temporal CIC detection (0.734+/-0.022 versus 0.639+/-0.027) but loses multi-class attribution to XGBoost. Under leave-one-family-out, the gate detects all nine UNSW families but drops below chance on CIC recon; CIC trees transfer better. Suricata resolves only about 0.1% of attacks on flow reconstructions and 0.2--2.2% on payload-bearing PCAPs; the strictly by-day Phase 2 recovers only the in-scope DoS/DDoS share on the wave day (recall 0.34, precision 0.97). Calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partly survives. We contribute a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.
papers.intro:

Three incumbent technology classes each miss at least one requirement.

papers.title: Higher-order tangent and secant numbers, special-value integrals, and a common zero attractor
papers.abstract: We study two families of coefficients associated with powers of the tangent function and with products of the secant and tangent functions, and develop a unified treatment of the corresponding higher-order tangent and secant numbers. The first part establishes a common identity for even derivatives of $\tanh x$ and odd derivatives of $\operatorname{sech}x$. Combined with integral formulae for these derivatives, this yields finite power-integral representations for the normalized values $ζ(2n+1)$ and $β(2n)$ and naturally introduces two polynomial families $P_n$ and $Q_n$. We determine several arithmetic and structural properties of these polynomials. In particular, we identify the exact content of $P_n$, prove that $Q_n$ is primitive, establish strict log-concavity and unimodality of their coefficient sequences, and describe their real zeros. For even indices each family has a unique negative real zero, and the two sequences of real zeros have the same limit. We also derive differential recurrences and generating functions for $P_n$ and $Q_n$. The generating functions lead to a global complex-singularity analysis. We construct a compact Jordan curve $Γ$ and prove that the complex zero sets of both $P_n$ and $Q_n$ converge to $Γ$ in Hausdorff distance. The normalized zero-counting measures converge weakly to the same equilibrium measure on $Γ$. We determine the logarithmic capacity of the enclosed compact set, give an explicit arclength density for the limiting measure, and compute its first moments. Numerical plots for $P_{20}$, $P_{50}$, $P_{100}$ and $P_{150}$ illustrate the zero-attractor theorem.

papers.title: A Consolidated Deployment Edition of a Microservice Core-Banking Platform: Composing Services by Reference into Three Hosts
papers.abstract: Microservices give teams independent deployment and scaling, but each deployed service also reserves compute and adds operational work. This paper examines a second deployment edition of a multi-tenant .NET core-banking platform. The existing edition runs as nine AWS ECS Fargate tasks; the alternative composes the five API services by project reference into one API host, alongside a consumer host and a background host. The service code remains in its original repositories, and both editions continue to be built from the same commits. We describe the composition mechanism, module manifest, start-up checks, request handling and configuration precedence, then compare the editions in an emulation of the AWS deployment. The composed edition exposes all 844 declared operations. Across 47 financial workload cases, both editions produced the same observed outcomes and matching ledgers. In read probes across five principal types, 230 of 231 endpoint results matched; the remaining difference was associated with the emulated load balancer. Eleven cross-tenant and write-authorisation cases also produced the expected outcomes in both editions. In the emulation, the composed edition delivered 2.3 times the read throughput and used less than half the memory. Estimated service-task compute at list prices was 11-24% lower, excluding the shared gateway, load balancer, data stores and other operating costs. The consolidation also enlarges the failure domain: one API-host crash takes all five modules offline. Of 16 injected faults, the edition's checks detected 10, behavioural tests detected five additional faults, and one fault escaped both. These findings concern one platform and an emulated deployment that mirrors its topology, task sizes and configuration; they are not production-AWS measurements.
papers.intro:
The platform studied here is a multi-tenant core-banking system written in .NET. Its capabilities (customers, channels, transactions, accounts and users, with consumers and a scheduler) were built as separate services in seven repositories, and it ships as nine ECS Fargate tasks behind an Ocelot gateway and an internal Application Load Balancer (ALB). Some customers asked for fewer moving parts. The answer is a second edition of the same product: one repository whose API host references the five API services’ projects and serves their controllers as MVC application parts, beside a consumer host for the three queue workers and a background host for the scheduler (Fig. 2). The nine-service edition is not retired; both editions ship from the same service repositories, so every fix made in a service reaches both.

This version keeps that architectural description, updated where the code has moved (Sections IV–VIII), and answers those questions by experiment. Both editions were built from the same commits and run side by side in an emulation of their AWS deployment, and compared differentially [1]: the same writes, the same reads, the same failures and the same load.

Terms. We keep three claims apart throughout. Route parity means that every operation a standalone service declares is served by the composed host at the same method and path. Tested behavioural equivalence means that the requests we sent produced matching outcomes, after a stated normalisation, in both editions. System-wide equivalence, that every possible request behaves alike, is not established by this study. We also keep four questions apart: whether the two editions behaved alike (equivalence), whether the behaviour followed the bank’s intended rules (compliance), whether each ledger stayed balanced (consistency), and whether each response matched what the test script expected. Passing one does not imply passing the others; Section X reports all four.

papers.title: Double KV Cache Optimization on Apple Silicon: Block-FP4, Radial Quantization, and Fused Metal Kernels
papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) cache capacity and memory traffic are primary bottlenecks in long-context autoregressive inference. We evaluate five cache paths on an Apple Silicon M5 Max using MLX: a native bf16 baseline, block-scaled E2M1 FP4, a Python reference implementing radial quantization with a QJL-style residual, sequential FP4-to-Polar composition, and a fused Metal Polar kernel. On Apple Silicon M5 Max, fused Metal PolarQuant achieves 46.8 tok/s at 3,456 B/token - 3.64x compression versus the bf16 baseline and 1.84x faster than the Python Polar reference (25.4 tok/s), while slightly outperforming block-FP4 (41.5 tok/s at 3.62x compression). Sequential composition of FP4 and Polar (Double Optimization) yields no additive benefit: 4,241 B/token at 15.1 tok/s, worse than FP4 alone on both axes. The fused path establishes that radial coding can be competitive when packing, rotation, and reconstruction are placed in one device kernel, but this result does not extend to longer contexts. At 32K and above, all compressed variants collapse to 1.5-14 tok/s because the current attention path repeatedly reconstructs the full cache, retaining cumulative O(N^2) decode work. At 64K, the Metal variant runs out of memory when a 33.5 GB allocation exceeds MLX's 22.6 GB Metal buffer limit. Fused scaled dot-product attention operating directly on compressed KV, together with chunked pre-allocation, is required for long-context viability. These results separate representation-level compression from kernel and allocator effects and identify the conditions under which low-bit KV caching helps on unified memory hardware.
papers.intro:
Autoregressive Transformer inference reuses the key and value tensors produced for earlier tokens. This KV cache avoids recomputing the entire prefix at every generation step, but its capacity grows linearly with sequence length and batch size. The cache is read repeatedly during decoding, so its footprint is also a bandwidth cost rather than merely a storage cost. Analytical and empirical studies of Transformer serving identify this state as a central constraint on long-context inference [14]. Multi-query attention reduces the number of key/value heads [15], and grouped-query attention interpolates between multi-head and multi-query designs [1], yet large contexts still leave substantial persistent state.

KV compression addresses the remaining state without changing model weights. The design space includes scalar and group-wise quantization, sparse outlier retention, token eviction, cross-layer sharing, geometric transforms, and compressed-domain attention. These approaches make different tradeoffs. A compact representation can save memory but lose throughput if every decode step reconstructs the entire cache. Conversely, a specialized kernel can make a less compact layout faster by avoiding framework dispatch, intermediate tensors, and repeated format conversion. The representation and the consuming attention kernel therefore have to be evaluated together.

Apple Silicon is a useful target for this comparison. CPU and GPU allocations share physical memory, MLX schedules lazy array graphs onto Metal, and the device exposes large unified-memory capacity without a discrete-host transfer. Those properties remove one class of PCIe bottlenecks while exposing allocator behavior and kernel granularity more directly. They also make it possible to test whether a custom Metal implementation changes the practical ranking of KV formats that look similar from byte accounting alone.

papers.title: Radial reduction, spherical splitting and root counts for two-sided quaternionic polynomials
papers.abstract: We study quaternionic polynomials whose coefficients may occur on both sides of the variable, using their degree in the four real coordinates. Such polynomials can have no roots, or many more isolated roots than their degree. A simple root has an invertible real derivative, and its sign is the sign of that derivative's determinant. For a radial family, the roots over a non-real target reduce to one real equation. We obtain a sharp root bound and follow a change in the signed root count as roots escape to infinity. The main results concern spherical root sets for which the polynomial derivative is invertible in the two normal directions. Under a small polynomial perturbation, a sphere splits into simple roots corresponding to the zeros of a tangent vector field, when the derivative of that field is invertible at every zero. We obtain a sharp bound in terms of the perturbation degree and a signed count of two or of minus two. For even degrees, the construction yields polynomials with a single leading power and lower-degree terms whose simple root counts, divided by the fourth power of the degree, tend to one as the degree grows. An explicit quartic has 132 simple roots, and this count persists under small coefficient perturbations. For gradient perturbations, the roots correspond to equilibrium directions of an energy on the sphere. This correspondence gives energy thresholds for root disappearance and bounds the critical directions of polynomial orientation profiles in diffusion magnetic resonance imaging.
